Her syphilis enzyme immunoassay is reactive, treponemal particle agglutination is reactive and the rapid plasma reagin titre is 1 in 32. Her booking screen at 11 weeks was non reactive on the same assays. She feels well, has had no rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no genital or oral ulcer and no hair loss, and she has never been diagnosed with or treated for syphilis. She reports no penicillin allergy and has taken amoxicillin previously without difficulty. She has one regular sexual partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital or oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, fundal height consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Syphilis enzyme immunoassay reactive, treponemal particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32, booking screen at 11 weeks non reactive, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat serology later
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin crosses the placenta poorly, so it does not treat congenital infection (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Repeat the serology in four weeks before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Both treponemal assays are reactive with a titre of 1 in 32, which is not a pattern requiring confirmation, and a month of delay at 28 weeks materially raises the risk of congenital infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Weekly intramuscular benzathine penicillin for a total of three doses
options.rationale: Seroconversion since an 11 week negative screen without any symptomatic stage means the duration cannot be established as under two years by history alone, and in pregnancy the safe course is the three dose weekly regimen, which also gives greater certainty of fetal treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin administered today
options.rationale: One dose is the regimen for infection confidently established as early, and a single dose has a higher rate of fetal treatment failure, so it is not used when the stage is uncertain in pregnancy (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Oral doxycycline twice daily for a total of fourteen days now
options.rationale: Doxycycline is the alternative for non pregnant patients with penicillin allergy, but tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy and do not reliably treat the foetus (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Congenital syphilis is preventable and is diagnosed in Australia often enough to have prompted expanded screening in areas of high incidence, with repeat testing in the third trimester and at birth in addition to the booking screen. Vertical transmission is highest in primary and secondary disease, approaching 100 per cent, and falls with increasing duration of latent infection but never disappears. Benzathine penicillin is the only agent proven to treat the foetus, so a woman with a genuine penicillin allergy is desensitised and then treated with penicillin rather than given an alternative. Treatment more than 30 days before birth is required for the infant to be regarded as adequately treated in utero, and titres are followed to confirm at least a fourfold fall. Partner notification and treatment are essential, since reinfection during the remainder of the pregnancy would undo the benefit.
key_points: Benzathine penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats fetal infection.
Latent syphilis of unknown duration is treated with three weekly doses.
Genuine penicillin allergy is managed by desensitisation, not by substituting another class.
Treatment must be completed more than 30 days before birth for the infant to be considered treated.
Partner notification and treatment prevent reinfection later in the pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: The Jarisch Herxheimer reaction occurs within 24 hours in a substantial minority and can provoke uterine contractions and fetal heart rate abnormalities, so women treated after 20 weeks are advised to attend for monitoring if they develop fever, rigors or contractions after the injection.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

subtopic_detail: Localising secondary amenorrhoea to the outflow tract when gonadotrophins are normal and withdrawal fails
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman whose periods have not returned to normal since a surgical evacuation of the uterus for retained products seven months ago, performed two weeks after the birth of her first child.

Before that pregnancy her cycles were regular and moderately heavy. For the first three months after the procedure she had only a few hours of light spotting each month, and for the last four months she has had nothing at all. She stopped breastfeeding five months ago. Each month around the time she expects a period she gets cramping lower abdominal pain for a day or two with no bleeding. A urine pregnancy test is negative and a course of oral progestogen followed by cessation produced no bleeding at all.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia, patent vagina and cervix on speculum examination, normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L (2-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 4.6 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 342 pmol/L (110-1500 follicular), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy with adhesiolysis under direct vision
options.rationale: Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol in the follicular range show the ovary is working, and a failed progestogen withdrawal with cyclical pain after intrauterine instrumentation localises the problem to the outflow tract, where hysteroscopy both confirms adhesions and treats them (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Anti Mullerian hormone measurement and repeat gonadotrophins
options.rationale: Premature ovarian insufficiency is the tempting explanation for secondary amenorrhoea, but it produces a raised follicle stimulating hormone with a low oestradiol, and both of hers are normal (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any procedure
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is insensitive for thin intrauterine adhesions and would not obviate hysteroscopy, which remains both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive with review again in six months
options.rationale: Suppressing an endometrium that is already unable to shed treats nothing, and six months of delay allows adhesions to become denser and harder to divide (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A repeat progestogen challenge after oestrogen priming first
options.rationale: The near pair is a hypo oestrogenic endometrium that is too thin to respond, which oestrogen priming would correct, but her oestradiol is already in the follicular range so priming would add nothing (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Amenorrhoea).

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through anatomically, from the hypothalamus down to the outflow tract, and the combination of normal gonadotrophins, normal oestradiol and a failed progestogen withdrawal points below the ovary. Intrauterine adhesions follow instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus far more often than a non pregnant one, because the endometrial basal layer is thin and the myometrium soft, and puerperal curettage carries the highest risk of all. Cyclical pain without bleeding is a useful pointer because functioning endometrium is still responding but the blood cannot escape. Treatment is hysteroscopic division under direct vision, followed by measures to keep the cavity walls apart during healing, and outcomes for menstruation are good while fertility outcomes depend on the extent of the disease at the outset.
key_points: Normal gonadotrophins with normal oestradiol exclude ovarian and most central causes.
A failed progestogen withdrawal with adequate oestrogen localises the problem to the endometrium or outflow tract.
Instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the dominant risk factor for adhesions.
Cyclical pain without bleeding suggests functioning endometrium behind an obstruction.
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure.
explanation.pearls: After adhesiolysis, a period of oestrogen therapy with or without a physical barrier keeps the raw cavity walls from re adhering, and a second look hysteroscopy at around two to three months is standard because recurrence rates reach a third in severe disease.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose and quantification after a mid pregnancy sensitising event
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 28 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 20 weeks and 3 days who slipped on wet steps yesterday evening and struck her abdomen against the handrail.

She presents 18 hours later because a friend told her she should be checked. She has had no vaginal bleeding, no leaking and no abdominal pain since the fall, and she reports normal fetal movements. Her booking bloods recorded blood group O with a negative red cell antibody screen, and she has not yet had any anti-D this pregnancy. Her uterus is soft and non tender, and the fetal heart rate is 148 beats per minute on hand held Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative at booking, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender uterus, fundal height consistent with dates, no bruising over the abdominal wall, no vaginal bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give 625 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
options.rationale: Abdominal trauma after 12 weeks is a sensitising event requiring 625 IU of anti-D as soon as possible and within 72 hours, with a quantification test sent at the same time to determine whether the bleed was large enough to need additional doses (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Give 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is the correct one for sensitising events in the first trimester, and using it after 12 weeks under doses a pregnancy in which the fetal red cell volume is considerably larger (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D only if the result is raised
options.rationale: The quantification test determines whether extra doses are needed, not whether the standard dose is given, and waiting for the result erodes the 72 hour window in which prophylaxis is effective (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D because more than 12 hours have already elapsed
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is given up to 72 hours after the event and is still worth giving beyond that if it has been missed, so an 18 hour delay is well inside the effective window (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Repeat the antibody screen and give anti-D if it is still negative
options.rationale: A repeat screen cannot be interpreted usefully at this point because passively acquired anti-D from prophylaxis is indistinguishable from immune anti-D on the screen, and delaying for the result serves no purpose (Source: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D alloimmunisation is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin both routinely in the third trimester and after any potentially sensitising event. Sensitising events include abdominal trauma, antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version, invasive prenatal procedures, miscarriage and termination, and the dose depends on gestation: 250 IU up to 12 weeks and 625 IU thereafter. Routine antenatal prophylaxis in Australia is given as 625 IU at 28 and again at 34 weeks, and this is additional to rather than instead of event based doses. Quantification of foeto maternal haemorrhage after events beyond 20 weeks determines whether the standard dose is adequate, since a large bleed requires further immunoglobulin calculated on the measured volume.
key_points: Anti-D is given within 72 hours of a sensitising event and remains worth giving if missed.
The dose is 250 IU up to 12 weeks and 625 IU after 12 weeks.
Quantification of foeto maternal haemorrhage decides whether extra doses are needed.
Routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is additional to event based doses.
Cord blood grouping after birth determines whether a postnatal dose is required.
explanation.pearls: Non invasive fetal RhD genotyping on maternal plasma is now available in Australia and can spare an RhD negative woman carrying an RhD negative foetus from prophylaxis altogether, but where it is unavailable prophylaxis proceeds on the assumption that the foetus is RhD positive.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
National Blood Authority Guidelines on Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Fertility sparing management of atypical endometrial hyperplasia with intensive surveillance
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman in clinic with the result of an endometrial pipelle biopsy taken three weeks ago for eight months of heavy irregular bleeding.

She has polycystic ovary syndrome with a lifelong pattern of four or five periods a year, a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 and no other medical history. She has one child, conceived after ovulation induction, and she and her partner have been trying for a second for the past two years. The histology reports endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis shows an endometrium of 16 mm with no myometrial invasion, no cervical involvement and normal adnexa, and there is no lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, bulky mobile uterus, no adnexal masses, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial biopsy showing hyperplasia with atypia, magnetic resonance imaging with endometrial thickness 16 mm and no myometrial invasion, haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-165), ferritin 12 mcg/L (20-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Observation with repeat endometrial sampling again in 12 months
options.rationale: Atypical hyperplasia progresses to carcinoma in a substantial proportion within a few years, so observation without treatment is not an option even when fertility is being preserved (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: A levonorgestrel intrauterine system with three monthly sampling
options.rationale: For a woman who has not completed her family, high dose local progestogen delivered by intrauterine system achieves higher regression rates than oral progestogen and is combined with endometrial sampling every three months until two consecutive negative biopsies are obtained (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy as planned
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the standard treatment for atypical hyperplasia in a woman who has completed her family, but oophorectomy in a 42 year old is not routine, and proceeding to surgery forecloses the pregnancy she is actively seeking (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone with sampling again in one year
options.rationale: Cyclical rather than continuous dosing is inadequate for atypical disease, and a twelve month surveillance interval is far too long when up to 40 per cent harbour a concurrent carcinoma (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive with sampling again in six months
options.rationale: Combined contraception provides insufficient progestogenic opposition for established atypia and carries additional risk at a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is classified as with or without atypia, and that single distinction drives everything: hyperplasia without atypia has a progression risk under five per cent over 20 years and is treated with progestogen, while atypical hyperplasia carries a concurrent carcinoma rate of up to 40 per cent at hysterectomy and a high progression risk. Standard management of atypia is total hysterectomy, with the ovaries usually conserved in premenopausal women. Fertility sparing treatment is legitimate but is a specialist decision requiring imaging to exclude invasive disease, high dose progestogen and intensive sampling every three months until regression is confirmed twice, followed by prompt referral for assisted conception because relapse rates after treatment are high. Weight loss and treatment of insulin resistance are part of the plan, since unopposed oestrogen from peripheral aromatisation and anovulation is what generated the lesion.
key_points: Atypia carries up to a 40 per cent rate of concurrent carcinoma at hysterectomy.
Hysterectomy is standard once the family is complete; ovaries are usually conserved before menopause.
Fertility sparing treatment uses the intrauterine progestogen system with three monthly sampling.
Two consecutive negative biopsies are required before conception is attempted.
Weight loss and management of anovulation address the underlying oestrogen excess.
explanation.pearls: After successful regression on fertility sparing treatment, referral for assisted conception is made without delay because relapse occurs in around a quarter within two years, and hysterectomy is recommended once childbearing is complete.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: First line ovulation induction agent in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who has been trying to conceive for 14 months. She has had four or five periods a year since her teens and shaves her chin every second day.

Her body mass index was 34 kg/m2 at her first visit six months ago and is now 31 kg/m2 after a supervised diet and exercise programme, and her cycles remain unchanged. Her partner's semen analysis was normal on two occasions. A hysterosalpingogram showed a normal cavity with free spill from both tubes. She is rubella immune, takes folic acid, and her thyroid function and prolactin are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, terminal hair over the chin and lower abdomen, no acanthosis nigricans, normal sized non tender uterus and adnexae
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 320 mIU/L (less than 500), total testosterone mildly raised, transvaginal ultrasound showing multifollicular ovaries with normal antral morphology, hysterosalpingogram with bilateral free spill

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Ovulation induction with letrozole and follicle tracking by ultrasound
options.rationale: An aromatase inhibitor is first line for ovulation induction in this condition on the strength of higher live birth rates than the older agent, particularly in women with a raised body mass index, and cycles are monitored to limit multiple follicular development (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Ovulation induction with clomifene and follicle tracking by ultrasound
options.rationale: The selective oestrogen receptor modulator was first line for decades and remains effective, but head to head trials show lower ovulation and live birth rates than the aromatase inhibitor, partly because its anti oestrogenic effect thins the endometrium and cervical mucus (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Metformin alone with a review of her cycles again in six months
options.rationale: Metformin improves menstrual regularity and metabolic parameters and can be added to ovulation induction, but as sole therapy it is inferior for achieving live birth (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Referral for in vitro fertilisation as the next treatment step
options.rationale: Assisted reproduction is third line in this setting, reserved for failure of oral agents and gonadotrophins or for a coexisting indication, and it carries a substantial risk of ovarian hyperstimulation in these women (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Ovulation induction with injectable gonadotrophins and monitoring
options.rationale: Gonadotrophins are second line after failure of an oral agent, and using them first exposes her to a higher multiple pregnancy and hyperstimulation risk with intensive monitoring that oral treatment avoids (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is the commonest cause of anovulatory infertility and is diagnosed on two of three criteria: oligo or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Lifestyle intervention comes first because a loss of five to ten per cent of body weight restores ovulation in a substantial proportion, and it improves the response to every subsequent treatment. Where lifestyle alone does not restore ovulation, pharmacological induction proceeds in a defined order, and treatment is only started once tubal patency and semen analysis are known so that a couple is not put through cycles that cannot succeed. Cycle monitoring is required because these ovaries are exquisitely sensitive and multiple pregnancy is the main avoidable complication.
key_points: Diagnosis requires two of three criteria after exclusion of thyroid, prolactin and adrenal causes.
Weight loss of five to ten per cent restores ovulation in a meaningful proportion of women.
An aromatase inhibitor is first line for ovulation induction, ahead of the older oral agent.
Semen analysis and tubal patency are established before induction begins.
Follicle tracking limits multiple pregnancy in ovaries that are highly sensitive to stimulation.
explanation.pearls: Letrozole is given on cycle days two to six and works by transiently lowering oestrogen to release the pituitary from negative feedback, and because its half life is around 45 hours it has cleared well before implantation, which is why the early teratogenicity concern was not borne out.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics before surgical evacuation in secondary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 26 year old woman who gave birth 12 days ago. She had a spontaneous vaginal birth at term and the placenta appeared complete at the time.

Her lochia had almost stopped by day eight but for the past two days she has been soaking a maternity pad every hour with bright red blood and passing clots the size of a golf ball. Her partner says the discharge smells offensive. She has had rigors overnight. Her uterus is tender and the fundus is palpable midway between the symphysis and the umbilicus. A transvaginal ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material 22 mm across within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender bulky uterus with the fundus midway to the umbilicus, open cervical os with active bright red loss, offensive discharge, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 122 mg/L (less than 5), high vaginal and endocervical swabs and blood cultures collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation with repeat full blood count and ultrasound in a week
options.rationale: Expectant management is reasonable for retained tissue found incidentally in a well woman with light loss, and this presentation with sepsis and heavy ongoing bleeding is the near pair that it must be distinguished from (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with evacuation by a senior obstetrician
options.rationale: Retained products with endometritis need broad spectrum intravenous cover started immediately, and because the bleeding is heavy and continuing, evacuation follows rather than waiting, performed by an experienced operator because the infected postpartum uterus perforates easily (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Immediate evacuation of the uterus before antibiotics are given
options.rationale: Instrumenting an infected uterus without antibiotic cover risks bacteraemia and septic shock, so the first dose goes in before the patient goes to theatre (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral antibiotics with discharge and community midwife review
options.rationale: Oral therapy at home is appropriate for mild endometritis in a woman who is afebrile and not bleeding heavily, and she is tachycardic, febrile, rigoring and anaemic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine with repeat ultrasound in seven days
options.rationale: A uterotonic may reduce loss transiently but does not clear retained tissue or treat the infection driving it, and a week of delay in a woman already at 92 g/L is unsafe (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth, and the two dominant causes, retained products and endometritis, usually coexist because retained tissue provides the substrate for infection. Ultrasound has limited specificity in the puerperium since clot and normal involuting decidua can look identical to retained tissue, so vascularity on colour Doppler is the finding that most raises the likelihood of true retained products. The decision to operate balances the risk of continued bleeding against the risk of perforation and later intrauterine adhesions, both of which are considerably higher in a soft infected postpartum uterus. Where the bleeding is settling and the woman is stable, antibiotics alone allow many cases to resolve without instrumentation.
key_points: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage spans 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth.
Retained products and endometritis usually coexist and are treated together.
Colour Doppler vascularity raises the likelihood that echogenic material is retained tissue rather than clot.
Antibiotics are started before instrumentation to avoid precipitating bacteraemia.
Evacuation of an infected soft uterus is performed by an experienced operator because of perforation risk.
explanation.pearls: Intrauterine adhesions follow puerperal curettage in up to a fifth of cases, far more than after a non pregnant procedure, which is why gentle suction with the largest safe cannula under ultrasound guidance is preferred to sharp curettage.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Choosing emergency contraception at four days with a raised body mass index
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who had unprotected intercourse four days ago, on day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle.

She has been using condoms alone and one broke. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and no unusual discharge, and a self collected swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea has been sent today with results due tomorrow. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She tells you she would like something more reliable going forward and is open to any method.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, normal sized anteverted uterus, no adnexal tenderness, no cervical motion tenderness, no abnormal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally as a single dose taken today
options.rationale: Doubling the dose is sometimes used at higher body weight, but the supporting evidence is weak and the underlying limitation, that it only works if given before the luteinising hormone surge, still applies on day 12 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Reassurance that emergency contraception is no longer effective
options.rationale: Four days is still inside the window for a copper device, so declaring the opportunity closed would deny her the most effective option available (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A copper intrauterine device inserted within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: The copper device can be inserted up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest calculated ovulation, has a failure rate below one per cent that is unaffected by body weight, and simultaneously provides the ongoing contraception she has asked for (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single dose taken today
options.rationale: This agent is licensed to 120 hours and is the better of the two oral options, but its efficacy falls as body mass index rises above 30 kg/m2 and it remains substantially less effective than the device (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose taken today
options.rationale: Oral levonorgestrel is licensed only to 96 hours and its efficacy declines markedly above a body mass index of 26 kg/m2, so both timing and body weight work against it here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception has three options in Australia and they differ in mechanism, window and reliability. The two oral agents work by delaying or preventing ovulation, which means both fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, and both lose efficacy as body weight rises. The copper intrauterine device works by a direct toxic effect on gametes and by preventing implantation, so it is unaffected by weight and by where the woman is in her cycle, and it is more than ten times more effective than either oral agent. A pending sexually transmitted infection result does not delay insertion; the device is inserted and treatment is given if the result returns positive. Any woman offered emergency contraception should also leave with a plan for ongoing contraception, since the encounter is often the only opportunity.
key_points: The copper device is effective up to five days after intercourse and is unaffected by body weight.
Oral levonorgestrel is licensed to 96 hours; ulipristal to 120 hours.
Both oral agents lose efficacy at higher body mass index and fail after the luteinising hormone surge.
A pending infection screen does not delay device insertion.
Every emergency contraception consultation includes a plan for ongoing contraception.
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator, so starting a progestogen containing method within five days after it blunts its effect, and hormonal contraception is deferred for that interval with condoms used in the meantime.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Referral for fetoscopic laser at an early stage of twin to twin transfusion syndrome
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 19 weeks and 2 days with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, attending for her routine fortnightly surveillance scan.

She feels well, has no abdominal tightening, no bleeding and no leaking. Her fundal height is larger than expected for dates and she has noticed her abdomen becoming rapidly more distended over the past fortnight. Today's scan reports the first twin with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm and a bladder that is not visible over 60 minutes of observation, and the second twin with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm and a persistently distended bladder. Umbilical artery Doppler waveforms show positive end diastolic flow in both twins, the ductus venosus waveforms are normal, and neither twin is hydropic.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound findings: Monochorionic diamniotic twins, twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with non visible bladder, twin two deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with distended bladder, positive end diastolic flow in both umbilical arteries, normal ductus venosus waveforms, no hydrops, cervical length 34 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Serial amnioreduction with weekly ultrasound surveillance instead
options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves maternal discomfort and pressure but leaves the shared placental anastomoses intact, and randomised comparison showed laser to give superior survival and less neurological morbidity (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Weekly ultrasound surveillance with review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Expectant surveillance is reasonable only for isolated discordant growth or for the mildest stage in selected cases, and untreated disease at this stage carries a perinatal mortality above 80 per cent (Source: International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology Practice Guidelines

options.text: Administer antenatal corticosteroids and plan birth at 26 weeks
options.rationale: Birth is not a treatment option at 19 weeks and steroids are given for anticipated preterm birth from 23 weeks, so this plan neither treats the condition nor is deliverable now (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Amniotic septostomy with weekly ultrasound surveillance instead
options.rationale: Deliberately perforating the dividing membrane equalises fluid volumes but creates a functionally monoamniotic pregnancy with cord entanglement risk and does not treat the vascular cause (Source: International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology Practice Guidelines

options.text: Urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre for laser ablation
options.rationale: A deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac with above 8 cm in the other before 20 weeks defines the syndrome, and once the donor bladder is no longer visible the disease has advanced beyond the earliest stage, at which point fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses gives the best survival (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates around 10 to 15 per cent of monochorionic pregnancies and arises from unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses within a shared placenta, which is why chorionicity determined in the first trimester dictates the entire surveillance schedule. Diagnosis requires a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac with above 8 cm in the other before 20 weeks, using 10 cm as the upper threshold after 20 weeks, and discordant growth alone is not sufficient. Staging runs from isolated fluid discordance, through loss of the donor bladder, abnormal Dopplers, hydrops, to demise of either twin. Fetoscopic laser ablation is the definitive treatment because it addresses the anastomoses themselves, and outcomes are best when it is performed in a high volume centre, which is why monochorionic pregnancies are scanned fortnightly from 16 weeks so that referral happens early.
key_points: Chorionicity is established in the first trimester and drives the surveillance schedule.
Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks is standard in monochorionic pregnancies.
Diagnosis requires deepest vertical pockets below 2 cm and above 8 cm before 20 weeks.
Loss of the donor bladder marks progression beyond the earliest stage.
Fetoscopic laser ablation treats the underlying anastomoses and outperforms amnioreduction.
explanation.pearls: Selective fetal growth restriction is the important near pair and shows discordant estimated weights with normal amniotic fluid volumes, whereas this condition is defined by the fluid discordance and may occur with barely discordant weights.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug choice by trimester in newly diagnosed hyperthyroidism
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 30 year old woman at 7 weeks in her first pregnancy, referred by her general practitioner with palpitations and weight loss.

She has lost 3 kg since her booking visit despite eating normally and describes her heart racing when she climbs the stairs at work. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist palms and a smooth symmetrically enlarged thyroid with a bruit over it. There is mild retraction of both upper eyelids and slight proptosis. Her vomiting settled at six weeks and she is now keeping food down, and there is no history of a molar pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 38 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 12.4 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody strongly positive
data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrical goitre with an audible bruit, fine outstretched hand tremor, bilateral lid retraction with mild proptosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propylthiouracil now and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
options.rationale: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism in the first trimester is treated with propylthiouracil because the alternative thionamide is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal and oesophageal atresia during organogenesis, with a switch considered after the first trimester to limit hepatotoxicity risk (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start carbimazole now and reassess the plan again after 16 weeks
options.rationale: This is the preferred agent outside pregnancy and after the first trimester, and the two are near pairs whose order is reversed by gestation, since its embryopathy risk is concentrated between 6 and 10 weeks (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start propranolol alone and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
options.rationale: A beta blocker controls tremor and tachycardia and is a useful adjunct for a few weeks, but it does not reduce thyroid hormone production and leaves the pregnancy exposed to the risks of untreated thyrotoxicosis (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange radioiodine ablation and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
options.rationale: Radioiodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and ablates the fetal thyroid, which begins concentrating iodine from around 10 to 12 weeks (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Withhold treatment now and reassess the plan again after 16 weeks
options.rationale: The near pair is transient gestational thyrotoxicosis from human chorionic gonadotrophin, which resolves without treatment, but that condition has no goitre, no eye signs and no receptor antibody, all of which are present here (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Hyperthyroidism in early pregnancy has two dominant causes that need opposite management. Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis reflects cross stimulation of the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor by human chorionic gonadotrophin, peaks around 10 weeks, is associated with hyperemesis and resolves spontaneously without antithyroid drugs. Autoimmune disease persists, has a goitre, sometimes eye signs, and a positive receptor antibody, and it requires treatment because untreated maternal thyrotoxicosis increases miscarriage, pre eclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction and heart failure. The antithyroid drug is titrated to keep free thyroxine in the upper part of the non pregnant reference range using the smallest possible dose, because both agents cross the placenta and can cause fetal hypothyroidism and goitre if the mother is over treated.
key_points: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester; carbimazole is preferred thereafter and outside pregnancy.
Radioiodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and for six months before conception.
Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis has no goitre, no eye signs and no receptor antibody.
The dose is titrated to keep free thyroxine at the upper end of the reference range.
Untreated disease raises risks of miscarriage, pre eclampsia, preterm birth and growth restriction.
explanation.pearls: Thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody crosses the placenta and is measured at 18 to 22 weeks and again at 30 to 34 weeks, because a titre more than three times the upper limit predicts fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis even in a mother whose own disease is well controlled or previously ablated.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Reduced liquor with a small foetus once membrane rupture has been excluded
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 29 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 33 weeks and 4 days, referred after a growth scan. She has felt normal movements today and has noticed no fluid loss and no wetness on her underwear.

She smokes eight cigarettes a day and her booking blood pressure was 108/64 mmHg. A sterile speculum examination shows no pooling of liquor in the posterior fornix and no fluid seen at the cervix on coughing, and a point of care test for placental protein in the vaginal fluid is negative.

The scan reports an estimated fetal weight on the third centile with an abdominal circumference below the third centile, a deepest vertical pocket of liquor of 1.6 cm, and an umbilical artery pulsatility index above the 95th centile with end diastolic flow still present. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight third centile, abdominal circumference below third centile, deepest vertical pocket 1.6 cm, umbilical artery pulsatility index above 95th centile with positive end diastolic flow, speculum and placental protein test negative, urinalysis no protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence erythromycin and expectant management for preterm membrane rupture
options.rationale: Latency antibiotics follow confirmed membrane rupture, and the absent pooling with a negative placental protein test makes rupture very unlikely, so the reduced liquor is placental in origin (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Arrange emergency caesarean birth today given the reduced liquor and small foetus
options.rationale: Delivery at 33 weeks with a reassuring cardiotocograph and preserved end diastolic flow trades a manageable surveillance problem for the substantial morbidity of iatrogenic prematurity (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal growth restriction).

options.text: Advise increased oral fluid intake and repeat the growth scan in four weeks
options.rationale: Maternal hydration raises liquor volume in idiopathic oligohydramnios but does nothing for placental insufficiency, and a four week interval is far too long once the umbilical artery Doppler is abnormal (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal growth restriction).

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids and start twice weekly Doppler and cardiotocograph surveillance
options.rationale: Early onset growth restriction with raised placental resistance but preserved end diastolic flow is managed by intensified surveillance with steroid cover in place, since deterioration to absent or reversed flow is what triggers birth and can occur within days (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal growth restriction).

options.text: Induce labour after corticosteroids with continuous monitoring in labour ward
options.rationale: A growth restricted foetus with raised placental resistance tolerates the contractions of induction poorly, and induction at this gestation is not indicated while surveillance remains reassuring (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal growth restriction).

explanation.summary: Reduced amniotic fluid in the third trimester has three broad explanations, membrane rupture, fetal renal tract abnormality, and placental insufficiency causing redistribution away from the kidneys, and the first step is always to exclude rupture with a speculum examination. Early onset growth restriction, defined as onset before 32 weeks, is strongly placental and follows a recognised sequence of deterioration: rising umbilical artery resistance, then absent and later reversed end diastolic flow, then changes in the ductus venosus, and finally an abnormal cardiotocograph. Because that sequence can unfold over days, surveillance is intensified rather than reassurance being taken from a normal trace on a single day. Antenatal corticosteroids are given because the probability of birth before 34 weeks is high, and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given when birth becomes imminent before 30 weeks. Timing of birth balances the risk of stillbirth against the morbidity of prematurity, and before 32 weeks the trigger is usually ductus venosus change or an abnormal cardiotocograph rather than the umbilical artery alone.
key_points: Exclude membrane rupture with a speculum examination before attributing reduced liquor to the placenta.
Early onset growth restriction deteriorates in a recognised Doppler sequence over days.
Raised umbilical artery resistance with preserved end diastolic flow calls for surveillance, not immediate birth.
Give antenatal corticosteroids when birth before 34 weeks is likely.
Absent or reversed end diastolic flow escalates both the frequency of surveillance and the plan for birth.
explanation.pearls: Smoking is the single most modifiable contributor to placental growth restriction in Australian practice, and cessation even in the third trimester measurably improves fetal growth velocity, so the referral to a quit service belongs in the same consultation as the surveillance plan.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
Safer Care Victoria: Fetal growth restriction

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of excessive amniotic fluid found on a third trimester scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 30 weeks and 2 days, referred because her abdomen measures 38 cm against a symphysis fundal height expectation of 30 cm. She says she has felt increasingly stretched and breathless lying flat for the last fortnight.

Her two previous babies weighed 3.4 kg and 3.6 kg at term. She had a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks that she was told was normal, and her blood pressure has been normal throughout with no protein on urinalysis. The uterus is soft and non tender, fetal parts are difficult to palpate through the fluid and the presentation is unstable. The scan today reports a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm with a single foetus, an estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile and a normally sited posterior placenta.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm, estimated fetal weight 60th centile, posterior placenta with no praevia, urinalysis no protein, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a detailed fetal anatomy review with repeat testing for gestational diabetes
options.rationale: The two causes that must be found are impaired glucose tolerance and a fetal anomaly interfering with swallowing or absorption, and a normal test three weeks ago does not exclude diabetes that has developed since, so both are pursued together (Source: RANZCOG: Polyhydramnios).

options.text: Reassure her that mild excess fluid is common and repeat the scan in four weeks
options.rationale: A deepest pocket above 8 cm is moderate rather than mild, and roughly a third of cases at this level have an identifiable cause that changes management for mother or baby (Source: RANZCOG: Polyhydramnios).

options.text: Perform amnioreduction by needle drainage to relieve the maternal breathlessness
options.rationale: Drainage is reserved for severe symptomatic accumulation causing respiratory compromise, and it carries risks of membrane rupture, abruption and preterm labour that are not justified for postural breathlessness (Source: RANZCOG: Polyhydramnios).

options.text: Prescribe oral indomethacin to reduce fetal urine output and the fluid volume
options.rationale: Indomethacin reduces fetal urine output but constricts the ductus arteriosus and is avoided beyond about 32 weeks, and it treats the fluid without addressing the cause (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Admit for induction of labour once antenatal corticosteroids have been given
options.rationale: Birth at 30 weeks for excess fluid alone imposes serious prematurity, and the accumulation itself is not an indication for delivery while mother and foetus are stable (Source: RANZCOG: Polyhydramnios).

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid in the third trimester reflects the balance between fetal urine production and fetal swallowing, so excess accumulates when urine output is high, as in maternal hyperglycaemia, or when swallowing or gut transit is obstructed, as in oesophageal or duodenal atresia and in some neuromuscular conditions. About half of cases are idiopathic, but the workup is still performed because the identifiable half changes management. Maternal glucose testing is repeated even after a normal earlier result, since gestational diabetes can develop later in the third trimester. Congenital infection, fetal anaemia from red cell alloimmunisation or parvovirus, and twin to twin transfusion in a multiple pregnancy are the further considerations. The obstetric consequences are the reason it matters: unstable lie, cord prolapse at membrane rupture, preterm labour from uterine distension, placental abruption on decompression and postpartum haemorrhage from an overdistended uterus.
key_points: Fetal urine output and swallowing set amniotic fluid volume, so excess points to one or the other.
Repeat glucose testing even after a normal earlier result, since diabetes can develop later.
A detailed anatomy review looks for obstruction to swallowing or gut transit.
About half of cases are idiopathic but the workup still identifies management changing causes.
Unstable lie, cord prolapse, preterm labour, abruption and postpartum haemorrhage are the practical risks.
explanation.pearls: Warn her to present immediately if the waters break, because the unstable lie created by the excess fluid makes cord prolapse a real risk at rupture, and that warning does more for outcome than any intervention offered antenatally.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Amniotic fluid volume

subtopic_detail: Investigation sequencing after an unexplained late intrauterine fetal death
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 30 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 38 weeks and 1 day. She came in this morning because she had felt no movements since yesterday afternoon, and ultrasound has confirmed there is no fetal heart activity.

Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated, with normal growth on a 34 week scan and normal blood pressure throughout. She has had no abdominal pain, bleeding or fever. Her blood group is A positive. She is distressed but composed, and she and her partner have asked you what happens next and whether they will ever know why. Induction of labour has not yet been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms absent fetal cardiac activity, urinalysis no protein, full blood count and coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation plan?

options.text: Arrange an inherited thrombophilia screen and antiphospholipid antibodies today
options.rationale: Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended after stillbirth because the association is weak and results are distorted by pregnancy, while antiphospholipid testing is reserved for a suggestive history and must be repeated after twelve weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth investigation).

options.text: Send placental tissue for histopathology after birth and take no maternal bloods
options.rationale: Placental histopathology is the single highest yield investigation and must be done, but omitting maternal testing forfeits the diagnoses that only maternal blood can make, including massive foetomaternal haemorrhage (Source: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death).
source_refs: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death

options.text: Send cord blood for karyotype after birth and defer all other investigations
options.rationale: Genetic testing is part of the panel, but cord blood after intrauterine death often fails to culture, so a placental or fetal tissue sample is preferred and it cannot stand alone as the whole workup (Source: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death).
source_refs: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death

options.text: Send maternal blood for a Kleihauer test now and offer autopsy with placental histopathology
options.rationale: Fetal cells clear from the maternal circulation over days so the Kleihauer must be taken before birth to be interpretable, and autopsy with placental histopathology is the pairing that yields a cause most often (Source: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death).
source_refs: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death

options.text: Request maternal serology for the full congenital infection panel as the priority
options.rationale: Broad untargeted infection serology has a low yield in the absence of maternal illness, growth restriction or hydrops, and prioritising it displaces the tests that actually explain most late deaths (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth investigation).

explanation.summary: About one in every 130 Australian pregnancies ends in stillbirth, and a systematic investigation identifies a probable cause in the majority when the full protocol is followed. The highest yield elements are placental histopathology, autopsy and cytogenetic testing, and consent for autopsy is offered to every family with an explanation that a limited or external examination is an alternative if a full examination is declined. Certain tests are time critical and must be taken before or at birth: the Kleihauer detects massive foetomaternal haemorrhage and becomes uninterpretable as fetal cells clear from the maternal circulation, and it should be sent before induction begins. The standard panel also includes maternal full blood count, glucose or glycated haemoglobin, bile acids, thyroid function, blood group and antibody screen, and targeted infection testing where the history or examination suggests it. Inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended, since it does not change management and generates anxiety in future pregnancies. Establishing a cause matters for the family's understanding and for the management of the next pregnancy, which is why the results are reviewed with them at a scheduled follow up.
key_points: Take the Kleihauer before birth, since fetal cells clear from the maternal circulation over days.
Placental histopathology and autopsy are the two highest yield investigations.
Offer autopsy to every family, including limited or external examination as alternatives.
Inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended after stillbirth.
Arrange a structured follow up appointment to discuss results and the next pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Send the Kleihauer before induction is started rather than after birth: massive foetomaternal haemorrhage explains a meaningful minority of otherwise unexplained late stillbirths and is the one diagnosis that is permanently lost by waiting a day.

sources.label: PSANZ: Clinical practice guideline for care around stillbirth and neonatal death
Safer Care Victoria: Stillbirth investigation and care

subtopic_detail: Setting and adjuncts for repair of an anal sphincter injury after instrumental birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite immediately after a forceps birth of a 4.1 kg baby to a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy. The second stage lasted two hours and a mediolateral episiotomy was performed.

Her epidural is still running and is providing good analgesia. On systematic examination with the woman in lithotomy and good lighting, the tear extends through the perineal body and you can see torn fibres of the external anal sphincter. On digital rectal examination the torn muscle involves rather more than half the thickness of the external sphincter, the internal sphincter is intact and the anal mucosa is intact. Estimated blood loss so far is 350 mL and the uterus is well contracted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tear through the perineal body with more than 50 per cent thickness of external anal sphincter torn, internal anal sphincter intact, anorectal mucosa intact, uterus contracted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the tear?

options.text: Repair in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration with absorbable suture
options.rationale: Local infiltration gives inadequate relaxation for sphincter apposition and poor lighting and assistance in the birth suite are associated with worse anatomical results (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair in theatre under regional anaesthesia with antibiotic cover and postoperative laxatives
options.rationale: This is the correct setting and the correct adjuncts, and it is the near pair to the answer, differing only in whether an experienced operator is specified, which is itself an independent determinant of continence outcome (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair in theatre by an experienced operator with antibiotics and postoperative laxatives
options.rationale: Sphincter repair is performed in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia by or under the supervision of a clinician trained in the technique, with a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotic and a postoperative laxative to protect the repair (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair the perineal body only and manage the sphincter tear conservatively with physiotherapy
options.rationale: Leaving a torn external sphincter unrepaired produces persistent faecal urgency and incontinence, and physiotherapy is an adjunct to repair rather than a substitute for it (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Pack the perineum and plan a delayed secondary repair with a colorectal surgeon
options.rationale: Delayed repair is reserved for the woman who presents late with established incontinence, and primary repair at the time of injury gives the better functional outcome (Source: RCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears green top guideline).
source_refs: RCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears green top guideline

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is classified by how much muscle is involved: a 3a tear involves less than half the thickness of the external sphincter, 3b more than half, 3c extends into the internal sphincter, and a fourth degree tear breaches the anorectal mucosa. Recognition depends on a systematic examination of every woman after vaginal birth, including a digital rectal examination, because a substantial proportion of these injuries are missed at the bedside and present later as faecal urgency or incontinence. Risk factors include first vaginal birth, forceps delivery, a birthweight above 4 kg, prolonged second stage, occipitoposterior position and shoulder dystocia. Repair happens in theatre with adequate anaesthesia and lighting, the external sphincter is repaired by overlapping or end to end technique with equivalent results, and the internal sphincter is repaired separately when torn. Postoperative care includes a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotic, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy, and follow up in a dedicated clinic where continence is assessed and the mode of birth for the next pregnancy is discussed.
key_points: Classification depends on the proportion of external sphincter torn and whether the internal sphincter or mucosa is involved.
Perform a digital rectal examination on every woman after vaginal birth to avoid missing the injury.
Repair in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia by a trained operator.
Give a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotic and postoperative laxatives.
Arrange follow up to assess continence and plan the mode of birth for the next pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Prescribe a stool softening laxative rather than constipating analgesia after the repair, since straining against a fresh sphincter repair is the mechanism by which an anatomically good result becomes a functionally poor one.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
RCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears green top guideline

subtopic_detail: Choosing the instrument for an assisted birth before 34 weeks gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 24 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 33 weeks and 4 days who is in spontaneous preterm labour. She has been fully dilated and pushing for 55 minutes and her epidural is working well.

The cardiotocograph has developed recurrent late decelerations over the last twelve minutes with reduced variability between them, and a fetal scalp lactate is not available at this hospital. She received a full course of antenatal corticosteroids two days ago and magnesium sulfate is running. On examination the head is direct occipitoanterior at station plus two centimetres below the ischial spines, with no caput and no moulding, and the bladder is empty. The consultant, the paediatric team and theatre have all been alerted and are present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph with recurrent late decelerations and reduced baseline variability, estimated fetal weight 2100 g, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mode of birth?

options.text: Assisted birth with forceps in the birth suite with the theatre team standing by
options.rationale: Vacuum extraction is not recommended before 34 weeks because the preterm skull is at high risk of cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage and intracranial bleeding, so forceps is the instrument of choice when an assisted birth is needed at this gestation (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth).

options.text: Assisted birth with a soft cup vacuum extractor applied at the flexion point
options.rationale: The soft cup reduces scalp trauma at term but does not remove the gestational restriction, which rests on the compliance of the preterm skull rather than on the cup material (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth).

options.text: Vacuum extraction first and forceps afterwards if the vacuum attempt is unsuccessful
options.rationale: Sequential use of two instruments multiplies neonatal trauma and is avoided at any gestation, and it compounds the specific objection to vacuum before 34 weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth).

options.text: Emergency caesarean section under the working epidural without an instrumental attempt
options.rationale: Caesarean birth with the head at plus two and no moulding is technically difficult and slower than an assisted birth, and it is the answer only if the instrumental criteria are not met (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth).

options.text: Oxytocin infusion with continued maternal pushing and repeat assessment in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Augmenting contractions in the presence of recurrent late decelerations worsens the hypoxic stress that is already present and delays a birth that is indicated now (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance).

explanation.summary: An assisted vaginal birth requires the whole set of prerequisites to be met before an instrument is applied: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, a known cephalic presentation and position, an engaged head at or below the ischial spines, adequate analgesia, an empty bladder, informed consent and a clinician competent with the chosen instrument in a place where an immediate caesarean is possible. The choice between vacuum and forceps normally turns on operator experience, the position of the head and the maternal and neonatal trade off, since vacuum causes fewer maternal sphincter injuries while forceps has a higher success rate. Gestational age overrides that usual reasoning: vacuum extraction is contraindicated before 34 weeks because the poorly ossified, highly compliant preterm skull is prone to cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage and intracranial haemorrhage. Every assisted birth is preceded by a plan for what happens if it fails, and a trial in theatre is chosen when success is uncertain. Failure to progress with the instrument after three pulls with no descent means abandoning the attempt rather than persisting.
key_points: Vacuum extraction is not used before 34 weeks because of the compliance of the preterm skull.
Forceps is the instrument of choice when an assisted birth is required preterm.
Sequential use of two instruments substantially increases neonatal trauma and is avoided.
All prerequisites must be met before any instrument is applied.
Abandon the attempt if there is no descent with three pulls of correctly applied traction.
explanation.pearls: Subgaleal haemorrhage is the specific vacuum related catastrophe: the subaponeurotic space can hold most of a newborn's blood volume, and preterm infants tolerate that loss least, which is what puts the gestational limit at 34 weeks rather than at a birthweight threshold.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Operative vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Treating a protozoal genital infection and its partner implications
stem:
You are the sexual health registrar seeing a 27 year old woman with three weeks of vaginal discharge, soreness and stinging when she passes urine. She has one regular male partner of two years and no other partners.

On speculum examination there is a frothy yellow green discharge pooling in the posterior fornix and the ectocervix is studded with punctate red areas. The vaginal pH is 5.5. A self collected vaginal swab reports nucleic acid detected for Trichomonas vaginalis, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected and no candida seen. She is not pregnant, takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no drug allergies. Her partner has no symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Frothy yellow green discharge, punctate cervical erythema, vaginal pH 5.5, no adnexal or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Trichomonas vaginalis nucleic acid detected, chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected, urine pregnancy test negative, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral metronidazole for her, with treatment of her partner at the same time
options.rationale: Oral nitroimidazole therapy cures the infection, and simultaneous partner treatment regardless of partner symptoms is required because asymptomatic male carriage is common and reinfection otherwise follows within weeks (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for five nights with review afterwards
options.rationale: Topical nitroimidazole reaches inadequate concentrations in the urethra and periurethral glands where the organism persists, and cure rates are well below those of oral therapy (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries for six nights with a topical antifungal cream
options.rationale: Antifungal treatment addresses candidiasis, which produces a thick white discharge with a normal vaginal pH rather than a frothy discharge with a pH of 5.5, and no yeast was seen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Single dose oral azithromycin for her and for her partner on the same day
options.rationale: A macrolide covers chlamydia, which was not detected here, and has no activity against this protozoan (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral metronidazole for her, with partner treatment only if he becomes symptomatic
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms in the partner leaves an untreated reservoir, since the majority of infected men have no symptoms at all and reinfect within a short interval (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted protozoal infection that is uncommon in most Australian metropolitan settings but remains prevalent in some remote communities, so local epidemiology shapes how strongly it is considered. The frothy discharge, raised vaginal pH and punctate cervical erythema are suggestive but insensitive, and nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced microscopy, which misses around half of cases. Treatment is oral because topical therapy does not reach the urethral and periurethral reservoirs. All current sexual partners are treated at the same time without waiting for their test results, and sex is avoided until both have completed treatment and been symptom free for seven days. Diagnosis of any sexually transmitted infection prompts a full screen, including chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology, because coinfection is common. In pregnancy the infection is associated with preterm birth and low birthweight, and treatment is still given.
key_points: Oral nitroimidazole therapy is required; topical treatment does not clear urethral reservoirs.
Treat all current partners simultaneously regardless of symptoms or test results.
Avoid sex until both partners have completed treatment and been symptom free for seven days.
Nucleic acid testing has replaced wet mount microscopy, which misses about half of cases.
Any positive result prompts a full sexually transmitted infection screen for coinfection.
explanation.pearls: Test of cure by nucleic acid testing is recommended at two weeks to three months in women because reinfection and treatment failure are both common, and testing earlier than two weeks can detect residual non viable organism DNA.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Managing provoked vestibular pain after repeated antifungal courses have failed
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman with fourteen months of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever she attempts intercourse or tries to insert a tampon. She has no pain at rest, and none when cycling or sitting through a work day.

She has taken four courses of oral fluconazole and used several antifungal creams, none of which changed the pain. She and her partner have stopped attempting sex and she is tearful describing the effect on their relationship. On examination the vulval skin looks entirely normal. Light touch with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain exactly, while the same touch on the labia majora and perineum is painless.
