The pelvic floor muscles are tender and she cannot relax them on request.

data_table.Examination: Vulval skin normal with no pallor, fissuring or architectural change, no discharge, cotton bud test positive at the posterior vestibule only, hypertonic tender pelvic floor musculature
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab with no candida or bacterial pathogen isolated, fungal culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of weekly oral fluconazole and review
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy treats recurrent candidiasis, and four previous courses with a negative fungal culture have already excluded that as the mechanism (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy alongside education and topical local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Pain provoked only by pressure at the vestibule with a hypertonic pelvic floor is managed with a multimodal program in which physiotherapy for the muscle component, explanation of central pain mechanisms and topical anaesthetic for penetration together carry the strongest evidence (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied nightly for three months
options.rationale: Topical steroid treats an inflammatory dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus, which would show pallor, fissuring or loss of architecture, and none of those changes is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer for vestibulectomy with vaginal advancement flap at the earliest opportunity
options.rationale: Surgery has a place only after a properly delivered multimodal program has failed over many months, and operating on an untreated hypertonic pelvic floor commonly leaves the pain unchanged (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Prescribe oral amitriptyline at night as sole therapy with dose escalation monthly
options.rationale: A tricyclic is a reasonable adjunct for neuropathic pain but as monotherapy it leaves the muscular and psychosexual components untreated, and the evidence for it in provoked vestibular pain is weak (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic).

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable disease to explain it, and it is subdivided by whether the pain is provoked or spontaneous, localised or generalised. Provoked vestibulodynia, in which pain occurs only on pressure at the vestibule, is the commonest form in women of reproductive age and is frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent thrush for years before assessment. The cotton bud test that maps pain precisely to the vestibule while sparing surrounding skin is the key examination finding, and normal vulval skin is expected rather than reassuring. Peripheral nociceptor sensitisation, central pain amplification and a secondary hypertonic pelvic floor all contribute, which is why single modality treatment usually disappoints. Management combines physiotherapy, education, topical measures, psychological and psychosexual therapy, and sometimes neuromodulating medication, with surgery held in reserve.
key_points: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of three months or more without an identifiable causative disease.
The cotton bud test localising pain to the vestibule with normal skin is the central finding.
Repeated antifungal courses with negative cultures are a common and unhelpful detour.
A secondary hypertonic pelvic floor is present in most women and responds to physiotherapy.
Vestibulectomy is reserved for failure of a properly delivered multimodal program.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the pain occurs with cycling, prolonged sitting or at rest: pain only on attempted penetration marks the provoked localised form that responds best to physiotherapy, while constant unprovoked burning suggests generalised vulvodynia and a greater role for neuromodulating medication.

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a fluctuant vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department for a 29 year old woman with three days of worsening swelling and pain at the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down and has walked in leaning on her partner.

Examination shows a tense, tender, fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across at the posterior aspect of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus, with surrounding erythema limited to the swelling itself. She is afebrile with normal observations and there is no induration extending into the perineum or thigh, no crepitus and no area of dusky skin. She has had one similar but smaller episode two years ago that settled with antibiotics alone. She is not pregnant and has no medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling of the posterior right labium majus, localised erythema, no perineal induration, no crepitus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di or flucloxacillin for seven days with analgesia and warm baths at home
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis without a collection, and a tense fluctuant abscess needs drainage because antibiotic penetration into pus is poor (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Needle aspiration of the collection under local anaesthesia in the department
options.rationale: Aspiration relieves pain briefly but the cavity refills because the tract seals over within a day, giving recurrence rates far above those of a technique that keeps the tract open (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a balloon tipped catheter left in situ
options.rationale: A small stab incision with a balloon tipped catheter left for four to six weeks drains the abscess and allows an epithelialised tract to form, which is what prevents recurrence, and it is done under local anaesthesia in the emergency department (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with a gauze wick changed daily by the practice nurse
options.rationale: Incision alone drains the pus but the incision closes over as it heals, so recurrence is common and this is the near pair that differs only by omitting the device that keeps the tract patent (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Marsupialisation of the gland in theatre on the next available operating list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is effective but requires a theatre slot and usually general anaesthesia, so it is kept for recurrent disease after simpler drainage has failed (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

explanation.summary: The greater vestibular glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the introitus and drain through short ducts; obstruction produces a cyst and secondary infection produces an abscess. Asymptomatic cysts in women under 40 need no treatment, while an abscess is drained. The principle that governs technique is that the drainage tract must stay open long enough to epithelialise, which is why a balloon tipped catheter left in place for four to six weeks or marsupialisation outperforms incision or aspiration alone. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, immunosuppression or a high risk of methicillin resistant organisms, and swabs are taken at drainage. A new vulval mass in a woman over 40, or one that is firm, fixed or irregular, warrants biopsy because carcinoma of the gland, though rare, presents this way. Rapidly spreading induration, pain out of proportion, crepitus or dusky skin should redirect the assessment towards necrotising infection.
key_points: A fluctuant abscess requires drainage; antibiotics alone are for cellulitis without a collection.
The tract must stay open for weeks to epithelialise, which is why catheter drainage beats simple incision.
Marsupialisation is reserved for recurrent disease or failure of catheter drainage.
Add antibiotics for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression.
A firm or irregular vulval mass in a woman over 40 needs biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
explanation.pearls: The balloon catheter stays in for four to six weeks, not days: removing it once the pain settles at one week defeats the purpose, because the epithelialised tract that prevents recurrence has not yet formed.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess
BMJ Best Practice: Bartholin cyst and abscess

subtopic_detail: Structuring induction and maintenance therapy for repeated culture proven vaginal yeast infection
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old teacher who has had five episodes of vulval itch with a thick white discharge in the past twelve months. Each episode was confirmed on high vaginal swab, each cleared within days of a topical antifungal, and each returned within six to ten weeks.

She uses no soap on the vulva, wears cotton underwear and has not used antibiotics for two years. She has one regular partner who has no symptoms. Her most recent swab grew Candida albicans with sensitivity to azoles, and no bacterial pathogen or trichomonas was detected. She is not pregnant, takes no immunosuppressant medication, and her glycated haemoglobin and human immunodeficiency virus serology are both normal.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with satellite lesions, thick adherent white discharge, vaginal pH 4.2
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab growing Candida albicans sensitive to azoles, glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Recommend oral lactobacillus probiotics daily with dietary sugar restriction
options.rationale: Probiotics and dietary measures have not been shown to prevent recurrence in controlled trials and delay effective suppressive therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: A single oral fluconazole dose taken at the onset of each future episode
options.rationale: Episodic treatment is appropriate for sporadic infection and is what she has effectively been doing, since it clears each attack without altering the pattern of recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries used twice weekly for the next six months
options.rationale: Topical maintenance is an alternative when oral therapy is contraindicated, such as in pregnancy, but adherence is poorer and it is not the first choice for a non pregnant woman (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Treat her partner with a topical antifungal at the same time as each episode
options.rationale: This is not a sexually transmitted infection and randomised evidence shows partner treatment does not reduce recurrence in the woman (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Oral fluconazole induction over one week then weekly maintenance for six months
options.rationale: Four or more culture proven episodes in a year defines recurrent disease, and induction followed by six months of suppressive weekly dosing is what breaks the cycle, with about half remaining free of recurrence after maintenance ends (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as four or more symptomatic episodes in twelve months, and confirmation by culture matters because a large proportion of women self treating for thrush have another cause entirely, including dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and vulvodynia. Speciation is part of that confirmation, since non albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, respond poorly to azoles and need alternative agents such as intravaginal boric acid or nystatin. Predisposing factors worth excluding are diabetes, immunosuppression, high dose oestrogen exposure and repeated antibiotic courses, but most women with recurrent disease have none of them. Treatment is a defined induction course followed by six months of weekly suppression, and around half of women remain in remission after suppression stops while the remainder relapse and may need longer maintenance. Fluconazole is avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy, where topical therapy is used instead.
key_points: Four or more culture proven episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease.
Confirm by culture and speciate, since non albicans species respond poorly to azoles.
Induction followed by six months of weekly oral suppression is the standard regimen.
Partner treatment does not reduce recurrence; this is not a sexually transmitted infection.
Exclude diabetes and immunosuppression, though most women have no predisposing condition.
explanation.pearls: Candida glabrata is the species to suspect when azole therapy repeatedly fails despite good adherence, and it is treated with intravaginal boric acid pessaries or nystatin rather than by escalating the fluconazole dose.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choosing between a history indicated suture and ultrasound surveillance in recurrent midtrimester loss
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the maternal fetal medicine clinic seeing a 31 year old woman at 13 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had three previous pregnancies that ended at 19, 21 and 20 weeks, and no living children.

On each occasion she described pressure and a watery discharge over a day or two, and was found to be several centimetres dilated with bulging membranes before she had any contractions. There was no bleeding, no fever and no abdominal pain on any of the three occasions, and placental histopathology after the second loss showed no chorioamnionitis. Her current pregnancy is a singleton with normal first trimester screening and a nuchal translucency within normal limits. Today's transvaginal cervical length is 34 mm with no funnelling and a mid vaginal swab shows normal flora.

data_table.Examination: Uterus consistent with dates, cervix closed on speculum examination, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal cervical length 34 mm with no funnelling, mid vaginal swab normal flora, first trimester combined screening low risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her cervix in this pregnancy?

options.text: Serial cervical length scans from 16 weeks with a suture if the length falls below 25 mm
options.rationale: Ultrasound indicated cerclage is the strategy for one or two previous losses or a shortened cervix without a definite history, and with three painless midtrimester losses the surveillance approach risks catching the cervix once it is already dilating (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: History indicated cervical cerclage placed now while the cervix is still long
options.rationale: Three consecutive painless midtrimester losses with progressive dilatation and no bleeding, contractions or infection is the pattern for which a history indicated suture at 12 to 14 weeks reduces preterm birth, and it is placed before any shortening occurs (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: Vaginal progesterone nightly from 16 weeks with no scans and no suture
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix found on scan, but it has not been shown to substitute for a suture where the history itself establishes cervical insufficiency (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: Cervical pessary inserted at 16 weeks and removed at 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Pessary trials have produced inconsistent results and it is not an established alternative to a suture in a woman with this history (Source: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline).
source_refs: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline

options.text: Reduced activity with pelvic rest and weekly review through the second trimester
options.rationale: Bed rest and activity restriction do not prevent preterm birth and carry real harms including venous thromboembolism, deconditioning and lost income (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis built on a pattern of painless progressive dilatation in the midtrimester leading to loss or extreme preterm birth, in the absence of labour, abruption or infection. The three cerclage categories are distinguished by what triggers them: history indicated sutures are placed electively at 12 to 14 weeks on the basis of previous losses, ultrasound indicated sutures follow a shortened cervix on surveillance, and rescue sutures are placed when dilatation with exposed membranes is found. Placental histopathology and the absence of contractions, bleeding and fever matter because infection driven and abruption driven losses have a different mechanism and do not benefit from a suture. First trimester aneuploidy screening is performed before an elective suture so that a chromosomally abnormal pregnancy is not sutured. Complications include membrane rupture, infection and cervical laceration if labour begins with the suture in place, so the suture is removed at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier if labour starts.
key_points: Painless progressive dilatation without labour, bleeding or infection defines the clinical pattern.
History indicated cerclage is placed at 12 to 14 weeks after three or more midtrimester losses.
Ultrasound indicated cerclage follows a short cervix in women with a less definitive history.
Complete first trimester screening before placing an elective suture.
Remove the suture at 36 to 37 weeks, or sooner if labour or membrane rupture occurs.
explanation.pearls: The suture must come out at the onset of labour: leaving it in place while a woman contracts against it is what produces cervical laceration and annular detachment, so removal instructions travel with the woman in her handheld record.

sources.label: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline
Safer Care Victoria: Preterm birth prevention

subtopic_detail: Timing birth by peak bile acid concentration in cholestasis of pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 33 weeks and 2 days. For twelve days she has been unable to sleep because of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet, and she has scratched the skin of her forearms until it bled.

There is no rash apart from linear excoriations. She has no right upper quadrant pain, headache or visual disturbance. Blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. Fetal growth is on the 45th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and the cardiotocograph is normal. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and a liver ultrasound shows normal ducts and no gallstones.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 156 U/L (less than 30 in pregnancy), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (2-24), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue the pregnancy to 39 to 40 weeks with weekly bile acid measurement
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk in this condition rises sharply once peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L, and continuing to term accepts the period of highest risk without benefit (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: A peak bile acid concentration at or above 100 micromol/L defines severe disease for which birth is recommended at 35 to 36 weeks, and ursodeoxycholic acid is offered in the interim for maternal itch though it does not alter perinatal outcome (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Deliver today by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Birth at 33 weeks exposes the baby to substantial prematurity for a risk that becomes material closer to term, and this condition is not in itself an indication for caesarean birth (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Prescribe emollients with a sedating antihistamine at night and review at term
options.rationale: Symptomatic measures are reasonable adjuncts for itch, but relying on them and deferring the timing decision ignores the bile acid concentration that drives the perinatal risk (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Commence oral dexamethasone for pruritus and continue routine antenatal care
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is less effective than ursodeoxycholic acid for itch in this condition and repeated maternal corticosteroid exposure for a symptomatic indication is not justified (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus that is worst on the palms and soles and at night, without a primary rash, and is confirmed by raised serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases. The clinically important variable is the peak bile acid concentration, because the association with stillbirth is concentrated in the severe group: risk is close to background below 40 micromol/L, modestly raised between 40 and 99, and rises steeply at 100 micromol/L and above. Timing of birth is therefore stratified, with birth around 38 to 39 weeks for mild disease, 36 to 37 weeks for moderate disease and 35 to 36 weeks for severe disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves maternal itch and biochemistry but a large randomised trial showed no reduction in perinatal death or preterm birth, so it is offered for symptoms rather than as protection. Other causes of itch and deranged liver tests, including pre-eclampsia, acute fatty liver, viral hepatitis and gallstone disease, are excluded before the diagnosis is settled, and the condition recurs in a majority of subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: Peak bile acid concentration stratifies risk and drives the timing of birth.
Bile acids at or above 100 micromol/L define severe disease with birth at 35 to 36 weeks.
Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itch but does not reduce stillbirth or preterm birth.
Itch of palms and soles without a primary rash is the characteristic presentation.
Exclude pre-eclampsia, acute fatty liver, viral hepatitis and biliary obstruction before settling the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Bile acids need not be fasting for the timing decision, and it is the highest value recorded across the pregnancy rather than the most recent one that determines which gestation band the woman falls into.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Follow up interval for an incidental simple adnexal cyst in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman referred after an ultrasound arranged for one episode of right sided abdominal pain that settled the same day and has not returned.

She has regular 29 day cycles with no bloating, early satiety or weight loss, and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Abdominal and pelvic examination is normal. The pelvic ultrasound was performed on day 7 of her cycle, and the findings for both ovaries and the uterus are recorded in her file.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no palpable mass, no ascites, cervix and uterus normal on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with a 6 cm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst, thin smooth wall, no solid areas or septations, no internal vascularity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Annual ultrasound surveillance while the cyst remains unchanged and asymptomatic
options.rationale: A simple unilocular anechoic cyst between 5 and 7 cm in a premenopausal woman carries a negligible risk of malignancy, so yearly imaging to confirm stability is sufficient and intervention is reserved for growth, symptoms or a change in morphology (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding
options.rationale: The malignancy index is designed for postmenopausal assessment, and CA125 rises with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and pelvic infection in premenopausal women, generating false alarms for a clearly benign morphology (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to obtain a histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Surgery on a benign appearing cyst removes normal ovarian cortex with it and reduces ovarian reserve in a woman who may want to conceive, for no diagnostic gain (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress and resolve the cyst
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception prevents new functional cysts forming but randomised evidence shows it does not hasten resolution of a cyst that is already present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in six weeks and discharge her if the cyst has resolved
options.rationale: A short interval rescan is the approach for cysts under 5 cm that are likely to be functional, and it is a near miss here because a 6 cm cyst warrants confirmation of stability over a longer horizon rather than a single early rescan (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

explanation.summary: Most adnexal cysts found in premenopausal women are functional and resolve without intervention, and the ultrasound morphology rather than the size alone determines how they are managed. A simple cyst is unilocular, anechoic, thin walled and avascular with no solid component or papillary projection, and this appearance is associated with a very low malignancy risk at any premenopausal size. Simple cysts under 5 cm generally need no follow up, those between 5 and 7 cm are followed with yearly imaging, and those above 7 cm are difficult to assess fully with ultrasound and prompt further imaging or a surgical opinion. Features that change the pathway are solid areas, papillary projections, thick septations, internal vascularity, ascites and any suggestion of peritoneal disease. Sudden severe pain with a known cyst raises torsion or rupture and is a separate acute problem needing prompt assessment, and larger cysts are more prone to torsion.
key_points: Morphology, not size alone, determines the management of an adnexal cyst.
Simple cysts under 5 cm in premenopausal women need no follow up.
Simple cysts of 5 to 7 cm are followed with yearly imaging.
CA125 is unreliable premenopausally and is not used to assess a clearly simple cyst.
Solid areas, papillary projections, thick septations, vascularity or ascites change the pathway.
explanation.pearls: Warn her about torsion rather than about cancer: a cyst of this size carries a real risk of sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, and that presentation needs assessment within hours, whereas the malignancy risk here is close to nil.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer clinical guidelines

subtopic_detail: Acting on endometrial thickness in a woman with bleeding after the menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman who had two episodes of light red vaginal bleeding in the past three weeks. Her last menstrual period was four years ago and she has taken no hormone therapy.

She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with a small amount of blood at the external os and no visible lesion, and her cervical screening test six months ago detected no oncogenic human papillomavirus. Bimanual examination finds a mobile, normal sized, non tender uterus with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrium measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion, normal ovaries and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with blood at the external os, mobile normal sized uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with endometrial thickness 9 mm and no focal lesion, cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the bleeding reflects atrophic change and review if it recurs
options.rationale: Atrophy is the commonest cause of bleeding after the menopause but it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and an endometrium of 9 mm requires tissue before that label can be applied (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months to see whether it thins
options.rationale: Repeat imaging delays diagnosis without adding information, since the measurement has already crossed the threshold that mandates sampling (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the reference range
options.rationale: CA125 has no role in the assessment of endometrial pathology and a normal value would falsely reassure in the presence of a thickened endometrium (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines

options.text: Commence a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Progestogen therapy is a treatment for confirmed hyperplasia without atypia, and inserting it before a histological diagnosis risks treating an unrecognised carcinoma (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines

options.text: Arrange endometrial sampling, proceeding to hysteroscopy if sampling is inadequate
options.rationale: Bleeding after the menopause with an endometrium above 4 mm requires histology, and outpatient sampling is the first line with hysteroscopy and directed biopsy when the sample is insufficient or bleeding persists (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

explanation.summary: Bleeding after the menopause carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma, and that risk alone justifies investigating every episode rather than the recurrent ones only. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first line test, and an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a woman not taking hormone therapy has a high negative predictive value that allows conservative management if bleeding does not recur. Above that threshold, or with persistent or recurrent bleeding whatever the thickness, histology is required. Outpatient sampling with a suction device is well tolerated and diagnoses most cancers, but it samples blindly, so an insufficient sample or a focal lesion on imaging leads to hysteroscopy with directed biopsy. Obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, late menopause, tamoxifen use and Lynch syndrome all raise the risk, and obesity operates through peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue. Most endometrial cancers present at an early stage precisely because they bleed early.
key_points: Every episode of bleeding after the menopause is investigated, not only recurrent episodes.
An endometrium of 4 mm or less without hormone therapy has a high negative predictive value.
Above 4 mm, or with persistent bleeding at any thickness, histology is required.
Blind sampling misses focal lesions, so hysteroscopy follows an inadequate sample or a focal finding.
Obesity, diabetes, nulliparity, tamoxifen and Lynch syndrome are the principal risk factors.
explanation.pearls: The 4 mm threshold applies only to women not taking hormone therapy: on sequential hormone therapy the endometrium is measured in the week after the progestogen phase, and on tamoxifen the ultrasound appearance is unreliable altogether so hysteroscopy is the investigation of choice.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines

subtopic_detail: Heavy bleeding on day twelve after a normal vaginal birth with an open cervical os and a tender uterus
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a woman who gave birth vaginally twelve days ago at term. Her lochia had almost stopped but this morning she soaked four maternity pads in two hours and passed two clots the size of a golf ball.

Her labour was spontaneous and the placenta was described at the time as appearing complete. She is breastfeeding, has a temperature of 38.2 degrees C and says her lower abdomen aches constantly and her discharge has an offensive smell. The uterus is palpable midway to the umbilicus and is tender, and the cervical os admits a fingertip. She is not dizzy at present and the bleeding has slowed to moderate. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L and her white cell count is 16.8 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable midway between symphysis and umbilicus and tender, offensive lochia, cervical os admits a fingertip, no vulval haematoma
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ergometrine and discharge her with advice to return if bleeding recurs
options.rationale: A uterotonic may slow the bleeding briefly but leaves the infection and any retained tissue untreated, and discharge before source control risks a return with sepsis. Ergometrine is also avoided where blood pressure is raised (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Take genital tract and blood cultures, start broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics and arrange pelvic ultrasound
options.rationale: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage with fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia is treated as endometritis, which frequently coexists with retained products, so antimicrobial therapy and imaging proceed together after cultures. Surgical evacuation is then decided on the ultrasound findings and the response to treatment (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Take her directly to theatre for immediate suction curettage of the uterine cavity without imaging
options.rationale: Curetting an infected soft postpartum uterus before antibiotics carries a substantial perforation and Asherman risk, and her bleeding is not torrential enough to demand immediate theatre. Emergency evacuation without imaging is reserved for haemodynamic instability (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin alone and review her again in general practice within the next two days
options.rationale: Narrow oral therapy does not cover the anaerobes and Gram negative organisms typical of postpartum endometritis, and her tachycardia with a raised inflammatory response warrants parenteral treatment. Oral therapy suits mild afebrile endometritis diagnosed early (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange transfusion of two units of packed red cells and repeat her full blood count in the morning
options.rationale: Transfusion treats a number rather than the cause and is not indicated at this haemoglobin in a woman who is not compromised, with oral or intravenous iron the appropriate replacement. It would be considered if bleeding continued with haemodynamic compromise (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is bleeding between 24 hours and twelve weeks after birth and is most often caused by endometritis, retained products of conception, or both together, with rarer causes including a uterine arteriovenous malformation and gestational trophoblastic disease. Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia point to infection, while an open cervical os and clot passage raise the probability of retained tissue. Ultrasound cannot reliably separate retained products from clot in the early puerperium, so findings are interpreted alongside the clinical picture rather than as a definitive test. Antibiotic therapy is started before any surgical evacuation because operating on an infected uterus increases perforation and adhesion risk. Persistent or heavy bleeding despite therapy is the trigger for evacuation, usually under ultrasound guidance.
key_points: Bleeding from 24 hours to twelve weeks postpartum is secondary postpartum haemorrhage
Endometritis and retained products commonly coexist and are treated together
Cultures precede antibiotics, and parenteral therapy is used when systemically unwell
Ultrasound findings in the puerperium are interpreted with caution because clot mimics retained tissue
Evacuation follows antibiotic cover unless bleeding is torrential
explanation.pearls: Send a high vaginal swab and blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose, and cover anaerobes explicitly, because Bacteroides and other anaerobic organisms are recovered in a large share of postpartum endometritis and are missed by amoxicillin alone.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant lump in a breastfeeding woman whose mastitis has not settled after two days of oral antibiotics
stem:
You are the doctor in a women's health clinic seeing a woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby. She was prescribed oral flucloxacillin two days ago for a red painful right breast and has taken every dose.

Her temperature has settled but the pain has become sharply localised and she now feels a lump that was not there yesterday. The upper outer quadrant contains a 4 cm tender area that is red and shiny, and it feels fluctuant with a smooth rounded edge that does not move with the skin. Milk expressed from that breast looks normal and the baby is feeding well and gaining weight. There is no cracked nipple, no axillary lymphadenopathy and no overlying skin necrosis. An ultrasound performed this morning shows a 38 by 30 mm collection with internal debris and no solid component.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuant tender 4 cm mass in the right upper outer quadrant with overlying erythema, no skin breakdown, no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Imaging: Breast ultrasound shows a 38 by 30 mm fluid collection with internal debris and no solid component

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange ultrasound guided needle aspiration of the collection and continue antibiotics and feeding
options.rationale: Needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance drains most lactational abscesses, can be repeated, and avoids the scarring and milk fistula associated with open surgery. Feeding or expressing from the affected breast continues because milk stasis perpetuates the infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Refer her for formal incision and drainage of the breast in theatre under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Open drainage is reserved for very large collections, overlying skin necrosis or abscesses that recur after repeated aspiration, and it produces more scarring and a longer interruption to feeding. Ultrasound guided aspiration is the first line drainage method (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Change the antibiotic to oral cefalexin and review her in the clinic again in three days time
options.rationale: An established collection will not resolve with any oral antibiotic because the drug cannot penetrate pus, so changing agents simply delays drainage. A change of antibiotic is appropriate for cellulitis that is failing therapy without a collection on imaging (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise her to stop feeding from the affected breast and suppress lactation with cabergoline
options.rationale: Stopping drainage of the breast worsens stasis and delays resolution, and abrupt suppression is not required for a treatable infection. Suppression is considered only when a woman has decided to wean for her own reasons (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Organise mammography with core biopsy of the lesion before undertaking any drainage procedure
options.rationale: Imaging has already shown a simple collection with no solid component in a clinically typical lactational abscess, so tissue sampling is not needed first. Biopsy becomes relevant if the mass persists after drainage or has solid areas, since inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis progresses to abscess in a small proportion of women, most often when treatment is delayed or when milk drainage from the affected segment is incomplete. The clinical shift is from diffuse hardness and fever to a discrete fluctuant mass, and ultrasound both confirms the collection and guides drainage. Aspiration with a wide bore needle, repeated every few days if required, achieves resolution in most cases while preserving breastfeeding. Antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus continue alongside drainage, and the aspirate is sent for culture because resistant organisms are increasingly seen. Persistent masses after adequate drainage must be investigated for malignancy, as inflammatory breast cancer can present during lactation.
key_points: A fluctuant mass appearing during treated mastitis signals abscess formation
Ultrasound guided aspiration is first line drainage and may be repeated
Antibiotics alone cannot clear an established collection
Continued feeding or expressing from the affected breast aids resolution
A residual mass after drainage requires imaging and biopsy to exclude malignancy
explanation.pearls: Send the aspirated pus for culture every time, because methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus is now recovered often enough in community lactational abscesses to change the antibiotic in a meaningful minority of women.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis and breast abscess
Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia at twenty eight weeks in a woman who cannot tolerate any oral iron preparation
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 31 year old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her routine bloods show a haemoglobin of 92 g/L with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L.

She has tried three different oral iron preparations since her booking visit, including alternate day dosing, and each produced severe nausea and constipation that she could not sustain beyond a fortnight. She is tired and breathless climbing stairs but has no chest pain or palpitations. She is vegetarian, has had no bleeding in this pregnancy, and her previous birth involved a postpartum haemorrhage of 900 mL. Her mean cell volume is 76 fL and her C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Her blood group is O positive with a negative antibody screen and there is no history of transfusion reaction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood group O positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a further oral iron preparation to be taken on alternate days with ascorbic acid
options.rationale: She has already failed three preparations including alternate day dosing, so a fourth trial predictably fails and wastes the weeks remaining before birth. Ascorbic acid modestly improves absorption but does nothing for the gastrointestinal intolerance that is the limiting problem (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion now and recheck her haemoglobin in about four weeks
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated for established iron deficiency anaemia with oral intolerance or failure, and is used from the second trimester onwards with a haemoglobin response over two to four weeks. Repleting stores before birth also lowers the transfusion risk that her previous postpartum haemorrhage makes relevant (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells to correct the anaemia in advance of her birth
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, and exposes her to alloimmunisation that could affect a future pregnancy. She has weeks available in which iron replacement can raise the haemoglobin instead (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Start vitamin B12 and folate supplementation and repeat the full blood examination in six weeks
options.rationale: Her low mean cell volume with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L identifies iron deficiency rather than a megaloblastic process, which would raise the cell volume instead. B12 assessment is worth adding in a long standing vegan diet but does not treat the deficiency present (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

options.text: Investigate for a haemoglobinopathy with electrophoresis before committing her to any iron therapy
options.rationale: A ferritin of 8 micrograms/L with a normal C reactive protein already establishes iron deficiency as the cause of the microcytosis, and iron studies must be interpreted before electrophoresis because deficiency itself distorts the haemoglobin A2 fraction. Screening is prompted by microcytosis with normal iron stores (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy and dietary intake rarely meets them, so iron deficiency is the commonest medical problem of the antenatal period and is associated with preterm birth, low birthweight and postpartum depression. Ferritin is the most useful single test but is an acute phase reactant, which is why a normal C reactive protein matters when interpreting a low value. Oral iron remains first line and alternate day dosing improves absorption by reducing hepcidin induction, but intolerance is common. Intravenous preparations replete stores in a single visit and are used in the second and third trimesters when oral therapy fails, is not tolerated, or when birth is too close for oral therapy to work. Adequate stores before birth reduce the likelihood of transfusion when postpartum haemorrhage occurs.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms/L indicates deficiency, and below 15 micrograms/L indicates absent stores
Intravenous iron is indicated for oral intolerance, oral failure, or late gestation presentation
Alternate day oral dosing improves fractional absorption by limiting hepcidin rise
Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, not for a number alone
Interpret haemoglobinopathy screening only after iron status is known
explanation.pearls: Expect a haemoglobin rise of about 20 g/L in two to four weeks after intravenous iron, and recheck ferritin no sooner than four weeks because the infused iron keeps the level artificially high before then.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Household exposure to chickenpox at sixteen weeks in a woman with negative varicella serology
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by a 29 year old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant. Her four year old nephew stayed at her house the night before last and developed a vesicular rash yesterday morning, which his own doctor has diagnosed as chickenpox.

She played with him for several hours on both days. She has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms today, and feels entirely well. She does not recall having chickenpox and was not vaccinated as a child. Her booking bloods, taken six weeks ago, include a varicella zoster immunoglobulin G that was reported as not detected. She has no immunosuppressive illness, takes no corticosteroids, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. It is currently 30 hours since her last contact with the child.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rash, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected, full blood examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give her the varicella vaccine today and arrange a second dose in four weeks as planned
options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated preparation and is contraindicated during pregnancy, so it cannot be used for post exposure protection here. Vaccination is offered instead in the postpartum period before discharge (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassure her that maternal antibody will protect the pregnancy and review her only if a rash appears
options.rationale: Her booking serology shows she has no protective antibody, which is precisely why she is at risk of severe varicella pneumonitis and of transmitting infection to the fetus. Reassurance without action would be appropriate only if immunoglobulin G had been detected (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Arrange zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and advise her to report any rash immediately
options.rationale: A seronegative pregnant woman with significant exposure should receive zoster immunoglobulin, ideally within 96 hours and up to ten days after contact, to attenuate maternal disease. Prompt reporting of a rash then allows oral aciclovir to be started within 24 hours of its onset (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral aciclovir immediately at treatment dose and continue it for the next seven days
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is started when a rash appears rather than at the point of exposure, since it is most effective within 24 hours of the first vesicles. Presumptive antiviral use is not the recommended post exposure strategy in a seronegative pregnant contact (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in pregnancy).

options.text: Organise amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing to assess the risk to the fetus
options.rationale: Invasive testing is not indicated in an exposed woman who has not developed infection, and it carries a procedure related loss risk. It is considered only after confirmed maternal varicella when detailed ultrasound raises concern about fetal involvement (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy is dangerous for both mother and fetus, with maternal pneumonitis carrying substantial mortality and first and early second trimester infection risking congenital varicella syndrome. Most Australian adults are immune, so the first step after an exposure is to establish serostatus, and a booking result showing no detectable immunoglobulin G answers that immediately. Seronegative women with significant exposure receive zoster immunoglobulin, which attenuates rather than prevents infection, and the window extends to ten days although earlier administration works better. If a rash develops, oral aciclovir started within 24 hours reduces the duration and severity of maternal illness. Infection between 28 weeks and delivery raises the separate problem of neonatal varicella, which requires immunoglobulin for the newborn.
key_points: Live vaccines including varicella are contraindicated in pregnancy
Zoster immunoglobulin is given to seronegative pregnant contacts, ideally within 96 hours and up to ten days
Aciclovir is for treatment once a rash appears, started within 24 hours of the first vesicles
Congenital varicella syndrome risk is highest with infection before 20 weeks and is around 1 to 2 per cent
Maternal infection from five days before to two days after birth requires immunoglobulin for the neonate
explanation.pearls: Offer varicella vaccination postpartum to any woman found seronegative at booking, giving the first dose before hospital discharge because the return rate for a deferred first dose is poor and breastfeeding is not a contraindication.

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis three months after birth in a breastfeeding woman with a painless gland
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman three months after the birth of her second child. She reports palpitations, sweating and irritability for the past three weeks and has lost 4 kg despite eating well.

She is fully breastfeeding. Her thyroid is not enlarged, not nodular and not tender, and she has no eye signs, no pretibial change and no thyroid bruit. She had a similar episode after her first birth that settled without treatment, though she then felt sluggish and cold for several months. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 34 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative and thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm per hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 per minute and regular, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, thyroid not palpable and non tender, no eye signs
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 34 pmol/L (10-20), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm per hour (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start carbimazole and titrate the dose against her thyroid function tests every four weeks
options.rationale: Thionamides block synthesis of new hormone and have no effect on hormone leaking from an inflamed gland, so they do not shorten this illness. They are the treatment when receptor antibodies are positive and the gland is overproducing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Prescribe propranolol for symptom control and recheck her thyroid function in four to six weeks
options.rationale: A painless destructive thyroiditis after birth with negative receptor antibodies is self limiting, so a beta blocker compatible with breastfeeding covers the symptomatic phase while the process runs its course. Repeat testing detects the hypothyroid phase that follows in a substantial proportion of women (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Refer her for radioactive iodine uptake scanning to establish the cause of her thyrotoxicosis
options.rationale: Radioisotope studies require interruption of breastfeeding and are not needed when negative receptor antibodies, a non tender gland and the postpartum timing already indicate a destructive process. Uptake scanning is reserved for cases where the distinction from Graves disease remains genuinely unclear and feeding has ceased (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Begin levothyroxine now in anticipation of the hypothyroid phase that typically develops later
options.rationale: Giving thyroid hormone during a thyrotoxic phase compounds the excess and worsens her symptoms, and not every woman progresses to a hypothyroid phase. Replacement is started when the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic or biochemically marked (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it over the following four weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for painful subacute thyroiditis where inflammation causes significant neck pain, and her gland is not tender with a normal sedimentation rate. Steroid exposure adds risk without changing the course of the painless postpartum form (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune destructive process affecting a few per cent of women in the year after birth, and it classically runs through a thyrotoxic phase at two to six months, a hypothyroid phase, and then recovery. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually positive and predict both recurrence in later pregnancies and long term hypothyroidism. The key clinical task is separating it from Graves disease, since the treatments differ entirely, and negative receptor antibodies with a non tender impalpable gland make destruction far more likely. Management is symptomatic with a beta blocker in the thyrotoxic phase and levothyroxine if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic. Around one in five affected women develop permanent hypothyroidism, so annual thyroid function testing is recommended thereafter.
key_points: Postpartum thyroiditis is destructive, so thionamides are ineffective
Negative receptor antibodies with a non tender gland distinguish it from Graves disease
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies predict recurrence and later permanent hypothyroidism
Propranolol is compatible with breastfeeding and covers the thyrotoxic phase
Radioisotope uptake studies require interruption of breastfeeding and are rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function annually after an episode, because roughly 20 per cent of women develop permanent hypothyroidism within a few years and the risk is highest in those with strongly positive peroxidase antibodies.

subtopic_detail: Urinary leakage with coughing and exercise in a parous woman with a normal post void residual
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes or plays netball. It began after her third vaginal birth and has worsened over two years to the point where she wears a pad on training days.

She empties her bladder about six times a day and once at night, and does not leak on the way to the toilet or when she hears running water. She has no dysuria, no haematuria and no pelvic pain. Examination shows a well oestrogenised vagina, no prolapse beyond the hymen, and leakage of urine from the urethra when she coughs with a comfortably full bladder. Her bladder scan afterwards shows a post void residual of 20 mL. Urine dipstick is negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, and her body mass index is 31 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Leakage from the urethra on coughing with a full bladder, no prolapse beyond the hymen, well oestrogenised vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 20 mL, urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, bladder diary shows six voids per day and one at night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic bladder relaxant and review her symptom diary in three months
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic drugs treat detrusor overactivity, which produces urgency and leakage on the way to the toilet rather than leakage synchronous with a cough. Her diary and provocation findings do not support that mechanism (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Refer her for urodynamic studies before any conservative treatment is offered to her
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear symptoms, prior failed surgery, or before an operation is planned, and it does not change the initial conservative plan. Her history and demonstrated leakage on coughing are sufficient for a working diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Arrange supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for at least three months
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for a minimum of three months is the first line treatment for stress incontinence and cures or improves symptoms in most women, with supervision producing substantially better results than a handout. Weight reduction and modification of fluid habits are addressed alongside it (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance

options.text: Refer her to a gynaecologist for a midurethral sling procedure to correct the urethral support
options.rationale: Surgery is considered only after an adequate trial of supervised conservative therapy has failed, and it requires detailed counselling about mesh related risks. Proceeding directly to operation bypasses a treatment that resolves symptoms for many women (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence in women).

options.text: Commence vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week and reassess her leakage after two months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen helps urogenital atrophy in the postmenopausal woman, and her epithelium is well oestrogenised with regular cycles. It has little effect on the sphincteric mechanism responsible for leakage on effort (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance).
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence in women is separated clinically into stress, urgency and mixed types, and this distinction determines the entire management pathway. Leakage that occurs simultaneously with a rise in intra abdominal pressure, without urgency and with a normal post void residual, indicates a sphincteric or support problem rather than detrusor overactivity. A bladder diary, urinalysis to exclude infection, and a post void residual are the basic assessment, and demonstrating leakage on coughing supports the diagnosis without urodynamics. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first line and is more effective than unsupervised exercises, with weight loss adding benefit in women with a raised body mass index. Surgery and continence pessaries are options after conservative therapy fails, and mesh procedures require explicit counselling in Australia.
key_points: Leakage synchronous with coughing and no urgency indicates stress incontinence
Basic assessment is a bladder diary, urinalysis and post void residual
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for three months or more is first line
Urodynamics is indicated for mixed or unclear pictures, or before planned surgery
Antimuscarinic drugs and vaginal oestrogen address different mechanisms and will not help here
explanation.pearls: Weight loss of 5 to 10 per cent reduces stress incontinence episodes by roughly half in women with a raised body mass index, which makes it worth negotiating alongside the physiotherapy referral rather than after it.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidance

subtopic_detail: Actinomyces like organisms reported on cytology in an asymptomatic copper intrauterine device user
stem:
You are the general practitioner phoning a 34 year old woman with the results of her cervical screening test. She has had a copper intrauterine device in place for four years and intends to keep it until it expires.

Her test detected oncogenic human papillomavirus of a type other than 16 or 18, and the reflex liquid based cytology reported no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy but noted actinomyces like organisms. She has no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge, and her periods are regular and unchanged in pattern. She has one regular partner and has never had pelvic infection. On examination her abdomen is soft and non tender, the device threads are visible at the cervix, and there is no cervical excitation or adnexal tenderness.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass or tenderness, device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus detected, not type 16 or 18; liquid based cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion with actinomyces like organisms noted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Remove the device now and send it for culture, then reinsert a new one after two weeks
options.rationale: Removal in an asymptomatic woman leaves her without contraception and the organism is a normal genital tract commensal, so culture of the device would not change management. Removal is indicated when pelvic infection is present or strongly suspected (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception).

options.text: Treat her with a two week course of oral amoxicillin and repeat her cytology afterwards
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not eradicate colonisation and repeat cytology is not the follow up test in the renewed screening program. Prolonged penicillin therapy is reserved for proven invasive actinomycosis, which presents with a pelvic mass and systemic illness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange pelvic ultrasound and refer her to gynaecology for assessment of possible pelvic infection
options.rationale: Imaging and referral are driven by symptoms or signs such as pelvic pain, fever or an adnexal mass, none of which she has. Investigating an incidental cytological finding generates anxiety and further tests without benefit (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception).

options.text: Leave the device in place without antibiotics and repeat the screening test in twelve months
options.rationale: Actinomyces like organisms are commonly seen with any intrauterine device and require no action in an asymptomatic woman, while the intermediate risk human papillomavirus result is managed by repeat testing in twelve months. She is counselled to return promptly if pelvic pain, fever or abnormal discharge develops (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen detected abnormalities

options.text: Refer her for immediate colposcopy because oncogenic human papillomavirus has been detected
options.rationale: Direct referral applies to type 16 or 18 detection or to a high grade cytological prediction, neither of which is present here. Other oncogenic types with a negative cytology are followed by a repeat test in twelve months (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen detected abnormalities).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen detected abnormalities

explanation.summary: Actinomyces species are commensals of the lower genital tract and are reported more often on cytology when a foreign body such as an intrauterine device is present, but colonisation is not infection. Invasive pelvic actinomycosis is rare, presents with pain, fever, weight loss and a mass, and is treated with prolonged penicillin plus device removal. In the asymptomatic woman the correct response is to explain the finding, keep the device and give clear return advice. The renewed Australian cervical screening program uses primary human papillomavirus testing, with direct colposcopy for types 16 or 18 and repeat testing at twelve months for other oncogenic types with negative or low grade cytology. Combining both results in a single plan avoids the common error of acting on the incidental cytological comment while missing the screening pathway.
key_points: Actinomyces like organisms on cytology in an asymptomatic device user need no treatment
Device removal and prolonged penicillin apply only to invasive pelvic actinomycosis
Human papillomavirus 16 or 18 detection prompts direct colposcopy referral
Other oncogenic types with negative cytology are repeated at twelve months
Give explicit return advice for pelvic pain, fever or abnormal discharge
explanation.pearls: Pelvic actinomycosis characteristically produces a firm mass that crosses tissue planes and discharges sulfur granules, and it is treated with intravenous benzylpenicillin followed by many months of oral therapy rather than a standard two week course.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen detected abnormalities

subtopic_detail: Discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at twenty weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy, which was confirmed at 11 weeks as monochorionic and diamniotic. She has noticed her abdomen enlarging quickly over the past fortnight and feels tight and breathless when lying flat.

Today's ultrasound shows one sac with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.4 cm and a normally filled fetal bladder, and the other sac with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm where the fetus is held against the uterine wall by its membrane and the bladder cannot be seen over 40 minutes of scanning. Umbilical artery Doppler indices are within normal limits in both fetuses, ductus venosus waveforms show forward flow throughout, and neither fetus is hydropic. Estimated fetal weights differ by 14 per cent. Her cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Imaging: Monochorionic diamniotic twins, recipient sac deepest vertical pocket 9.4 cm with visible bladder, donor sac deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with non visible bladder, normal umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers, no hydrops, estimated fetal weight discordance 14 per cent, cervical length 32 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue fortnightly ultrasound surveillance in your unit and intervene only if Dopplers deteriorate
options.rationale: Waiting for Doppler abnormality allows progression to the stage where one or both fetuses die or sustain neurological injury, and the disease can advance within days. Surveillance alone is the strategy for isolated growth discordance without a fluid discrepancy (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform serial amnioreduction from the larger sac to relieve her symptoms and prolong the pregnancy
options.rationale: Amnioreduction treats the consequence of the shunt rather than the shunt itself and gives inferior survival and neurological outcomes compared with definitive treatment. It remains an option only where the definitive procedure is unavailable or technically impossible (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Give a course of antenatal corticosteroids and arrange delivery by caesarean section this week
options.rationale: Birth at 20 weeks is pre viable, so delivery converts a treatable condition into the certain loss of both fetuses. Steroids and planned birth become relevant only in the periviable range and beyond (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Offer selective reduction of the smaller fetus by cord occlusion to protect the co twin from harm
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for advanced disease with an unsalvageable fetus, severe early growth restriction, or discordant anomaly, and it sacrifices a fetus who may survive intact after definitive treatment. Both fetuses here have normal Dopplers and no hydrops (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Refer her urgently to a fetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser of the placental anastomoses
options.rationale: A deepest pocket above 8 cm in one sac with under 2 cm in the other establishes twin to twin transfusion, and the absent donor bladder makes this at least stage II disease, for which laser ablation of the connecting vessels is the treatment of choice between 16 and 26 weeks. Laser targets the underlying vascular communication and gives better survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes than any drainage based approach (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
New England Journal of Medicine: Eurofoetus trial of endoscopic laser surgery

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion complicates around one in ten monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies and arises from unbalanced flow across placental vascular anastomoses, producing hypovolaemia and oliguria in the donor and volume overload with polyuria in the recipient. Australian practice is fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in monochorionic pregnancies precisely to detect it before decompensation. Diagnosis rests on the fluid criteria of a deepest vertical pocket over 8 cm in one sac and under 2 cm in the other, not on growth discordance, which is a separate condition. The Quintero system then stages severity by bladder visibility, Doppler abnormality, hydrops and fetal death. Fetoscopic laser between 16 and 26 weeks is the definitive treatment and doubled survival compared with amnioreduction in the trial that established it.
key_points: Diagnosis requires a deepest vertical pocket over 8 cm in one sac and under 2 cm in the other
Growth discordance alone is a different problem and does not define this condition
A non visible donor bladder indicates stage II disease or higher
Fetoscopic laser between 16 and 26 weeks is the definitive treatment
Amnioreduction is a fallback with inferior survival and neurological outcomes
explanation.pearls: Monochorionic pregnancies need ultrasound every two weeks from 16 weeks, since the interval between a normal scan and stage III disease can be under a fortnight and maternal symptoms appear only once the recipient sac is already grossly overfilled.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
New England Journal of Medicine: Eurofoetus trial of endoscopic laser surgery

subtopic_detail: Abdominal distension and reduced urine output nine days after oocyte retrieval and fresh embryo transfer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department assessing a 32 year old woman who had oocyte retrieval eleven days ago and a fresh embryo transfer nine days ago. Thirty two oocytes were collected.

Over the past three days her abdomen has swollen so that none of her clothes fit, she has gained 4 kg, and she now feels short of breath when she lies down. She has vomited twice today and has passed only a small amount of dark urine since last night. Her abdomen is distended and tense with shifting dullness, and there is no guarding or rebound. Her calves are soft and non tender and there is no chest pain. Her serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin is 340 IU/L, and bedside ultrasound shows large ovaries with ascites extending above the umbilicus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.49 (0.33-0.45), white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 108 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), beta human chorionic gonadotropin 340 IU/L
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged ovaries bilaterally with ascites extending above the umbilicus, no pleural effusion seen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide to shift the fluid and monitor her urine output on the ward
options.rationale: The intravascular compartment is depleted despite the ascites, so a loop diuretic worsens haemoconcentration and thrombotic risk. Diuretics are considered only after intravascular volume has been restored and oliguria persists with rising pressures (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome).

options.text: Discharge her with oral rehydration advice and arrange review in the fertility clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Haemoconcentration, hyponatraemia, oliguria and tense ascites define severe disease requiring inpatient care, and an early pregnancy will drive it further for weeks. Outpatient management with daily weight and abdominal girth suits mild to moderate cases only (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome).

options.text: Start a dopamine agonist to reduce vascular permeability and review her again in the morning
options.rationale: Cabergoline reduces the incidence of the syndrome when given around the trigger in high risk cycles but does not treat established severe disease. Prevention and treatment are separate decisions in this condition (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome).

options.text: Admit her for intravenous crystalloid, thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin and fluid balance
options.rationale: Severe disease is managed with volume replacement guided by haematocrit and urine output, strict fluid balance, and heparin prophylaxis because a haematocrit of 0.49 in a newly pregnant woman carries a high thrombotic risk that persists for weeks. Paracentesis is added if the ascites is tense enough to compromise breathing or renal perfusion after volume replacement (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome).
