options.text: Arrange laparoscopy to exclude ovarian torsion and to drain the ascitic fluid under direct vision
options.rationale: There is no localised pain, guarding or unilateral tenderness to suggest torsion, and surgery on grossly enlarged fragile ovaries risks haemorrhage. Drainage when needed is performed percutaneously under ultrasound guidance rather than operatively (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome).

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome follows gonadotropin stimulation and is mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor, which increases capillary permeability so that fluid moves from the intravascular space into the peritoneal and pleural cavities. The paradox that drives management is intravascular depletion with visible fluid overload, meaning the patient needs volume replacement while looking oedematous. Early onset disease relates to the trigger injection, while late onset disease is driven by rising human chorionic gonadotropin from an implanting pregnancy and is more severe and more prolonged. Thrombosis, including unusual sites such as the internal jugular and subclavian veins, is the most feared complication and prophylactic heparin is standard in severe disease. High oocyte yield, polycystic ovary syndrome and a high antral follicle count identify women in whom prevention strategies such as an agonist trigger, freeze all cycles and cabergoline are used.
key_points: The syndrome causes intravascular depletion despite third space fluid accumulation
Haematocrit, urine output and sodium guide severity and the response to fluids
Late onset disease driven by a new pregnancy is more severe and lasts longer
Thromboprophylaxis is standard in severe disease because thrombosis risk is high and prolonged
Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and are avoided before volume repletion
explanation.pearls: Thromboprophylaxis in severe disease continues for several weeks and is extended to the end of the first trimester when pregnancy has occurred, because the thrombotic risk outlasts the ascites by a considerable margin.

subtopic_detail: Ruptured membranes at thirty four weeks in a woman known to carry group B streptococcus
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite to see a 30 year old woman at 34 weeks and two days in her second pregnancy. She felt a gush of clear fluid four hours ago and continues to leak.

Speculum examination confirms a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with no cord and a closed cervix. A vaginal and rectal swab taken at 33 weeks for a previous episode of reduced fetal movements grew group B streptococcus. She has no uterine tenderness, no offensive discharge and no contractions. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 140 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Her white cell count is 9.8 x10^9/L and her C reactive protein is 4 mg/L. The baby is cephalic with an estimated fetal weight on the fiftieth centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), vaginal and rectal swab positive for group B streptococcus at 33 weeks
data_table.Imaging: Cephalic presentation, estimated fetal weight on the fiftieth centile, normal liquor volume around the fetus before rupture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manage her expectantly until 37 weeks with weekly swabs and twice weekly cardiotocography
options.rationale: Expectant management to 37 weeks is a reasonable option after 34 weeks in women who are not colonised, but known group B streptococcus carriage with ruptured membranes raises the risk of early onset neonatal sepsis with every additional day. Colonisation is the feature that tips this decision (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Start oral erythromycin for ten days and review the plan for birth at 36 weeks of gestation
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs latency in early preterm rupture before 34 weeks and is not the agent used for intrapartum prophylaxis against this organism. Using it here both selects the wrong drug and defers birth in a colonised woman (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids and tocolysis, then reassess her again in 48 hours on the ward
options.rationale: Tocolysis has no role once membranes have ruptured and she is not contracting, and it delays birth without neonatal benefit. Corticosteroids may still be given at this gestation but are not a reason to defer the decision about timing (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Arrange caesarean section today because ruptured membranes at this gestation contraindicate labour
options.rationale: Ruptured membranes with a cephalic presentation and a reassuring trace is not an indication for operative birth, and caesarean adds maternal morbidity without reducing neonatal sepsis. Operative birth is reserved for the usual obstetric indications (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and proceed to induction of labour without further delay
options.rationale: At 34 weeks or beyond with confirmed group B streptococcus colonisation and ruptured membranes, expediting birth with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis gives the lowest combined risk of neonatal sepsis and prematurity related morbidity. Prophylaxis should run for at least four hours before birth where the clinical situation allows (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus and prevention of early onset neonatal disease).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus and prevention of early onset neonatal disease
RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes before 34 weeks is usually managed expectantly with erythromycin, corticosteroids and surveillance for chorioamnionitis, because the risks of prematurity outweigh those of infection. From 34 weeks the balance narrows and Australian practice individualises the decision, with the large Australian led trial of expectant management showing less neonatal respiratory morbidity but more maternal and neonatal infection when birth was deferred. Known group B streptococcus colonisation shifts that balance decisively toward birth, since the organism is the leading cause of early onset neonatal sepsis and the protective effect of intrapartum antibiotics depends on birth occurring while they are running. Chorioamnionitis at any gestation mandates immediate birth with broad spectrum antibiotics regardless of the colonisation status. Surveillance for infection uses maternal observations, fetal heart rate and symptoms rather than serial inflammatory markers, which perform poorly.
key_points: Before 34 weeks, expectant management with erythromycin and corticosteroids is standard
From 34 weeks the decision is individualised, weighing infection against respiratory morbidity
Confirmed group B streptococcus colonisation with ruptured membranes favours expediting birth
Intrapartum benzylpenicillin ideally runs for at least four hours before birth
Chorioamnionitis mandates immediate birth with broad spectrum antibiotics at any gestation
explanation.pearls: Intrapartum benzylpenicillin reduces early onset neonatal group B streptococcal disease by around 80 per cent when the first dose is given at least four hours before birth, which is why the antibiotic is started before the induction rather than once labour is established.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus and prevention of early onset neonatal disease

subtopic_detail: Collapse immediately after delivery of the placenta with a fundus that cannot be palpated abdominally
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite three minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at term. The midwife applied controlled cord traction and the placenta delivered, and the woman immediately became grey and clammy and says she feels a crushing pressure low in her pelvis.

Blood loss so far is estimated at 1200 mL and continues. On abdominal palpation you cannot feel a fundus at all, and there is a cup shaped depression where it should be. On vaginal examination a firm rounded mass fills the vagina and the placenta has separated from it completely. Two large bore cannulas are in place and crystalloid is running. Her pulse is 46 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 74/40 mmHg, which the midwife notes is out of proportion to the volume lost so far.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 46 per minute, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on 6 L per minute by mask, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No palpable uterine fundus abdominally with a cup shaped depression, firm rounded mass filling the vagina, placenta completely separated, ongoing bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing, group and hold sent, massive haemorrhage protocol activated

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Replace the uterus manually through the cervix straight away while resuscitation continues
options.rationale: Immediate manual replacement is the priority because the cervical ring contracts within minutes and makes reduction progressively harder, and restoring the uterus relieves the vagal stimulation causing her bradycardia and hypotension. Uterotonic drugs are deliberately withheld until the uterus is back in place because a contracted uterus cannot be replaced (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Give intramuscular ergometrine and start an oxytocin infusion to control the ongoing bleeding
options.rationale: Uterotonics tighten the cervical ring around the inverted fundus and can make replacement impossible without laparotomy. They are given immediately after successful replacement to keep the uterus in position (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Apply bimanual uterine compression and continue it until the anaesthetic team can attend her
options.rationale: Compression is the holding measure for atony with a correctly positioned uterus and does nothing when the fundus has passed through the cervix. Applying it delays the manoeuvre that actually corrects the problem (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid and transfuse two units of red cells before examining her further
options.rationale: Both measures belong in the resuscitation running alongside, but neither addresses the anatomical cause and delay makes replacement harder every minute. Tranexamic acid is given within three hours of a postpartum haemorrhage as an adjunct, not as the definitive step (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Transfer her to theatre for laparotomy so the uterus can be repositioned from within the abdomen
options.rationale: Abdominal approaches such as the Huntington or Haultain procedures are used only after vaginal replacement, including hydrostatic reduction under anaesthesia, has failed. Going straight to laparotomy wastes the window in which simple manual reduction succeeds (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is rare but immediately life threatening, and it is recognised by the combination of a fundus that cannot be palpated, a mass in the vagina and shock that appears disproportionate to the measured blood loss. The bradycardia is vagally mediated by traction on the peritoneum and infundibulopelvic ligaments, distinguishing this from the tachycardia of pure hypovolaemia. Prompt manual replacement using the Johnson manoeuvre, pushing the fundus back through the cervix with the palm while lifting toward the umbilicus, succeeds in most cases if done within minutes. Uterotonics are withheld until the uterus is replaced and then given immediately to prevent recurrence. If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic reduction with warmed fluid under anaesthesia, with or without a tocolytic to relax the cervical ring, precedes any surgical approach.
key_points: Absent fundus with a vaginal mass and disproportionate shock defines uterine inversion
Bradycardia rather than tachycardia reflects the vagal mechanism
Replace first and give uterotonics second, since a contracted uterus cannot be reduced
Hydrostatic reduction under anaesthesia is the next step if manual replacement fails
Laparotomy is reserved for failure of vaginal approaches
explanation.pearls: Replace the part of the fundus that inverted last before the part that inverted first, pressing on the portion nearest the cervical ring, because reducing the centre first simply thickens the ring and blocks the manoeuvre.

subtopic_detail: Scant periods with cyclical pain six months after surgical evacuation for retained products of conception
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who gave birth fourteen months ago. She had a 1500 mL postpartum haemorrhage and underwent suction evacuation of retained products at day nine, which was repeated a fortnight later for continued bleeding.

Her periods returned six months ago as a single day of brown staining and have since become one or two hours of light spotting each cycle. Every month, two days before the spotting, she gets deep central pelvic cramping that lasts about 36 hours and settles when the spotting starts. She stopped breastfeeding four months ago, has not resumed contraception and would like another pregnancy. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, oestradiol, prolactin and thyroid stimulating hormone are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, normal vulva and vagina, cervix appears normal, uterus anteverted, normal size, non tender
data_table.Investigations: Beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (3-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 5.1 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 320 pmol/L (100-400 follicular), prolactin 240 mIU/L (100-500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that lactational suppression explains the pattern and review her again in six months
options.rationale: She stopped breastfeeding four months ago and her gonadotropins and oestradiol show normal ovarian cycling, so suppression of the axis is excluded. Further waiting delays treatment while adhesions mature and become harder to divide (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill for three months to establish a regular bleeding pattern
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy cannot restore an endometrium that has been replaced by fibrous adhesions, and it also blocks the pregnancy she is seeking. Cyclical hormones treat anovulatory bleeding disturbance, which her normal hormone profile argues against (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Perform a progestogen withdrawal test and diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency if she does not bleed
options.rationale: A withdrawal test cannot distinguish an unresponsive endometrium from an outflow obstruction, and her normal follicle stimulating hormone with a normal oestradiol already excludes ovarian insufficiency. The near pair to keep separate here is a hormonal cause versus a structural one (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

options.text: Refer her for hysteroscopy so the cavity can be inspected and any adhesions divided at the same time
options.rationale: Repeated instrumentation of a puerperal uterus is the classic cause of intrauterine adhesions, and normal ovarian hormones with cyclical pain preceding scant flow indicate a normally cycling endometrium meeting an obstructed cavity. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the treatment, allowing adhesiolysis under direct vision (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).
source_refs: Human Reproduction Update: Intrauterine adhesions after pregnancy related curettage

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to characterise the uterus before any intervention
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to define congenital uterine anomalies rather than to detect intrauterine adhesions, which it images poorly. Saline infusion sonohysterography is the non invasive alternative when hysteroscopy must be deferred (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management).

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea or markedly reduced flow after uterine instrumentation, particularly curettage of a recently pregnant uterus, should raise intrauterine adhesions before any endocrine cause is entertained. The puerperal endometrium is thin and vulnerable, so evacuation after postpartum haemorrhage or for retained products carries the highest risk, and a repeat procedure multiplies it. The diagnostic logic is that normal gonadotropins and oestradiol with cyclical symptoms indicate ovulation is occurring, placing the lesion in the outflow tract. Cyclical pain reflects trapped menstrual blood behind partial obstruction. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis restores menses in most women and improves subsequent fertility, though adhesions recur in a significant minority and postoperative strategies to keep the cavity apart are used.
key_points: Instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the dominant risk factor for intrauterine adhesions
Normal gonadotropins and oestradiol place the problem in the outflow tract, not the ovary
Cyclical pain preceding scant flow suggests obstructed menstrual outflow
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the definitive treatment
Magnetic resonance imaging is for congenital anomalies and images adhesions poorly
explanation.pearls: Delaying any repeat evacuation until at least a few weeks postpartum, and using ultrasound guidance when it is unavoidable, is the main preventive measure, since adhesion risk is highest when the endometrium is curetted between two and four weeks after birth.

sources.label: Human Reproduction Update: Intrauterine adhesions after pregnancy related curettage

subtopic_detail: Markedly increased nuchal translucency at twelve weeks with a structurally normal appearing fetus
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 38 year old woman who is 12 weeks and four days into her first pregnancy. She had a combined first trimester screening test three days ago.

The nuchal translucency measured 4.6 mm with a crown rump length of 63 mm, and the fetus appeared structurally normal with a visible nasal bone and normal ductus venosus flow. Her biochemistry gave a combined risk of 1 in 15 for trisomy 21. She and her partner say they want as much information as possible as early as possible, and would consider termination for a serious abnormality. She has no family history of genetic disease and her booking bloods, including her blood group, were unremarkable. She is well and the pregnancy is a spontaneous conception.

data_table.Imaging: Nuchal translucency 4.6 mm at a crown rump length of 63 mm, nasal bone present, normal ductus venosus a wave, no structural abnormality visible, single live fetus
data_table.Investigations: Combined first trimester screening risk 1 in 15 for trisomy 21, blood group A positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about further testing?

options.text: Arrange non invasive prenatal testing of cell free DNA and proceed further only if it is high risk
options.rationale: Cell free DNA screening interrogates a small number of chromosomes and would miss the copy number variants, rare aneuploidies and single gene disorders that a translucency of this size is associated with. It is the better choice when the translucency is normal and the risk comes from age or biochemistry alone (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Repeat the nuchal translucency measurement in two weeks and decide on testing from that result
options.rationale: The measurement is only valid between a crown rump length of 45 and 84 mm, so it cannot meaningfully be repeated later, and translucency often resolves while the underlying abnormality remains. Waiting also removes the option of a first trimester diagnostic procedure (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Defer all further testing until the detailed morphology scan at twenty weeks demonstrates the anatomy
options.rationale: A normal morphology scan reduces but does not exclude a genetic diagnosis, and deferring removes the earlier and safer testing window the couple have said they want. Anatomy assessment complements genetic testing rather than replacing it (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Book amniocentesis at fifteen weeks as the safest way to obtain a definitive genetic result for her
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is a legitimate diagnostic route with a comparable loss rate in experienced hands, but it delays a definitive answer by nearly three weeks in a couple who have asked for the earliest possible information. It becomes the preferred option when the presentation is later or when placental mosaicism would confuse the result (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

options.text: Offer chorionic villus sampling now with chromosomal microarray testing of the sample obtained
options.rationale: A translucency of 3.5 mm or more carries a wide range of causes beyond the common trisomies, including copy number variants and structural cardiac disease, so a diagnostic sample analysed by microarray is the test that answers the question. Sampling in the first trimester delivers the result in the window the couple have identified as important to them (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Prenatal diagnosis policy

explanation.summary: Nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more is a marker of a broad group of conditions rather than of trisomy 21 alone, and roughly a third of affected fetuses have a chromosomal abnormality while many of the remainder have structural heart disease, skeletal dysplasia, a genetic syndrome or a copy number variant. This is the reason a diagnostic test with chromosomal microarray outperforms screening based on cell free DNA in this setting, since screening reports only on the chromosomes it targets. Chorionic villus sampling is available from 11 weeks and amniocentesis from 15 weeks, and both carry a procedure related loss rate of well under one per cent in experienced units. Even after normal genetic results, a fetus with increased translucency needs a detailed cardiac assessment because the association with congenital heart disease persists. Counselling should set out what each test can and cannot exclude before a choice is made.
key_points: Increased nuchal translucency is a marker for a broad range of genetic and structural conditions
Cell free DNA screening reports only on targeted chromosomes and misses copy number variants
Chromosomal microarray on a diagnostic sample is the higher yield test in this situation
Chorionic villus sampling from 11 weeks gives an earlier answer than amniocentesis from 15 weeks
Fetal echocardiography is indicated even when genetic testing returns normal
explanation.pearls: A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more justifies a fetal echocardiogram at around 20 weeks regardless of the genetic result, because congenital heart disease is found in roughly 3 to 5 per cent of these pregnancies with normal chromosomes.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal abnormalities

subtopic_detail: Itch of the palms and soles without a rash at 34 weeks with a raised serum bile acid level
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 34 weeks and two days. For the past twelve days she has had itching that is worst in the evening and overnight, mainly on her palms and the soles of her feet, and she has been scratching until she bleeds.

Her skin shows excoriation marks over her forearms and shins but no primary rash, and there are no lesions in the abdominal striae. Her blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and her urine dipstick shows no protein. Her serum bile acids taken non fasting are 42 micromol/L with an alanine aminotransferase of 96 U/L, and her full blood count, coagulation profile and hepatitis and viral serology are all within normal limits. A liver ultrasound shows no gallstones and normal ducts. The foetus is growing along the 40th centile with a normal cardiotocograph.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142 per minute
data_table.Investigations: Serum bile acids 42 micromol/L (less than 19), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), prothrombin time within normal limits, viral hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound with no gallstones and normal intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the remainder of her pregnancy?

options.text: Repeat bile acid levels weekly and plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks gestation
options.rationale: The excess perinatal risk in this condition tracks with the peak bile acid concentration, and levels below 100 micromol/L carry a stillbirth rate close to the background population rate, so birth is planned at 38 to 39 weeks rather than earlier. Serial levels matter because a rise into the severe range shifts that plan forward (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Arrange birth by caesarean section within 48 hours given the stillbirth risk
options.rationale: Immediate birth at 34 weeks trades a very small excess stillbirth risk at this bile acid level for the certain respiratory and neurodevelopmental costs of late preterm delivery, and the mode of birth is not itself altered by the diagnosis. Urgent birth belongs to levels of 100 micromol/L or more with other complicating features (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Start weekly cardiotocography and continue the pregnancy to 41 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Cardiotocography and ultrasound surveillance do not predict the sudden fetal demise associated with this condition, which is thought to be an arrhythmic event rather than a progressive hypoxic one, so normal traces provide false reassurance. Expectant management to 41 weeks also abandons the timing benefit that drives the whole plan (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Give betamethasone now and plan induction of labour at 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Birth at 36 weeks is reserved for bile acids of 100 micromol/L or above, or for lesser elevations complicated by intractable itch, deranged coagulation or a coexisting problem such as pre-eclampsia. Neither the level of 42 micromol/L nor the normal coagulation profile here meets that threshold (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Treat with topical emollients alone and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Emollients and antihistamines address the symptom but a four week interval abandons the surveillance that determines timing of birth, and bile acids can climb into the severe range within days. Symptom relief is part of the plan, not a substitute for it (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy).
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Itch without a primary rash in the second half of pregnancy, worst on palms and soles and at night, should prompt measurement of serum bile acids and liver transaminases. The diagnosis is important because it is one of the few pregnancy conditions where the timing of birth is chosen on a laboratory number, and the 2021 individual participant data meta analysis reframed practice by showing stillbirth risk rises materially only once peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but the PITCHES randomised trial found no reduction in adverse perinatal outcomes, so it is offered for symptom control rather than to change the timing plan. Vitamin K is considered when the prothrombin time is prolonged or steatorrhoea is present. Itch and biochemistry resolve within days to weeks after birth, and persistence beyond six weeks warrants hepatology referral.
key_points: Itch of the palms and soles without a primary rash is the classic presentation
Peak bile acids below 100 micromol/L carry near background stillbirth risk
Birth is planned at 38 to 39 weeks for mild disease and 35 to 36 weeks at 100 micromol/L or above
Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden demise associated with this condition
Ursodeoxycholic acid helps the itch but does not improve perinatal outcomes
explanation.pearls: Serum bile acids need not be fasting for diagnosis, but a non fasting sample can run up to about 30 per cent higher than a fasting one, so a borderline non fasting result near 19 micromol/L is worth repeating fasting before committing a woman to a changed birth plan.

subtopic_detail: Six months of monthly abdominal pain and now urinary retention in a fourteen year old who has never bled, with normal breast and pubic hair development
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a fourteen year old girl with twelve hours of severe lower abdominal pain and an inability to pass urine since last night.

Her mother says she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting three or four days at about the same time each month for the past six months, each episode a little worse than the last, and that she has been sent home from school with it twice. She has never had a menstrual period. Her breast development and pubic hair are those of a girl in the later stages of puberty and she had a growth spurt two years ago. She is not sexually active and her urine pregnancy test is negative. On abdominal examination there is a smooth tender mass arising from the pelvis and reaching midway to the umbilicus, and the bladder is palpable above it. On inspection of the external genitalia there is a smooth bluish membrane bulging outward at the vaginal opening, which becomes tenser when she coughs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development, smooth tender suprapubic mass reaching midway to the umbilicus with a separately palpable distended bladder, bluish membrane bulging at the vaginal opening that tenses on coughing
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, full blood count and C reactive protein within normal limits, bladder scan showing 620 mL of retained urine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incise the membrane in the emergency department under local anaesthetic
options.rationale: A limited incision under local anaesthetic in an awake adolescent risks incomplete drainage, re closure of the opening and an examination that cannot properly exclude a more complex obstructive anomaly. It also fails the standards of consent and dignity that apply to genital surgery in a young person (Source: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract

options.text: Request a karyotype and hormone profile before any surgical intervention
options.rationale: Endocrine and chromosomal investigation is directed at primary amenorrhoea with absent or incomplete secondary sexual characteristics, and this girl has completed most of puberty with cyclical pain, which indicates a functioning axis and an outflow obstruction. Her acute retention also cannot wait for laboratory results (Source: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract

options.text: Refer for urgent hymenotomy in theatre under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea, normal secondary sexual characteristics, a pelvic mass and a bulging bluish membrane is obstructed menstrual outflow, and surgical incision of the membrane under anaesthesia drains the accumulated blood and relieves the retention. It is done in theatre so the opening can be fashioned to stay patent and the vagina and cervix inspected to exclude a more complex anomaly (Source: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract

options.text: Arrange an MRI of the pelvis before deciding on any surgical treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when the anatomy is uncertain, such as a suspected transverse vaginal septum, vaginal agenesis or an obstructed hemivagina, but a visible bulging membrane at the introitus with a distended vagina above it makes the diagnosis at the bedside. Delaying for imaging leaves her in retention (Source: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress further bleeding
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression stops further accumulation but leaves the existing collection undrained and the retention unrelieved, and it defers rather than treats the obstruction. It has a role only as a temporary measure while definitive surgery is arranged in a complex anomaly (Source: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and cyclical pain points to an outflow tract obstruction rather than an endocrine cause, because the presence of breast development and a growth spurt demonstrates a functioning hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis. An imperforate hymen is the commonest such obstruction, occurring in roughly one in a thousand to two thousand girls, and menstrual blood accumulates in the vagina and then the uterus over months to years. Presentation is with cyclical pain, a lower abdominal mass and often urinary retention or constipation from pressure on the bladder neck and rectum, and the diagnosis is made by inspecting the vulva, which is frequently omitted. Treatment is surgical incision under general anaesthetic with an opening fashioned to remain patent, and the accumulated blood drains as old dark blood over hours. Differentials that require different surgery are a transverse vaginal septum, cervical agenesis and an obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis, so renal tract imaging is arranged as part of the workup.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain indicates outflow obstruction
Inspection of the vulva makes the diagnosis and is often omitted
Urinary retention arises from pressure on the bladder neck
Surgery is performed under general anaesthesia with an opening fashioned to stay patent
A transverse vaginal septum or obstructed hemivagina requires different surgery and renal imaging
explanation.pearls: Examine the external genitalia of any girl presenting with cyclical abdominal pain and no periods, because this diagnosis is routinely missed through several months of investigation for appendicitis, constipation and urinary tract infection when a thirty second inspection would settle it.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Congenital anomalies of the female genital tract
Royal Children's Hospital: Gynaecology in adolescence

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth at 38 weeks for a woman on insulin whose estimated fetal weight sits just below the threshold that would prompt discussion of caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the diabetes in pregnancy clinic reviewing a 32 year old woman at 38 weeks and one day in her second pregnancy. Gestational diabetes was diagnosed at 26 weeks and she has been on insulin since 30 weeks, currently 22 units of isophane at night with three pre meal rapid acting doses.

Her capillary glucose diary over the past fortnight shows fasting readings between 4.8 and 5.2 mmol/L and two hour postprandial readings between 6.1 and 6.8 mmol/L. Her first baby was born vaginally at 39 weeks weighing 3620 g with no difficulty at the shoulders and no perineal trauma beyond a second degree tear. A growth ultrasound performed yesterday gives an estimated fetal weight of 4350 g on the 98th centile with a normal amniotic fluid index and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. On abdominal examination the presentation is cephalic with the head three fifths palpable, and vaginal examination shows a cervix 2 cm long, soft, mid position and 1 cm dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 145 per minute
data_table.Investigations: Fasting capillary glucose 4.8-5.2 mmol/L (target less than 5.1), two hour postprandial 6.1-6.8 mmol/L (target less than 6.7), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)
data_table.Imaging: Estimated fetal weight 4350 g on the 98th centile, amniotic fluid index 14 cm, umbilical artery Dopplers within normal limits, cephalic presentation

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding the timing and mode of her birth?

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean section this week because of the estimated weight
options.rationale: Discussion of planned caesarean for suspected macrosomia in diabetes is triggered at an estimated fetal weight of about 4500 g, and this estimate of 4350 g sits below it with a previous uncomplicated vaginal birth in her favour. Third trimester weight estimates also carry an error of around 10 to 15 per cent in either direction, which is why they anchor a conversation rather than a decision (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and reassess her again at 40 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Insulin treated gestational diabetes carries a stillbirth risk that rises through the late term period, which is why birth is planned rather than awaited once 38 to 39 weeks is reached. Waiting also allows further fetal growth in the fortnight when it accelerates fastest (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Repeat the growth scan in two weeks and decide on the timing after that
options.rationale: A repeat scan would report at 40 weeks, past the window in which birth is recommended for insulin treated disease, and serial estimates in the same fortnight do not improve accuracy enough to change the plan. The decision here rests on the insulin requirement and gestation rather than on a refined weight estimate (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Recommend induction of labour this week after discussing the options with her
options.rationale: Insulin treated gestational diabetes is an indication for birth at 38 to 39 weeks, and with a favourable cervix, a cephalic presentation and a previous vaginal birth of a 3620 g baby, induction is the appropriate route at an estimated weight below the caesarean discussion threshold. Induction for suspected macrosomia also reduces shoulder dystocia without increasing caesarean rates in randomised data (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Stop her insulin now and plan an induction of labour at 41 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Insulin is continued antenatally while glucose targets require it and is stopped after birth rather than before it, since withdrawal now would allow the maternal hyperglycaemia that drives fetal insulin mediated growth to resume. Planning birth at 41 weeks compounds this by extending the exposure (Source: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management).
source_refs: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management

explanation.summary: Timing of birth in gestational diabetes is graded by whether pharmacological treatment is required, because insulin or metformin treated disease carries the higher stillbirth risk and is planned for birth at 38 to 39 weeks, while diet controlled disease with normal growth can usually reach 40 to 41 weeks. Suspected macrosomia is a separate axis, and the evidence for elective caesarean rests on an estimated fetal weight of about 4500 g in diabetes or 5000 g without it, thresholds that acknowledge how imprecise third trimester estimation is. The Australian approach to a large baby with a favourable cervix and a previous vaginal birth is induction rather than caesarean, and randomised evidence supports reduced shoulder dystocia with induction for suspected macrosomia. Intrapartum care includes hourly capillary glucose monitoring with a dextrose and insulin infusion if levels exceed target, and insulin is ceased immediately after birth. The neonate needs early feeding and blood glucose monitoring for neonatal hypoglycaemia.
key_points: Insulin treated gestational diabetes prompts planned birth at 38 to 39 weeks
Diet controlled disease with normal growth can usually continue to 40 to 41 weeks
Caesarean discussion for macrosomia in diabetes starts around an estimated weight of 4500 g
Third trimester weight estimates carry an error of roughly 10 to 15 per cent
Insulin is ceased after birth, not before, and the baby needs glucose monitoring
explanation.pearls: Check the maternal capillary glucose hourly in established labour and aim to keep it between 4 and 7 mmol/L, since intrapartum hyperglycaemia in the hours before birth is what drives reactive neonatal hypoglycaemia regardless of how well controlled the pregnancy was.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management

subtopic_detail: A three day history of a painful swelling at the vaginal opening in a woman who cannot sit down
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 28 year old woman with three days of increasing pain and swelling at the opening of her vagina on the right side. She says it started as a small tender lump and has become so painful in the past day that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably, and she has not been able to sleep.

She has had no vaginal discharge, no urinary symptoms and no fevers or sweats, and her last cervical screening test two years ago was negative for human papillomavirus. On examination there is a tense fluctuant tender swelling about 4 cm across at the posterior part of the right vaginal opening, displacing the opening across the midline. The overlying skin is stretched and shiny but is not erythematous beyond the swelling itself and there is no induration extending into the surrounding tissue. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy and her temperature is 36.9 degrees C.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant tender 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus displacing the introitus across the midline, no surrounding cellulitis or induration, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate a walled off collection and are indicated only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness, immunosuppression or pregnancy, none of which is present here. Treating with antibiotics alone leaves the collection under tension and the pain unrelieved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Aspirate the swelling with a wide bore needle and send the fluid for culture
options.rationale: Simple aspiration gives immediate relief but the cavity reseals within days and recurrence rates approach 100 per cent, which is the specific problem that placing a drain solves. It differs from the preferred approach only in that it makes no attempt to create a lasting drainage tract (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Advise warm baths and simple analgesia with review in 48 hours if no better
options.rationale: Conservative measures suit a small asymptomatic cyst or a very early inflammatory lump that has not yet formed a collection, whereas a tense fluctuant 4 cm abscess preventing sitting and sleeping needs drainage now. Waiting risks spontaneous rupture through the skin with a poorly healing sinus (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Incise and drain the abscess and insert a Word catheter for four to six weeks
options.rationale: Incision through the vaginal mucosa just outside the hymenal ring with insertion of a balloon tipped catheter drains the collection immediately and keeps the tract open long enough for an epithelialised opening to form, dropping recurrence to roughly 10 to 20 per cent. It can be done under local anaesthetic in the emergency department without a theatre booking (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next available gynaecology theatre list
options.rationale: Gland excision is reserved for repeated recurrence after simpler drainage procedures or for a suspicious solid mass, because it carries risks of bleeding from the vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia. In a woman over 40 with a persistent mass, biopsy at the time of drainage would be the relevant addition rather than primary excision (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess).

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal opening and drain through short ducts, so duct obstruction produces a cyst and secondary infection produces an abscess. The organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a sexually transmitted pathogen, though gonorrhoea and chlamydia should be considered and tested for where the history suggests risk. Definitive management is drainage with a procedure that keeps the tract open, either a balloon tipped catheter or marsupialisation, because simple incision or needle aspiration alone recurs in the great majority of cases. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression. In a woman over 40 a persistent solid or irregular mass in this location warrants biopsy, since adenocarcinoma of the gland is rare but presents this way.
key_points: Drainage is the treatment for a fluctuant abscess and antibiotics alone are not
Needle aspiration or plain incision alone recurs in the great majority of cases
A Word catheter is left for four to six weeks to allow the tract to epithelialise
Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic illness or pregnancy
A persistent solid mass in a woman over 40 should be biopsied
explanation.pearls: Make the incision inside the hymenal ring on the vaginal mucosal surface rather than on the vulval skin, because an incision placed on the skin side creates a chronically discharging sinus that will not close.

subtopic_detail: A single ulcerated area that has not healed on potent topical steroid while the surrounding vulval itch is well controlled
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 64 year old woman in clinic who has had biopsy proven lichen sclerosus for three years, treated with clobetasol propionate ointment used intermittently as directed.

She tells you the itch that used to wake her at night has settled completely everywhere except one spot on the right side, which has been sore rather than itchy for about ten weeks and stings when she passes urine. She has applied the ointment to that area every night for the last six weeks with no improvement. On examination there is the expected pale atrophic change with loss of the labia minora and early narrowing of the vaginal opening, and within it on the right labium majus there is a 12 mm ulcer with a firm rolled edge that bleeds lightly when touched. The base of the ulcer feels indurated between finger and thumb. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy and no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Pale atrophic vulval skin with loss of the labia minora and early introital narrowing, 12 mm ulcer on the right labium majus with a firm rolled edge and indurated base that bleeds on contact, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and inflammatory markers within normal limits, urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes
data_table.Medications: Clobetasol propionate 0.05 per cent ointment applied nightly to the affected area for six weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase the topical corticosteroid to twice daily and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Escalating potent topical steroid for an area that has already failed six weeks of daily treatment is the classic reason invasive disease is diagnosed late in this condition. A localised area behaving differently from surrounding well controlled skin is the signal to biopsy rather than to treat harder (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Take an urgent biopsy of the ulcerated area and refer her to a specialist unit
options.rationale: An indurated non healing ulcer with a rolled edge arising within lichen sclerosus that has otherwise responded to treatment requires histology, because roughly 2 to 5 per cent of women with this condition develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma and it arises in exactly this way. Biopsy is taken from the edge of the ulcer including adjacent skin rather than from the necrotic centre (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Start topical tacrolimus ointment for six weeks and reassess the ulcer then
options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are a second line option for lichen sclerosus that has not responded to potent steroid, but they are avoided over an undiagnosed lesion because of the theoretical malignancy concern and they would delay histology by a further six weeks. Steroid failure in a single site means biopsy, not a different immunosuppressant (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders).

options.text: Swab the ulcer for herpes simplex and start oral valaciclovir empirically now
options.rationale: Herpetic ulceration is typically multiple, shallow and painful with a soft base and resolves or evolves within one to two weeks, whereas this is a solitary indurated lesion present for ten weeks. The induration and rolled edge are the features that separate the two (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe a topical antifungal cream and review her again in four weeks time
options.rationale: Candidal vulvitis produces erythema, fissuring and itch with discharge rather than a discrete indurated ulcer, and there is no discharge here. Another four weeks of empirical topical treatment repeats the delay already incurred (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval dermatosis that causes itch, pale atrophic skin, fissuring and progressive architectural change with loss of the labia minora, burial of the clitoris and introital narrowing. Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line and, used properly, both relieves symptoms and reduces long term scarring, and there is evidence that adherent maintenance treatment lowers the risk of malignant transformation. That risk is the reason women need long term review: about 2 to 5 per cent develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, typically arising in differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia rather than through a human papillomavirus pathway. Any area that ulcerates, thickens, becomes fixed or fails to respond to adequate treatment must be biopsied regardless of how well the rest of the vulva is doing. Pain replacing itch at a single site is a particularly useful change in symptom quality to ask about.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime vulval squamous cell carcinoma risk of about 2 to 5 per cent
Any non healing, indurated or fixed area needs biopsy irrespective of treatment response elsewhere
Escalating topical steroid over an undiagnosed lesion is the usual cause of diagnostic delay
Biopsy is taken from the edge of the lesion with adjacent skin, not the necrotic centre
Vulval cancer in this setting arises through differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia rather than human papillomavirus
explanation.pearls: A change in symptom quality from itch to soreness or burning at one specific site is the single most useful history question in long standing lichen sclerosus, because it precedes the visible ulcer in many women who later prove to have invasive disease.

subtopic_detail: Two years of cramping pain confined to the first two days of each period in a sixteen year old missing school
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old girl who has come with her mother about painful periods. Her periods started at twelve and became regular at fourteen, arriving every 28 to 30 days and lasting five days.

For the past two years she has had cramping lower abdominal pain that begins a few hours before the bleeding starts, is worst on the first day, and has settled by the end of the second day. It is associated with nausea and loose stools on the first day, and she has missed one or two days of school in most months this year. She has no pain at any other time in the cycle, no pain with bowel movements or urination outside her period, and she is not sexually active. Abdominal examination is normal with no masses and no tenderness today, and she is on day nineteen of her cycle. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g when the pain starts with little effect.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen with no palpable mass, normal external genitalia, no pelvic examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start regular ibuprofen beginning as the pain starts each cycle
options.rationale: Prostaglandin driven myometrial contraction produces this pattern, and a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug taken regularly rather than as needed inhibits its synthesis and relieves pain in about 70 to 80 per cent of adolescents. Her failure on paracetamol does not predict failure on this class because the mechanisms differ (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound before starting any medical treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the history suggests a secondary cause, such as pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, or failure of first line treatment, and none of those applies to pain confined to the first two days. A transabdominal scan also has limited sensitivity for the conditions being sought (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression is an effective second line option and a reasonable first choice when contraception is also wanted, but it is not the standard first step for uncomplicated pain of this pattern. Continuous use without a hormone free interval belongs to management of suspected endometriosis rather than to initial treatment (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Refer her for diagnostic laparoscopy to look for endometriosis now
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is considered after failure of both a non steroidal agent and hormonal treatment, or where symptoms point to a secondary cause, because a general anaesthetic and a negative finding are otherwise likely. Pain strictly confined to the first two days without acyclical symptoms is the pattern least associated with endometriosis (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Prescribe codeine with paracetamol to be taken on the worst days
options.rationale: Opioids are not recommended for menstrual pain in adolescents because they do not address prostaglandin mediated contraction, worsen the nausea and constipation already present, and carry dependence risk. Codeine is also contraindicated under 18 years in several settings owing to variable metabolism (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea typically begins six to twenty four months after menarche once ovulatory cycles establish, and is characterised by cramping suprapubic pain starting just before or with the bleeding and lasting one to three days, often with nausea, diarrhoea and headache from systemic prostaglandin effects. Secondary causes are suggested by pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, heavy or irregular bleeding, onset at menarche without a pain free interval, or failure of first line treatment, and these prompt imaging and specialist referral. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line and work best when started at the first sign of pain and continued regularly through the worst forty eight hours rather than taken reactively. Hormonal treatment with a combined pill, progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device is second line or first line where contraception is also required. Repeated school absence is itself an indication to treat actively rather than to reassure.
key_points: Primary dysmenorrhoea begins six to twenty four months after menarche with ovulatory cycles
Pain confined to the first one to three days of bleeding is the characteristic pattern
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs taken regularly are first line
Acyclical pain, dyspareunia or treatment failure prompt imaging and referral
Opioids have no place in routine management of menstrual pain in adolescents
explanation.pearls: Advise starting the non steroidal agent at the first twinge or the day before bleeding is expected and continuing it regularly for 48 to 72 hours, because these drugs prevent prostaglandin synthesis rather than reversing its effects and taking them once the pain is established is why most adolescents report they do not work.

subtopic_detail: An intensely itchy blistering eruption beginning around the umbilicus at 32 weeks with normal liver biochemistry
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy with a two week history of an intensely itchy rash. It started as raised red patches immediately around her navel and has spread outward across her abdomen and onto both thighs.

Over the past four days the patches have developed tense fluid filled blisters up to a centimetre across, several of which have burst and crusted. Her first pregnancy four years ago was uncomplicated with no skin problems. On examination there are urticarial plaques with tense bullae distributed over the periumbilical skin, flanks and proximal thighs, with the umbilicus itself clearly involved, and her abdominal striae are spared. Her palms, soles, face and mucous membranes are clear. Her serum bile acids, transaminases and full blood count are all within normal limits, and fetal growth and the cardiotocograph are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 86 per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148 per minute
data_table.Examination: Urticarial plaques with tense bullae over the periumbilical skin, flanks and proximal thighs, umbilicus involved, striae spared, palms soles face and mucosae clear, extensive excoriation
data_table.Investigations: Serum bile acids and transaminases within normal limits, full blood count with eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), urine dipstick negative for protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her this is a benign pregnancy rash and prescribe a topical steroid
options.rationale: The common benign eruption of pregnancy begins in the abdominal striae and characteristically spares a rim of skin around the umbilicus, which is the reverse of the distribution here, and it does not produce tense bullae. Treating without a diagnosis also misses the neonatal and maternal implications that follow from the alternative (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Measure serum bile acids and plan birth at 37 weeks for her symptoms
options.rationale: Cholestasis of pregnancy causes itch without any primary rash and her bile acids and transaminases are already normal, so repeating them adds nothing. A visible blistering eruption directs the workup to the skin rather than the liver (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Prescribe an oral antihistamine with emollients and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: Antihistamines and emollients provide only partial symptom relief in a blistering autoimmune eruption, which usually requires systemic corticosteroid, and a two week delay allows further blistering and excoriation. Symptomatic treatment without histology also leaves the fetal surveillance plan unmade (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin
options.rationale: Tense bullae arising from urticarial plaques centred on the umbilicus with sparing of the striae is the pattern of an autoimmune blistering disease of pregnancy, and linear complement C3 deposition along the basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin is the diagnostic finding. Confirming it matters because the condition is associated with fetal growth restriction and preterm birth, needs systemic corticosteroid, and produces a transient blistering rash in around 10 per cent of newborns (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange induction of labour this week to bring the rash to an end
options.rationale: Birth at 32 weeks for a maternal skin condition trades established prematurity against a rash that is treatable with corticosteroid, and the eruption commonly flares at delivery in any case rather than resolving immediately. Serial growth surveillance with treatment is the appropriate response (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy).
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare autoimmune blistering disease driven by antibodies against collagen XVII in the hemidesmosome, usually presenting in the second or third trimester with intense itch and urticarial plaques that begin at the umbilicus and evolve into tense bullae. Its principal differential is polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which begins in abdominal striae, spares the umbilicus, occurs typically in a first pregnancy or a multiple pregnancy, and does not blister. Diagnosis is by direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showing linear C3 along the basement membrane zone, with circulating antibodies detectable on indirect testing. Treatment is potent topical corticosteroid for mild disease and systemic prednisolone for extensive or blistering disease, and pregnancies are monitored for growth restriction and preterm birth. The condition characteristically flares at the time of birth, recurs in subsequent pregnancies often earlier and more severely, and can flare with the combined oral contraceptive pill or menstruation.
key_points: Umbilical involvement with tense bullae distinguishes it from polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption begins in the striae and spares the umbilicus without blistering
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear C3 at the basement membrane
Associated with fetal growth restriction and preterm birth, so growth surveillance is needed
About one in ten neonates develop a transient blistering rash that resolves spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Warn the woman that the eruption typically flares in the days around birth rather than settling, and that it can recur with menstruation or the combined oral contraceptive pill, so a progestogen only or non hormonal method is preferred afterwards.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Dermatoses of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of vomiting at nine weeks with a 3 per cent weight loss in a woman still tolerating some oral fluid
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at nine weeks in her first pregnancy who has been vomiting for three weeks. She vomits four or five times a day, mostly in the mornings, and feels nauseated for much of the rest of the day.

She has been eating dry crackers before getting up, taking small frequent meals and using ginger tablets for a fortnight without much benefit. She is still able to keep down about a litre of fluid a day and has not vomited blood. She weighed 62 kg before the pregnancy and weighs 60 kg today. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no urinary symptoms and no diarrhoea. Her thyroid is not enlarged and she has no tremor or lid lag. Her urine dipstick shows ketones at one plus with no nitrites or leucocytes, and her thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.09 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine. An ultrasound this morning confirmed a single intrauterine pregnancy with a normal heartbeat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick ketones one plus with no nitrites or leucocytes, thyroid stimulating hormone 0.09 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine pregnancy with fetal heart activity and no molar features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Admit her for intravenous rehydration and intravenous antiemetics today
options.rationale: Admission is indicated when a woman cannot maintain oral hydration, has lost more than 5 per cent of body weight, or has electrolyte disturbance or ketosis with clinical dehydration, and she is tolerating a litre a day with normal electrolytes. Admitting first also skips the oral step that resolves most cases (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start ondansetron 4 mg orally as required and review her in one week
options.rationale: Ondansetron is effective but is positioned as a second or third line agent in Australian practice because of a small absolute increase in orofacial clefting reported with first trimester exposure, so it is used after the first line combination has failed. The counselling that goes with it is unnecessary if the earlier step works (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start oral doxylamine with pyridoxine and review her in one week
options.rationale: This combination has the longest safety record of any antiemetic in pregnancy and is first line once non pharmacological measures have failed, which they have after a fortnight of ginger and dietary change. Her weight loss of 3 per cent with tolerated oral intake and normal electrolytes places her in the moderate category managed as an outpatient (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start prednisolone 40 mg orally daily and taper over the next fortnight
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are a last resort for refractory hyperemesis after multiple agents have failed and are avoided before ten weeks because of a reported association with orofacial clefting. Starting them before any antiemetic has been trialled inverts the ladder (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start carbimazole for her suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone level
options.rationale: A suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine in the first trimester reflects cross stimulation of the thyroid receptor by human chorionic gonadotrophin and resolves as levels fall after about twelve weeks. Treating it would produce iatrogenic hypothyroidism in a euthyroid woman (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy).
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Nausea and vomiting affects around 70 to 80 per cent of pregnancies, typically beginning before nine weeks and settling by sixteen to twenty weeks, and severity is best graded with a validated score such as the Pregnancy Unique Quantification of Emesis alongside weight loss and ketosis. Hyperemesis gravidarum is the severe end and is defined by persistent vomiting with weight loss over 5 per cent, dehydration and electrolyte or acid base disturbance. Management is stepwise, beginning with dietary and lifestyle measures, then doxylamine with pyridoxine, then metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, then ondansetron, with corticosteroids reserved for refractory disease. Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis is common and needs no treatment because it reflects the structural similarity between human chorionic gonadotrophin and thyroid stimulating hormone. Women admitted for rehydration need thiamine before any dextrose containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and this is the most consequential omission in the condition.
key_points: Grade severity by weight loss, ability to tolerate fluids, ketosis and electrolytes
Doxylamine with pyridoxine is the first line pharmacological treatment
Ondansetron is second or third line in Australia because of a small clefting signal
A suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine needs no treatment
Weight loss beyond 5 per cent with dehydration indicates admission
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any dextrose containing intravenous fluid to a woman admitted with prolonged vomiting in pregnancy, because glucose loading a thiamine depleted woman can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain at the moment of attachment on day twelve with a wedge shaped nipple after feeds
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman twelve days after the birth of her first baby. She has come because feeding has become so painful that she has been dreading each feed and has started giving one bottle of formula overnight.

She describes a sharp stabbing pain at the instant the baby latches on that eases considerably once the milk starts flowing, and that has gone by the time the feed ends. There is no burning between feeds and no shooting pain into the breast afterwards. On examination both nipples have a linear crack at the base and, immediately after she takes the baby off, the nipple comes out compressed into a wedge with a white crease across the tip. The areolae are not red or shiny and there is no scaling. The baby's mouth is clear with no white plaques, and he has regained his birth weight and is having six heavy nappies a day.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Linear fissure at the base of each nipple, nipple compressed into a wedge shape with a transverse white crease immediately after the feed, areolae not erythematous or shiny, no scaling or satellite lesions, breasts soft with no localised lump or erythema
data_table.Infant: Birth weight regained by day twelve, six heavy nappies daily, oral cavity clear with no plaques, tongue elevates to the palate with the mouth open

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Observe a full feed and correct attachment with lactation support
options.rationale: Pain confined to the moment of attachment with a nipple that emerges compressed and creased indicates that the nipple is being drawn against the hard palate rather than deep to the junction with the soft palate, which is a positioning problem and the cause of the fissures. Watching an entire feed is the only way to identify and correct it, and the fissures heal once the mechanical cause is removed (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe topical miconazole for her nipples and oral gel for the baby
options.rationale: Nipple candidiasis causes burning pain that persists between feeds and often radiates into the breast, with shiny or flaking areolae and usually oral plaques in the baby, and none of those features is present. Treating for the wrong cause leaves the mechanical trauma to continue (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole for her and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal treatment is reserved for deep breast pain thought to be candidal that has not responded to topical treatment, and it differs from the topical option only in the depth of the infection it targets. Neither applies to pain that stops when the feed does (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise nipple shields for every feed and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: A shield can be a short term measure while damaged nipples heal, but used without correcting the attachment it perpetuates the shallow latch, and it is associated with reduced milk transfer and earlier weaning. It manages the symptom while entrenching the cause (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe topical mupirocin to the cracks and continue feeding as she is
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic is appropriate when a fissure shows honey coloured crusting, spreading erythema or purulent discharge suggesting secondary bacterial infection, none of which is described here. Continuing to feed unchanged also guarantees the fissures reopen at every feed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Nipple pain is the commonest reason Australian women stop breastfeeding earlier than they intended, and the great majority of it is mechanical rather than infective. The timing of the pain is the most useful piece of history: pain at attachment that eases as the feed progresses points to a shallow latch, whereas burning that persists between feeds with radiating breast pain suggests candidal infection, and pain with blanching then colour change of the nipple after feeds suggests vasospasm. A nipple that emerges compressed, creased or wedge shaped is direct evidence of compression against the hard palate. Assessment requires observing a complete feed rather than examining the nipple alone, and correction focuses on bringing the baby to the breast chin first with a wide gape so the nipple sits deep in the mouth. Persistent difficulty despite skilled support prompts assessment for tongue tie, but the great majority resolve with positioning alone.
key_points: The timing of nipple pain relative to the feed identifies the cause
Pain only at attachment with a compressed creased nipple indicates a shallow latch
Candidal pain burns between feeds and usually involves shiny or flaking areolae
Observing a full feed is essential and cannot be replaced by examining the nipple
Nipple shields without attachment correction perpetuate the problem
explanation.pearls: Look at the shape of the nipple in the first seconds after the baby comes off the breast, because a nipple that is round and everted has been positioned correctly while one shaped like a new lipstick has been compressed against the hard palate throughout the feed.

subtopic_detail: Worsening wheeze at 28 weeks in a woman who stopped her inhaled preventer early in pregnancy, speaking in short phrases
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 27 year old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy with two days of worsening wheeze and breathlessness following a head cold.

She has had asthma since childhood and was well controlled on budesonide with formoterol before conceiving, but she stopped the preventer at eight weeks because she was worried about the effect on the baby and has been using salbutamol alone, most recently every three to four hours. She is sitting upright and can speak only in short phrases, using her accessory muscles. Her chest has widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry at both bases. Her peak expiratory flow is 210 L/min against a recorded personal best of 470 L/min. Her oxygen saturation is 93 per cent on room air, her respiratory rate is 28 per minute and the cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 155 per minute with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, fetal heart rate 155 per minute
