data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 210 L/min against a personal best of 470 L/min, arterial pH 7.46 with partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mmHg (pregnancy reference 28-32), no consolidation on chest radiograph with abdominal shielding
data_table.Examination: Speaking in short phrases, accessory muscle use, widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced basal air entry, cardiotocograph with normal baseline variability and accelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol alone and avoid systemic corticosteroid in pregnancy
options.rationale: Withholding systemic corticosteroid is the central error in this scenario, since prednisolone is extensively metabolised by placental 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase so that fetal exposure is a small fraction of the maternal dose. Maternal hypoxia poses a far greater risk to the foetus than the drug (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate as the first treatment for her wheeze
options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct for severe or life threatening exacerbations that have not responded to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid treatment, not a first line agent. Using it first delays the interventions with the largest and fastest effect (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Give oxygen with repeated salbutamol and start systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated exactly as it is outside pregnancy, with oxygen targeted to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent, repeated or continuous inhaled salbutamol with ipratropium for severe episodes, and systemic corticosteroid given early. Her inability to complete sentences with a peak flow at 45 per cent of personal best places her in the severe category where the corticosteroid is the intervention that changes the trajectory (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange urgent delivery of the baby to relieve her respiratory distress
options.rationale: Birth at 28 weeks carries substantial prematurity risk and does not treat bronchoconstriction, and the cardiotocograph here is reassuring. Delivery is considered only for a deteriorating mother requiring ventilation or for fetal compromise that persists despite maternal treatment (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Give nebulised adrenaline and observe her for the next four hours
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is used for upper airway obstruction such as croup or angio oedema rather than for lower airway bronchospasm, where a selective beta2 agonist is both more effective and better tolerated. Four hours of observation without corticosteroid also wastes the window in which it acts (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of women with asthma worsen during pregnancy, and the strongest predictor of an exacerbation is stopping the preventer, which around a quarter of pregnant women do out of concern about the medication. Poorly controlled asthma is associated with pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and low birth weight, whereas the inhaled and systemic drugs used to treat it have reassuring safety records. Acute management is identical to the non pregnant algorithm, with the additional points that maternal oxygen saturation is kept at or above 94 per cent because the foetus sits on the steep part of its own dissociation curve, and that the woman is nursed with left lateral tilt after twenty weeks. Physiological hyperventilation of pregnancy means the normal partial pressure of carbon dioxide is around 28 to 32 mmHg, so a value in the normal non pregnant range signals impending failure. Continuous fetal monitoring is used in severe episodes, and every discharge includes restarting the preventer with a written action plan.
key_points: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated the same as outside pregnancy
Systemic corticosteroid is given early and is not withheld because of pregnancy
Target maternal oxygen saturation at or above 94 per cent to protect fetal oxygenation
A partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the normal non pregnant range signals deterioration
Preventer cessation is the leading cause of exacerbation in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Take the peak flow as a percentage of the woman's own personal best rather than a predicted value, since peak expiratory flow itself is essentially unchanged by pregnancy and a reading below 50 per cent of personal best defines a severe exacerbation at any gestation.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: A first unaccompanied antenatal visit at 26 weeks with grip pattern bruising and a request that nothing be written down
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 24 year old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy. She has attended every previous appointment with her partner, who has answered most of the questions on her behalf, and today she has come alone for the first time because he is at work.

While you are measuring her blood pressure you notice several oval bruises on the inner aspect of both upper arms. When you ask about them she becomes tearful and tells you that two nights ago her partner pushed her against a wall and held her by the arms during an argument, that this has happened four or five times over the past year, and that he checks her phone each evening and gives her a set amount of cash each week. She says he has never hurt their two year old. She asks you not to write any of this in her notes and says she does not want the police involved and is not leaving him. Her abdomen is soft and non tender and the cardiotocograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142 per minute
data_table.Examination: Multiple oval bruises of differing ages on the inner aspect of both upper arms, soft non tender abdomen with fundal height appropriate for dates, no vaginal bleeding or loss
data_table.Social: Two year old child at home, partner attends all appointments and answers on her behalf, weekly cash allowance and daily phone checking described

lead_in: What would you do first?

options.text: Assess her immediate safety and offer referral to a family violence service
options.rationale: A structured safety assessment covering escalation, threats, weapons, strangulation, separation plans and where she will go tonight is the first task, because level of danger determines everything that follows, and specialist family violence services provide risk assessment and safety planning that general antenatal care cannot. Doing this while she is unaccompanied is essential, since asking these questions with the partner present is unsafe (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence).

options.text: Contact the police so that they can act on the assault she has described
options.rationale: Reporting an adult's assault against her wishes removes her control at the point she has trusted a clinician for the first time and is associated with escalation, since the period around disclosure and separation is when the risk of serious harm is highest. Police involvement is offered and supported rather than imposed (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence).

options.text: Notify child protection immediately because a two year old lives in the home
options.rationale: The risk to the child is a genuine and mandatory part of the assessment, and exposure to family violence meets notification thresholds in several jurisdictions, but that determination follows the safety assessment rather than replacing it. Notifying before assessing the risk also forfeits the chance to do it with her knowledge and with a specialist service involved (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence).

options.text: Advise her to leave the relationship today and arrange emergency accommodation
options.rationale: Directing a woman to leave without a safety plan increases her risk, because separation is the period of greatest danger, and a plan she has not chosen is rarely followed. Accommodation is one option within a plan she leads rather than the instruction that opens the conversation (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence).

options.text: Arrange couples counselling for the two of them with a relationship service
options.rationale: Joint counselling is contraindicated where there is family violence because it presumes shared responsibility for the relationship's problems and creates a forum in which she may be punished afterwards for what she says. This is the intervention most likely to cause direct harm of the five listed (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence).

explanation.summary: Family violence commonly begins or escalates during pregnancy and is associated with antepartum haemorrhage, placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and maternal death, which is why routine enquiry in the antenatal period is standard practice across Australian maternity services. Enquiry is made only when the woman is alone, with a professional interpreter rather than a family member if one is needed, and the immediate response is validation, a safety assessment and an offer of specialist referral rather than advice to leave. Controlling behaviours such as monitoring a phone, restricting money and answering on a woman's behalf are core features rather than background detail, and coercive control is now a criminal offence in several Australian jurisdictions. Documentation is a clinical and medico legal obligation and cannot be omitted at a woman's request, but records can be kept in a way that limits access, and she should be told what will be written and why. Children in the household are always considered, and notification thresholds and mandatory reporting duties differ between states and territories.
key_points: Enquiry occurs only when the woman is alone and never through a family interpreter
Safety assessment precedes any referral, notification or advice about leaving
Separation is the period of highest risk, so leaving is planned rather than instructed
Couples counselling is contraindicated where family violence is present
Documentation is required despite a request to omit it, with access limited where possible
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about non fatal strangulation, since it is one of the strongest single predictors of later homicide and women rarely mention it unprompted, describing it instead as being grabbed around the neck.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Family violence in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Four months of bleeding after intercourse with a smooth lesion protruding from the external os and a recent negative screening test
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who has had light bleeding after intercourse on most occasions over the past four months. She describes it as a smear of fresh blood on wiping afterwards, lasting less than a day.

Her periods are regular every 28 days with no change in flow, and she has no bleeding between periods at any other time. She has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill for six years without missing doses and has had two previous vaginal births. Her last cervical screening test fourteen months ago was negative for human papillomavirus. On speculum examination there is a smooth glistening pedunculated lesion about 12 mm long protruding through the external os on a narrow stalk, which bleeds lightly when touched with a swab. The remainder of the cervix looks healthy with no irregularity, ulceration or friable mass, and there is no abnormal discharge. Tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Smooth glistening pedunculated cervical lesion 12 mm long on a narrow stalk protruding through the external os, bleeding lightly on contact, remaining cervix smooth with no irregularity or ulceration, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test fourteen months ago negative for human papillomavirus, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative, haemoglobin within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat her cervical screening test today and manage on the result
options.rationale: A screening test detects human papillomavirus in an asymptomatic population and was negative fourteen months ago, and a negative repeat would not explain the bleeding or remove the lesion. Symptomatic bleeding is investigated on its own merits rather than through the screening program (Source: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

options.text: Refer her for colposcopy and take no action at this appointment
options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated when the cervix looks suspicious with irregularity, ulceration or a friable mass, or where screening is abnormal, and here the surface is smooth with a discrete benign appearing lesion on a stalk. Referral without removing the lesion also leaves the bleeding untreated for months (Source: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

options.text: Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and review her in three months
options.rationale: Hormonal contraception can cause unscheduled bleeding, but that is typically intermenstrual rather than strictly after intercourse, and stopping it does nothing about a visible lesion that bleeds on contact. She would also need alternative contraception for a trial that is unlikely to help (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

options.text: Remove the polyp in clinic and send it for histological examination
options.rationale: A pedunculated polyp on a narrow stalk that bleeds on contact explains her postcoital bleeding and can be avulsed in clinic by grasping the stalk with sponge forceps and twisting, which is both diagnostic and curative. Histology is mandatory because a small proportion harbour dysplasia or malignancy despite a benign appearance (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

options.text: Refer her for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling under anaesthetic
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding and at risk factors for endometrial pathology, and she has regular cycles with bleeding only after intercourse. Hysteroscopy has a role where a polyp appears to arise from the endocervical canal or where symptoms persist after removal (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

explanation.summary: Postcoital bleeding is caused most often by cervical ectropion, cervical polyps, cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhoea, or vaginal atrophy, but cervical cancer must be excluded in every case because it is the diagnosis that cannot wait. The critical principle is that a negative human papillomavirus screening result does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic woman, since a small proportion of cervical cancers are not associated with the virus and false negatives occur, so the appearance of the cervix drives the decision. A visibly abnormal, irregular, ulcerated or friable cervix is referred for colposcopy and biopsy regardless of the screening result, whereas a discrete benign appearing polyp on a stalk can be removed in clinic. All removed tissue goes for histology. Persistent postcoital bleeding after treatment of an apparent cause is itself an indication for specialist referral rather than reassurance.
key_points: A negative human papillomavirus test does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic woman
The appearance of the cervix determines whether colposcopy is needed
A pedunculated polyp on a narrow stalk can be avulsed in clinic
All removed cervical tissue is sent for histological examination
Test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in every case of postcoital bleeding
explanation.pearls: Postcoital bleeding that persists after an apparent cause has been treated warrants specialist referral even with negative screening and normal histology, because that pattern is how the small number of screen negative cervical cancers are eventually found.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

subtopic_detail: Non-immune rubella serology identified on booking bloods
stem:
You are reviewing a 29 year old woman at 12 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her booking bloods. Her rubella IgG is reported as non-immune, although her childhood record documents two doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.

She feels well, has had no rash or fever, and has had no known contact with anyone with a rash illness. She works in an accounting office with no contact with young children. Her hepatitis B surface antigen, syphilis and HIV serology are negative, she is varicella immune, and her blood group is O positive. She asks whether she can simply have the vaccine now to protect the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG non-immune; varicella IgG immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; syphilis and HIV serology negative; blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the vaccine now, since the risk from a live vaccine in pregnancy is only theoretical
options.rationale: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, and although inadvertent administration has not been shown to cause congenital rubella syndrome, deliberate administration is not acceptable when the dose can safely be given after birth. Inadvertent exposure is managed with reassurance rather than termination. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the vaccine now and advise her to avoid pregnancy for the next 28 days
options.rationale: The 28 day rule applies to a woman who is not yet pregnant, and it cannot be applied to someone already 12 weeks pregnant. Applying the interval here reveals a misreading of when the precaution operates. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer vaccination and give it after birth before she leaves the maternity unit
options.rationale: The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but should be given in the immediate postpartum period, which is the reliable opportunity to protect future pregnancies, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication. In the meantime she is advised to avoid contact with anyone who has a rash illness and to present early if exposed. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give normal human immunoglobulin now to provide passive protection during pregnancy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin does not reliably prevent infection or congenital rubella syndrome and is not recommended as routine prophylaxis for a non-immune pregnant woman. Its limited role is after a significant confirmed exposure where termination would not be considered. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Repeat the antibody test at 28 weeks and vaccinate only if she remains non-immune
options.rationale: Repeat testing will not change management because vaccination remains contraindicated throughout pregnancy regardless of the result. Serial testing is used to detect seroconversion after a documented exposure, not to decide on routine vaccination. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaccination in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Rubella serology is checked at every antenatal booking not to protect the current pregnancy, which cannot be vaccinated, but to identify women who need immunisation afterwards so that future pregnancies are protected. Congenital rubella syndrome causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects and intellectual disability, with the risk of severe defects highest when infection occurs before 12 weeks and falling substantially after 16 weeks. A non-immune result despite documented vaccination is common, reflecting waning of measurable antibody rather than absent protection, but management follows the serology. The vaccine is live attenuated and therefore contraindicated in pregnancy, so the dose is given in the immediate postpartum period before discharge, where uptake is highest, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication. Women who are not yet pregnant are advised to avoid conception for 28 days after the dose, and inadvertent vaccination in early pregnancy is managed with reassurance because no case of congenital rubella syndrome has been attributed to the vaccine.
key_points: Booking serology identifies women for postpartum vaccination, not for treatment in this pregnancy
The vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated during pregnancy
Give the dose before discharge after birth, when uptake is highest; breastfeeding is not a contraindication
The 28 day conception interval applies only to women who are not currently pregnant
Risk of severe congenital defects is highest with infection before 12 weeks
explanation.pearls: Advise a non-immune pregnant woman to present immediately if she is exposed to a rash illness, because diagnosis of maternal rubella depends on paired serology and IgM taken close to the exposure rather than on the booking result.

subtopic_detail: Vaccination advice at a routine second trimester antenatal visit
stem:
You are reviewing a 31 year old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy at a routine antenatal visit. She received an influenza vaccine at 12 weeks in this pregnancy and has no allergies.

During her first pregnancy three years ago she was given a whooping cough vaccine at 30 weeks, and she asks whether she needs it again so soon. Her three year old is fully immunised on schedule. She has had no contact with anyone with a prolonged cough and feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with iodine; influenza vaccine given at 12 weeks this pregnancy; diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine given at 30 weeks of her previous pregnancy three years ago

lead_in: What should you advise about whooping cough vaccination?

options.text: Give a diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine during this pregnancy now
options.rationale: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy irrespective of the interval since the last one, because maternal antibody wanes and it is transplacental transfer in this pregnancy that protects this newborn. The optimal window of 20 to 32 weeks allows time for antibody transfer before birth. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer vaccination until after the birth and vaccinate her and household contacts then
options.rationale: Vaccinating around the birth relies on reducing transmission from contacts rather than protecting the infant directly, and gives no transplacental antibody. This cocooning approach is the fallback for women who were not vaccinated during pregnancy. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Advise that no further dose is needed because she was vaccinated three years ago
options.rationale: Antibody from a previous pregnancy has waned and does not cross the placenta in this one, so a prior dose does not protect this baby. The minimum interval concern that applies to other tetanus containing vaccines does not override the recommendation in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer the dose until 36 weeks so that her antibody levels peak closer to the birth
options.rationale: Vaccinating late leaves insufficient time for antibody production and placental transfer, and offers no protection at all to a baby born preterm. Doses after 32 weeks are still given if the opportunity was missed, but they are second best. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaccination in Pregnancy)

options.text: Check her pertussis serology and vaccinate only if her antibody titres are found low
options.rationale: Serology is not recommended for this purpose because no protective antibody threshold is established and results would not change the recommendation to vaccinate. Testing would only delay a vaccine that is indicated regardless of the result. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Pertussis causes its most severe disease in infants under six months, who are too young to have completed their own primary course, and the majority of infant deaths occur before the first scheduled dose at six weeks. Maternal vaccination works by generating antibody that crosses the placenta, and it is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of how recently a previous dose was given, because transfer only benefits the infant of the pregnancy in which the vaccine was administered. The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks, which allows time for the maternal antibody response and for active placental transfer, and vaccination in this window prevents the large majority of infant cases. Doses given after 32 weeks are still worthwhile but produce lower infant antibody levels, and vaccination before 20 weeks may result in waning before birth. Influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of pregnancy, and both vaccines are safe and funded, with the wider household encouraged to be up to date as an additional layer.
key_points: A dose is recommended in every pregnancy regardless of the interval since the last
The optimal window is 20 to 32 weeks to allow antibody production and placental transfer
Protection works through transplacental antibody, so it is pregnancy specific
Infants are most vulnerable before their first scheduled dose at six weeks
Serological testing has no role because no protective threshold is defined
explanation.pearls: Vaccinating in the 20 to 32 week window rather than at 36 weeks matters most for babies born preterm, who otherwise arrive before any meaningful transplacental antibody has been transferred.

subtopic_detail: Fever and a discharging abdominal wound six days after caesarean section
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman who presents six days after an emergency caesarean performed at full dilatation. She reports two days of increasing pain at the wound with fever and a discharge that has stained her dressing.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she had gestational diabetes managed with insulin. On examination the lower transverse wound has erythema extending 4 cm beyond the incision line with surrounding induration, and serous fluid discharges from the lateral third when gentle pressure is applied. The uterus is non-tender, lochia is not offensive, and there is no calf tenderness or leg swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.3 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Open and drain the infected wound segment and commence intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A collection under an infected wound will not resolve on antibiotics alone, so the discharging portion is opened along its length to drain and allow healing by secondary intention, with a swab taken at the same time to guide therapy. Her fever, tachycardia and inflammatory response justify the intravenous route rather than oral treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

options.text: Prescribe oral cephalexin and arrange community nurse review of the wound in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy without drainage leaves the collection in place and understates a systemic inflammatory response with fever and tachycardia. This approach suits mild cellulitis around an intact wound in a well patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT abdomen and pelvis before any antimicrobial treatment is commenced
options.rationale: The infection is clinically evident at the wound and imaging would delay both drainage and antibiotics without changing the immediate plan. Cross sectional imaging is indicated when a deep pelvic collection or uterine dehiscence is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for endometritis and observe the wound expectantly
options.rationale: Endometritis produces a tender uterus with offensive lochia, both of which are absent, so treating the wrong site leaves the wound collection undrained. The two complications can coexist, which is why both are examined for explicitly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for immediate return to theatre for full wound resuture under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Primary closure of an infected wound traps bacteria and leads to breakdown, so these wounds are managed open with secondary healing or delayed closure. Theatre is required when there is fascial dehiscence or suspected necrotising infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean Section)

explanation.summary: Surgical site infection complicates a meaningful proportion of caesarean births and is the most common cause of readmission afterwards, with raised body mass index, diabetes, prolonged labour, emergency surgery at full dilatation and prolonged rupture of membranes all increasing risk. Infection typically declares itself between days four and eight, after discharge from hospital, so the presentation is usually to a general practice or emergency department rather than the maternity ward. The essential principle is that antibiotics alone do not treat a collection, so an infected wound with fluctuance or discharge is opened and drained, swabbed, and then managed open with dressings to heal by secondary intention. Assessment must also distinguish and exclude endometritis, deep pelvic collection, venous thromboembolism and, rarely, necrotising soft tissue infection, since pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapidly spreading discolouration demands immediate surgical review. Prevention is largely achieved through prophylactic antibiotics given before the skin incision rather than after cord clamping, along with skin preparation and glycaemic control.
key_points: Infection usually appears between days four and eight, after hospital discharge
Raised body mass index, diabetes and emergency surgery at full dilatation raise the risk
Antibiotics alone will not resolve a collection; the wound must be opened and drained
Endometritis is distinguished by a tender uterus and offensive lochia
Pain out of proportion with rapidly spreading change suggests necrotising infection
explanation.pearls: Prophylactic antibiotics given within the 60 minutes before skin incision, rather than after cord clamping, roughly halve the rate of maternal infection without adverse neonatal effects, and this timing is now standard Australian practice.

subtopic_detail: Maternal exposure to a childhood exanthem and surveillance for fetal anaemia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 33 year old childcare worker at 15 weeks in her second pregnancy. Ten days ago several children in her room developed a bright red facial rash followed by a lace-like rash on their limbs, and one was diagnosed by a general practitioner.

She has had mild joint aches in both hands for three days but no rash and no fever. Her booking bloods showed rubella immunity and negative syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV serology. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Examination reveals no rash, no lymphadenopathy and a uterus consistent with dates. Urgent serology now returns parvovirus B19 IgM positive with IgG negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; rubella IgG immune; full blood count within normal limits; ultrasound today shows a single live foetus with normal anatomy, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the high risk of severe congenital malformation
options.rationale: This infection does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome, and the risk is transient fetal anaemia rather than structural anomaly, so this advice is factually wrong and would cause avoidable harm. Structural teratogenesis is the concern with rubella, not with this virus. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

options.text: Reassure her that the normal scan today excludes any risk to the foetus from this infection
options.rationale: Anaemia and hydrops typically develop two to six weeks after maternal infection, so a normal scan at 10 days provides no reassurance about the weeks that follow. A single normal scan is adequate only once the surveillance window has passed. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

options.text: Commence maternal intravenous immunoglobulin to prevent transplacental viral transmission
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no established role in preventing transmission or treating fetal infection with this virus, and no antiviral therapy exists. Treatment is directed at the consequence, fetal anaemia, rather than at the virus. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction to confirm fetal infection
options.rationale: Confirming fetal infection does not change management because surveillance and intervention are driven by evidence of anaemia rather than by the presence of viral genome. The procedure adds a miscarriage risk without altering the plan. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler for the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: The serology confirms recent maternal infection, and the risk to the foetus is aplastic anaemia leading to hydrops during a window of roughly two to 12 weeks afterwards, detected non-invasively by a rising peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery. Detecting anaemia before hydrops allows intrauterine transfusion, which is the intervention that saves these pregnancies. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy matters because the virus targets erythroid precursors, and the short fetal red cell lifespan combined with rapid expansion of red cell mass makes the foetus vulnerable to profound aplastic anaemia. Around half of adults are already immune, and IgG positivity with negative IgM indicates past infection and no risk. The virus is not teratogenic, so structural anomaly is not the concern; instead the risks are fetal anaemia, hydrops and loss, and these are greatest when infection occurs before 20 weeks. The interval from maternal infection to hydrops is typically two to six weeks and can extend to 12, which defines the surveillance period. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median identifies significant anaemia non-invasively and triggers referral for intrauterine transfusion, after which survival is good and long term outcomes for survivors are generally normal.
key_points: The virus causes fetal anaemia by suppressing erythroid precursors, not congenital malformation
IgG positive with IgM negative indicates past infection and immunity, requiring no action
Hydrops develops two to 12 weeks after maternal infection, so one normal scan is insufficient
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity detects anaemia non-invasively before hydrops appears
Intrauterine transfusion is the treatment and carries good survival when performed in time
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median is the trigger for referral for intrauterine transfusion, and it detects anaemia well before ascites or pericardial effusion appear on the scan.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital: Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus and Perinatal Infections

subtopic_detail: Febrile illness in the second trimester after high risk food exposure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 27 year old woman at 24 weeks who presents with three days of fever, aching muscles, headache and loose stools. She attended a family gathering five days ago where she ate soft cheese, prepacked sliced ham and a rockmelon fruit platter.

She reports normal fetal movements and no abdominal pain, no vaginal bleeding and no fluid loss. There is no dysuria and no frequency. On examination her chest is clear, there is no renal angle tenderness and the uterus is soft and non-tender. Urinalysis shows no nitrites, no leucocytes and no protein. A midstream urine has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 106/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 152/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), C-reactive protein 64 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures taken; cardiotocography not indicated at this gestation and fetal heart auscultated as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cephalexin for presumed urinary tract infection and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Her urinalysis is clean with no frequency, dysuria or loin tenderness, so a urinary source is unlikely, and cephalosporins have no reliable activity against Listeria monocytogenes. This regimen suits asymptomatic bacteriuria or cystitis in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral paracetamol and oral fluids and review if symptoms persist beyond a week
options.rationale: Symptomatic management alone risks missing an infection that can cause fetal loss, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis, and the classic presentation is precisely this non-specific febrile illness. Supportive care alone is reasonable only once a serious bacterial cause has been excluded. (Source: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy)
source_refs: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy

options.text: Take blood cultures and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin empirically
options.rationale: A febrile pregnant woman with a compatible food exposure and no other source must be treated empirically for listeriosis, because bacteraemia can seed the placenta and the maternal illness is often mild while fetal consequences are severe. High dose penicillin or amoxicillin is the treatment of choice and blood culture is the diagnostic test. (Source: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy)
source_refs: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy

options.text: Send stool for culture and withhold antibiotics until an organism has been identified
options.rationale: Stool culture is insensitive for this organism because it is a normal gut coloniser, and waiting for results allows placental infection to progress. Stool testing is more useful when a specific enteric pathogen outbreak is suspected. (Source: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy)
source_refs: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for culture to establish whether intrauterine infection has occurred
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is invasive, delays therapy and does not change the immediate decision to treat the mother with antibiotics. It has a role in suspected chorioamnionitis where the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and delivery timing depends on it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Listeriosis is uncommon but disproportionately affects pregnant women, who are roughly 10 to 20 times more susceptible than the general population because of the cell mediated immune changes of pregnancy. The maternal illness is typically mild and non-specific, presenting as fever with myalgia, headache and sometimes gastrointestinal upset, which means the diagnosis depends on maintaining a low threshold rather than on a distinctive clinical picture. The organism crosses the placenta and can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and severe early onset neonatal sepsis or meningitis, so the stakes are entirely fetal. Blood culture is the key investigation, and empirical high dose penicillin or amoxicillin should be started while results are pending because cephalosporins, the usual empirical choice in pregnancy, are intrinsically inactive against this organism. Prevention through food advice is the mainstay, avoiding soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and fruit, cold cured and sliced meats, pate, and chilled seafood.
key_points: Pregnancy markedly increases susceptibility while keeping the maternal illness mild and non-specific
Blood culture is the diagnostic test; stool culture is insensitive and unhelpful
Cephalosporins are intrinsically inactive, so standard empirical regimens fail
High dose penicillin or amoxicillin is the treatment of choice and should not await results
Consequences are predominantly fetal: miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis
explanation.pearls: Any unexplained fever in pregnancy warrants a blood culture and empirical amoxicillin cover for Listeria, because ceftriaxone, the reflex empirical choice, has no activity against it and a missed case can present later as neonatal meningitis.

sources.label: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Interpreting maternal serology after an abnormal second trimester ultrasound
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman at 22 weeks whose morphology scan reports fetal ventriculomegaly with periventricular echogenicity, an echogenic bowel and an abdominal circumference below the third centile. She has a two year old in childcare.

She recalls a week of sore throat and tiredness around 12 weeks that she attributed to a virus. She has had no rash and no known contact with anyone with a rash illness. Her booking serology showed rubella immunity, and syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV were negative. Serology now shows cytomegalovirus IgM positive with IgG positive and low IgG avidity.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Cytomegalovirus IgM positive, IgG positive, IgG avidity low; toxoplasma IgM negative; parvovirus B19 IgG positive with IgM negative; full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What does the serology result indicate and what should follow?

options.text: Past infection before conception, so the scan findings need an alternative explanation
options.rationale: Low avidity indicates recently acquired antibody, whereas past infection produces high avidity IgG, and this distinction is the entire purpose of the avidity assay. Past infection would make congenital disease much less likely but not impossible through reactivation. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy

options.text: A false positive IgM result, so serology should simply be repeated in four weeks
options.rationale: IgM alone can persist or cross react, which is why avidity testing is performed, and a low avidity result alongside the ultrasound findings makes a false positive an untenable explanation. Repeat testing without acting would waste the window for fetal assessment. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy

options.text: Recent primary maternal infection, and amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction
options.rationale: Low IgG avidity with positive IgM dates the infection to within roughly the preceding three months, matching her illness at 12 weeks, and the ultrasound findings raise the probability of fetal infection substantially. Amniocentesis after 21 weeks and at least six weeks from maternal infection confirms fetal infection and guides counselling and neonatal planning. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Prenatal Assessment of Congenital Infection

options.text: Recent primary maternal infection, and immediate delivery to allow neonatal antiviral therapy
options.rationale: Delivery at 22 weeks is not viable and antiviral therapy does not reverse established central nervous system damage, so this offers no benefit at enormous cost. Neonatal antiviral treatment is considered after birth at term in symptomatic congenital infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Assessment of Congenital Infection)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Assessment of Congenital Infection

options.text: Reactivation of latent maternal infection, which carries no meaningful risk to the foetus
options.rationale: Reactivation carries a much lower transmission risk than primary infection but is not risk free, and the low avidity here points to primary rather than recurrent infection. Distinguishing the two matters because it changes the counselling on transmission probability substantially. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, yet routine antenatal screening is not recommended in Australia because there is no proven intervention that reliably prevents transmission. Primary maternal infection carries a transmission risk of roughly 30 to 40 per cent, far higher than reactivation or reinfection, so distinguishing the two determines the counselling. Because IgM can persist for months and cross react, avidity testing is essential: low avidity indicates infection within about the last three months, while high avidity effectively excludes recent primary infection. Amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction is the diagnostic test for fetal infection and should be performed after 21 weeks and at least six weeks after the estimated maternal infection to avoid false negatives from delayed fetal urinary excretion. Ultrasound and fetal MRI findings such as ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcification, microcephaly and growth restriction predict symptomatic disease, and prevention rests on hygiene advice for women with young children in childcare.
key_points: Primary maternal infection carries a transmission risk of about 30 to 40 per cent
IgG avidity dates the infection: low avidity means recent primary infection
Amniocentesis is performed after 21 weeks and at least six weeks after maternal infection
Ultrasound abnormalities predict symptomatic congenital disease and guide counselling
It is the leading infectious cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Hand hygiene after handling a toddler's saliva, nappies or toys is the only proven preventive measure, since young children in childcare shed the virus for months and are the usual source of maternal primary infection.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital: Cytomegalovirus in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Prenatal Assessment of Congenital Infection

subtopic_detail: Antenatal planning for a woman with type 3 female genital cutting
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy. She was born in Somalia, arrived in Australia four years ago, and underwent genital cutting as a young child in her country of birth.

Through a professional interpreter she describes taking several minutes to pass urine and having had three urinary infections in the past year. She has never had a vaginal examination and is frightened about giving birth. With her consent, examination shows a horizontal band of scar tissue across the vaginal opening with a residual aperture of approximately 1 cm, and no ulceration or discharge. Her uterus is consistent with dates and the pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Horizontal scar band across the introitus with a residual aperture of about 1 cm; no ulceration, no discharge, no cyst; uterus consistent with 22 weeks

options.text: Arrange elective caesarean at 39 weeks to avoid perineal complications entirely
options.rationale: Cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean, and operative birth exposes her to surgical risk while leaving the urinary symptoms and the narrowed opening unaddressed for the future. Caesarean is reserved for the usual obstetric indications. (Source: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting

options.text: Defer any action antenatally and perform deinfibulation during the second stage
options.rationale: Deinfibulation in the second stage is possible but is performed under pressure, with less adequate analgesia and no opportunity for counselling or consent in advance. It is the fallback when a woman presents in labour undiagnosed, not the planned approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting

options.text: Offer antenatal deinfibulation performed by a clinician experienced in the procedure
options.rationale: Opening the scar in the second trimester, with an accredited interpreter and full informed consent, relieves the urinary symptoms, allows vaginal examination and monitoring in labour, and reduces the risk of obstructed birth and severe tearing. Performing it antenatally rather than during labour permits proper analgesia, counselling and healing. (Source: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting
Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception Guidance

options.text: Notify police, since her circumstances require mandatory reporting of an offence
options.rationale: Reporting an adult woman for a procedure performed on her as a child in another country is neither required nor appropriate and would destroy the therapeutic relationship. Child protection obligations arise if a female child is judged to be at risk, which is a separate assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting

options.text: Plan a midline episiotomy at birth without prior examination or discussion with her
options.rationale: A midline incision through scarred tissue risks extension into the anal sphincter, and an anterior rather than midline incision is used when deinfibulation is needed at birth. Proceeding without prior discussion also removes her consent from a decision with lasting consequences. (Source: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting

explanation.summary: Female genital mutilation and cutting is classified into four types, of which type 3, involving narrowing of the vaginal opening by creating a covering seal, carries the greatest obstetric and urological consequences. Australia has a substantial population of women affected by procedures performed overseas before migration, and the clinical priorities are respectful communication through an accredited interpreter rather than a family member, accurate documentation of the type, and a plan made well before labour. Antenatal deinfibulation, usually offered in the second trimester, relieves urinary and menstrual difficulty, permits vaginal examination and fetal monitoring, and reduces the risk of obstructed labour, severe perineal tearing and postpartum haemorrhage. Performing the procedure in an unhurried antenatal setting allows adequate analgesia, informed consent and time to heal, whereas doing it in the second stage is a fallback for women who present undiagnosed. Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful in Australia, and clinicians should discuss this sensitively while assessing whether any female children in the family are at risk, which is a child protection rather than a policing question.
key_points: Type 3 cutting narrows the vaginal opening and causes urinary, menstrual and obstetric problems
Use an accredited interpreter rather than a family member for these consultations
Antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester is preferred to opening the scar in labour
Cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean section
Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful, and child protection concerns are assessed separately
explanation.pearls: If deinfibulation is required at birth, the incision is made anteriorly along the midline of the scar rather than as a posterior midline episiotomy, because cutting posteriorly through scarred tissue readily extends into the anal sphincter.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Female Genital Mutilation and Cutting
Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception Guidance

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain in the third trimester with a non-diagnostic ultrasound
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 28 year old woman at 27 weeks who has had 18 hours of abdominal pain that began around the umbilicus and has settled into the right side of her abdomen, higher than she expected. She has vomited twice and has eaten nothing since yesterday.

She reports normal fetal movements, no vaginal bleeding, no fluid loss and no contractions. There is no dysuria, frequency or loin pain. On examination she is tender in the right flank and right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding, and the uterus is soft and non-tender between palpations. Urinalysis shows no nitrites, no leucocytes and no blood, and ultrasound reports the appendix not visualised, no renal tract dilatation and normal fetal biometry.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 104/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), neutrophils 12.6 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), lipase within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to define the cause of her abdominal pain
options.rationale: CT would answer the question but delivers ionising radiation to the foetus when an equally accurate alternative without radiation is available. It is reserved for situations where that alternative is unavailable and the diagnosis cannot safely wait. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in Pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange MRI of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast and involve the surgical team
options.rationale: When ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix in a pregnant woman with a compatible history, non-contrast MRI is the recommended next imaging test because it is accurate, avoids ionising radiation and reliably excludes the alternatives. Early surgical involvement matters because delay markedly increases the risk of perforation and fetal loss. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for pyelonephritis and reassess her again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis is a common differential in pregnancy but typically produces loin tenderness with an abnormal urinalysis, and hers is entirely clean. Treating empirically for the wrong diagnosis would consume the hours in which perforation risk rises steeply. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in 12 hours and manage her pain with regular simple analgesia
options.rationale: Non-visualisation of the appendix is expected in the second half of pregnancy as the caecum is displaced and bowel gas obscures the view, so repeating the same test is unlikely to add information. Serial ultrasound is reasonable only when the clinical suspicion is low. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in Pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without further imaging being performed first
options.rationale: Operating without imaging accepts a substantial negative exploration rate and its associated risk of preterm labour when a safe and accurate test is available. Immediate surgery is justified when there is peritonism or haemodynamic instability suggesting perforation. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Appendicitis is the most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy, and it is dangerous precisely because pregnancy erodes every diagnostic anchor the clinician normally relies on. The enlarging uterus displaces the caecum upwards and laterally so pain localises higher than the usual point, nausea and anorexia are attributed to pregnancy itself, and a mild leucocytosis is physiological with the upper limit rising to around 16 x10^9/L, so the white cell count loses much of its discriminating value. Ultrasound is the appropriate first imaging test but frequently fails to visualise the appendix after the first trimester, and non-visualisation must not be read as a negative result. Non-contrast MRI is the recommended second line, with accuracy comparable to CT and no ionising radiation, and it also identifies alternative causes. The stakes justify the urgency, since fetal loss rates rise from a few per cent with simple appendicitis to well over 20 per cent once perforation occurs, and delay to theatre is the main driver of perforation.
key_points: The appendix is displaced upwards, so pain localises higher than the classic point
A white cell count up to about 16 x10^9/L is physiological in pregnancy
Non-visualisation of the appendix on ultrasound is common and does not exclude the diagnosis
Non-contrast MRI is the recommended second line test, avoiding ionising radiation
Perforation raises fetal loss from a few per cent to over 20 per cent
explanation.pearls: Delay to theatre, not the operation itself, drives the harm: fetal loss climbs above 20 per cent once perforation occurs, so a pregnant woman with a compatible history and a non-diagnostic ultrasound needs MRI the same day rather than overnight observation.

subtopic_detail: Offensive discharge and bleeding in a woman using a vaginal support device
stem:
An 81 year old woman is brought to your clinic by her daughter with six weeks of blood stained, offensive vaginal discharge. She has had a ring pessary in place for uterovaginal prolapse and has not attended for review in almost three years after her usual clinic appointments lapsed.

She has no pain, no fever and no urinary symptoms, and is otherwise well and independent. On speculum examination the pessary is in situ and the vaginal walls are thin and pale, with a 2 cm area of granulation and superficial ulceration at the posterior fornix where the device sits. The cervix appears healthy. There is no mass palpable abdominally and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Ring pessary in situ, no offensive necrotic tissue beyond the ulcerated area, uterus not descended below the introitus with the pessary removed, no adnexal masses palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the pessary in place, prescribe an antifungal pessary and review in six weeks
options.rationale: The appearance is of mechanical erosion rather than candidiasis, and leaving the device in place allows the ulceration to deepen and potentially fistulate. Antifungal therapy would be appropriate for typical curd-like discharge with vulval itch. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Refer for urgent vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair as definitive prolapse treatment
options.rationale: Surgery is not the immediate answer to a pessary related erosion, which usually heals with device removal and topical oestrogen, and it carries substantial risk at her age. Surgical repair is considered later if she cannot tolerate a device and remains symptomatic. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Remove the pessary, commence topical vaginal oestrogen, and biopsy any non-healing lesion
options.rationale: Erosion from a neglected pessary heals once the pressure is removed and the atrophic epithelium is restored with topical oestrogen, and a planned review allows reinsertion once the vagina is healed. Biopsy of a lesion that does not heal is essential because vaginal carcinoma can present identically in this age group. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Replace the pessary with a larger size to reduce movement and prescribe oral antibiotics
options.rationale: A larger device increases the pressure on already ulcerated tissue and worsens the erosion, and there is no cellulitis or systemic infection to justify antibiotics. Size adjustment is done at a routine review on healthy vaginal skin. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness before any local treatment
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is the priority when postmenopausal bleeding has no visible local cause, whereas here a visible ulcerated lesion explains the bleeding and must be addressed and sampled. Imaging would follow if bleeding continued after the erosion healed. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Vaginal pessaries are an effective and underused conservative treatment for pelvic organ prolapse, particularly in older women or those unsuitable for surgery, but they require ongoing review because complications arise almost entirely from neglect. Standard practice is removal, inspection and cleaning at intervals of three to six months, with topical oestrogen used in postmenopausal women to maintain epithelial thickness and reduce erosion. A neglected device can cause ulceration, bleeding, offensive discharge, incarceration, and in extreme cases fistula formation into the bladder or rectum. The critical safety principle is that a visible lesion in a postmenopausal woman must never simply be attributed to the device: vaginal and cervical malignancy present with identical bleeding and discharge, so any area that fails to heal after removal and oestrogen therapy requires biopsy. Once healed, the pessary can usually be refitted successfully with a structured review schedule.
key_points: Pessaries need review every three to six months; complications arise from neglect
Topical oestrogen in postmenopausal women reduces erosion and improves tolerance
Remove the device to allow erosion to heal rather than replacing or upsizing it
A lesion that fails to heal must be biopsied to exclude vaginal carcinoma
Neglected devices can become incarcerated or erode into the bladder or rectum
explanation.pearls: Never attribute postmenopausal bleeding to a pessary without a plan to reassess: re-examine four to six weeks after removal and topical oestrogen, and biopsy anything still present, because vaginal carcinoma mimics erosion exactly.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

subtopic_detail: Painful vulval and vaginal erosions with scarring in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 61 year old woman attends your clinic with 14 months of vulval soreness and burning that is worse on urination and makes intercourse impossible. She has tried two courses of antifungal cream and a barrier ointment without benefit.

She also reports painful gums that bleed when brushing and a rough patch inside her cheek. On examination there is loss of the labia minora with early adhesion of the introitus, and glazed red erosions with a fine white lacy border at the introitus and lower vagina. The clitoral hood is not fused and there are no white parchment-like plaques on the perineum or perianal skin. A vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogens.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions at the introitus and lower vagina with a reticulate white border; loss of labia minora; buccal mucosa shows a white lacy pattern; no perianal involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an extended course of oral fluconazole for resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.rationale: Two antifungal courses have failed and swabs show no candida, so continuing this line ignores the negative result and the mucosal findings elsewhere. Extended fluconazole is appropriate for microbiologically confirmed recurrent candidiasis. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review the symptoms after three months
options.rationale: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes pallor, dryness and thinning rather than glazed erosions with a lacy white border, and it does not affect the mouth. Vaginal oestrogen is a useful adjunct here but will not control the underlying inflammatory disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the introital adhesions before any medical treatment starts
options.rationale: Operating on actively inflamed mucosa leads to recurrent scarring and poor healing, so inflammation must be controlled first. Surgery has a limited role later for persistent adhesions once the disease is quiescent. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Prescribe an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid and arrange biopsy with long term review
options.rationale: Erosive mucosal disease with a reticulate white border affecting both the vulva and the mouth requires an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid as first line therapy, with biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy given the long duration. Lifelong surveillance is needed because of a recognised risk of squamous cell carcinoma in affected skin. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

options.text: Prescribe topical lidocaine gel and refer to a pelvic pain service for vulvodynia management
options.rationale: Vulvodynia is defined by pain without visible pathology, and she has clear erosions, scarring and mucosal disease, so a pain-only pathway would leave destructive inflammation untreated. Topical anaesthetic is a symptomatic adjunct at best. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen planus and lichen sclerosus are the two inflammatory dermatoses that scar the vulva, and separating them matters because the erosive form of lichen planus involves the vagina and other mucosal surfaces while lichen sclerosus does not. Lichen sclerosus produces white parchment-like plaques in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus with clitoral hood fusion, whereas erosive lichen planus produces glazed red erosions with a reticulate white border at the introitus and in the vagina, often with oral involvement and gingivitis. Vaginal involvement is important because adhesions can obliterate the vagina entirely if untreated. Both conditions are treated first line with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, usually as a reducing regimen, and both carry a small but definite risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma that mandates ongoing review. Biopsy is indicated where the diagnosis is uncertain, where disease fails to respond to adequate treatment, or where a lesion looks suspicious.
key_points: Erosive lichen planus involves the vagina and mouth; lichen sclerosus spares both
A reticulate white border around glazed erosions is the characteristic sign
Lichen sclerosus shows a figure of eight distribution with perianal involvement and hood fusion
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line for both conditions
Both carry a risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma requiring long term surveillance
explanation.pearls: Vaginal involvement is what makes erosive lichen planus dangerous: untreated adhesions can obliterate the vagina, so vaginal dilators and topical corticosteroid are used alongside vulval treatment rather than after it.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

subtopic_detail: Interpreting an abnormal thyroid stimulating hormone in early pregnancy
stem:
You review a 32 year old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy who had thyroid function tested by her general practitioner because of fatigue. She has no goitre, no cold intolerance, no constipation and no dry skin, and her weight is stable.

She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease and has never had neck irradiation. She takes a pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine. On examination her pulse is regular, there is no tremor, no lid lag and no palpable thyroid enlargement. She is anxious about the result and asks whether her baby will be affected.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 5.8 mIU/L (pregnancy specific upper limit for the first trimester 4.0), free thyroxine 13.1 pmol/L (10.0-20.0), thyroid peroxidase antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence levothyroxine now and repeat thyroid function testing in four weeks
options.rationale: A thyroid stimulating hormone above the pregnancy specific reference limit with a normal free thyroxine and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies is the combination in which treatment is recommended, because antibody positivity predicts progression to overt hypothyroidism as gestational demand rises. Repeat testing at four weeks allows titration during the period of greatest fetal dependence. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function test in the second trimester without commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Deferring treatment wastes the first trimester, during which the foetus depends entirely on maternal thyroxine for neurodevelopment, and antibody positivity makes deterioration likely rather than possible. Watchful waiting is reasonable only when antibodies are negative and the elevation is marginal. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that the result is normal for pregnancy and requires no further action
options.rationale: This misreads the reference interval, since the pregnancy specific upper limit is lower than the non-pregnant one because human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the thyroid and suppresses the pituitary hormone. A value of 5.8 mIU/L is therefore clearly abnormal in the first trimester. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake scanning to define the underlying cause
options.rationale: Radionuclide scanning is contraindicated in pregnancy and ultrasound does not alter management when the antibody result already indicates autoimmune thyroiditis. Imaging is indicated for a palpable nodule or goitre. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Increase her dietary iodine intake and recheck thyroid function after eight weeks
options.rationale: She already takes an iodine containing supplement, and iodine repletion does not correct autoimmune thyroid failure. Dietary iodine advice addresses deficiency in populations with inadequate intake rather than antibody mediated disease. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Thyroid physiology changes substantially in pregnancy, with human chorionic gonadotropin weakly stimulating the thyroid receptor and thereby suppressing the pituitary hormone, so pregnancy specific reference intervals are lower than non-pregnant ones and applying the wrong interval is a frequent source of error. Subclinical hypothyroidism means an elevated thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine, and the decision to treat rests substantially on thyroid peroxidase antibody status, since antibody positive women are far more likely to progress to overt hypothyroidism as gestational demand increases. Fetal thyroid hormone production does not begin until around 12 weeks, so the developing brain depends entirely on maternal supply through the first trimester, which is why treatment is started promptly rather than deferred. Women already on levothyroxine before conception typically require a dose increase of 25 to 30 per cent as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Antibody positive women also carry an increased risk of postpartum thyroiditis and need thyroid function checked after delivery.
key_points: Pregnancy specific reference intervals are lower; using non-pregnant ranges causes missed diagnoses
Thyroid peroxidase antibody status drives the treatment decision in subclinical hypothyroidism
The fetal thyroid does not function until around 12 weeks, so early maternal supply is critical
Radionuclide scanning is contraindicated during pregnancy
Antibody positive women require postpartum thyroid function testing
explanation.pearls: A woman already taking levothyroxine needs roughly a 25 to 30 per cent dose increase from the moment pregnancy is confirmed, most simply achieved by taking two extra tablets per week while awaiting formal review.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Antiseizure medication review in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 27 year old woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures attends your clinic to discuss becoming pregnant in the next year. She has been seizure free for four years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having previously failed a trial of levetiracetam because of intolerable irritability.

She drives to work and describes her independence as very important to her. She takes no other medicines and does not smoke or drink. She has read online that her medicine is dangerous in pregnancy and has already stopped taking it three days ago without telling anyone. She has had no seizures since stopping and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, ceased three days ago by the patient; no folate supplement; no other regular medicines

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Advise her to restart her medicine today and arrange urgent neurology review for a planned switch
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal risks breakthrough seizures and status epilepticus, which carry greater immediate danger to her than the teratogenic risk of a medicine taken before conception, so restarting while a supervised change is organised is the safest step. A cross-taper to a lower risk agent is then planned with contraception maintained until she is stable. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy)

options.text: Support her decision to remain off treatment given four years of seizure freedom
options.rationale: Seizure freedom on treatment is not evidence that treatment can be stopped, and withdrawal after four years still carries a substantial relapse rate that is highest in the first months. Planned withdrawal is a specialist decision made with driving and safety implications discussed in advance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence high dose folic acid and advise her to conceive as soon as possible while off treatment
options.rationale: Folate is important but does not protect against seizures, and encouraging conception during an unsupervised medication gap places both her and a pregnancy at risk. Folate should be started once a stable regimen is in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy)

options.text: Substitute levetiracetam at full dose today given her plan to conceive within the year
options.rationale: An abrupt switch without cross-tapering risks breakthrough seizures, and she has already failed this agent for behavioural side effects, making it a poor choice without specialist reassessment. Any change requires overlapping titration under supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange serum valproate concentration measurement before deciding on any change to therapy
options.rationale: Drug levels do not guide management here because she has already stopped the medicine and the decision rests on seizure risk rather than concentration. Levels are more useful for assessing adherence or toxicity during ongoing therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiseizure medicines, with major congenital malformation rates around 10 per cent and a substantial risk of impaired neurodevelopment in exposed children, which is why regulatory authorities require that it not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other options have failed and pregnancy prevention is in place. The clinical dilemma arises when a woman is well controlled on it, because abrupt cessation is genuinely dangerous and uncontrolled generalised seizures in pregnancy risk maternal injury, fetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The correct approach is never to stop abruptly but to restart, then cross-taper to a lower risk agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam under specialist supervision, with effective contraception maintained throughout the change and until control is confirmed. High dose folic acid is recommended before conception for women taking antiseizure medicines. Pregnancy itself alters drug handling, and lamotrigine concentrations in particular fall substantially, requiring dose increases and postpartum reduction.
key_points: Never stop an antiseizure medicine abruptly; withdrawal seizures are the immediate danger
Valproate carries roughly a 10 per cent malformation rate plus neurodevelopmental risk
Changing agents requires a supervised cross-taper with contraception maintained throughout
