explanation.pearls: In the primary HPV NCSP algorithm an isolated cytology finding on an HPV-negative sample does not change management - the five-year negative predictive value for CIN3 or worse of an HPV-negative sample exceeds 99%.

sources.label: RACGP Red Book preventive health guide

subtopic_detail: Lactational breast abscess management with ongoing breastfeeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman four weeks postpartum. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her first baby who is thriving on the 50th centile. Three days ago she felt a hard painful red patch in her left upper outer quadrant and was started on oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day and warm compresses by an out-of-hours doctor.

Despite good adherence, her fever has continued and the area has now formed a distinct rounded lump that is tender and fluctuant. She has not had chills for the last six hours. She is otherwise well, without cellulitis beyond the affected quadrant, no nipple crack and no rash. She is very keen to continue breastfeeding and is still latching the baby to the affected breast, which is painful but tolerated.

Bedside ultrasound performed in your clinic shows a 3.5 cm x 2.8 cm hypoechoic collection with internal echoes at 3 cm depth, with no involvement of the areola.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.3 degC
data_table.Examination: Erythema and induration left upper outer quadrant, discrete 3.5 cm fluctuant lump, no cellulitis beyond quadrant, no lymphangitis, no crack in the nipple
data_table.Investigations: Bedside breast ultrasound: 3.5 cm x 2.8 cm hypoechoic collection with internal echoes at 3 cm depth, no involvement of the areola

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral flucloxacillin at the same dose and add oral metronidazole for anaerobic cover, reviewing her in clinic at 72 hours before considering drainage
options.rationale: A drainable collection larger than 3 cm will not resolve with oral antibiotics alone. Delayed drainage risks sinus formation, further breast tissue destruction and possible skin ulceration. Antibiotic modification without drainage is insufficient once fluctuance and imaging confirm an abscess. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

options.text: Perform ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration under local anaesthesia, send pus for culture, continue oral flucloxacillin and support ongoing breastfeeding
options.rationale: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is the first-line drainage for a lactational breast abscess under about 5 cm without skin necrosis. It preserves cosmesis, permits ongoing breastfeeding, and carries lower recurrence than incision. Antibiotics remain because the surrounding tissue is still cellulitic. Culture guides ongoing therapy. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update
eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Arrange emergency incision and drainage in theatre under general anaesthesia and advise the mother to formula-feed the baby until the surgical wound has fully healed
options.rationale: Formal incision and drainage under general anaesthesia is reserved for large abscesses over 5 cm, abscesses with skin necrosis, or those that fail image-guided aspiration. Cessation of breastfeeding increases the risk of milk stasis and recurrence and is not required for either drainage approach. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

options.text: Advise complete cessation of breastfeeding on the affected side, prescribe cabergoline to suppress milk supply, and continue oral flucloxacillin without drainage
options.rationale: Cabergoline suppression is contraindicated by the patient's clear preference to continue breastfeeding and is medically unnecessary. Ongoing milk removal from the affected breast (feeding, hand expression) accelerates resolution. The abscess still requires drainage. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Refer for urgent core biopsy of the mass to exclude inflammatory breast carcinoma before proceeding to any percutaneous or surgical drainage of the lesion
options.rationale: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is a red-flag differential in non-lactating women with erythema and peau d'orange, or when a suspected abscess does not resolve after adequate drainage and antibiotics. It is not the first-line workup for a fluctuant lump with a clear ultrasound abscess appearance in the fourth postpartum week. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis affects around 15% of breastfeeding women in the first six weeks. Most cases respond to milk removal, warm compresses and oral flucloxacillin, but a proportion progress to abscess formation and require drainage. Bedside ultrasound is diagnostic and quantifies size. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration is first-line for abscesses under about 5 cm without skin necrosis; it preserves cosmesis, allows continued breastfeeding, and has an aspiration-to-cure rate over 80% with repeat aspirations as needed. Larger abscesses, skin necrosis, or aspiration failure escalate to formal incision and drainage. Breastfeeding from the affected breast should continue where tolerated, as milk stasis worsens outcomes and expressed milk supports supply.
key_points: Mastitis unresponsive to 48-72 hours of antibiotics and milk removal warrants ultrasound to look for abscess.
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is first line for lactational abscess under 5 cm without skin necrosis.
Continue breastfeeding from the affected breast; formula-only is not indicated.
Repeat aspirations may be needed every 2-3 days until pus has resolved.
Non-resolving mass after adequate drainage and antibiotics: consider inflammatory breast cancer and refer for imaging plus biopsy.
explanation.pearls: A hypoechoic collection over 3 cm with internal echoes on bedside ultrasound is a lactational abscess until proven otherwise - continue flucloxacillin, aspirate under ultrasound guidance, and keep the mother breastfeeding on the affected side.

sources.label: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update
eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for Group B streptococcus with previous affected sibling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman at 36 plus 3 weeks in the antenatal clinic. Her first baby, now three years old, had culture-confirmed Group B streptococcal early-onset sepsis at 20 hours of life and made a full recovery after IV benzylpenicillin. In her current pregnancy the routine 36 week rectovaginal screening swab reports Group B streptococcus not detected.

She has no known drug allergies, no significant medical history, and no prior preterm birth. Her BMI is 24 kg/m^2. She is planning a vaginal birth in a public tertiary hospital with continuous CTG monitoring available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Antenatal screening: 36-week rectovaginal Group B streptococcus swab: NOT detected; urine culture from booking negative
data_table.Obstetric history: First baby with culture-confirmed early-onset GBS sepsis at 20 hours; treated to recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every four hours until birth, commenced in labour or at membrane rupture whichever is earlier during this admission
options.rationale: Previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a RANZCOG standalone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis irrespective of current screening. First-line agent is IV benzylpenicillin with a 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g four-hourly, starting in established labour or at membrane rupture, and continuing until birth. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is required because the current 36-week rectovaginal swab is negative and screening supersedes prior obstetric history
options.rationale: A previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a standalone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of the current pregnancy's screening result. The vertical transmission risk is judged too high to rely on culture alone. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times a day from 37 weeks continued until the onset of labour to eradicate any low-level Group B streptococcal genital colonisation
options.rationale: Antenatal oral antibiotics do not durably eradicate GBS colonisation and are not part of the Australian prophylaxis pathway. Intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis is what reduces vertical transmission and early-onset disease. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg every eight hours from admission in labour, given the severity of the Group B streptococcal disease that occurred in her previous baby
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for women with a documented immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin AND either clindamycin resistance on GBS isolate or clindamycin susceptibility unknown. Severity of prior disease does not change the first-line agent. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 39 weeks to bypass the birth canal and avoid the need for any intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis during her labour
options.rationale: A prior baby with GBS sepsis is not itself an indication for caesarean. Elective caesarean on intact membranes before labour eliminates the immediate intrapartum transmission risk but does not obviate GBS prophylaxis in women with strong risk factors, and adds surgical morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

explanation.summary: Group B streptococcus colonises the maternal genital tract in around 20% of Australian women and is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. RANZCOG endorses a risk-and-screening hybrid: 35-37 week rectovaginal swab identifies most carriers, with intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin offered to carriers, women with GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, women with a previous baby who had invasive GBS disease, and unbooked women in preterm labour or with prolonged rupture of membranes over 18 hours or intrapartum fever above 38 degrees regardless of screening. Effective prophylaxis requires the first dose at least four hours before birth. Alternative agents are chosen by penicillin allergy severity and antibiogram.
key_points: Previous baby with invasive GBS disease = standalone indication for IAP regardless of current swab.
First-line IAP: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth.
Effective prophylaxis requires at least four hours between first dose and delivery.
Penicillin non-severe hypersensitivity: cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours.
Penicillin severe hypersensitivity: clindamycin if isolate susceptible, otherwise IV vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: A prior baby with invasive GBS disease overrides a negative current-pregnancy swab: give IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every four hours from established labour or rupture of membranes, aiming for at least four hours before birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

subtopic_detail: Investigation pathway after three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman in the outpatient clinic. She and her partner have had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages over the last two years at 8, 6 and 9 weeks; all were confirmed with a positive urine pregnancy test and each was managed expectantly with confirmed complete miscarriage on transvaginal ultrasound.

She has regular 28 day menstrual cycles and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m^2, she does not smoke or drink alcohol and takes no medications. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her partner is fit and well.

She saw a naturopath privately and had a karyotype on the tissue from the most recent loss which reports a euploid 46 XY specimen.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Non-tender abdomen; normal external genitalia; uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual
data_table.Prior investigations: Product of conception karyotype from third loss: 46 XY euploid

lead_in: Which set of investigations is most appropriate as first-line workup?

options.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing and detailed semen analysis as first-line, deferring maternal blood work until the paternal contribution has been clarified
options.rationale: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not routinely recommended in recurrent pregnancy loss workup and has an uncertain evidence base for changing management. Maternal-side treatable causes take priority. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C and S, antithrombin, homocysteine and MTHFR polymorphism screen only
options.rationale: Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is NOT recommended in recurrent miscarriage: results do not alter management, MTHFR is now specifically discouraged, and false positives lead to unnecessary anticoagulation exposure. Reserve for a personal or family VTE history. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: TORCH serology, cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, and toxoplasma IgG and IgM as the initial workup before any structural investigation
options.rationale: TORCH infections are not causes of recurrent first-trimester miscarriage. Screening produces prevalence findings without therapeutic implications and delays workup of the causes that do matter. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis with bacterial and mycoplasma culture and empirical treatment with a two-week course of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: The evidence for chronic endometritis as a cause of recurrent pregnancy loss and for empirical doxycycline is limited and this is not a RANZCOG first-line investigation. Consider only in the context of investigation-negative recurrent loss with tertiary specialist input. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody screen on two occasions twelve weeks apart, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and pelvic imaging with three-dimensional ultrasound or hysterosalpingography
options.rationale: RANZCOG and ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines identify treatable causes: antiphospholipid syndrome (needs two positive tests 12 weeks apart), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced translocations and uterine cavity anomalies. This is the evidence-based first-line panel that changes management. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined by RANZCOG as three or more consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. The evidence-based workup targets treatable or prognostically important conditions: antiphospholipid syndrome (repeat testing 12 weeks apart to satisfy classification criteria), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced chromosomal translocations, and uterine cavity anomalies (septum, submucosal fibroid, adhesions). Approximately half of couples end investigation with no identified cause; supportive care with early-pregnancy ultrasound in the next conception is offered and cumulative live-birth rates remain reasonable. Empirical progesterone (400 mg vaginally twice daily) started with a positive test may be offered per the RANZCOG algorithm to women with a history of recurrent miscarriage and early pregnancy bleeding.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage per RANZCOG: three or more consecutive first-trimester losses.
First-line workup: APLS (twice, 12 weeks apart), TFTs, parental karyotype, uterine cavity imaging.
Routine inherited thrombophilia and MTHFR screening are NOT recommended.
Empirical vaginal progesterone can be offered when bleeding occurs in the next pregnancy.
About 50% remain unexplained; supportive care and early scan the primary intervention.
explanation.pearls: Do NOT order MTHFR or routine thrombophilia in recurrent miscarriage - the evidence supports lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus anti-beta-2 glycoprotein-I repeated at 12 weeks, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and uterine cavity imaging.

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia detected at second trimester scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old primigravida in the maternal-fetal medicine clinic at 32 plus 4 weeks. Her pregnancy was conceived by fresh embryo transfer following IVF and has been otherwise uncomplicated with a normal fetal anomaly scan.

A tertiary transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler was arranged after the 20 week anomaly scan reported a low-lying velamentous cord insertion. Today's scan confirms a velamentous cord insertion in the lower posterior segment with a fetal vessel running unprotected across the internal os on colour Doppler. The placenta is otherwise 3.6 cm from the internal os and there is no morbidly adherent appearance.

She has no bleeding, no contractions and no rupture of membranes. Booking bloods and glucose tolerance test are normal. Fetal growth is on the 55th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler and reactive cardiotocograph. She lives 45 minutes from the tertiary hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, fetal heart rate 138 /min
data_table.Ultrasound: Velamentous cord insertion, fetal vessel over internal os (vasa praevia); placental edge 3.6 cm from os; EFW 55th centile; UA Doppler normal; AFI 14 cm
data_table.CTG: Baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit at 32 weeks for inpatient monitoring with a completed course of antenatal corticosteroids, aim for planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends inpatient admission for confirmed vasa praevia from around 30-32 weeks with a completed corticosteroid course, given the risk of catastrophic fetal haemorrhage at rupture of membranes. Planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks balances perinatal exsanguination risk against prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Continue outpatient antenatal follow-up with weekly CTG from 36 weeks, aim for spontaneous labour and vaginal birth at term with continuous intrapartum monitoring
options.rationale: Vaginal birth in vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50% because rupture of the fetal vessel at membrane rupture leads to rapid fetal exsanguination. Planned caesarean before labour is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange an emergency cervical cerclage at 33 weeks to reinforce the lower uterine segment, and plan spontaneous vaginal birth at term
options.rationale: Cerclage does not treat vasa praevia and is not indicated. The condition is a fetal vessel problem, not a cervical competency problem. Vaginal birth remains contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks with amniotomy avoided until the presenting part is well applied, and immediate caesarean for any bleeding
options.rationale: Attempted vaginal birth places the foetus at unacceptable risk of exsanguination at any spontaneous or artificial membrane rupture. Induction of labour does not mitigate this risk and is contrary to RANZCOG guidance. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean at 39 weeks after a second course of corticosteroids at 38 weeks to minimise iatrogenic prematurity
options.rationale: Delaying planned caesarean to 39 weeks in vasa praevia substantially increases the probability of spontaneous labour or rupture of membranes with catastrophic fetal haemorrhage. RANZCOG recommends birth by 35+6 weeks. Two courses of corticosteroids beyond 34 weeks are not routine. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os, either from a velamentous cord insertion (type I) or between placental lobes in a bilobed or succenturiate placenta (type II). Antenatal diagnosis by second-trimester ultrasound with follow-up transvaginal colour Doppler transforms outcomes: undiagnosed vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50%, diagnosed cases with planned caesarean carry a survival rate approaching 100%. RANZCOG advises inpatient admission from 30-32 weeks (individualised for distance from hospital and clinical stability), a completed corticosteroid course, and planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks. Emergency caesarean with massive transfusion capability follows any antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes or spontaneous labour.
key_points: Vasa praevia carries perinatal mortality above 50% when undiagnosed; near 100% survival with planned birth.
Type I: velamentous cord insertion. Type II: vessels between lobes.
Admit from 30-32 weeks; complete antenatal corticosteroids by 34 weeks.
Planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks (SMFM 34-37, RANZCOG typically 34-36).
Emergency caesarean for any bleeding, rupture of membranes, or labour.
explanation.pearls: In a confirmed vasa praevia, plan the caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after an antenatal corticosteroid course and admit the mother from around 32 weeks - waiting until 39 weeks converts a survivable situation into a fetal exsanguination emergency.

subtopic_detail: Post-caesarean pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in obesity
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman on the postnatal ward six hours after an emergency in-labour caesarean for fetal distress. She is her second baby. Her BMI at booking was 41 kg/m^2 and her measured weight today is 118 kg. She had gestational diabetes managed with insulin.

She had a category 2 caesarean at 39 plus 2 weeks under spinal anaesthesia; the estimated blood loss was 900 mL and the wound was closed with staples. She lost 1300 mL total by 4 hours postpartum but her haemodynamics and urine output are now stable, she is not bleeding actively per vaginam, and the postnatal haemoglobin is 105 g/L.

She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no known thrombophilia, and no current epidural in situ. She is exclusively breastfeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Postnatal bloods: Haemoglobin 105 g/L (115-165), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), INR 1.0
data_table.Anticoagulant history: No anticoagulation antepartum; last thromboprophylaxis assessment antenatally scored as intermediate risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for six weeks as VTE prophylaxis rather than low molecular weight heparin because of the risk of postpartum haemorrhage after this caesarean
options.rationale: Aspirin is not an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent under RANZCOG or RCOG guidance. Low molecular weight heparin at a weight-adjusted dose is standard for postpartum women meeting risk thresholds, once haemostasis is secured. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Oral rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for six weeks postpartum, with a switch to warfarin only if her breastfeeding continues beyond that time and further prophylaxis is needed
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants including rivaroxaban are not recommended in breastfeeding women because transfer into breast milk is either significant or inadequately characterised. LMWH is breastfeeding-compatible. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Standard-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for ten days from the day after her surgery, with graduated compression stockings continued for the full six weeks
options.rationale: The RANZCOG weight-adjustment schedule delivers approximately 0.6 mg/kg for extended prophylaxis; 40 mg is under-dosing for 118 kg. Ten days does not meet the guideline recommendation of six weeks postpartum LMWH for women with multiple moderate risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice a day for six weeks postpartum given her obesity, gestational diabetes and category 2 caesarean earlier today
options.rationale: Therapeutic dose LMWH is reserved for confirmed or high-clinical-suspicion VTE, mechanical valve prophylaxis, or specific antiphospholipid syndrome scenarios. It carries substantial bleeding risk and is not indicated for postpartum prophylaxis in the absence of documented VTE. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Weight-adjusted enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for six weeks, commencing at least four hours after any neuraxial catheter is removed and haemostasis is secured
options.rationale: Emergency in-labour caesarean plus BMI over 40 plus current weight over 90 kg constitutes multiple moderate-risk factors, meeting the RANZCOG threshold for six weeks postpartum LMWH. Weight-based dosing per RANZCOG is 0.6 mg/kg once daily rounded to available vial size for weights 91-130 kg, approximating enoxaparin 80 mg. Timing after neuraxial anaesthesia respects catheter removal rules. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy and the puerperium raise VTE risk fourfold antenatally and up to twentyfold postnatally, with the peak in the first six weeks post-delivery. RANZCOG stratifies risk by antenatal and postnatal factors: BMI at booking above 30, emergency caesarean, prolonged labour, immobility, peripartum haemorrhage requiring transfusion, pre-eclampsia, prior VTE and known thrombophilia. Women with multiple moderate risk factors after caesarean receive weight-adjusted enoxaparin for six weeks postpartum; LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin except in renal failure. Neuraxial block timing rules apply: first prophylactic LMWH dose is given at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and prophylactic dosing precedes any subsequent catheter removal by at least 12 hours.
key_points: Multiple moderate risk factors (emergency CS + BMI > 40 + weight > 90 kg) meet RANZCOG threshold for 6 week postpartum LMWH.
Weight-adjusted enoxaparin approximates 0.6 mg/kg daily; 91-130 kg dose is around 80 mg daily.
Aspirin is NOT an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent.
DOACs are not recommended while breastfeeding; LMWH and warfarin are compatible.
Timing after neuraxial block: at least 4 hours after catheter removal for LMWH.
explanation.pearls: For postpartum VTE prophylaxis at booking BMI over 40, use enoxaparin 0.6 mg/kg daily (about 80 mg for 118 kg) for six weeks - the risk peak is in the first six weeks post-delivery, and shorter courses miss the majority of pulmonary emboli.

subtopic_detail: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after two prior caesareans
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36 year old woman at 28 plus 3 weeks in a metropolitan tertiary hospital antenatal clinic. She has had two previous lower segment caesarean sections. The current pregnancy was conceived spontaneously and is her third; her second baby was born 18 months ago.

Today's ultrasound reports an anterior placenta covering the internal os with multiple placental lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear space, focal thinning of the myometrium to 1 mm behind the placenta with bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder wall on colour Doppler. Fetal growth is on the 60th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

She has no bleeding, no contractions, and no rupture of membranes. Her booking bloods and gestational diabetes screen were normal. She lives 20 minutes from the tertiary centre.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, fetal heart rate 142 /min
data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta covering internal os; multiple placental lacunae (Finberg grade 3); loss of retroplacental clear space; myometrium 1 mm; bladder wall bridging vessels
data_table.Booking bloods: Haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165), platelets 235 x10^9/L (150-400), ABO A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue outpatient antenatal care with a repeat ultrasound at 34 weeks and aim for elective caesarean at 38 plus 6 weeks in a suitably resourced tertiary hospital
options.rationale: Delaying elective caesarean to 39 weeks in suspected placenta accreta spectrum substantially increases the probability of an emergency haemorrhage. RANZCOG and international guidance both recommend planned birth between 34 and 36 weeks after a completed corticosteroid course. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Confirm ultrasound with MRI placenta, complete antenatal corticosteroids at 34 weeks, and plan a multidisciplinary caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in an accreta centre
options.rationale: Placenta praevia with two prior caesareans plus lacunae, loss of clear space, bridging vessels and myometrial thinning meets the ultrasound criteria for likely placenta accreta spectrum. MRI adds surgical planning information. Planned birth at 34+0-35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with multidisciplinary team, blood bank preparation and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Arrange bilateral uterine artery embolisation under interventional radiology now and plan vaginal birth after two caesareans at 37 weeks with placenta left in situ post-birth
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia. Prophylactic pre-birth embolisation is not standard practice for antenatally suspected accreta spectrum in Australia; balloon catheters may have a role intraoperatively at select centres, not as an outpatient antenatal intervention. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Admit at 30 weeks for weekly transvaginal cervical length and daily cardiotocography, aiming for spontaneous labour and vaginal birth at term with continuous fetal monitoring
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia and additionally with suspected accreta. Cervical length screening does not alter management here and daily CTG antenatally in an otherwise stable pregnancy adds no value. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Arrange emergency caesarean today under general anaesthesia with immediate abdominal hysterectomy, given the very high risk of catastrophic obstetric haemorrhage at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Emergency delivery at 28 weeks in a stable woman inflicts substantial prematurity morbidity unnecessarily. Planned delivery at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in a suitably resourced centre is the standard, with emergency intervention reserved for antepartum haemorrhage or labour. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is defined by abnormal placental adherence (accreta), invasion into myometrium (increta) or through it (percreta). Prior caesarean plus a current anterior placenta praevia is the leading risk profile; two prior caesareans raises accreta risk to around 40%. Antenatal ultrasound features include placental lacunae (Finberg grade), loss of the retroplacental clear space, myometrial thinning, bladder wall interruption and bridging vessels. MRI is not diagnostic in isolation but adds surgical planning value. Standard care is planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with obstetrics, gynaecological oncology or urology, anaesthesia, interventional radiology, blood bank and neonatal intensive care coordinated. Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ is the usual surgical strategy; conservative management with the placenta left in situ and expectant care is offered in select cases.
key_points: Two prior caesareans plus anterior praevia carries around 40% accreta risk.
Key ultrasound features: lacunae (grade 3), loss of clear space, myometrial thinning, bridging vessels.
MRI supports surgical planning, not diagnosis in isolation.
Planned caesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in an accreta centre.
Standard strategy is caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with two prior caesareans and an anterior placenta praevia showing lacunae, loss of the clear space, and bridging vessels at 28 weeks, the correct sequence is MRI plus corticosteroids plus transfer to a placenta accreta centre for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0-35+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta with concurrent atony despite pharmacological uterotonics
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a delivery suite room 40 minutes after the vaginal birth of a term baby to a 31 year old woman on her third pregnancy. She has had two prior spontaneous vaginal births without complication. The placenta has not delivered despite active management with IM oxytocin 10 units, controlled cord traction and maternal effort.

The midwife reports 900 mL of estimated ongoing PV loss over the last 15 minutes with a boggy uterus that briefly firms with fundal massage then relaxes. A second dose of intramuscular oxytocin has been given and an IV infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's is running at 250 mL/h. The umbilical cord is intact and the placenta is felt as a discrete mass in the mid-uterine cavity on abdominal palpation.

She is pale, cool peripherally, with fingertip capillary refill three seconds and no epidural in situ. Two 16 gauge IV cannulae have been sited; four units of cross-matched red cells are already in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degC
data_table.Estimated blood loss: 1600 mL total; 900 mL in last 15 minutes; ongoing
data_table.Bedside: Bladder scanner 40 mL, uterus boggy at umbilicus firms briefly to fundal massage, cord intact, placenta palpable in mid-cavity, no visible cervical or vaginal tear
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165); coagulation not yet available; fibrinogen not yet available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a further 250 microgram intramuscular ergometrine, insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon, and reassess her response to combined pharmacological therapy over the next 30 minutes
options.rationale: A Bakri balloon has no role while the placenta remains in the uterus; the tamponade cannot form around a foreign body of that size. Continued pharmacological uterotonics without addressing the retained placenta will not stop the bleeding and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol, transfer to theatre for manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia with concurrent intravenous tranexamic acid and antibiotics
options.rationale: The woman is haemodynamically unstable with a retained placenta and atonic haemorrhage. Manual removal under anaesthesia is the definitive treatment; delay adds ongoing exsanguination. Simultaneous massive transfusion activation, IV tranexamic acid within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial) and prophylactic antibiotics (single-dose cefazolin plus metronidazole) form the standard package. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Attempt umbilical vein injection of 30 units of oxytocin diluted in 30 mL of normal saline via a catheter to encourage placental separation before considering manual removal
options.rationale: Umbilical vein oxytocin has weak evidence of benefit for retained placenta and no role in an unstable haemorrhaging woman. The definitive treatment remains theatre transfer for manual removal. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Perform bedside manual removal of the placenta in the delivery room using nitrous oxide analgesia only, and transfuse packed red cells to her as soon as they become available
options.rationale: Bedside manual removal without adequate anaesthesia is painful, unsafe, and produces incomplete removal; it also delays the surgical response if bleeding does not settle. RANZCOG mandates regional or general anaesthesia in an appropriately equipped theatre. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Arrange interventional radiology for uterine artery embolisation before surgical intervention, with vasopressor support to maintain her blood pressure in the meantime here
options.rationale: Interventional radiology is not the first-line response to retained placenta with ongoing haemorrhage. The retained placenta must be removed; embolisation is considered after removal if atony or focal bleeding persists. Vasopressor use without volume resuscitation and definitive haemostasis worsens end-organ perfusion. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined by RANZCOG as failure of placental delivery beyond 30 minutes of active third-stage management. In an actively bleeding woman it converts a common third-stage problem into an obstetric emergency, because the partially-separated placenta prevents effective uterine contraction and creates open sinuses at the placental bed. Definitive treatment is manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia. The standard concurrent package is massive transfusion protocol activation for major PPH, tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial shows a mortality benefit), and single-dose prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole). Ongoing atony after removal escalates through uterotonic ladder, uterine balloon tamponade, uterine compression sutures, uterine artery embolisation, and finally hysterectomy.
key_points: Retained placenta: no delivery of placenta within 30 minutes of active third-stage management.
In a bleeding woman, retained placenta prevents uterine contraction; manual removal is the definitive treatment.
Give IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of birth for any PPH (WOMAN trial mortality benefit).
Uterine balloon tamponade requires an empty uterus, not one containing a retained placenta.
Post-removal atony ladder: oxytocin infusion -> ergometrine -> carboprost -> tamponade -> compression sutures -> embolisation -> hysterectomy.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth reduces death from bleeding by around a third in the WOMAN trial; the retained placenta must be removed in theatre first, because uterine balloon tamponade cannot form around a placenta.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

subtopic_detail: PPH first uterotonic escalation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite three minutes after a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. The mother is a 30 year old para 2 who laboured for eight hours; active management of the third stage was performed with 10 units intramuscular oxytocin at anterior shoulder delivery, and the placenta was delivered complete at four minutes. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72; there has been no antenatal hypertension.

The midwife reports estimated blood loss of 900 mL in the last two minutes, ongoing brisk trickle from the vaginal introitus, and a uterus that is soft to palpation above the umbilicus.

On your rapid review the mother is pale, alert, with brisk fresh vaginal bleeding and no perineal trauma visible on inspection. There is no calf swelling and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus at umbilicus, brisk fresh vaginal bleeding, placenta appears complete on tray inspection, no perineal or vaginal wall trauma
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-160), venous access 16 gauge x 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units and continue bimanual uterine compression by the treating team
options.rationale: Escalation to a second-line uterotonic acting on a different receptor is more effective than repeating oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram, a synthetic prostaglandin F2 alpha, as next step
options.rationale: Carboprost is third-line in Australian sequencing (after oxytocin and ergometrine) because of significant bronchospasm,. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Administer misoprostol 800 microgram rectally as the immediate next uterotonic escalation step now
options.rationale: Misoprostol has a role when parenteral uterotonics are unavailable or ergot is contraindicated; it acts slowly (peak eff. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Give IV oxytocin 5 units by slow injection then infusion of 40 units over 4 hours plus ergometrine 250 microgram
options.rationale: Australian PPH sequencing: intravenous oxytocin bolus plus infusion escalates the initial uterotonic, and ergometrine (a. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; AMH: Uterotonics)

options.text: Proceed to theatre for examination under anaesthesia before adding any further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Uterotonic escalation is done in parallel with examination under anaesthesia; deferring pharmacology until theatre waste. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Primary PPH management follows the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) and a stepwise uterotonic ladder: oxytocin (intravenous bolus plus infusion) as first-line, ergometrine.
key_points: Tone first (uterine atony is the commonest cause) - massage plus escalating uterotonics.
Oxytocin first-line, ergometrine second unless hypertension/cardiac disease, carboprost third.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly is second-line PPH pharmacology only if the mother is normotensive and has no cardiac disease; it acts on alpha-adrene.

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice with heavy menstrual bleeding and migraine with aura
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 28 year old woman in a mid-morning appointment for contraception review and heavy periods. She is nulliparous, in a stable relationship, and wants effective contraception without pregnancy for at least three years. Her cycles are regular at 28 days with seven days of heavy flow soaking through pads at two hourly intervals for the first three days; ferritin is 12 microgram/L. She has migraine with aura roughly monthly since her mid-teens; her body mass index is 24; she does not smoke.

On direct enquiry she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no breast or cervical cancer history, and no unexplained vaginal bleeding.

Cervical screening is up to date and normal; pelvic examination is unremarkable with a normal-size uterus and no adnexal mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, normal thyroid, non-tender abdomen, normal-size mobile anteverted uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-200), TSH 1.4 mIU/L, urine hCG negative, recent HPV screen negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive option would you first recommend?

options.text: Progestogen-only pill norethisterone 350 microgram daily plus tranexamic acid during menstrual days
options.rationale: The traditional low-dose progestogen-only pill requires a three-hour dosing window and is user-dependent; it does not re. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with ethinyloestradiol 30 microgram plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) in migraine with aura at any age because of incr. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; UKMEC)

options.text: Copper intrauterine device with 10-year duration and no menstrual loss reduction benefit at all
options.rationale: The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but typically INCREASES menstrual blood loss and pain, and would worsen. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks with bone-density monitoring
options.rationale: Depot progestin is safe in migraine with aura and reduces bleeding, but bone mineral density falls with prolonged use an. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; AMH)

options.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device 52 mg with 5-year duration and menstrual loss reduction
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD is the most effective non-permanent contraception (failure under 0.2%) AND is first-line ho. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; Family Planning Alliance Australia)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk.
key_points: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
LNG-IUD is first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding in Australia.
Copper IUD increases menstrual blood loss and worsens iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg LNG-IUD reduces menstrual blood loss by about 90% at 12 months and rescues ferritin, all while providing the most effective reversible contraception.

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with unknown status
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 27 year old woman at 34 weeks and 2 days by dating scan with regular contractions every four minutes and ruptured membranes 30 minutes before arrival. This is her second pregnancy; the first was an uncomplicated term vaginal birth. Her antenatal care was fragmented and no group B streptococcus screening swab has been performed this pregnancy.

She has no penicillin allergy on direct questioning. Her observations are stable and she is afebrile. Fetal cardiotocography is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min, moderate variability and accelerations. Cervical examination confirms 4 cm dilatation with clear liquor.

Her first-child pregnancy did not include GBS screening either; that child was born at term without early-onset neonatal GBS disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 140 /min, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: White cells 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 4 mg/L (<5), high vaginal swab has NOT been performed this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management with respect to group B streptococcus?

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every four hours until birth of the baby
options.rationale: Preterm labour at 34 weeks with unknown GBS status meets the Australian risk-based indication for intrapartum antibiotic. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Take a high vaginal swab now and hold intrapartum antibiotics until the culture result returns after birth
options.rationale: Cultures take 24-48 hours; delaying antibiotics until results arrive misses the intrapartum window in preterm labour. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Do not give intrapartum antibiotics because she is afebrile, CRP is normal, and her prior child had no disease
options.rationale: Preterm labour under 37 weeks with unknown GBS status is a stand-alone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Commence intravenous ampicillin 2 g loading then 1 g every four hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily
options.rationale: This is empirical intra-amniotic infection therapy, not GBS prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral azithromycin 1 g orally in the birth suite as intrapartum GBS prophylaxis today
options.rationale: Azithromycin is used in caesarean labour antibiotic prophylaxis (with cefazolin) to reduce endometritis, not for GBS pro. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

explanation.summary: Australian GBS prophylaxis uses a risk-based approach when universal screening at 35 to 37 weeks is unavailable or the woman presents in preterm labour.
key_points: Preterm labour under 37 weeks with unknown GBS status triggers empirical intrapartum prophylaxis.
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g q4h until birth; cefazolin if non-severe penicillin allergy.
Clindamycin only for severe penicillin allergy AND documented clindamycin-susceptible GBS isolate.
explanation.pearls: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intravenously every 4 hours for at least 4 hours pre-delivery is the Australian GBS prophylaxis window that meaningfully reduces neonatal.

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage with fetal exsanguination pattern
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 32 year old primigravida at 37 weeks and 3 days. She reports a sudden gush of vaginal fluid at home 20 minutes ago that appeared blood-stained, followed by cessation of fetal movements. She was well until the event. Her routine anomaly scan noted a low-lying placenta with a bilobed morphology and a single-vessel cord; a follow-up scan at 32 weeks reported the placenta had migrated away from the internal os.

She is haemodynamically stable and denies pain. Speculum examination shows a small pool of blood-stained liquor in the vaginal vault and a closed cervix with no active bleeding.

Cardiotocography is being applied as you arrive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 88 /min, reduced variability, sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin (maternal) 132 g/L, Kleihauer-Betke result pending, coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Trial of labour with continuous CTG monitoring given the maternal haemodynamic stability and painless bleed
options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern indicates fetal hypovolaemia and severe anaemia. Labour will lose the baby. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Category 1 emergency caesarean section with paediatric team briefed for neonatal resuscitation and transfusion
options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern after painless ruptured membranes with blood-stained liquor is vasa praevia w. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Arrange urgent bedside ultrasound to localise the placenta before deciding on mode of delivery in birth suite
options.rationale: Ultrasound wastes the survival window in vasa praevia with active exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Give intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg for fetal lung maturity and admit for observation before delivery
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not treat fetal exsanguination and 37 weeks is past the routine steroid window. Delivery cannot wait. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Perform emergency artificial rupture of membranes to accelerate delivery vaginally in the birth suite now
options.rationale: Membranes are already ruptured and the fetal circulation is compromised. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal os, either overlying a velamentous cord insertion (Type I) or between lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta.
key_points: Vasa praevia: painless antepartum haemorrhage at rupture PLUS sinusoidal or bradycardic CTG.
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes; delay costs the baby.
Neonate needs immediate resuscitation and blood transfusion for anaemia.
explanation.pearls: A sinusoidal CTG with painless blood-stained liquor after membrane rupture is vasa praevia fetal exsanguination; the baby is born by category 1 caesarean and t.

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia with severe features and magnesium sulfate indication
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old primigravida at 33 weeks and 5 days admitted from clinic for further assessment of hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 and she was previously well; there is no personal or family history of hypertension. Today at clinic her blood pressure was 168/108 on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since yesterday morning and mild epigastric discomfort described as heartburn.

On examination her tendon reflexes are brisk with two beats of ankle clonus. There is mild pitting pedal oedema. Fetal cardiotocography shows a reassuring baseline of 138/min with moderate variability and accelerations.

Proteinuria on dipstick is 3+; a random protein-to-creatinine ratio is 82 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 138 /min, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 148 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.41 mmol/L, urine protein-to-creatinine 82 mg/mmol, LDH 620 U/L (<250), coagulation within normal limits, blood film without schistocytes

lead_in: In addition to antihypertensive control and planning delivery, what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses every 15 minutes for blood pressure control, no magnesium
options.rationale: Antihypertensive control is essential but does not prevent eclamptic seizures; magnesium is a separate pharmacological i. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intravenous diazepam 5 mg for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is superior for eclamptic sei. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for at least 24 hours
options.rationale: Pre-eclampsia with severe features (BP >=160/110, headache, epigastric pain, platelets <100, ALT >2x normal, hyperreflex. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer any further intervention pending steroid completion
options.rationale: Betamethasone is indicated for fetal lung maturity at this gestation, but administering steroids without magnesium sulf. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Give aspirin 150 mg orally to reduce placental thromboxane production and delay progression of pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin is preventive (started before 16 weeks in women at high risk); it has no acute role once pre-eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by any of BP >=160/110, thrombocytopaenia (platelets <100), impaired liver function (transaminases twice upper limit), progressive renal insufficien.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria include BP >=160/110 OR end-organ features (platelets <100, ALT >2x no.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/h reduces eclamptic seizures (MAGPIE).
Continue magnesium 24 hours after delivery or last seizure.
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour is the Australian first-line for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia; continue for 24 hours post-.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome - moderate outpatient vs admission
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman referred by her fertility unit five days after transvaginal oocyte retrieval. She had 21 oocytes retrieved and her human chorionic gonadotropin trigger was a full agonist replacement rather than recombinant hCG, and she has not yet had embryo transfer. She reports abdominal distension, mild dyspnoea when lying flat, and reduced urine output.

On examination her abdomen is distended, non-tender, with shifting dullness but no guarding. Her weight is up 3.5 kg from oocyte retrieval baseline. Chest expansion is symmetrical with dullness at the right base.

Her body mass index is 22 and she is otherwise well. Bedside ultrasound shows large multi-follicular ovaries (right 12 cm, left 11 cm) and moderate ascites; a small right pleural effusion is noted on chest X-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, no guarding, dullness right lung base
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 46% (36-46), white cells 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), coagulation within normal limits, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient monitoring, oral fluid intake targets and next-day fertility unit review appointment
options.rationale: Rising haematocrit (46%), hyponatraemia (130), oliguria on history, pleural effusion, weight gain >3 kg, dyspnoea and ta. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Perform urgent bilateral ovarian cystectomy to reduce ovarian volume and third-space losses in the acute phase
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for ovarian torsion, cyst rupture with haemodynamic instability, or ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Give a 500 mL 0.45% saline bolus and start furosemide 40 mg intravenously to correct oedema and third-spacing
options.rationale: Diuresis in OHSS is contraindicated while patients are intravascularly deplete (rising haematocrit, third-space losses). (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

options.text: Admit for IV crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin, daily haematocrit, and paracentesis if respiratory decline
options.rationale: Moderate to severe OHSS is a high-VTE-risk state (haemoconcentration, oestradiol effect, immobility) and requires admiss. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement; RCOG green-top guideline)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of dexamethasone 8 mg to reduce vascular permeability and third-space losses
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have not shown clinically important benefit in OHSS and are not standard therapy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome ranges from mild (self-limiting) to critical (respiratory failure, thrombosis, acute renal failure).
key_points: OHSS is a hypercoagulable, haemoconcentrated, third-space-loss state.
Admission for moderate to severe disease; VTE prophylaxis with LMWH.
Crystalloid volume replacement guided by haematocrit and urine output.
explanation.pearls: In moderate OHSS with haematocrit above 45%, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation plus VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin is the Australian standard; diuretics and h.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite when the midwife calls you emergently to bay 4. A 38 year old para 3 delivered vaginally 12 minutes ago at 40 weeks after a two hour second stage; the placenta was delivered complete at seven minutes with routine oxytocin. She had felt breathless and 'panicked' immediately after the birth, coughed twice, then became agitated, then unresponsive.

On arrival she has agonal breathing, pulse is impalpable at the femoral, and there is torrential fresh vaginal bleeding from a soft boggy uterus and oozing from her cannula sites and speculum-untouched perineum.

CPR has been commenced by the midwife with 30:2. IV access is already available.

data_table.Vital signs: Impalpable central pulse, SpO2 unrecordable, agonal breaths, GCS 3
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus, torrential vaginal bleeding, bleeding from cannula and perineum, no obvious trauma
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 74 g/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 62 x10^9/L, INR 2.4

lead_in: What is the single best pattern of immediate management?

options.text: Administer thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg intravenously since pulmonary embolism is the likely mechanism here
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in a bleeding coagulopathic patient is contraindicated and worsens haemorrhage. (Source: RCOG green-top AFE)

options.text: Give 500 mL crystalloid bolus, single ergometrine 250 microgram IM, and defer massive transfusion for 20 minutes
options.rationale: This underuses balanced blood products in a coagulopathic obstetric collapse and gives ergometrine (contraindicated in c. (Source: RANZCOG obstetric emergencies)

options.text: Prioritise B-Lynch suture in theatre without perimortem caesarean, continuing chest compressions during transfer
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean is the priority to restore maternal cardiac output; B-Lynch is a specific tone-focused surgical tec. (Source: ANZCOR adult ALS)

options.text: Give recombinant activated factor VIIa 90 microgram/kg first-line to reverse coagulopathy before red cell transfusion
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not a first-line agent for obstetric haemorrhage or AFE; balanced red cells, plasma, platelet. (Source: NBA patient blood management)

options.text: Continue ALS with left uterine displacement, activate massive transfusion 4:4:1, tranexamic acid, perimortem caesarean
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiovascular collapse plus coagulopathy is the diagnosis and requires simultaneous cardio. (Source: RANZCOG obstetric emergencies; ANZCOR)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, catastrophic obstetric emergency presenting within minutes of labour, delivery or the immediate postpartum with hypoxia, hypotension, arrest and.
key_points: AFE: sudden peripartum collapse plus coagulopathy plus bleeding from puncture sites.
Massive transfusion protocol with 4:4:1 red cells:plasma:platelets and cryoprecipitate for fibrinoge.
Perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes of maternal arrest.
explanation.pearls: In a peripartum collapse with coagulopathy activate massive transfusion protocol at 4:4:1 and cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L, and prepare for pe.

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture during trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite reviewing a 34 year old para 1 at 40 weeks and 4 days who is undergoing a trial of labour after a previous lower segment caesarean section for breech at term. Labour was induced with an oxytocin infusion four hours ago after spontaneous rupture of membranes with clear liquor at admission. Her cervix was 5 cm at review one hour ago; contractions have been every three minutes.

The midwife has escalated because the mother has a sudden change: contractions have paused for three minutes, and the mother reports a burning sensation across her lower abdomen 'unlike the earlier pain'. The cardiotocograph baseline has fallen from 138 to 72 /min over 90 seconds and is not recovering.

On examination the presenting part is no longer palpable at 0 station on vaginal examination (previously station 0); abdominal palpation reveals an easily palpated fetal part in the maternal upper abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 72 /min for 90 seconds with reduced variability and no recovery
data_table.Examination: Presenting part no longer engaged, easily palpable fetal parts in maternal upper abdomen

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management?

options.text: Cease oxytocin, give terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously, and mobilise category 1 caesarean team
options.rationale: Sudden change in pain character, loss of station, palpable fetal parts abdominally and prolonged fetal bradycardia in. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC; RCOG green-top VBAC)

options.text: Continue the oxytocin infusion and reassess after another two contractions with fresh CTG interpretation
options.rationale: Uterine rupture requires immediate cessation of oxytocin (which contributes to rupture through hyperstimulation) and cat. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Perform intrauterine resuscitation with left lateral position, IV fluid bolus and oxygen; reassess in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is appropriate for reversible fetal decelerations without rupture features. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Prepare for instrumental vaginal delivery with rotational forceps when the next contraction pattern resumes
options.rationale: Instrumental delivery from station 0 with an unrestored contraction pattern and possible ruptured uterus is not feasible. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Give ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly to restore uterine tone and reassess bleeding in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Ergometrine increases uterine contraction and worsens rupture; it is a postpartum agent, not an intrapartum one. (Source: AMH: Uterotonics)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture in a trial of labour after caesarean carries substantial maternal and perinatal mortality.
key_points: VBAC uterine rupture: sudden pain change, loss of station, palpable fetal parts, prolonged bradycar.
Immediate: cease oxytocin, tocolysis, category 1 caesarean.
Ergometrine is intrapartum-contraindicated in this scenario.
explanation.pearls: In a suspected uterine rupture during VBAC, terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously buys transfer time to theatre; category 1 caesarean is the definitive step.

subtopic_detail: PPH active management uterotonic choice
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a rural birth suite ten minutes after the vaginal delivery of a term 3.6 kg baby to a 32 year old G2P2 woman with a labour lasting seven hours. Third stage was actively managed with oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery and the placenta appeared complete after controlled cord traction at eight minutes.

Estimated blood loss is now 900 mL of fresh red loss with clots. On examination the fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. A rapid inspection of the vagina and cervix shows no lacerations and the perineum is intact. She is talking to you and holding her baby but says she feels lightheaded.

Her antenatal blood pressure was consistently 145/95 without medication and she was investigated for chronic hypertension. She has no known drug allergies. IV access has been secured with a wide bore cannula, bloods including group and hold are drawn and 500 mL of Hartmann's is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus above the umbilicus, placenta complete on inspection, no genital tract laceration, perineum intact
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 units IM given at delivery, ongoing oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours in progress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to give?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram with fundal massage and continued oxytocin infusion currently running
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease because of the risk of hypertensive crisis, stroke and myocardial ischaemia; this woman has documented chronic hypertension. (Source: AMH: Ergometrine)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram with fundal massage, repeat every 15 minutes to maximum eight doses
options.rationale: RANZCOG stepwise PPH management gives ergometrine as second line, then carboprost when ergometrine fails or is contraindicated by hypertension; a history of chronic hypertension makes ergometrine contraindicated so carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic here. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; eTG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Bimanual uterine compression alone and reassess in 15 minutes without additional pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Bimanual compression is a temporising manoeuvre used alongside pharmacological escalation for ongoing PPH; using it in place of additional uterotonic wastes time and does not address the uterine atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the only additional pharmacological therapy given now
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid should be given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours as an adjunct, not instead of a second line uterotonic; the atony must be treated pharmacologically at the same time. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device without giving any additional pharmacological uterotonic
options.rationale: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is second line after failure of medical management and preparation for theatre; pharmacological escalation to a second uterotonic is appropriate before mechanical intervention in a stable woman with atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Uterine atony causes the majority of primary PPH. RANZCOG stepwise pharmacological escalation is fundal massage, oxytocin (given), ergometrine (contraindicated by chronic hypertension), carboprost, then misoprostol. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours of birth as an adjunct. Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used if medical measures fail. Do not give ergometrine in hypertensive, pre-eclamptic or cardiac disease.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth for any PPH over 500 mL
Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used with, not instead of, pharmacology
explanation.pearls: The AMH warns that ergometrine and combination Syntometrine can precipitate hypertensive crisis in eclamptic women - remember to check the antenatal blood pressure before reaching for the ampoule.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 28 year old G1P0 at 34+2 weeks referred by her GP for elevated blood pressure and a severe frontal headache that started this morning. She has had two episodes of blurred vision and mild right upper quadrant discomfort since arrival.

Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 with normal booking bloods. Home readings over the past week have run 138-148/88-96. She is on no regular medications and reports no allergies.

On admission her blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg confirmed on repeat reading with a size appropriate cuff. Urinalysis shows 3+ proteinuria with a spot protein creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol (<30). CTG is reassuring at 145 bpm baseline with normal variability. She is neurologically alert with brisk reflexes and no clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC, fetal HR 145 /min
data_table.Examination: Alert, brisk reflexes without clonus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema documented
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 152 U/L (<45), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.14-0.34), LDH 380 U/L (<250)

lead_in: Alongside intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control, what is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, plus antenatal betamethasone
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms and HELLP features (platelets under 100, ALT over 70) requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis (Magpie trial protocol) alongside blood pressure control and betamethasone before delivery planning. AMH uses the AU spelling magnesium sulfate. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy statement)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin loading 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis with oral maintenance postnatally
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is the evidence based seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia (Magpie trial) with clear superiority over phenytoin; phenytoin is not first line and gives worse outcomes. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Nifedipine 10 mg orally as sole antihypertensive and admit for observation without seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: This woman meets criteria for severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features and neurological symptoms and requires magnesium sulfate; a blood pressure agent alone leaves her unprotected against eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia without corticosteroids or magnesium loading dose
options.rationale: Delivery is planned but stabilisation with magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives comes first, and at 34+2 weeks betamethasone should be given if delivery can be safely delayed for 24 hours; skipping stabilisation increases maternal and neonatal risk. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg intravenous now and reassess her neurological state and reflexes in one hour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are used to abort an active eclamptic seizure only if magnesium fails; they cause maternal sedation and respiratory depression and have no role in prevention. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: This woman has severe pre-eclampsia at 34+2 weeks with cerebral symptoms (headache, blurred vision), HELLP features (platelets 92, ALT 152, LDH raised) and blood pressure well over the severe threshold of 160/110. Management is simultaneous control of blood pressure with IV labetalol or hydralazine, seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate per the Magpie protocol, and antenatal corticosteroids as delivery is planned within 24-48 hours after stabilisation. Delivery mode is determined by cervix and fetal status; caesarean is not automatic.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria: BP 160/110, HELLP, neurological symptoms, or end organ dysfunction
Magnesium sulfate load 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/hour infusion (Magpie protocol)
Monitor magnesium clinically: reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output
Betamethasone if delivery may be delayed 24-48 hours between 24 and 34+6 weeks
explanation.pearls: The AU spelling is magnesium sulfate (INN in AMH), not sulphate - and magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically, not by routine serum levels.

subtopic_detail: GDM initial dietary trial before pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old G1P0 at 27+3 weeks in the antenatal diabetes clinic. Her booking BMI was 31 kg/m2 and her mother was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 45. She was screened at 26 weeks with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test after skipping first trimester HbA1c.

OGTT results: fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), one hour 11.0 mmol/L (<10.0), two hour 8.9 mmol/L (<8.5). She meets ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes.

She reports no polydipsia, polyuria or infections. She is asymptomatic with no vision changes. She has been offered diabetes educator and dietitian input which she can attend within one week.

Today's dating scan showed appropriate for gestational age foetus with no polyhydramnios. Blood pressure and proteinuria are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC, fetal HR 148 /min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, symphyseal fundal height 27 cm, fetal movements reported normal
data_table.Investigations: As above; HbA1c today 5.6% (<5.7 non-pregnant), urea and creatinine normal, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in four weeks to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
options.rationale: A single positive OGTT meeting ADIPS criteria makes the diagnosis and delaying management for a repeat test exposes mother and foetus to four weeks of untreated hyperglycaemia; there is no diagnostic need for confirmation. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily now and titrate up to 2 g daily over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first line at diagnosis in the absence of severe hyperglycaemia; ADIPS calls for a trial of medical nutrition therapy with self monitoring first, with metformin or insulin added if glucose targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Start subcutaneous long acting insulin at 0.2 units/kg at bedtime now with morning glucose review
