options.rationale: Insulin is first line pharmacotherapy when nutrition therapy fails or when there is severe hyperglycaemia at diagnosis; the OGTT here is mildly elevated and a trial of medical nutrition therapy is indicated first. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

options.text: Refer to diabetes educator and dietitian and start four times daily home glucose monitoring with review
options.rationale: ADIPS first line management of newly diagnosed GDM is medical nutrition therapy, physical activity and home glucose self monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets (fasting under 5.0 and two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L) are not met within one to two weeks. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

options.text: Plan a category 1 induction of labour at 39 weeks now without additional glucose monitoring in the interim
options.rationale: Delivery timing decisions in GDM depend on glycaemic control, fetal growth and complications during ongoing pregnancy, not on the diagnosis alone; this bypasses the need for glucose management and monitoring in the interim. (Source: RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnostic criteria for GDM on a 75 g OGTT are fasting 5.1, one hour 10.0, two hour 8.5 mmol/L (any one). First line management is medical nutrition therapy from a dietitian, structured physical activity and home glucose self monitoring four times daily targeting fasting under 5.0 and one hour post prandial under 7.4 (or two hour under 6.7). Pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) is added if targets are not met within 1-2 weeks, or immediately for severe hyperglycaemia or fetal macrosomia. Insulin remains first line pharmacotherapy in AU, with metformin used in specific settings after counselling on placental transfer.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1h 10.0, 2h 8.5 mmol/L
Glucose targets on treatment: fasting under 5.0, 1h post prandial under 7.4, 2h under 6.7
MNT first, pharmacotherapy if targets missed at 1-2 weeks
Insulin first line pharmacotherapy in AU, metformin alternative
explanation.pearls: Metformin crosses the placenta but the MiG trial and long term follow up show broadly reassuring neonatal outcomes; AU practice still starts with insulin more often than metformin, unlike some UK pathways.

subtopic_detail: Progestogen only pill in breastfeeding
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 30 year old woman for her six week postnatal check after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a healthy term baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and plans to continue for at least six months. She wants to resume contraception before she and her partner become sexually active again.

She had one previous pregnancy that ended in a first trimester miscarriage. She has no history of migraine, venous thromboembolism, hypertension, cardiac or liver disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m2 and blood pressure today is 118/74. She smokes five cigarettes daily and has cut down from twenty during the pregnancy.

She does not want an intrauterine device at this stage due to needle phobia and wants a method she can start today. She has not resumed periods.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Well healed episiotomy, uterus involuted, no pelvic tenderness, no varicose veins
data_table.Investigations: Nil today; postnatal bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to prescribe today?

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today after signed consent and post procedure observation
options.rationale: The implant is safe and effective but requires a subdermal insertion which she declined for the same reason as the IUD; the pill matches her stated preference and MEC category 1 status. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today with a three month review to reassess breastfeeding
options.rationale: MEC AU category 3 (risks outweigh benefits) for combined pill in the first six weeks postpartum in a breastfeeding woman due to venous thromboembolism and lactation concerns; category 2 after 6 weeks but not first choice while breastfeeding. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular given today with review in 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA is safe in breastfeeding but requires an injection which she declined for other reasons and has a slower return to fertility and bone mineral density concerns with long use; the pill better matches her preference. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

options.text: Advise lactational amenorrhoea method alone until she has fully weaned her infant off breastfeeding
options.rationale: LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months, and even then has a failure rate of about 2% in typical use; she needs a defined method as she does not want to rely on breastfeeding pattern alone. (Source: FSRH postnatal contraception guideline)

options.text: Progestogen only pill starting today with no additional precautions if fully breastfeeding and amenorrhoeic
options.rationale: MEC AU category 1 for progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum; it does not affect lactation and can be started immediately with no additional precautions if within 21 days postpartum or amenorrhoeic. It is also compatible with smoking under 15/day if under 35. (Source: MEC AU 2021; FSRH progestogen only pill guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: MEC AU categorises contraception in breastfeeding women. Progestogen only methods (pill, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUS) are all category 1 or 2 from any time postpartum and do not impair lactation. Combined hormonal methods are category 3 in the first six weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (VTE and lactation concerns) and category 2 from 6 weeks onwards. If she declines devices, the progestogen only pill is a category 1 first choice that can start today. Contraception should be discussed by six weeks postpartum because ovulation can return before menses.
key_points: MEC AU 1: progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum
MEC AU 3: combined pill in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding
Ovulation may return before menses so contraception before day 21 if not breastfeeding
LAM is 98% effective only if exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months
explanation.pearls: The progestogen only pill window in AU is often quoted as 3 hours for older levonorgestrel pills and 12 hours for desogestrel and drospirenone - check the product prescribed.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage antiphospholipid workup
stem:
You are the O and G registrar seeing a 34 year old woman in the early pregnancy clinic six weeks after her third consecutive first trimester miscarriage. Her first pregnancy at 24 ended in a miscarriage at 8 weeks with a normal karyotype on products of conception. Her second at 26 miscarried at 10 weeks with a similar karyotype result. The most recent miscarriage at 12 weeks was managed medically with no complications.

She reports one episode of provoked deep vein thrombosis after a long haul flight two years ago that was treated with three months of rivaroxaban and has not recurred. She smokes ten cigarettes daily.

She is not currently pregnant and her partner has fathered another child in a previous relationship. Recent parental karyotypes were normal. A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound showed a normal uterine cavity with no septum. Thyroid function and prolactin are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, cardiovascular examination normal, no lower limb swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide future pregnancy care?

options.text: Empirical low molecular weight heparin from a positive pregnancy test without further diagnostic workup
options.rationale: Empirical LMWH in the absence of documented antiphospholipid syndrome or heritable thrombophilia has not been shown to reduce miscarriage in trials (SPIN, ALIFE); prescribing it exposes her to needle burden and bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ALIFE trial NEJM 2010)

options.text: Hysteroscopy with septum resection to exclude uterine cavity abnormality missed on ultrasound
options.rationale: A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound has already shown a normal cavity with no septum and no further imaging is needed unless the ultrasound was unclear; empirical resection has no evidence of benefit without a documented lesion. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody screen: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 GP1 IgG and IgM
options.rationale: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage workup includes antiphospholipid antibody screening after 3 or more first trimester losses; diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome requires a positive test confirmed on repeat 12 weeks later, and treatment (aspirin plus low molecular weight heparin) reduces subsequent loss. Her provoked DVT is not itself diagnostic without APL. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ISTH APS classification criteria 2023)

options.text: Send further parental karyotypes and array comparative genomic hybridisation on parental blood samples
options.rationale: Parental karyotypes have already returned normal and repeat testing is not indicated; array comparative genomic hybridisation is a cytogenetic tool for products of conception rather than parental blood in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

options.text: Advise assisted reproductive technology with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy screening
options.rationale: PGT-A has not been shown to improve live birth rate in couples with unexplained recurrent miscarriage and normal parental karyotypes; empirical use adds cost, cycle burden and does not address a potentially treatable cause like APS. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive first trimester losses or two or more with any second trimester loss) warrants structured workup: pelvic imaging for uterine anomaly, parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibody screen and thyroid and prolactin. In this case the cavity is normal, karyotypes are normal and endocrine screen is normal, so the outstanding test is APL antibodies. APS diagnosis needs a positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti beta 2 glycoprotein 1 antibody confirmed at 12 weeks. Treatment with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from a positive pregnancy test improves live birth rate in obstetric APS.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage: 3 or more first trimester OR 2 or more with any second trimester loss
Workup: pelvic imaging, parental karyotype, APL antibodies, thyroid, prolactin
APS diagnosis: positive APL confirmed at 12 weeks
Empirical LMWH in unexplained recurrent miscarriage is not evidence based
explanation.pearls: The ISTH APS classification criteria 2023 use domain scoring so a single positive result is not enough - two positive results 12 weeks apart, at least one at moderate to high titre, is needed to confirm.

subtopic_detail: ICP delivery timing by bile acid tier
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old G2P1 at 35+4 weeks referred by her midwife for severe generalised itch that started three weeks ago and is worse at night. It affects her palms and soles most. She has no rash on examination beyond scratch marks. Her first pregnancy was affected by intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy at 34 weeks and she was induced at 37 weeks with a live vigorous infant.

Today's bloods show a fasting serum bile acid of 108 micromol/L (<10) rising from 62 last week. ALT is 168 U/L (<45), GGT is 92 U/L (<50). Total bilirubin and INR are within normal limits.

Ultrasound today shows a singleton cephalic foetus with estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler within normal limits. Cardiotocograph is reassuring at 140 bpm baseline with normal variability and accelerations. She has been counselled about fetal risks and started on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily last week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC, fetal HR 140 /min
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations without primary rash, no jaundice, uterus soft with normal fundal height, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Fasting bile acids 108 micromol/L (was 62), ALT 168 U/L, GGT 92 U/L, INR 1.0, viral hepatitis screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Continue expectant management until spontaneous labour or 40 weeks gestation with weekly bloods
options.rationale: Bile acids over 100 micromol/L carry an absolute stillbirth risk that rises from 37 weeks onwards; expectant management until spontaneous labour or 40 weeks is inconsistent with contemporary AU and UK practice for severe ICP. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

options.text: Plan expedited delivery at 36 weeks by induction of labour with continuous intrapartum CTG monitoring
options.rationale: RCOG and RANZCOG endorsed bile acid stratification identifies severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 micromol/L as carrying a stillbirth risk that is materially higher than background from 36 weeks; delivery at 36 weeks is recommended with continuous intrapartum CTG. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section this evening under general anaesthesia for fetal indication
options.rationale: There is no acute fetal compromise on CTG, Doppler or growth to warrant category 1 delivery tonight; the timing decision here is elective planning at 36 weeks, not emergency birth. (Source: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.text: Plan induction at 39+0 weeks and continue outpatient bile acid monitoring every week until delivery
options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks is appropriate for mild ICP with bile acids under 40 micromol/L; severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 requires earlier delivery to reduce stillbirth risk. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

options.text: Discontinue ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat bile acids in one week before deciding delivery timing
options.rationale: PITCHES showed UDCA does not reduce fetal composite outcomes but many centres continue it for maternal itch; stopping it does not change delivery timing which is driven by the peak bile acid tier. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; PITCHES Lancet 2019)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is stratified by peak bile acid: mild (under 40), moderate (40-99) and severe (100 or more micromol/L). Stillbirth risk rises sharply above 100 micromol/L from about 37 weeks. Contemporary guidance recommends delivery at 36 weeks for severe ICP, 38-39 weeks for moderate and 39-40 weeks for mild disease. UDCA improves maternal pruritus and biochemistry but the PITCHES trial did not show reduction in composite fetal outcomes; it is not a substitute for delivery timing. Continuous intrapartum CTG is recommended given the small but definable stillbirth risk.
key_points: Severe ICP: bile acids 100 or more, deliver at 36 weeks
Moderate ICP: 40-99, deliver 38-39 weeks
Mild ICP: under 40, deliver 39-40 weeks
UDCA improves itch but does not remove need for timed delivery
explanation.pearls: Peak bile acids drive the plan - so ongoing measurement matters even after treatment starts, because tier can escalate.

sources.label: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

subtopic_detail: Ectopic methotrexate criteria
stem:
You are the O and G registrar reviewing a 27 year old G1P0 in the early pregnancy assessment unit with two days of mild left iliac fossa pain and a small amount of dark brown vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was seven weeks ago. She has never had an ectopic before and has no history of pelvic infection, tubal surgery or IUD use.

Ultrasound today shows an empty uterus, a 2.4 cm mass in the left adnexum without a fetal pole or fetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid. Serum beta hCG today is 1820 IU/L. She is haemodynamically stable and pain scores 3/10 on paracetamol.

She lives 20 minutes from the hospital, has reliable transport and a partner at home. She has no chronic liver, renal or haematological disease. Full blood count and liver and renal function are within normal limits. She has been counselled about medical, surgical and expectant management options in a shared decision making conversation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed, minimal dark blood in the vault
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 1820 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-160), platelets 258 x10^9/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Uterine evacuation with dilation and curettage to establish the location of the pregnancy definitively
options.rationale: The pregnancy is not intrauterine on ultrasound so curettage of an empty uterus is not indicated and can delay treatment of the extrauterine pregnancy; location has already been established sonographically. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy on the current admission under general anaesthesia and postoperative care
options.rationale: Surgical management is preferred for haemodynamic instability, severe pain, contraindications to methotrexate or when medical management fails; in a stable woman meeting all methotrexate criteria, medical management avoids surgical morbidity and preserves the contralateral tube. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy on the current admission with tubal preservation and postoperative followup
options.rationale: Salpingostomy carries a persistent trophoblast rate around 4-15% and adds no live birth benefit over salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy; it is not preferred over methotrexate in a stable woman meeting medical criteria. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly outpatient beta hCG monitoring only and no immediate intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for women with declining beta hCG under 1000, an asymptomatic clinical picture and clear evidence of resolution; a rising or stable hCG at 1820 with a visible adnexal mass has too high a rupture risk to observe without treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: IM methotrexate 50 mg/m2 single dose with beta hCG on day 4 and day 7 and clear return advice
options.rationale: This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, no contraindications and normal bloods. Single dose methotrexate has resolution rates around 85-90% in appropriately selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS; eTG: Ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic pregnancy are: hCG under 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemodynamic instability, reliable follow up, no contraindications (liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression) and normal baseline blood tests. Single dose regimen is methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with beta hCG on day 4 and day 7; success is a fall of at least 15% between days 4 and 7. Failure or rise triggers a second dose or surgery. Anti-D immunoglobulin should be considered if Rh negative.
key_points: hCG threshold for methotrexate: under 5000 IU/L
Mass size threshold: under 3.5 cm
Requires no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow up
Contraindications: liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L (or the presence of cardiac activity, or mass at or above 3.5 cm, or instability, or contraindications to methotrexate) - not the older 3000 IU/L figure.

subtopic_detail: MCDA twin pregnancy - TTTS surveillance and delivery
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine registrar reviewing a 31 year old G2P1 at 26+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy for a fortnightly ultrasound. Chorionicity was established at 12 weeks by lambda sign absence and thin intertwin membrane. Anatomy scan at 20 weeks was normal in both twins with concordant growth. Two weeks ago twin A had estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile with maximum vertical amniotic pocket 3.8 cm and twin B on the 40th centile with 4.2 cm pocket.

Today twin A has estimated fetal weight on the 25th centile with maximum vertical pocket 1.4 cm and an empty bladder that has not filled across a 30 minute scan window. Twin B has estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile with maximum vertical pocket 9.6 cm and a distended bladder. Umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end diastolic flow in twin A and normal flow in twin B. Ductus venosus and middle cerebral artery Doppler are normal in both.

Both twins have reassuring cardiotocograph tracings. She has no contractions and cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC, fetal HRs A 148 /min B 152 /min
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, no contractions, cervix long and closed on transvaginal scan
data_table.Investigations: As above; full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Selective fetal reduction of twin A by bipolar cord occlusion during elective fetal medicine intervention
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for cases with severe growth restriction and imminent demise of the donor threatening the recipient by exsanguination through anastomoses, or major structural anomaly; laser is offered before reduction as it preserves both twins where possible. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Amnioreduction alone with a further scan in one week to reassess Quintero staging and Doppler
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is inferior to laser for TTTS at 16-26 weeks (Eurofoetus trial: survival of at least one twin 76% laser vs 51% amnioreduction) and delays definitive therapy; if a fetal therapy centre is inaccessible amnioreduction is a temporising measure at best. (Source: Eurofoetus trial NEJM 2004)

options.text: Administer betamethasone and plan delivery within 48 hours by caesarean section for fetal indication
options.rationale: At 26+3 weeks with reassuring CTGs and normal ductus venosus flow, immediate delivery carries very high extreme prematurity morbidity that is worse than the risk of transferring for laser therapy; delivery is reserved for irretrievable Doppler deterioration or fetal distress. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

options.text: Urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
options.rationale: TTTS stage III (Quintero: oligohydramnios pocket under 2 in donor, polyhydramnios pocket over 8 in recipient, empty donor bladder plus abnormal Doppler with absent end diastolic flow) at 16-26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of intertwin anastomoses; laser improves at least one twin survival compared with amnioreduction (Eurofoetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is at the outer margin and referral is time critical. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement; ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

options.text: Increase surveillance to weekly biometry and Doppler without intervention on both twins for two weeks
options.rationale: TTTS with abnormal Doppler is a treat now diagnosis, not a watch and wait; without laser the composite mortality of untreated stage III TTTS at this gestation approaches 80-90%. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates 10-15% of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies and is staged by the Quintero classification: stage I (oligo-poly), II (donor bladder not visible), III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), IV (hydrops), V (demise). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated by fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the intertwin anastomoses which has been shown superior to serial amnioreduction (Eurofoetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is right at the upper margin of the classic laser window; urgent transfer to a fetal therapy centre is time critical.
key_points: MCDA chorionicity mandates fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks
Quintero staging: I oligo-poly, II bladder gone, III abnormal Doppler, IV hydrops, V demise
Stage II+ at 16-26 weeks: fetoscopic laser preferred over amnioreduction
Delivery is a fallback when laser is not feasible or when demise is imminent
explanation.pearls: The absence of the lambda sign at 11-13 weeks confirms monochorionicity - a determination that cannot be reliably made retrospectively later in pregnancy, which is why every twin pregnancy must have chorionicity documented at the nuchal scan.

subtopic_detail: Vaginal birth after caesarean eligibility criteria per RANZCOG
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in a district hospital antenatal clinic. A 33 year old woman is 36 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy in cephalic presentation. Her first birth was 3 years ago by lower segment caesarean for breech at term with a low transverse incision documented in the operative report. She had no wound complications and her postnatal recovery was uncomplicated. This pregnancy has been uneventful with normal glucose tolerance test, normal blood pressure, normal ultrasound growth, and a normally sited placenta anteriorly not overlying the previous scar.

She is keen to plan a vaginal birth this time and asks about eligibility. The birth suite is midwife led with an on site obstetric registrar 24 hours, a general theatre with 30 minute recall for elective work, and continuous cardiotocograph monitoring available. Anaesthetics can be on site within 15 minutes overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysial fundal height 35 cm, cephalic, longitudinal lie, fetal heart 142 /min, no palpable contractions
data_table.Investigations: Fetal ultrasound 34 weeks estimated fetal weight 55th centile, placenta anterior high, cervix long closed

lead_in: Which single feature makes planned vaginal birth after caesarean in this hospital inappropriate?

options.text: The indication for her previous caesarean was breech presentation at term with a low transverse uterine scar
options.rationale: The indication for the previous caesarean does not itself preclude a planned vaginal birth after caesarean; a low transverse scar with a resolved non recurring indication is a good candidate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The inter delivery interval since the previous caesarean is 3 years with no complications during that time
options.rationale: An inter delivery interval of 18 to 24 months and above is considered acceptable; 3 years does not preclude a planned vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The current pregnancy is at 36 weeks with a cephalic singleton and normal fetal growth on scan
options.rationale: 36 weeks is not a preclusive gestation; term vaginal birth after caesarean is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: Anaesthetics and theatre availability with a 30 minute recall for elective work rather than immediate in house response
options.rationale: RANZCOG requires the ability to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of a decision, meaning immediate access to anaesthetics and theatre for uterine rupture. A 30 minute recall for elective theatre with 15 minute anaesthetic on call overnight does not meet that immediate response requirement and makes planned vaginal birth after caesarean inappropriate at this facility. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The anteriorly located placenta is not overlying the previous caesarean scar on the recent morphology scan
options.rationale: An anterior placenta not overlying the scar and normally sited does not preclude planned vaginal birth after caesarean; placenta accreta risk with anterior placenta over the scar would. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean requires a low transverse uterine scar, a resolved or non recurring indication, appropriate inter delivery interval, continuous cardiotocograph monitoring and immediate access to obstetric, anaesthetic and theatre teams to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of the decision. Facility rather than obstetric factors are the reason planned vaginal birth after caesarean is declined here. Anterior placenta not overlying the scar is safe; anterior placenta overlying the previous caesarean scar prompts placenta accreta workup. Inter delivery interval and previous indication are not disqualifying in this scenario.
key_points: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of decision is a RANZCOG facility requirement for vaginal birth after caesarean.
Low transverse scar with resolved indication is a favourable feature.
Anterior placenta over the scar (not off the scar) prompts placenta accreta workup.
explanation.pearls: A 30 minute theatre recall for elective work is not the immediate response needed for uterine rupture; refer to a facility with in house theatre for planned vaginal birth after caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean
NSW Health Maternity - vaginal birth after caesarean

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic choice in a woman with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 29 year old primigravida in early labour at 39 weeks gestation. She had a vaginal group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks that was positive. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy (immediate anaphylaxis with tongue swelling and hypotension after an intramuscular procaine penicillin dose as a teenager). Her group B streptococcus isolate has been sensitivity tested and is reported as susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin (inducible resistance detected on D test), and sensitivity to vancomycin not requested by the laboratory.

She is contracting every 5 minutes with intact membranes. The birth suite midwife asks for the antibiotic order to give now. There is no other allergy and no other medical comorbidity. She has had no doses of prophylaxis yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, intact membranes, cephalic, fetal heart 138 /min
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab positive; sensitivities susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance, no vancomycin sensitivity reported

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, no allergy modification needed
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is contraindicated because of her documented immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula in this labour
options.rationale: Cephalosporins share a small cross reactivity with penicillins and are relatively contraindicated when the reaction was immediate anaphylaxis; select an alternative not sharing the beta lactam core. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula throughout this labour period
options.rationale: The isolate is resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance; clindamycin cannot be relied on for group B streptococcus prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Oral erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours starting now and continued until delivery of the infant in this labour
options.rationale: Erythromycin has variable resistance in group B streptococcus and poor placental transfer; it is not recommended as intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes until delivery, per AU guidance
options.rationale: With immediate penicillin anaphylaxis and clindamycin resistance on D test, vancomycin is the recommended prophylaxis at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes until delivery. Sensitivity to vancomycin does not need to be reported for empiric intrapartum use. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: The Australasian intrapartum prophylaxis pathway for group B streptococcus uses benzylpenicillin as first line; a woman with immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin has cephalosporins relatively contraindicated. Clindamycin may be used only when the isolate is sensitive and no inducible resistance is detected on D test; where either is unavailable or resistance is present, vancomycin is the recommended alternative. Erythromycin is no longer routinely recommended. Vancomycin is dosed at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes to reduce infusion related hypersensitivity. Adequate prophylaxis is at least one dose 4 hours before birth.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line; anaphylaxis is a hard contraindication.
Clindamycin requires proven susceptibility and no inducible resistance on D test.
Vancomycin is the fallback where clindamycin cannot be used, 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over 60 minutes.
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance, intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis is vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

subtopic_detail: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome outpatient vs inpatient management
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman in the emergency department 6 days after a fresh embryo transfer following a gonadotrophin cycle. She has abdominal distension, nausea, some vomiting and reduced urine output over the last day. She has no chest pain and no leg swelling. She has had two large volume fluids over the past 24 hours. Her pain is manageable with paracetamol.

Her weight is 4 kg above baseline. She is tolerating oral fluids in small amounts between vomits. Her most recent transabdominal ultrasound shows bilateral ovaries measuring 9 cm each, moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, no pleural effusion visible. Her home is 30 minutes from the tertiary hospital and she lives with her partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with generalised tenderness, no peritonism, bowel sounds present, mild dyspnoea when supine
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.44 L/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, beta hCG 210 IU/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan now?

options.text: Discharge with oral fluid guide, daily weight, daily urine output diary and same next day gynaecology review
options.rationale: This is moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with weight gain <5 kg, haematocrit <0.45 L/L, normal renal function, adequate oral intake, no pleural effusion or thromboembolism and a stable social situation; outpatient management with structured monitoring is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 200 mL/hour and diagnostic paracentesis of the pouch of Douglas fluid
options.rationale: Paracentesis is reserved for severe or critical ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with respiratory compromise, tense ascites, or oliguria refractory to conservative therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for intravenous 25 percent albumin infusion and dopamine renal dose for prevention of oliguric renal injury
options.rationale: Neither high dose albumin nor dopamine renal dose are supported for prevention of renal injury in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and both add risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for empirical broad spectrum antibiotics for possible ovarian abscess complicating this stimulation cycle
options.rationale: Ovarian abscess is not a routine consideration in this scenario; markers are not consistent with sepsis and empirical antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for immediate laparoscopy to detorse and possibly resect the enlarged ovaries prior to further deterioration
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a specific surgical emergency with characteristic pain, and prophylactic surgery of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is graded by symptoms, haemoconcentration, ascites, renal function and thromboembolic markers. Moderate cases with haematocrit under 0.45 L/L, weight gain under 5 kg, adequate urine output, ability to tolerate oral fluids and stable social supports can be managed as outpatients with a daily weight and urine diary, thromboprophylaxis in high risk cases and a same next day review. Admission is reserved for severe features (haematocrit >=0.45 L/L, oliguria, pleural effusion, hyponatraemia, coagulopathy). Paracentesis, albumin infusion and prophylactic surgery are all reserved for specific severe scenarios.
key_points: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (haematocrit <0.45, urine output preserved) can be managed as outpatient with structured monitoring.
Severe features prompt admission: haematocrit >=0.45, oliguria, pleural effusion, coagulopathy, tense ascites.
Prophylactic laparoscopy of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable.
explanation.pearls: A moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with haematocrit 0.44 L/L, tolerating oral fluid and preserved urine output goes home with a monitoring diary and next day review.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

subtopic_detail: Second line uterotonic choice with hypertensive contraindication
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar in the birth suite immediately after the vaginal delivery of a 3.9 kg live infant to a 34 year old woman. Third stage was actively managed with prophylactic oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly. The placenta appears complete at 8 minutes with no obvious retained tissue. Over 5 minutes there is a rapid trickle of blood, estimated blood loss 850 mL, and the uterus is boggy. A syntocinon infusion 40 units in 1 L 0.9 percent saline has been commenced running at 250 mL/hour. Bimanual compression is being performed by the senior midwife. The estimated blood loss continues to rise.

Her antenatal record shows two clinic readings of 158/98 mmHg and 156/94 mmHg during the third trimester and she is currently on labetalol 200 mg twice daily for gestational hypertension. She has no asthma, no cardiac disease, no known contraindication to prostaglandins. Repeat blood pressure 3 minutes ago was 154/96 mmHg. Placenta reviewed and complete.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116 /min, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy 22 weeks size, rising fundus, bimanual compression in progress, no visible cervical or perineal tear on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin pre-labour 110 g/L (115-165), platelets 220 x10^9/L, fibrinogen not yet available; group O positive

lead_in: Which second line uterotonic is most appropriate now?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg with intravenous metoclopramide 10 mg antiemetic cover given now for the acute bleed
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia because of ergot mediated vasoconstriction and severe hypertensive crisis risk; her blood pressure and gestational hypertension exclude this. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microg (15 methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) now, repeat at 15 minutes if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension; it can be repeated every 15 minutes up to a total of 2 mg with asthma being the main contraindication to consider. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Rectal misoprostol 800 microg alone as the next uterotonic agent and hold further parenteral agents at this time
options.rationale: Misoprostol may be used but has slow onset and is less effective as monotherapy in ongoing bleeding; parenteral carboprost is preferred when available in ongoing haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units now and observe for 15 minutes before further uterotonic escalation this bleed
options.rationale: Repeating oxytocin in a woman already on an oxytocin infusion at 250 mL/hour with ongoing haemorrhage is not the next step; escalate to a different uterotonic mechanism. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate 200 microg now to relax the uterus and allow prompt manual removal in this bleed
options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate is a uterine relaxant used for a trapped placenta or uterine inversion, not for atonic bleeding after a complete placenta. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage after adequate oxytocin needs a different uterotonic mechanism. Ergometrine causes ergot mediated vasoconstriction and precipitates hypertensive crisis in women with pre eclampsia or hypertension. Carboprost (15 methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) is the preferred second line agent when ergometrine is contraindicated; the main contraindication for carboprost itself is asthma. Misoprostol 800 microg rectally is an option in low resource settings or where parenteral prostaglandin is unavailable. Concurrent tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia.
Carboprost 250 microg intramuscularly, repeat every 15 minutes to 2 mg total, asthma is the main contraindication.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is a standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: A woman with gestational hypertension and ongoing atonic postpartum haemorrhage gets carboprost as the second line uterotonic, not ergometrine.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia identification and delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32 year old primigravida at 32 weeks gestation in the high risk clinic. The morphology scan at 20 weeks had noted a bilobed placenta and a low lying placenta 22 mm from the internal os, and a follow up transvaginal scan at 30 weeks was arranged. That scan showed the placenta 40 mm from the os but visualised unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal os anteriorly. Colour Doppler confirmed fetal arterial waveform on the vessels traversing the os. The rest of the pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal glucose tolerance test.

She reports no bleeding and normal fetal movements. She lives 40 minutes from the tertiary maternity unit. She and her partner ask about the plan for the rest of the pregnancy and birth. Antenatal corticosteroids have not been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysial fundal height 31 cm, fetal heart 148 /min, no palpable contractions, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound 30 weeks: bilobed placenta, placenta clear of the internal os but unprotected fetal vessels crossing the os with fetal arterial Doppler; fetal growth 40th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Serial growth scans and planned vaginal birth at 40 weeks with expectant management if labour begins spontaneously
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated in vasa praevia because rupture of membranes can precipitate fetal exsanguination; delivery must be by planned caesarean before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Immediate caesarean this week at 32 weeks gestation with antenatal corticosteroid loading given intrapartum only
options.rationale: 32 weeks is too early to deliver an asymptomatic woman with vasa praevia and no evidence of bleeding or labour; corticosteroids given intrapartum are too late for maximal benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Admit at 32 to 34 weeks for antenatal corticosteroids and inpatient monitoring, plan elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient monitoring (particularly for women living far from a maternity unit) and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity against catastrophic haemorrhage from ruptured fetal vessels at membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Outpatient management until 39 weeks with a caesarean planned then if she has not laboured spontaneously by that date
options.rationale: Planned caesarean at 39 weeks carries an unacceptable risk of spontaneous rupture of membranes and fetal exsanguination in the interval; delivery must be planned before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Weekly cardiotocograph plus vaginal ultrasound reassessment, delivery only when fetal vessels move clear of the os
options.rationale: Fetal vessels overlying the internal os do not resolve reliably and expectant management delays needed delivery; planned early caesarean is the intervention. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is characterised by unprotected fetal vessels traversing or lying close to the internal cervical os. Membrane rupture with these vessels present precipitates fetal exsanguination within minutes. Australian guidance recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient admission where the woman lives at a distance from a maternity unit, and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity risk against catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Vaginal birth is contraindicated. Suspicion is triggered on morphology scan features such as bilobed placenta, low lying placenta or velamentous cord insertion, then confirmed on transvaginal colour Doppler.
key_points: Vasa praevia risk factors: bilobed placenta, low lying placenta, velamentous cord insertion.
Vaginal birth contraindicated; deliver by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids.
Consider inpatient admission from 32 weeks if geography or bleeding raises risk.
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is delivered by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, not at term.

sources.label: SMFM Consult Series 37: Diagnosis and management of vasa previa

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate toxicity clinical assessment vs level
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar overnight on the birth suite. A 27 year old primigravida at 35 weeks with severe pre eclampsia had a loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous over 20 minutes 3 hours ago, followed by a maintenance infusion at 1 g/hour. Blood pressure is now under 155/95 mmHg with intravenous labetalol. She had a witnessed eclamptic seizure earlier this shift. She is under continuous cardiotocograph. Urine output has been 25 mL in the last hour, having previously been 40 to 60 mL/hour. Her most recent creatinine was 88 micromol/L.

On assessment she is drowsier than 2 hours ago. Her deep tendon reflexes are absent at the patellae and biceps. Her respiratory rate has fallen. Fetal heart is 138 /min with normal variability. Repeat magnesium levels have been sent but the result is not yet available. Calcium gluconate is available in the emergency drug drawer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 150/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 10 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, absent patellar and biceps reflexes, no muscle fasciculation, no jaundice, fetal heart 138 /min normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine transaminase 62 U/L, magnesium level pending; urine output 25 mL in last hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase magnesium sulfate infusion to 2 g/hour empirically for possible seizure recurrence, reduce blood pressure to 130/80 mmHg
options.rationale: The clinical picture is magnesium toxicity, not seizure recurrence; increasing the infusion worsens toxicity, and aggressive blood pressure reduction below 140/90 risks fetal compromise. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Continue infusion at current rate pending the pending magnesium level, review clinical status in one hour with midwifery
options.rationale: Waiting for a level in the face of areflexia, respiratory depression and oliguria risks respiratory arrest; clinical toxicity mandates action before the level returns. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg to induce diuresis to clear magnesium faster and reduce accumulation of drug
options.rationale: Loop diuresis carries risk of hypotension and does not immediately antagonise the neuromuscular effect; calcium gluconate is the antagonist to give during clinical toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Stop magnesium sulfate, give intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes, support ventilation, reassess reflexes hourly
options.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and reduced urine output are clinical signs of magnesium toxicity; the appropriate step is to stop the infusion, give calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes as an antagonist, and support respiration and monitor closely without waiting for the level. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Administer intravenous diazepam 5 mg as an anticonvulsant substitute and continue magnesium sulfate at a reduced rate
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are second line for magnesium refractory seizures; here the clinical problem is magnesium toxicity not seizure and diazepam risks compound respiratory depression. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in a pre eclamptic woman on magnesium sulfate is a clinical diagnosis: loss of patellar reflexes, reduced respiratory rate, drowsiness and oliguria all indicate rising levels. Because renal clearance dominates elimination, oliguria drives accumulation. The clinical assessment does not wait for the level; the infusion is stopped and intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes antagonises the neuromuscular effect. Ventilatory support is added if respiration is compromised. Once stable the infusion may be recommenced at a lower rate with closer monitoring and dose adjustment for renal function.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity is clinical: absent reflexes, respiratory depression, oliguria.
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes; stop the infusion first.
Oliguria drives accumulation; adjust the rate for reduced renal clearance.
explanation.pearls: Absent patellar reflexes and respiratory rate 10 /min on magnesium sulfate is toxicity: stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes.

sources.label: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Magnesium sulfate in pre eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite of a tertiary hospital. A 38 year old woman had spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago in the second stage of labour. Immediately after rupture she became agitated, then unresponsive with sudden hypoxaemia and hypotension. She is now intubated and receiving cardiopulmonary resuscitation with return of spontaneous circulation after 4 minutes. Immediate perimortem caesarean birth was performed at 5 minutes; foetus is transferred to the resuscitaire. The uterus is boggy with a large amount of ongoing dark and clotting-poor vaginal bleeding and generalised oozing from the venepuncture sites and around the endotracheal tube.

Massive transfusion protocol has been activated. First red cells and fresh frozen plasma are hanging. Tranexamic acid 1 g is running. Anaesthetics and intensive care are attending. The next set of coagulation results has just arrived and are markedly abnormal. Cardiac output has been restored on noradrenaline 20 microg/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 88/48 mmHg on noradrenaline, respiratory rate mechanical, SpO2 92% on FiO2 1.0, temperature 36.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, ongoing vaginal bleeding, oozing venepuncture sites, bilateral bibasal crackles on chest auscultation, no visible perineal laceration
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 62 g/L (115-165), platelets 42 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0), INR 2.8, activated partial thromboplastin time 78 s, D dimer >20 mg/L, arterial pH 7.10 lactate 8 mmol/L

lead_in: In addition to ongoing red cells and fresh frozen plasma, which single next intervention is most likely to reduce mortality?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microg/kg intravenous bolus as a haemostatic agent to control bleeding rapidly now
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII is not first line in amniotic fluid embolism and has an increased thrombotic and pulmonary vascular complication risk in this setting; correction of fibrinogen and platelets and empirical haemostatic products come first. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Continuous cell salvage from the surgical field with re infusion to reduce donor red cell exposure through this bleed
options.rationale: Cell salvage is a useful adjunct in obstetric haemorrhage but does not correct the coagulopathy and does not treat the pulmonary vasoconstrictive component of amniotic fluid embolism; it is not the priority. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Intravenous ergometrine 500 microg immediately to reverse uterine atony contributing to the ongoing haemorrhage
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in this haemodynamic and pulmonary state; the pulmonary vasoconstriction would worsen right ventricular failure. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Intravenous heparin 5000 unit bolus to address the disseminated intravascular coagulation contributing to this bleed
options.rationale: Anticoagulation would worsen active haemorrhage and is not indicated in amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation which is predominantly consumptive and fibrinolytic. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Cryoprecipitate 10 units targeted to fibrinogen above 2 g/L with concurrent platelets to keep platelets above 50
options.rationale: Fibrinogen falls first and fastest in amniotic fluid embolism related consumptive coagulopathy; targeted cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen above 2 g/L reduces mortality more than fresh frozen plasma alone at low fibrinogen. Concurrent platelets are kept above 50 x10^9/L in the actively bleeding patient. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism has three overlapping phases: sudden cardiopulmonary collapse from pulmonary vasoconstriction and right ventricular failure, hypoxia and neurological dysfunction, and consumptive coagulopathy with a marked and early drop in fibrinogen. Management is supportive: airway and ventilation, haemodynamic support with noradrenaline and consideration of pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L with cryoprecipitate and platelets above 50 x10^9/L. Ergometrine, heparin and recombinant activated factor VII are variously contraindicated or unproven; the primary haemostatic priority is fibrinogen replacement.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy is fibrinogen consumption first; cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L.
Ergometrine is contraindicated because of pulmonary vasoconstriction risk.
Anticoagulation is not indicated during active haemorrhage from amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation.
explanation.pearls: In amniotic fluid embolism with fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, cryoprecipitate targeted to above 2 g/L is the survival step; do not give ergometrine, heparin or recombinant activated factor VII.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism
National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guideline Module 5 Obstetrics

subtopic_detail: Elective delivery timing and mode in asymptomatic placenta praevia at term
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman gravida 3 para 2 at 34 weeks gestation with a persistent complete anterior placenta praevia confirmed on transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks. She has had no vaginal bleeding. She has two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term. She has no other medical history. She has been counselled about risk of antepartum haemorrhage. She has been asked to avoid intercourse and heavy lifting.

She attends the antenatal high risk clinic today asking about delivery timing and mode. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no features of morbidly adherent placenta. Her booking blood group is O positive with negative antibody screen. Her partner is A positive. She has iron and folate supplementation. Her haemoglobin is 118 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, fundus at 34 weeks, symphysis fundal height 33 cm, fetal heart 148 /min regular, no vaginal blood on outer clothing at review
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound complete anterior placenta praevia, cervix 3.4 cm closed, fetal biometry on 50th centile, umbilical artery Doppler normal, magnetic resonance imaging no features of morbidly adherent placenta

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean at 36+0 weeks with a cell salvage strategy in place, plus antenatal betamethasone before caesarean
options.rationale: 36+0 is earlier than the RANZCOG recommended timing for asymptomatic placenta praevia and requires antenatal steroids because of prematurity risk; timing without prior bleeding is 36+0 to 37+6 in some guidance but Australian practice defaults to 37+0 to 37+6 for asymptomatic praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; no antenatal betamethasone required unless earlier delivery becomes necessary before 37 weeks
options.rationale: Asymptomatic placenta praevia is delivered by elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in AU per RANZCOG. Antenatal betamethasone is not routinely given if delivery is planned at 37 weeks or later. If earlier delivery becomes necessary (bleeding, preterm labour) before 34+6 weeks, a betamethasone course is given. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks with a plan for expectant induction of labour if she goes into labour before then
options.rationale: 39+0 is too late for placenta praevia because of the accumulating risk of unplanned antepartum haemorrhage requiring emergency caesarean; 37 to 37+6 is standard. Induction is contraindicated in complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Trial of vaginal delivery from 39+0 weeks because she has two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term without complication
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia regardless of parity; caesarean is mandated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 34+0 weeks with a plan for antenatal betamethasone plus magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection given prematurity
options.rationale: 34+0 is inappropriately early without a clinical trigger and exposes the neonate to prematurity morbidity; timing is 37 to 37+6 unless bleeding or other complication mandates earlier delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic placenta praevia at term is delivered by elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in AU per RANZCOG, balancing the maternal risk of antepartum haemorrhage against neonatal prematurity morbidity. Symptomatic praevia (bleeding) or high risk features (previous bleed, low anterior placenta with previous caesarean) may prompt delivery from 34 to 36+6 weeks, in which case antenatal betamethasone is given. Cell salvage, cross matched blood, senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement and a written surgical plan are standard for high risk cases. Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete praevia regardless of parity. Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess for accreta if the placenta is anterior and overlies a previous scar.
key_points: Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in asymptomatic praevia.
Antenatal betamethasone if delivery is expected before 34+6 weeks.
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia regardless of parity.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic complete placenta praevia at term: elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; antenatal betamethasone reserved for expected delivery before 34+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Optimal Timing of Elective Birth statement

subtopic_detail: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia management in a postmenopausal woman keen to avoid surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with 6 months of postmenopausal bleeding. She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m^2 and is on metformin for type 2 diabetes. She has no personal history of breast cancer. She has no personal or family history of endometrial or ovarian cancer. She has never used hormone replacement therapy or tamoxifen. She is not a smoker. She has hypertension on ramipril. She has completed her family. She is asking about non surgical options.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy has returned reporting atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia); there is no invasive component identified on biopsy. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a normal appearing myometrium and no adnexal pathology. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m^2, abdomen soft, no palpable adnexal mass, cervix nulliparous appearing, no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness 14 mm, hysteroscopy directed biopsy atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia), magnetic resonance imaging normal myometrium and adnexa, haemoglobin A1c 6.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg daily for 6 months with hysteroscopy monitoring at 3 monthly intervals only
options.rationale: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate is less effective than levonorgestrel intrauterine device for endometrial hyperplasia and does not avoid the need for hysterectomy in postmenopausal atypical hyperplasia. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device with 3 month hysteroscopy monitoring and continued therapy for 12 months minimum
options.rationale: Conservative management with levonorgestrel intrauterine device is reserved for premenopausal women wishing to preserve fertility or those unfit for surgery; in a postmenopausal woman who has completed her family, hysterectomy is first line. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line management for postmenopausal atypical endometrial hyperplasia
options.rationale: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) carries a 25 to 40 percent coexisting invasive endometrial cancer rate at hysterectomy specimen and a high progression risk to invasive cancer. In a postmenopausal woman who has completed her family, total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line treatment. Conservative levonorgestrel intrauterine device therapy is reserved for premenopausal women wishing to preserve fertility or those unfit for surgery. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Reassure and offer 6 monthly transvaginal ultrasound with an endometrial thickness cut off of 5 mm as her indication to repeat biopsy
options.rationale: Surveillance without treatment is inappropriate for atypical hyperplasia in a postmenopausal woman; hysterectomy is definitive and is first line. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Endometrial ablation with second generation device balloon therapy in day surgery under general anaesthetic as definitive management
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is not appropriate for treatment of atypical hyperplasia because it obscures future endometrial assessment and does not address coexisting invasive disease risk. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

explanation.summary: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) carries a 25 to 40 percent risk of coexisting invasive endometrial cancer at hysterectomy and a high progression risk to invasive cancer. Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line treatment in postmenopausal women or women who have completed their family. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered at hysterectomy at some AU centres. Conservative levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device management with 3 monthly hysteroscopy monitoring is reserved for premenopausal women who want to preserve fertility or women unfit for surgery. Non atypical hyperplasia is managed with progestogen and endometrial surveillance; regression is expected in more than 80 percent within 12 months.
key_points: Atypical hyperplasia: 25 to 40 percent coexisting endometrial cancer at hysterectomy specimen.
Postmenopausal atypical hyperplasia: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is first line.
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device conservative therapy reserved for premenopausal fertility preservation or unfit for surgery.
explanation.pearls: Postmenopausal atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia): total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is definitive first line; the 25 to 40 percent coexisting endometrial cancer risk mandates surgery.

sources.label: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia
European Society for Medical Oncology Endometrial Cancer Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Immediate manoeuvres for umbilical cord prolapse at full dilation in a term singleton
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar attending a 28 year old woman gravida 2 para 1 in the labour ward at 39 weeks gestation. She has been in the second stage of labour for 20 minutes with the head at station +1 and ruptured membranes 45 minutes ago. Immediately after a spontaneous surge of amniotic fluid the midwife notes a loop of pulsating cord in the vagina. Cardiotocograph shows immediate profound decelerations to 60 /min lasting more than 2 minutes. She has no known allergies. She has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth 2 years ago at term.

Epidural is in situ and functional. Theatre has been alerted. Anaesthetics have been called. Blood is available on standby. The paediatric team is on the way for resuscitation. She is fully dilated with vertex presentation and no shoulder dystocia risk factors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Fully dilated, vertex station +1, cord palpable in vagina and pulsating, loop of cord visible externally
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph profound deceleration to 60 /min lasting >2 minutes, no bleeding, fetal scalp electrode not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediately push the cord back inside the vagina above the presenting part and prepare for a planned category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: Manual replacement of the cord above the presenting part is not recommended because of vasospasm risk and unreliable outcome; manual elevation of the presenting part and appropriate positioning is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)

options.text: Elevate the presenting part with a gloved hand and adopt knee to chest position, plan immediate assisted vaginal delivery if feasible
options.rationale: Immediate manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand plus a knee to chest (or exaggerated Sim) position relieves cord compression while the plan is enacted. If she is fully dilated with a vertex at station +1 in an experienced obstetrician's hands, an assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) is faster than a caesarean and is the recommended mode. Otherwise, urgent category 1 caesarean is performed. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)

options.text: Wrap the cord in warmed saline soaked gauze and delay urgent delivery pending intrapartum ultrasound assessment of the fetal heart
options.rationale: Keeping the cord moist is a supportive measure but does not replace urgent delivery; delay to await ultrasound is inappropriate given the profound deceleration. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)

options.text: Instruct the woman to actively push with contractions in the left lateral position to expedite vaginal delivery of the fetal head
options.rationale: Active pushing may increase cord compression; the aim is to relieve pressure on the cord and deliver rapidly by the fastest safe mode. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)

options.text: Insert a Foley catheter and fill the bladder with 500 mL saline as the sole immediate manoeuvre before proceeding to theatre now
options.rationale: Bladder filling with 500 mL saline lifts the presenting part off the cord as a bridging measure specifically when transfer to theatre is expected to be prolonged; it is not the sole immediate action and manual elevation of the presenting part is faster. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is a category 1 obstetric emergency. Immediate manoeuvres are manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord, positioning the woman knee to chest or exaggerated Sim to relieve cord compression, and calling for urgent delivery. If she is fully dilated with a vertex at low station in an experienced obstetrician's hands, an assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) is the fastest mode; otherwise category 1 caesarean is performed. Bladder filling with 500 mL saline is a bridging technique if transfer to theatre is expected to be delayed (rural or prolonged transport), and tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneous may be considered if uterine relaxation is needed as a bridging step. Keep the cord warm and moist and avoid excess handling.
key_points: Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord plus knee to chest position is the immediate action.
Fastest safe mode: assisted vaginal delivery at low station full dilation, otherwise category 1 caesarean.
Bladder filling 500 mL is a bridging technique if delivery is delayed.
explanation.pearls: Cord prolapse at full dilation with vertex at +1: manual elevation of the presenting part plus knee to chest position, then assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) as the fastest safe mode; category 1 caesarean if delivery is not immediately feasible.

sources.label: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Green Top Guideline on Umbilical Cord Prolapse

subtopic_detail: Discriminating asymptomatic uterine dehiscence from uterine rupture at trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman gravida 2 para 1 with one previous transverse lower segment caesarean 3 years ago. She is undergoing a trial of labour after caesarean at 40 weeks. She has been in labour for 8 hours; the cardiotocograph is reassuring; her contractions are 4 in 10, moderate to strong. She is 8 cm dilated with a well applied vertex at station 0. She reports mild suprapubic discomfort persistent between contractions but is otherwise well.
