She has an epidural in situ providing effective analgesia. Vaginal blood loss is normal.

A bedside ultrasound performed for parental reassurance shows the lower segment scar with an area of thinning (2 mm) but continuous serosa overlying it. There is no free fluid. Fetal heart tracing is category I. Blood pressure and pulse are stable. She has no shoulder pain. She has no gross haematuria on urinary catheter.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus contracting regularly, cervix 8 cm dilated vertex station 0, no vaginal bleeding above normal show, no palpable fetal parts abdominally, uterine tone normal between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph category I, bedside ultrasound lower segment scar thinned to 2 mm with continuous serosa, no free fluid, urinary catheter clear urine, haemoglobin 116 g/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section for suspected uterine rupture and activation of massive transfusion protocol at this point today
options.rationale: Uterine rupture is defined by disruption of the serosa with fetal or placental parts extruding; findings here are of dehiscence with intact serosa and stable maternal and fetal parameters; category 1 caesarean is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Perform manual palpation of the uterine scar transvaginally under general anaesthetic to assess for continuity before further management
options.rationale: Manual transvaginal palpation is not routine before delivery in trial of labour after caesarean; scar integrity is assessed clinically and by ultrasound. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Give tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously and continue with the trial of labour after caesarean without further review
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated without an abnormal cardiotocograph or evidence of hyperstimulation; it is used to buy time in confirmed fetal distress before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Increase oxytocin augmentation to 8 mU/min to accelerate labour and reduce the total time the scar is exposed to contractions today
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation increases uterine rupture risk in trial of labour after caesarean and requires careful indication and senior obstetric supervision; it is not increased in response to a suspected scar concern. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric review; act on evolving features suggesting rupture
options.rationale: Uterine dehiscence with intact serosa on ultrasound, a reassuring cardiotocograph and stable maternal and fetal parameters can continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph monitoring and senior obstetric awareness. Uterine rupture is diagnosed clinically by loss of station of the presenting part, acute fetal distress (particularly prolonged deceleration or bradycardia), maternal haemodynamic collapse, vaginal bleeding out of keeping, and severe abdominal pain that persists between contractions. Ultrasound scar thinning alone is not diagnostic. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis, not a radiological one. It is characterised by loss of station of the presenting part, acute fetal distress (particularly prolonged deceleration or bradycardia), maternal haemodynamic collapse, vaginal bleeding out of keeping, and severe abdominal pain persisting between contractions. Uterine dehiscence is asymptomatic scar thinning or incomplete disruption with intact serosa and is a not uncommon finding at repeat caesarean; scar thinning alone on ultrasound is not diagnostic of impending rupture and is not an indication for delivery in the absence of clinical features. Trial of labour after caesarean is continued with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric awareness. Rupture is treated with immediate category 1 caesarean and repair.
key_points: Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis: loss of station, prolonged deceleration, haemodynamic collapse, severe persistent abdominal pain.
Dehiscence is asymptomatic scar thinning with intact serosa and is not itself an indication for delivery.
Confirmed rupture: immediate category 1 caesarean and repair with senior obstetric involvement.
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound scar thinning with intact serosa and a reassuring cardiotocograph is dehiscence, not rupture: continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric review; rupture is diagnosed clinically by loss of station, prolonged deceleration, maternal collapse or severe persistent abdominal pain.

sources.label: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Practice Bulletin on Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery

subtopic_detail: Maternal cardiac arrest at 30 weeks requiring perimortem caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar attending a code blue on the medical ward for a 32 year old primigravida at 30 weeks gestation who has collapsed 30 seconds ago. She was admitted 2 days ago with severe pre-eclampsia at 30 weeks. She has been receiving magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour infusion since admission. She is now pulseless. Advanced life support has commenced with high quality chest compressions, ventilation via bag valve mask, and manual left uterine displacement. Adrenaline 1 mg has been given intravenously. An initial rhythm check shows pulseless electrical activity.

The medical emergency team is present. The neonatology team is being called. Theatre is 5 floors away. There is a category 1 caesarean scalpel pack at the bedside. The obstetric consultant is en route from home. She has been in cardiac arrest for approximately 2 minutes now. There is no return of spontaneous circulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse absent, blood pressure not recordable, respiratory rate assisted by bag valve mask, SpO2 not tracing during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Gravid uterus at umbilicus, pulseless electrical activity on cardiac monitor, effective chest compressions ongoing, manual left uterine displacement in progress
data_table.Investigations: Not available in acute resuscitation; magnesium level from earlier today 2.4 mmol/L (therapeutic pre-eclampsia range 2.0-3.5)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next intervention if there is no return of spontaneous circulation?

options.text: Transport her urgently to theatre for caesarean once the theatre team has scrubbed and prepared the sterile equipment on standby
options.rationale: Transport delays perimortem caesarean and worsens both maternal and fetal outcomes; perimortem caesarean is performed at the site of the arrest. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Insert a supraglottic airway and continue advanced life support for a further 5 minutes before proceeding to perimortem caesarean
options.rationale: Definitive airway is a parallel priority in advanced life support but must not delay perimortem caesarean; airway placement is done in parallel with the perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Give a further 1 mg adrenaline and continue advanced life support for 10 minutes before perimortem caesarean is considered
options.rationale: Waiting 10 minutes worsens both maternal and fetal outcomes; the 4 minute rule is a maternal resuscitation intervention, not a fetal one, and is initiated as soon as return of spontaneous circulation is not achieved. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Discontinue magnesium sulfate and administer calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent by intravenous injection now over 3 minutes
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously is given for suspected magnesium toxicity contributing to arrest but is not the definitive next step above perimortem caesarean; both may be done but the perimortem caesarean is the highest priority action if there is no return of spontaneous circulation. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Perform perimortem caesarean at the bedside aiming to deliver by 4 minutes into cardiac arrest, do not transport to theatre
options.rationale: The 4 minute rule states that perimortem caesarean should commence by 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest with a viable foetus at or beyond 20 to 24 weeks (fundus at or above the umbilicus) with delivery by 5 minutes. It is a maternal resuscitation intervention (aortocaval decompression improves cardiac output up to 25 percent) and is performed at the bedside without transport, without full sterility and without waiting for anaesthesia because the mother is arrested. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: The 4 minute rule for perimortem caesarean states that if there is no return of spontaneous circulation by 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest with a viable foetus at or beyond 20 to 24 weeks (uterus at or above the umbilicus), a perimortem caesarean is commenced with delivery by 5 minutes. It is a maternal resuscitation intervention because aortocaval decompression improves cardiac output up to 25 percent. It is performed at the bedside without transport, without full sterility and without waiting for anaesthesia because the mother is arrested. Chest compressions and defibrillation are continued during the procedure and manual left uterine displacement is maintained until the abdomen is opened. Suspected magnesium toxicity is treated with calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel.
key_points: Perimortem caesarean starts at 4 minutes of arrest, aim delivery by 5 minutes.
Performed at the bedside; do not transport; continue chest compressions.
Suspected magnesium toxicity: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel.
explanation.pearls: Maternal cardiac arrest at 30 weeks: perimortem caesarean at bedside starting at 4 minutes of arrest with delivery by 5 minutes; continue chest compressions and give calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel if magnesium toxicity is suspected.

sources.label: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy
American Heart Association Scientific Statement on Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion identified antenatally requires multidisciplinary planning
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine registrar reviewing a 37 year old woman gravida 4 para 3 at 30 weeks gestation with three previous caesareans. She had an in vitro fertilisation pregnancy. Ultrasound at 20 weeks noted anterior placenta praevia. Magnetic resonance imaging at 28 weeks demonstrated an anterior placenta praevia with loss of the retroplacental clear space, disruption of the bladder wall interface, hypertrophic subplacental vessels, and focal bulging of the placenta into the bladder consistent with placenta percreta with bladder invasion. She has had no vaginal bleeding. She has not received antenatal steroids.

She has been referred to your quaternary obstetric centre. Multidisciplinary review is planned for this week. She is otherwise well. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L; she is on iron replacement. She has no known allergies. Her BMI is 27 kg/m^2. She has a longstanding preference to preserve fertility but is prepared to consider hysterectomy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, no palpable bladder, no vaginal blood, no clinical anaemia, no palpable adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging placenta percreta with bladder invasion, ultrasound anterior praevia and lacunar spaces, haemoglobin 108 g/L, group O positive with antibody screen negative

lead_in: Which combination best matches the AU recommended peri-operative plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean at 37+0 weeks by local obstetrician alone with a plan to remove the placenta manually as usual after delivery of the baby
options.rationale: Local single obstetrician management is inadequate for placenta percreta with bladder invasion; multidisciplinary quaternary centre care is essential, and 37+0 does not allow for the increased unplanned delivery risk. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)

options.text: Elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks with a plan for placental removal, no hysterectomy is planned regardless of intraoperative findings today
options.rationale: 39+0 is too late in placenta accreta spectrum (risk of unplanned labour and antepartum haemorrhage) and attempted placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage; caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 35+6 weeks is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)

options.text: Elective vaginal induction at 39+0 weeks with plan for uterine artery embolisation as needed intra-operatively, no caesarean planned initially
options.rationale: Vaginal induction is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum; caesarean is mandated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)

options.text: Elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal betamethasone, cell salvage, and planned intraoperative caesarean hysterectomy
options.rationale: In placenta accreta spectrum with high risk features (multiple prior caesareans, in vitro fertilisation pregnancy, bladder invasion), RANZCOG advises planned delivery at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids at a quaternary centre with a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team, cross matched blood with cell salvage, senior gynaecology surgery, urology on standby for bladder involvement, and planned caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ or performing a controlled removal. Fertility preservation is not appropriate given morbidly adherent bladder invasion. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)

options.text: Elective caesarean at 32+0 weeks with immediate hysterectomy regardless of fetal maturity or antenatal corticosteroid course status today
options.rationale: 32+0 imposes significant neonatal prematurity morbidity without a specific clinical trigger; timing is 34+0 to 35+6 with antenatal corticosteroids unless bleeding or preterm labour supervenes. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with high risk features (multiple caesareans, in vitro fertilisation pregnancy, bladder invasion) is delivered at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks at a quaternary centre with a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team, antenatal corticosteroids, cross matched blood, cell salvage, senior gynaecology surgery, urology on standby, interventional radiology (uterine artery balloon occlusion available), and planned caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ or performing controlled removal. Attempted routine placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage. Preoperative counselling includes hysterectomy, transfusion, bladder repair or cystectomy, ureteric injury and intensive care. Fertility preservation is not appropriate in true percreta with organ invasion.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum with bladder invasion: elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids.
Quaternary centre, placenta accreta spectrum team, cell salvage, urology on standby, planned caesarean hysterectomy.
Attempted placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage; leave the placenta in situ or controlled removal.
explanation.pearls: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion: elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal betamethasone, cell salvage, planned caesarean hysterectomy at a quaternary centre with the placenta accreta spectrum team and urology on standby.

sources.label: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum

subtopic_detail: Severe preeclampsia with severe features at 27 weeks: expectant vs immediate delivery
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine registrar reviewing a 26 year old primigravida at 27+3 weeks with new severe pre-eclampsia. Blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg despite oral labetalol 200 mg 8 hourly and nifedipine 40 mg 12 hourly. She has proteinuria 4+ on dipstick and a protein creatinine ratio 340 mg/mmol. She has mild frontal headache which resolved with paracetamol. She has no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, no oliguria. Platelets are 148 x10^9/L, liver enzymes normal, creatinine 78 micromol/L, uric acid 0.42 mmol/L. Fetal growth is on the 10th centile, umbilical artery Doppler is normal with a positive end diastolic flow, biophysical profile is 8 of 10, cardiotocograph is category I.

Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis has started. She has received a first dose of betamethasone. She is asking about delivery timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, symphysis fundal height 26 cm, no epigastric tenderness, no clonus, brisk deep tendon reflexes 3+, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Protein creatinine ratio 340 mg/mmol, platelets 148 x10^9/L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, uric acid 0.42 mmol/L, ultrasound estimated fetal weight 10th centile, umbilical artery Doppler positive end diastolic flow, biophysical profile 8

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes as immediate delivery is required for all severe pre-eclampsia regardless of gestational age and current status
options.rationale: Immediate delivery is not mandated in all severe pre-eclampsia at 27 weeks; expectant management under close surveillance improves neonatal outcomes when maternal and fetal conditions are stable and antihypertensive control is achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Change to oral methyldopa 500 mg 6 hourly and manage as an outpatient with weekly clinic review of blood pressure and urinalysis testing
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 27 weeks with blood pressure 168/112 mmHg requires inpatient management; outpatient management is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Expectant management with close inpatient monitoring, complete steroid course, escalate antihypertensives, deliver at 34 weeks or earlier if criteria trigger
options.rationale: In severe pre-eclampsia at less than 34 weeks with severe hypertension but no persistent uncontrolled hypertension, HELLP syndrome, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, eclampsia, abruption or non reassuring fetal status, expectant management with close inpatient monitoring, complete antenatal steroid course, escalated antihypertensives and delivery at 34 weeks (or earlier if criteria trigger) improves neonatal outcomes. Fetal wellbeing surveillance includes daily cardiotocograph, weekly umbilical artery Doppler and growth every 2 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Induction of labour after prostaglandin ripening within the next 48 hours regardless of fetal weight or cervical status assessment result
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 27 weeks worsens neonatal outcomes when expectant management criteria are met; induction is also inappropriate before completing an antenatal steroid course. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Add aspirin 150 mg daily and discharge home for weekly outpatient blood pressure review and repeat proteinuria testing at general practice
options.rationale: Aspirin is a prevention strategy from before 16 weeks in high risk women, not a treatment for established severe pre-eclampsia; inpatient management is required. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: In severe pre-eclampsia with severe features at less than 34 weeks, expectant management under close inpatient surveillance with antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and titrated antihypertensives improves neonatal outcomes and is recommended when maternal and fetal conditions are stable. Delivery is triggered by eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, uncontrolled hypertension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, abruption, non reassuring cardiotocograph, absent or reversed umbilical artery end diastolic flow, or gestational age at or beyond 34 weeks. Antihypertensive targets are 140 to 155 mmHg systolic and 90 to 105 mmHg diastolic. Persistent visual disturbance, epigastric pain, headache resistant to simple analgesia and clonus are red flags.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia at <34 weeks: expectant management with steroids, magnesium and antihypertensives when maternal and fetal criteria are met.
Deliver at 34 weeks or earlier for eclampsia, HELLP, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, uncontrolled hypertension, abruption or non reassuring cardiotocograph.
Blood pressure targets: systolic 140 to 155 mmHg and diastolic 90 to 105 mmHg.
explanation.pearls: Severe pre-eclampsia at 27+3 with stable maternal and fetal status: expectant management with steroids, magnesium sulfate, escalated antihypertensives; deliver at 34 weeks or earlier if HELLP, eclampsia, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, abruption or absent umbilical artery end diastolic flow.

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: High grade squamous vulval intraepithelial neoplasia treatment selection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman with a persistent pruritic vulval lesion at the right labia minora. She was referred with an ill defined 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque with slight thickening but no ulceration or invasion. She has never had cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. She is a current smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 20 years). She has never been vaccinated against human papillomavirus. She is otherwise well. She has no immunosuppression. She wishes to preserve the anatomy of the vulva where safe. She is not planning further pregnancies.

Colposcopy and biopsy under local anaesthetic have returned reporting vulval high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive) with no invasive component. There is no adjacent lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. Examination of the vagina and cervix is normal. No inguinal lymphadenopathy is palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Ill defined 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque with mild thickening right labia minora, no ulceration, no palpable inguinal nodes, vagina and cervix normal
data_table.Investigations: Colposcopy directed biopsy vulval high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive), no invasive component

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Wide local excision with a 5 mm negative peripheral margin as the definitive management strategy for high grade squamous vulval lesions
options.rationale: Wide local excision remains an option and is preferred when occult invasion is suspected, but topical imiquimod is a valid conservative option for unifocal usual type high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion without suspicion of invasion, particularly when anatomy preservation is desired. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)

options.text: Reassurance and clinical review at 12 months without treatment given no evidence of invasion and expectant management is a valid option
options.rationale: High grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion has significant progression risk to invasive cancer; treatment is indicated rather than expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)

options.text: Vulvectomy (simple total) as a preventative measure to remove all human papillomavirus infected epithelium in this current smoker with HPV 16
options.rationale: Simple vulvectomy is not appropriate for a unifocal high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; it is disfiguring and reserved for extensive multifocal disease or invasion. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)

options.text: External beam radiotherapy 45 Gy in 25 fractions to the vulva and inguinofemoral nodes as first line treatment for high grade lesions
options.rationale: Radiotherapy is reserved for invasive vulval cancer, not vulval intraepithelial neoplasia; it is not first line for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)

options.text: Topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 16 weeks and re-biopsy any residual lesion; smoking cessation and colposcopy follow up
options.rationale: Topical imiquimod 5 percent applied three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks (typically 16 weeks) is a first line option for unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion of usual type without suspicion of invasion, especially when preservation of anatomy is important. Wide local excision remains an alternative and is preferred when occult invasion is suspected. Smoking cessation reduces recurrence, and post treatment colposcopy at 6 months and then annually is required. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia of usual type (high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, human papillomavirus related) is most common in premenopausal women and is a precursor for vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Treatment options for unifocal disease without suspicion of invasion are topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks or wide local excision with a 5 mm peripheral margin. Wide local excision is preferred when there is suspicion of occult invasion, at symptomatic thickened or ulcerated lesions, or when compliance with topical therapy is a concern. Smoking cessation reduces recurrence, and follow up colposcopy at 6 months then annually detects recurrence. Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (lichen sclerosus associated) has a higher progression rate and is treated by wide local excision.
key_points: Unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion of usual type: topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks or wide local excision with a 5 mm margin.
Wide local excision is preferred when occult invasion is suspected.
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (lichen sclerosus associated) has higher progression risk and is treated by wide local excision.
explanation.pearls: Unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive): topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 16 weeks with smoking cessation and colposcopy follow up at 6 months and annually.

sources.label: European Society of Gynaecological Oncology guidelines for vulval intraepithelial neoplasia

subtopic_detail: Third line uterotonic choice for atonic postpartum haemorrhage after first line failure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 32 year old G3 P2 woman has just delivered a healthy 3900 g baby by uncomplicated vaginal birth after a spontaneous labour. Active management of the third stage was performed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units at the anterior shoulder. Ten minutes after placental delivery she has ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding estimated at 1200 mL. The placenta appears complete on inspection.

Her past history includes essential hypertension well controlled on amlodipine and a healthy body mass index of 26. She has no bronchospastic disease. Her uterus is felt to be poorly contracted and her fundus is at 2 cm above the umbilicus. An intravenous oxytocin bolus of 5 units has been given and an infusion of 40 units in 1 L Hartmann solution is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Uterus: Poorly contracted, fundus 2 cm above umbilicus, ongoing brisk bleeding after oxytocin bolus and infusion
data_table.Genital tract: Placenta complete on inspection, no cervical or vaginal laceration identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Bilateral uterine artery embolisation now before any further uterotonic escalation because pharmacological options in AU practice have already failed her
options.rationale: Embolisation is a later step for ongoing bleeding after failed medical and mechanical therapies; ergometrine, tranexamic acid and mechanical measures come first. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg before ergometrine because it works faster and can be repeated every 15 minutes to a total dose of 2 mg to arrest bleeding
options.rationale: Carboprost is a third line uterotonic in AU practice, used if ergometrine is contraindicated or ineffective, not before ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular misoprostol 800 mcg rectally alone without ergometrine because it has fewer contraindications than the injectable ergot alkaloid agents
options.rationale: Misoprostol is considered when ergometrine is contraindicated and injectable options are unavailable; it is not the preferred second line agent when oxytocin fails. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes to promote uterine relaxation and improve placental site healing before further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate causes uterine relaxation and would worsen atony; it is not a treatment for PPH. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg after checking that there is no contraindication and giving intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g as an adjunct
options.rationale: In atonic PPH after oxytocin, ergometrine is the second line uterotonic if not contraindicated, and tranexamic acid 1 g is given within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian escalation for atonic postpartum haemorrhage is oxytocin (5 units intravenous bolus then 40 units in 1 L Hartmann infusion), then ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular or slow intravenous if there is no contraindication (hypertension, pre-eclampsia, cardiac disease), then carboprost 250 mcg intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 2 mg. Tranexamic acid 1 g is given intravenously within 3 hours of onset. Mechanical measures including bimanual compression, intrauterine balloon tamponade and, in refractory cases, uterine artery embolisation or B Lynch suture and hysterectomy are escalated in parallel. Well controlled essential hypertension is a relative but not absolute contraindication to ergometrine and requires blood pressure monitoring.
key_points: Escalation: oxytocin bolus and infusion, then ergometrine, then carboprost.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours of PPH onset.
Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) run in parallel to pharmacological escalation.
explanation.pearls: Atonic PPH after oxytocin: give ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular next unless contraindicated, add tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours and prepare mechanical measures early.

subtopic_detail: Immediate antihypertensive choice for severe range blood pressure in pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 26 year old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents with a 2 day history of headache and epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was 108/64 mmHg. Today her blood pressure has been 166/112, 172/108 and 168/110 mmHg over the past 30 minutes on repeated automated cuff. Urinary protein creatinine ratio is 78 mg/mmol.

She has brisk reflexes but no clonus and no visual disturbance. Fetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. Bloods show platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L. She is on no regular medication and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/110 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Reflexes: Brisk, no clonus, no visual disturbance
data_table.Laboratory: Platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L, urinary protein creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive management?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and start magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading, then a 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis at this stage
options.rationale: In severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia, intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus (repeatable) plus magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis is a first line combination in AU. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Oral atenolol 50 mg once and observe for one hour to confirm response before adding any parenteral agent or magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention
options.rationale: Oral beta blocker with a slow onset is not appropriate for severe range blood pressure; magnesium sulfate should also not be delayed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure below 90 mmHg and hold magnesium sulfate until an eclamptic seizure occurs
options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate is not a first line agent in severe pre-eclampsia; magnesium is given for seizure prophylaxis with severe features, not only after a seizure. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediately for rapid onset and repeat every 15 minutes as needed to bring blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg within one hour
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine risks abrupt hypotension and fetal compromise; immediate release oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg is acceptable but sublingual dosing is not recommended. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to reduce vascular volume and lower blood pressure and defer magnesium sulfate to prevent worsening of the pre-eclamptic profile
options.rationale: Furosemide is not indicated for severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia and worsens intravascular depletion; magnesium sulfate should not be deferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe range hypertension (systolic 160 mmHg or higher, or diastolic 110 mmHg or higher) in pre-eclampsia requires urgent antihypertensive therapy to prevent maternal stroke. In Australian practice the first line agents are intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus (doubling doses to 80 mg), hydralazine 5 to 10 mg intravenous, or immediate release oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg (not sublingual). Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis when there are severe features, typically a 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion. Definitive management is delivery, with timing individualised by gestation, fetal wellbeing and maternal severity.
key_points: Severe range: systolic at or above 160 or diastolic at or above 110 mmHg needs urgent treatment.
Intravenous labetalol, hydralazine or immediate release nifedipine (not sublingual) are first line.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis with severe features.
explanation.pearls: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks with sustained blood pressure over 160/110 mmHg: give intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and magnesium sulfate 4 g loading followed by 1 g/hour infusion, and plan delivery.

sources.label: RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Statement

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic decision in labour without antenatal group B streptococcus screening result
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 28 year old G2 P1 woman at 39 plus 2 weeks presents in spontaneous active labour with intact membranes and cervix 5 cm dilated. She had preterm rupture of membranes at 34 weeks in her previous pregnancy with a healthy 2600 g baby who was well. She missed her 36 week antenatal appointment and there is no group B streptococcus swab result available.

She has no penicillin allergy. Fetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. She has been afebrile and well throughout labour and the amniotic fluid, once membranes rupture 30 minutes later, is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Labour: Cervix 5 cm, spontaneous active labour, membranes rupture 30 minutes after admission with clear fluid
data_table.Screening: No group B streptococcus swab result available; no prior colonisation, no prior GBS neonatal disease, no bacteriuria this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and observe her carefully because she is at term, was afebrile with clear amniotic fluid and has no laboratory evidence of colonisation this pregnancy
options.rationale: Under AU risk based practice, unknown status at term labour is treated to prevent neonatal early onset GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 1 g stat now and repeat every 6 hours in labour because oral therapy achieves adequate placental transfer without needing intravenous access
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is not used for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis; intravenous benzylpenicillin achieves rapid neonatal cover. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give intrapartum intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading, then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery because unknown GBS status at term labour is a treat indication
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance treats unknown GBS status at term labour based on risk factors; the safer AU practice is intrapartum benzylpenicillin when swab is not available. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Send a rectovaginal swab now for polymerase chain reaction group B streptococcus screening and only start antibiotics once the result becomes positive later
options.rationale: In active labour, decisions cannot wait for swab or polymerase chain reaction turnaround; intrapartum prophylaxis is decided on risk factors and status now. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g single dose only at admission and no further antibiotic during labour because coverage is achieved for the full duration
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not first line and is not given as a single intramuscular dose for GBS prophylaxis; benzylpenicillin infusion every 4 hours is standard. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

explanation.summary: Australia uses a risk based approach to intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis (per RANZCOG). Indications include a positive antenatal swab, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, a previous baby with GBS disease, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes at 18 hours or more, intrapartum fever at or above 38 degC, and unknown status at term labour. First line intrapartum antibiotic is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery. Cefazolin is used in non anaphylactic penicillin allergy and clindamycin (if susceptibility confirmed) or vancomycin in severe allergy.
key_points: Unknown GBS status in term labour is a treat indication under the AU risk based approach.
First line agent: intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours.
Cefazolin for non severe penicillin allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin for severe allergy.
explanation.pearls: Term labour with no GBS swab result available: start intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading and 1.8 g every 4 hours; do not wait for a swab result once labour is established.

subtopic_detail: Selecting a reversible contraceptive in a woman with migraine with aura and heavy menstrual bleeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old nulliparous woman in a routine appointment. She has had migraine with visual aura for 5 years, occurring twice a month, and typical migraine without aura around her periods. She has heavy menstrual bleeding (a saturated pad every 2 hours for 3 days of each period) and no bleeding between periods. Pelvic ultrasound was normal 4 months ago.

She is a non smoker with body mass index 24 and blood pressure 116/72 mmHg. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She would like reliable contraception and would like heavy periods addressed if possible. She is in a monogamous relationship and has no sexually transmitted infection risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Cycle: Regular 28 day cycle, heavy days 1 to 3, saturated pad every 2 hours; pelvic ultrasound normal 4 months ago
data_table.Comorbidity: Migraine with visual aura twice monthly, non smoker, body mass index 24, no venous thromboembolism history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend first?

options.text: Progestogen only pill (desogestrel 75 mcg daily) alone with tranexamic acid 1 g up to 4 times daily on the heaviest three days to reduce menstrual blood loss
options.rationale: The progestogen only pill is safe in migraine with aura and tranexamic acid reduces heavy bleeding, but this combination is less effective than the levonorgestrel intrauterine device for both aims. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 30 mcg and levonorgestrel 150 mcg, taken continuously to reduce menstrual flow and eliminate the withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: Migraine with aura at any age is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Transdermal combined oestrogen and progestogen patch changed weekly for a total 3 weeks per month, with a hormone free week to allow scheduled withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: Transdermal combined contraception still contains oestrogen and is contraindicated in migraine with aura for the same stroke risk reason. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device, discussing that this reduces menstrual blood loss and provides highly effective contraception for 5 to 8 years of use
options.rationale: In migraine with aura, combined hormonal contraception is category 4; the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device is safe, reduces menstrual blood loss and provides long acting reversible contraception. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks with iron supplementation as needed for menstrual blood loss issues over the first three months
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is safe in aura and reduces bleeding but is less effective than the levonorgestrel intrauterine device for heavy menstrual bleeding and has bone density and delayed fertility issues. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is UK Medical Eligibility Criteria category 4 (unacceptable risk) for any combined hormonal contraception because of the elevated ischaemic stroke risk, regardless of age or route. Safe alternatives include the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device, copper intrauterine device, subdermal etonogestrel implant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and the progestogen only pill. The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device is preferred when heavy menstrual bleeding is also present because it reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90 percent at 12 months and provides highly effective long acting reversible contraception for 5 to 8 years. Tranexamic acid or non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be added.
key_points: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception at any age.
52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device gives long acting reversible contraception and cuts menstrual blood loss.
Other progestogen only options (pill, implant, depot) are safe but less effective at reducing bleeding.
explanation.pearls: Migraine with visual aura plus heavy menstrual bleeding: recommend the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device first because combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated by UKMEC and the intrauterine device treats both aims.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing after a sensitising event in a rhesus negative woman at 20 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the day assessment unit. A 25 year old G2 P0 woman who is O rhesus negative attends at 20 plus 4 weeks after a bicycle fall in which she landed on her right side. She has right lower quadrant abdominal bruising and mild abdominal discomfort but no vaginal bleeding and no uterine contractions. Fetal cardiotocograph is not yet reactive at this gestation but the fetal heart rate is 148 /min on Doppler.

Ultrasound shows a normal single foetus of appropriate size and a normally sited placenta with no retroplacental collection. Her partner is presumed rhesus positive. Her booking bloods showed no antibodies. She has not received any anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Abdomen: Right lower quadrant bruising, uterus non tender, no contractions
data_table.Ultrasound: Single foetus of appropriate size, normally sited placenta, no retroplacental haematoma, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D management now?

options.text: Give 625 IU intravenous anti-D immunoglobulin now because intravenous administration reaches placental exchange faster than intramuscular delivery to reduce sensitisation risk
options.rationale: Anti-D is given intramuscularly in AU standard practice; intravenous is not required and the AU product is licensed intramuscularly. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Give 1500 IU (300 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now as the routine 28 week prophylaxis dose because trauma is likely to have caused a large foetomaternal haemorrhage
options.rationale: The routine 28 and 34 week prophylaxis is 625 IU (125 mcg) in AU, not 1500 IU; and dosing after a sensitising event before 28 weeks is 625 IU with Kleihauer for additional dose. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Send a Kleihauer-Betke test only and hold anti-D immunoglobulin until the result becomes positive because there is no bleeding at the moment and no retroplacental haemorrhage
options.rationale: Anti-D must be given within 72 hours; waiting for a Kleihauer result before giving the initial dose is unsafe as sensitisation may be missed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure and arrange her routine 28 week anti-D immunoglobulin appointment without additional dose today, because the ultrasound is normal and there is no vaginal bleeding
options.rationale: Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event regardless of bleeding; giving anti-D now is required to prevent sensitisation. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Give 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer-Betke test to determine whether additional anti-D is needed based on the fetal red cell dose
options.rationale: Potentially sensitising events after 12 weeks require anti-D 625 IU with Kleihauer to guide additional dosing per NBA guidance. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Rhesus D negative women receive anti-D immunoglobulin routinely at 28 and 34 weeks (625 IU or 125 mcg per NBA), after birth of a rhesus positive baby (625 IU) and after any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma, external cephalic version, invasive procedures and antepartum bleeding. Under 12 weeks: 250 IU is used (only if invasive procedures such as chorionic villus sampling). At or after 12 weeks: 625 IU with a Kleihauer-Betke test to detect large foetomaternal haemorrhage requiring additional doses. Anti-D should be given within 72 hours of the sensitising event.
key_points: At or after 12 weeks: 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D within 72 hours of a sensitising event.
Send a Kleihauer-Betke test to detect additional foetomaternal haemorrhage requiring more anti-D.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is 625 IU each dose in Australia.
explanation.pearls: Abdominal trauma at 20 weeks in a rhesus negative woman: give 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours and send a Kleihauer-Betke test to guide additional dosing.

subtopic_detail: First response to overt umbilical cord prolapse at full dilatation in a hospital birth suite
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 30 year old G3 P2 woman at 39 plus 5 weeks is being cared for by a midwife in the second stage of labour with a cephalic presentation. Membranes rupture spontaneously with a gush of clear liquor. On the next vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating cord below the presenting part. Fetal heart rate on cardiotocograph is 78 /min with reduced variability.

She is fully dilated with the vertex at station 0. Theatre is 4 minutes from the birth suite and there is no anaesthetist in the room. She has had an uneventful pregnancy and has not received any antenatal corticosteroids.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Fetal heart rate 78 /min for 2 minutes, reduced variability, no decelerations before the rupture
data_table.Vaginal examination: Full dilatation, vertex station 0, pulsating cord palpable below presenting part

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Elevate the presenting part manually off the cord vaginally, position her knee to chest or head down and call for immediate assisted vaginal delivery if head is at spines
options.rationale: At full dilatation with vertex at spines, first response is manual elevation of the presenting part and preparation for immediate assisted vaginal delivery if feasible, otherwise category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Wait for spontaneous progress with active pushing and encourage strong contractions with oxytocin augmentation as head is at spines and vaginal delivery may occur naturally soon
options.rationale: Delay risks fatal cord compression; oxytocin augmentation worsens compression during contractions and is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Push the cord back into the uterus gently through the introitus using a warm saline soaked pad and continue expectant management with fetal monitoring for the next hour
options.rationale: Cord replacement is not recommended (vasospasm) and expectant management risks fetal death; immediate delivery is required. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Call for immediate transfer to theatre for category 1 caesarean without any manual elevation because vaginal elevation of the presenting part increases the risk of maternal infection
options.rationale: Manual elevation is standard bridging until delivery whether vaginal or caesarean; infection risk does not outweigh the acute fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter and fill the bladder with 500 mL of normal saline to elevate the presenting part before deciding on mode of delivery for her infant
options.rationale: Bladder filling is used only when transfer is prolonged (usually from home or a peripheral unit); it is not the first response in a hospital birth suite with theatre available. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency because cord compression causes acute fetal hypoxia. First response is manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord vaginally, positioning the mother knee to chest or Trendelenburg (or left lateral with head down), stopping any oxytocin infusion, calling for help and preparing for delivery. Mode of delivery depends on progress: at full dilatation with an engaged head and no other contraindication, assisted vaginal delivery is often quickest; otherwise category 1 caesarean. Bladder filling is a technique reserved for prolonged transfer situations, not routine hospital birth suite response.
key_points: Manual elevation of the presenting part is the first action to relieve cord compression.
At full dilatation and head at spines, assisted vaginal delivery may be quicker than caesarean.
Bladder filling is used when transfer is prolonged, not as first response in a hospital.
explanation.pearls: Cord prolapse at full dilatation with vertex at spines: elevate the presenting part manually, stop oxytocin and prepare for immediate assisted vaginal delivery or category 1 caesarean, whichever is faster.

sources.label: RCOG Cord Prolapse Green Top Guideline No 50

subtopic_detail: Choice between medical and surgical management of an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment service. A 26 year old woman presents with 3 days of mild right iliac fossa pain and 1 day of light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago and her home pregnancy test is positive. She lives 10 minutes from the hospital and has reliable transport. She has no shoulder tip pain.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a right adnexal mass 2.4 cm with no fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG is 3200 IU/L. Her haemoglobin is 128 g/L (115 to 165) and she is O rhesus positive. She is on no regular medications and has no chronic renal, hepatic or haematological disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, right adnexal mass 2.4 cm without fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid, ovaries otherwise normal
data_table.Laboratory: bhCG 3200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 165), rhesus positive, no renal, hepatic or haematological disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy today because a bhCG above 3000 IU/L is the AU threshold at which surgical management is required for an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy
options.rationale: The AU surgical threshold is bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher (per RANZCOG); at 3200 with a small mass and no rupture, methotrexate is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 single dose with day 4 and day 7 bhCG follow up, contraception counselling and clear return advice for any pain or bleeding progression
options.rationale: Unruptured tubal ectopic with bhCG below 5000, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm and reliable follow up meets RANZCOG criteria for single dose methotrexate. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG and no medical or surgical intervention because the mass is small and pain is mild and the pregnancy is likely to self resolve completely
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic patients with low and falling bhCG (typically under 1000 IU/L) and a small resolving mass; her bhCG at 3200 with pain is too high. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Give a single dose of misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally to complete resolution of the tubal pregnancy and repeat bhCG in 48 hours to confirm response before further steps
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a uterotonic for miscarriage of intrauterine pregnancy; it is not a treatment for tubal ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy today to preserve future fertility even though this is her first pregnancy and her contralateral tube appears normal on the transvaginal ultrasound
options.rationale: Salpingectomy is preferred in a contralateral healthy tube because salpingostomy carries higher recurrence and persistent trophoblast risk; and methotrexate is a valid non surgical option here. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Medical management of unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy with single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 is appropriate when RANZCOG criteria are met: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass less than 3.5 cm, minimal pain, no significant haemoperitoneum and reliable follow up, with no medical contraindications (renal, hepatic or haematological disease, breast feeding, immunodeficiency). bhCG is checked at day 4 and day 7; a fall of 15 percent between days 4 and 7 indicates response. Contraception is advised for 3 months. Surgical management (usually laparoscopic salpingectomy) is required for rupture, haemodynamic instability, failed medical therapy, bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher, or significant pain.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria include bhCG below 5000 and mass under 3.5 cm with no fetal cardiac activity.
Follow up bhCG on days 4 and 7 with 15 percent fall indicating response.
Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the other tube is normal.
explanation.pearls: Unruptured ectopic at bhCG 3200 IU/L with mass under 3.5 cm and reliable follow up: give single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 and repeat bhCG at day 4 and day 7.

subtopic_detail: First hour management of maternal sepsis from pyelonephritis at 22 weeks with an equivocal lactate
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the emergency department. A 27 year old G1 P0 woman at 22 plus 2 weeks presents with 24 hours of fevers, right loin pain and rigors. She has vomited three times and reports feeling dizzy standing up. She has a background of one prior urinary tract infection at 12 weeks that was treated with cephalexin.

On examination she is flushed and unwell looking. She has right renal angle tenderness and no uterine tenderness. Fetal cardiotocograph is not attempted at this gestation but fetal heart rate is 148 /min on Doppler. Bedside urinalysis is positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood. Serum lactate is 2.4 mmol/L on capillary sample; white cell count 18 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 178 mg/L (below 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.2 degC
data_table.Renal: Right renal angle tenderness, urinalysis positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood, no flank mass, no obstruction on ultrasound within 30 minutes
data_table.Laboratory: Lactate 2.4 mmol/L, white cell count 18 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 178 mg/L (below 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous betamethasone 11.4 mg for fetal lung maturation and delay antibiotics until after antenatal corticosteroid administration in this 22 week gestation pregnancy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are given from 24 weeks (or from 22 weeks with resuscitation planning) and do not take priority over sepsis management; antibiotics must not be delayed. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours because she is at 22 weeks and gentamicin should be avoided in pregnancy due to eighth cranial nerve toxicity risk to the foetus
options.rationale: Sepsis needs intravenous therapy; short course gentamicin in pregnancy is not contraindicated when treating serious maternal infection. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g stat and observe over 4 hours before considering fluid resuscitation to prevent iatrogenic pulmonary oedema in a pregnant woman with mild acidosis
options.rationale: Delaying fluids and monotherapy without gentamicin cover is not the AU standard; the sepsis pathway mandates the fluid bolus and appropriate combination therapy within one hour. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg with intravenous ampicillin 2 g within 1 hour after blood cultures, 500 mL crystalloid bolus and repeat lactate at 2 hours per Australian sepsis pathway
options.rationale: AU sepsis pathway in pregnancy requires antibiotics within one hour after cultures; gentamicin with ampicillin covers Enterobacterales and enterococci for pyelonephritis in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg plus meropenem 1 g stat as broad spectrum cover because pyelonephritis in pregnancy demands empirical carbapenem plus vancomycin coverage
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus carbapenem is reserved for severe sepsis with multidrug resistant risk factors or failed first line therapy; not first line for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Sepsis in pregnancy is managed by the same principles as non pregnant sepsis but with tighter physiological thresholds. The AU pathway requires blood cultures then broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics within one hour of recognition, a 500 mL crystalloid bolus (repeated to 30 mL/kg if hypotensive), lactate measurement and reassessment, source control, and fetal surveillance if appropriate for gestation. Empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy is intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg (adjusted for renal function and weight) with intravenous ampicillin or amoxicillin to cover Enterobacterales and enterococci. Short course gentamicin is not contraindicated when treating serious maternal infection. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is an alternative if aminoglycoside cannot be given.
key_points: Antibiotics within one hour of sepsis recognition after blood cultures; 500 mL crystalloid bolus.
Empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy: intravenous gentamicin plus ampicillin.
Repeat lactate after fluid; escalate if not clearing or hypotension persists.
explanation.pearls: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy with lactate 2.4 mmol/L and tachycardia: draw blood cultures, give 500 mL crystalloid bolus and intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg plus ampicillin 2 g within one hour of sepsis recognition.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis loading and maintenance in a woman with severe pre-eclampsia at 34 plus 3 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a metropolitan tertiary hospital reviewing a 32 year old primigravid woman at 34 plus 3 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia. She reports headache and epigastric pain today. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg and today it is 168/112 mmHg on repeat measurement 15 minutes apart. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and spot protein to creatinine ratio is 92 mg per mmol.

Other bloods show platelets 118 x10^9/L (150 to 400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), alanine aminotransferase 88 U/L (5 to 45) and urate 0.41 mmol/L. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. She has no known allergies. Intravenous labetalol has been commenced for blood pressure control and antenatal corticosteroid course is being organised. There is no known contraindication to magnesium sulfate and creatinine clearance is preserved.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 96 /min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg on repeat, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), ALT 88 U/L (5-45), urate 0.41 mmol/L
data_table.Neurological: Headache, epigastric pain, brisk reflexes with 3 beats of ankle clonus
data_table.Fetal: Cardiotocograph baseline 145 /min, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Give intramuscular magnesium sulfate 5 g into each buttock as a total loading dose of 10 g and repeat 5 g every 4 hours without any intravenous maintenance infusion pending delivery of the baby
options.rationale: Intramuscular Pritchard regimen is a resource limited fallback; the AU intravenous regimen (4 g load then 1 g/h) is preferred where infusion pumps and monitoring are available. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Withhold magnesium sulfate and use intravenous diazepam 10 mg bolus at seizure onset only because prophylactic magnesium sulfate is not evidence based in severe pre-eclampsia without an antecedent eclamptic seizure
options.rationale: Magpie trial evidence supports prophylactic magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia; benzodiazepines are second line at seizure. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Load with intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 5 minutes and follow with a maintenance intravenous infusion at 2 g per hour targeting therapeutic serum magnesium of 3.0 to 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: The AU loading dose is 4 g over 20 minutes with 1 g per hour maintenance; therapeutic monitoring is by clinical signs (reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output) rather than routine magnesium levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Load with intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes and follow with a maintenance intravenous infusion at 1 g per hour for at least 24 hours after delivery with clinical monitoring
options.rationale: The RANZCOG AU regimen for severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis is 4 g load over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after delivery, monitored by reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g bolus and titrate maintenance infusion between 2 g and 3 g per hour to serum magnesium level with the primary purpose of lowering the maternal blood pressure
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is a seizure prophylactic, not an antihypertensive; blood pressure is treated separately with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia meets criteria when hypertension (blood pressure at least 160/110 mmHg) is accompanied by any severe feature such as symptoms (headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain), thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L, transaminase above twice the upper limit of normal, creatinine rising above baseline, pulmonary oedema or fetal compromise. Prophylactic magnesium sulfate reduces the risk of eclampsia by around 60 percent based on the Magpie trial. The Australian regimen is 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour maintenance for 24 hours after delivery. Clinical monitoring (deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate above 12, urine output above 100 mL in 4 hours) replaces routine serum magnesium level measurement. Magnesium is a seizure prophylactic; blood pressure is controlled separately with labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine.
key_points: AU magnesium sulfate regimen: 4 g intravenous load over 20 minutes then 1 g/h for 24 hours after delivery.
Monitor by clinical signs (reflexes, respiratory rate above 12, urine output above 100 mL/4 h).
Magnesium is a seizure prophylactic, not an antihypertensive; treat blood pressure separately.
explanation.pearls: The Australian magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis regimen is 4 g intravenous load over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after delivery, monitored by reflexes and respiratory rate rather than by routine serum magnesium levels.

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis timing and interval for a Group B Streptococcus positive woman in early labour at 39 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29 year old parous woman at 39 plus 2 weeks in early labour with 4 hours of regular contractions and ruptured membranes 90 minutes ago at home. She is Group B Streptococcus (GBS) positive on a routine 36 week vaginal and rectal swab. She has no penicillin allergy. Her previous baby was well and there was no invasive GBS disease. Cervical examination is 3 cm dilated, cephalic, well applied.

Cardiotocograph shows a normal reactive trace with a baseline of 140 per minute. Temperature is 36.8 degC and she is well. She lives 20 minutes from hospital. The midwife requests advice on intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Estimated fetal weight is average for gestation and her body mass index is 24 kg per m2. She has no significant comorbidities and no other antibiotic use during the pregnancy or the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Obstetric: 39+2 weeks, parous, cephalic, 3 cm dilated, membranes ruptured 90 minutes ago
data_table.Microbiology: 36 week vaginal/rectal swab GBS positive; no penicillin allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Give a single intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g stat and no further doses for the duration of labour to cover Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis and avoid the need for repeat intravenous antibiotic dosing during labour
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not the AU first line for GBS prophylaxis in a non allergic woman; benzylpenicillin loading and 4 hourly dosing is standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Withhold intrapartum antibiotics and reassess only if maternal fever develops during labour or if the second stage is delayed beyond 3 hours or membranes rupture greater than 18 hours prior to birth
options.rationale: Culture based GBS colonisation at 36 weeks is itself an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of clinical risk factors developing. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours for the duration of labour with a first dose immediately in the antenatal ward before transfer of care to the birth suite for continuing intrapartum care
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate intrapartum fetal blood levels for GBS prophylaxis; the intravenous route is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours for the duration of labour for suspected penicillin allergy with anaphylactic reaction risk despite the woman reporting no penicillin allergy at booking
options.rationale: Clindamycin is second line for anaphylactic penicillin allergy only; a non allergic woman should receive benzylpenicillin. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, aiming for at least one full dose delivered 4 hours or more before delivery to achieve adequate prophylaxis
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a non allergic woman is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours; a dose given at least 4 hours before delivery is optimal for neonatal blood levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus)

explanation.summary: Group B Streptococcus is the leading cause of early onset neonatal sepsis in Australia. RANZCOG endorses a culture based screening strategy with combined vaginal and rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. Positive colonisation, previous baby with invasive GBS disease and GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy are indications for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of other risk factors. Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours is first line in non allergic women; at least one dose given 4 hours or more before delivery achieves adequate transplacental levels. Cefazolin is used for low risk penicillin allergy and clindamycin (with susceptibility) or vancomycin for high risk allergy. Oral or single dose regimens do not achieve adequate fetal blood levels.
key_points: AU regimen (non allergic): benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery.
Aim for at least one full dose 4 hours or more before delivery for adequate fetal blood levels.
Cefazolin for low risk penicillin allergy; clindamycin (with susceptibility) or vancomycin for high risk allergy.
explanation.pearls: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous load then 1.8 g every 4 hours is the AU intrapartum GBS regimen; the dose interval optimisation is the 4 hour rule (at least one dose 4 hours before delivery).

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis dosing and timing in an unsensitised RhD negative primigravida
stem:
You are the general practitioner obstetric shared care doctor reviewing a 29 year old primigravid woman at 27 plus 5 weeks. She is RhD negative on her booking group and antibody screen with no anti-D or other red cell antibodies detected. Her partner is RhD positive. Booking bloods otherwise showed haemoglobin 122 g/L, ferritin 42 microgram/L and normal glucose challenge test. She has had no antenatal bleeding, no invasive procedures and no abdominal trauma.

At today's visit she is well, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, symphysis fundal height 27 cm and fetal heart rate 148 per minute. Cell free fetal DNA to determine fetal RhD group has not been performed at her clinic and is not routinely funded in her state. She has no known allergies. Her next scheduled antenatal visit is at 32 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 82 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Booking bloods: Group O RhD negative, no red cell antibodies, haemoglobin 122 g/L, ferritin 42 microgram/L
data_table.Obstetric: 27+5 weeks primigravida, no bleeding, no trauma, no invasive procedures
data_table.Fetal: Symphysis fundal height 27 cm, fetal heart 148 /min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D regimen?

options.text: Give one dose of anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly today at 28 weeks and repeat a second dose of anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly at 34 weeks after a further antibody screen has been performed
options.rationale: The AU National Blood Authority regimen for RhD negative pregnant women is 625 IU intramuscularly at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks with a preceding antibody screen at each dose. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Give a single 1500 IU intramuscular anti-D dose today and no further doses until after delivery when a Kleihauer test is performed to determine the need for any supplementary doses in the postnatal period
options.rationale: AU uses split 625 IU regimen at 28 and 34 weeks; a single 1500 IU dose is a UK schedule and is not the funded AU option under the National Blood Authority. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Defer anti-D until 34 weeks and give a single 625 IU intramuscular dose at that visit only because the earlier 28 week dose is no longer required in current Australian antenatal prophylaxis practice today
options.rationale: The 28 week dose is a core part of the AU two dose regimen; deferring loses first trimester and second trimester silent sensitisation coverage. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Defer any anti-D until fetal RhD group is confirmed by cell free fetal DNA and only give anti-D if the fetal RhD group returns as RhD positive on the non invasive prenatal test result today
options.rationale: Non invasive fetal RhD typing is available but is not universally funded and is not required to proceed with routine 28 week prophylaxis under AU guidance. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Perform an antibody screen today, defer anti-D and reassess in 2 weeks with a repeat antibody screen to look for the appearance of anti-D before administering any prophylactic dose in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Antibody screening is performed before each anti-D dose but the 28 week dose itself should not be delayed once the screen is negative. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Anti-D prophylaxis prevents alloimmunisation in RhD negative women carrying an RhD positive foetus. In Australia the National Blood Authority funds a two dose antenatal regimen of 625 IU intramuscularly at 28 and 34 weeks, each preceded by an antibody screen. Additional doses are given for sensitising events including antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version, invasive procedures (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis), abdominal trauma and after delivery of a confirmed RhD positive baby (with a Kleihauer test to guide additional doses if a large foeto-maternal haemorrhage is suspected). Non invasive fetal RhD typing by cell free DNA is available in some jurisdictions but is not required for routine prophylaxis.
key_points: AU regimen: anti-D 625 IU intramuscular at 28 weeks and 34 weeks, each after an antibody screen.
Additional doses for sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, trauma, invasive procedures, delivery).
Kleihauer test after delivery guides additional postnatal dose for large foeto-maternal haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: The AU National Blood Authority anti-D antenatal schedule is two 625 IU intramuscular doses (28 and 34 weeks), each preceded by an antibody screen; sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, invasive procedures) require an additional dose.

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacological therapy for uterine atony postpartum haemorrhage of 800 mL at 10 minutes after normal vaginal delivery
stem:
