You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 34 year old parous woman has just delivered a healthy 3.8 kg baby by normal vaginal delivery after a 6 hour labour. Third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Ten minutes after delivery the estimated blood loss is 800 mL with ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding.

The midwife reports the uterus is soft and poorly contracted on palpation. Blood pressure is 108/62 mmHg (baseline 118/72), heart rate 108 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air. Bimanual examination shows the placenta appears complete on inspection, no cervical, vaginal or perineal lacerations visible on speculum, and no clots retained in the vagina. She had a normal antenatal course with no known bleeding disorder. She has an 18 gauge peripheral intravenous cannula and full blood count and coagulation samples are being collected.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg (baseline 118/72), respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Uterine: Uterus soft and poorly contracted, ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding
data_table.Assessment: Placenta complete on inspection, no visible cervical/vaginal/perineal lacerations, no retained clots
data_table.Loss: Estimated blood loss 800 mL at 10 minutes postpartum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Give intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram now and prepare to repeat every 15 minutes to a maximum of eight doses if bleeding continues without additional uterotonic therapy in the interim
options.rationale: Carboprost is a second line uterotonic used after oxytocin and ergometrine have failed; it is contraindicated in asthma. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's solution at 250 mL per hour with immediate uterine massage while preparing intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram as second line
options.rationale: First line for uterine atony after active management is intravenous oxytocin infusion plus fundal massage; ergometrine is second line unless contraindicated by hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus over 10 minutes now and defer any further uterotonic administration until the tranexamic acid effect has been assessed at 30 minutes after the initial dose
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an important adjunct within 3 hours but does not replace uterotonics as first line for atonic postpartum haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give sublingual misoprostol 800 microgram immediately as the first line pharmacological agent for atonic postpartum haemorrhage and reassess bleeding at 20 minutes after the sublingual dose has been given
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a resource limited or adjunct option; intravenous oxytocin is first line where available. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately as the first line intervention for atonic postpartum haemorrhage before any additional pharmacological uterotonic therapy is trialled or administered
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is used after failure of pharmacological measures (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost) or when medical therapy is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Uterine atony causes around 70 percent of primary postpartum haemorrhage. First line management is a coordinated response with fundal massage, an intravenous oxytocin infusion (40 IU in 1000 mL crystalloid at 250 mL per hour), simultaneous exclusion of retained products and lacerations, and prompt escalation. Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular is second line unless the woman is hypertensive. Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular is third line and is contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces mortality from postpartum haemorrhage. Balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation, B-Lynch suture and hysterectomy follow if pharmacological measures fail. Call for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and haematology support early.
key_points: First line for atony: intravenous oxytocin infusion (40 IU/L at 250 mL/h) plus fundal massage.
Second line: ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular (avoid in hypertension).
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces mortality; not a first line uterotonic.
explanation.pearls: In postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony, start an intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1 L at 250 mL/h plus fundal massage first; escalate to intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram if bleeding continues (avoid if hypertensive).

subtopic_detail: Expectant management timing decision in confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 33 plus 2 weeks without chorioamnionitis
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old parous woman at 33 plus 2 weeks with confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 6 hours ago. The diagnosis was made on speculum showing pooling of clear liquor and positive placental alpha microglobulin 1 test. There are no contractions. Cardiotocograph is reactive with no decelerations.

Maternal temperature is 36.8 degC, heart rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, C reactive protein 8 mg/L (below 5) and white cell count 9.6 x10^9/L. Group B Streptococcus swab at 34 weeks was not performed as this rupture is her first presentation. She has no allergies. She has already received the first dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg 4 hours ago and the second dose is scheduled at 24 hours. The maternity unit has neonatal intensive care level 3 on site with respiratory support and ventilation available for babies born from 32 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Bloods: C reactive protein 8 mg/L (below 5), white cell count 9.6 x10^9/L
data_table.Fetal: Cardiotocograph reactive, no decelerations, no contractions
data_table.Rupture: Confirmed clear liquor on speculum, positive placental alpha microglobulin 1 test 6 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin E2 today because ongoing expectant management beyond 32 weeks confers no additional fetal benefit and increases the risk of maternal and neonatal chorioamnionitis significantly
options.rationale: The PPROMT trial and RANZCOG guidance support expectant management to 37 weeks in the absence of infection or fetal compromise; immediate induction at 33 plus 2 without infection is not first line. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Perform an emergency caesarean section this evening once the second corticosteroid dose is complete because vaginal birth after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes carries an unacceptable rate of neonatal sepsis at this gestation
options.rationale: Route of delivery is decided by usual obstetric indications; caesarean is not the default for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and does not reduce sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Admit for expectant management with intravenous cefazolin then oral erythromycin per protocol, complete the corticosteroid course, monitor for infection and plan delivery at 37 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis
options.rationale: AU practice for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without infection or fetal compromise is expectant management to 37 weeks with intravenous then oral antibiotics, corticosteroids, and daily surveillance for chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Commence intramuscular magnesium sulfate 4 g load and 1 g per hour infusion for fetal neuroprotection now and continue for the full 24 hour infusion prior to any subsequent delivery decision at this gestation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given for imminent preterm delivery below 30 weeks; at 33 plus 2 weeks with no labour it is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Give tocolysis with intravenous atosiban 6.75 mg bolus and infusion for 48 hours to prolong the pregnancy until the corticosteroid course completes and neonatal intensive care support is optimised
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without active labour and may mask infection; her cardiotocograph shows no contractions. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes affects around 3 percent of pregnancies. In Australia, RANZCOG guidance (informed by the PPROMT trial) supports expectant management until 37 weeks in the absence of infection, placental abruption or fetal compromise, because immediate delivery at 34 to 36 weeks increases neonatal respiratory distress without reducing neonatal sepsis. Management includes antenatal corticosteroids (before 34 weeks), latency antibiotics (usually intravenous benzylpenicillin then oral erythromycin per unit protocol), daily maternal observations and fetal surveillance, and Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis in labour. Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is reserved for imminent birth below 30 weeks. Tocolysis is not indicated in the absence of active labour and may mask evolving chorioamnionitis.
key_points: Expectant management to 37 weeks is the AU default in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without infection or fetal compromise.
Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if under 34 weeks; latency antibiotics per protocol.
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection only for imminent birth below 30 weeks; no tocolysis in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without labour.
explanation.pearls: Expectant management to 37 weeks (with corticosteroids under 34 weeks and latency antibiotics) is the RANZCOG default for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes in the absence of infection or fetal compromise, following PPROMT trial evidence.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

subtopic_detail: Suspected complete hydatidiform mole with markedly elevated beta hCG, hyperemesis and classic ultrasound features at 9 weeks
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27 year old primigravid woman at 9 plus 2 weeks by dates with severe hyperemesis, dark brown vaginal discharge for 3 days and passage of a grape like fragment yesterday. She has no significant medical history. She is on oral pyridoxine and doxylamine for nausea with limited benefit.

On examination she is dehydrated, pulse 108 per minute, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, temperature 36.8 degC. Uterus is palpable 4 cm above the pubic symphysis (larger than dates). Serum beta hCG is 380000 IU/L (expected 20000 to 120000 at 9 weeks). Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus, no fetal parts, an echogenic intrauterine mass with numerous small anechoic spaces described by the radiologist as a snowstorm pattern, no obvious fetal heart activity and bilateral 5 cm theca lutein cysts. Thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.02 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and free thyroxine is 24 pmol/L (10 to 20). Full blood count and coagulation are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Ultrasound: Enlarged uterus, no fetal parts, echogenic intrauterine mass with numerous small anechoic spaces (snowstorm), no fetal cardiac activity, bilateral 5 cm theca lutein cysts
data_table.Biochemistry: Beta hCG 380000 IU/L (expected 20000-120000), TSH 0.02 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 24 pmol/L (10-20)
data_table.Clinical: Severe hyperemesis, dark brown discharge 3 days, passage of grape-like fragment, uterus larger than dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe methotrexate 50 mg per m2 intramuscular single dose today for medical management of a presumed ectopic pregnancy or non viable intrauterine pregnancy before considering any surgical intervention or referral
options.rationale: Molar pregnancy is not an ectopic pregnancy; methotrexate is not the initial treatment of a hydatidiform mole (suction curettage is) and may be used later for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Arrange elective surgical evacuation by dilatation and sharp curettage in 2 weeks time as an outpatient day surgery procedure with a general practitioner review at 6 weeks after the procedure has been completed
options.rationale: Sharp curettage risks uterine perforation in molar pregnancy; suction curettage is the preferred technique and evacuation should not be delayed 2 weeks given ongoing bleeding and hyperthyroid symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Give intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's solution to induce expulsion of the molar tissue without any subsequent surgical intervention or gynaecology admission for further inpatient care
options.rationale: Oxytocin infusion pre-evacuation increases the risk of embolic spread of trophoblastic tissue; suction evacuation is definitive and oxytocin is used cautiously after cervical dilatation. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Admit today for suction curettage of the uterine contents under general anaesthesia with histopathology, group and hold, and enrol in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial hCG surveillance
options.rationale: Suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology is the AU first line for complete hydatidiform mole; enrolment in the state registry ensures serial beta hCG surveillance for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Perform total abdominal hysterectomy urgently today for definitive management of the suspected molar pregnancy and to prevent the development of subsequent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in this patient population
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is reserved for women who have completed childbearing or for chemoresistant disease; it is not the first line for a molar pregnancy in a 27 year old primigravida. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

explanation.summary: Complete hydatidiform mole classically presents with vaginal bleeding, uterus larger than dates, markedly elevated beta hCG, hyperemesis and biochemical hyperthyroidism from beta hCG cross reactivity with the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm or cluster of grapes appearance with theca lutein cysts. First line management is suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology and group and hold; oxytocin is used cautiously after cervical dilatation to reduce blood loss without precipitating trophoblastic embolisation. After evacuation, enrolment in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG measurement (weekly until normal for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months) allows early detection of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Contraception is required during surveillance; the intrauterine device is avoided until beta hCG normalises.
key_points: Complete hydatidiform mole: uterus larger than dates, beta hCG very elevated, snowstorm ultrasound, biochemical hyperthyroidism.
First line: suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology.
Enrol in state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG surveillance.
explanation.pearls: Enrol every complete hydatidiform mole in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG (weekly until normal for 3 weeks then monthly for 6 months); avoid intrauterine device contraception until beta hCG normalises.

subtopic_detail: Antenatal referral and delivery planning for a woman with three prior caesarean sections and a low anterior placenta at 32 weeks with placenta accreta spectrum features on ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practitioner obstetric shared care doctor reviewing a 36 year old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had three previous lower segment caesarean sections and is otherwise well. Her 32 week transvaginal ultrasound performed today shows an anterior placenta praevia (edge covering the internal os) with placental lacunae, loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic zone and bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder wall. The reporting sonographer flags high suspicion of placenta accreta spectrum.

Her current haemoglobin is 108 g/L, ferritin 22 microgram/L, blood group A RhD positive with no antibodies. Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She has no antepartum bleeding to date, no contractions and a normal cardiotocograph. She lives 45 minutes from the tertiary centre where she previously delivered. She has been given information about the ultrasound findings and asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 82 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta praevia over internal os, placental lacunae, loss of retroplacental hypoechoic zone, bridging vessels to bladder wall
data_table.Obstetric: G4P3 with three prior caesarean sections, 32 weeks, no bleeding or contractions
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, ferritin 22 microgram/L, group A RhD positive, no antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue routine general practitioner shared care with a repeat ultrasound at 36 weeks to reassess for resolution of the low placental position and plan delivery in the local community hospital
options.rationale: Placenta accreta spectrum features with three prior caesareans and anterior praevia is high risk; local hospital delivery misses the multidisciplinary team required. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Admit today for immediate elective lower segment caesarean section under general anaesthesia at 32 weeks to remove the placenta before the risk of massive antepartum haemorrhage increases with advancing gestation
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 32 weeks incurs preterm neonatal morbidity without benefit in the absence of active bleeding; planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after multidisciplinary planning is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Perform amniocentesis at 34 weeks to confirm fetal lung maturity and only proceed to delivery once the lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio is confirmed as mature at greater than 2 for the current pregnancy
options.rationale: Amniocentesis for lung maturity is not routinely used in AU; timing is by gestation and clinical status with antenatal corticosteroids where appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary maternal fetal medicine unit for consideration of elective classical caesarean section with immediate hysterectomy at 39 weeks by the general obstetric team on call
options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks is too late (risk of labour or bleeding); planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 by a dedicated placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team is standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids and cell salvage plus massive transfusion protocol readiness
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG standard is referral to a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team with planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks under antenatal corticosteroids, with cell salvage and massive transfusion protocol ready. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) risk rises steeply with the number of previous caesarean sections and coexisting placenta praevia. Antenatal ultrasound features include placental lacunae (Swiss cheese appearance), loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic zone, thinning or interruption of the bladder wall interface and bridging vessels. Magnetic resonance imaging is used adjunctively. Standard Australian management is referral to a tertiary maternal fetal medicine unit with a dedicated placenta accreta spectrum team, antenatal corticosteroids and planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks (earlier for bleeding or preterm labour). Intraoperative preparation includes cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol readiness, interventional radiology for uterine artery occlusion balloons and multidisciplinary theatre team.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum risk rises with number of previous caesarean sections plus placenta praevia.
AU planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids in a tertiary centre.
Prepare cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol and interventional radiology support.
explanation.pearls: Placenta accreta spectrum with an anterior praevia over prior caesarean scars is planned for caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks in a tertiary centre with cell salvage and massive transfusion protocol activated preoperatively.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of amniotic fluid embolism presenting as intrapartum collapse with disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem:
You are the obstetric consultant urgently called to the birth suite where a 33 year old parous woman at 40 weeks has just delivered a live baby by normal vaginal delivery after 30 minutes of second stage. Immediately after delivery she developed sudden onset dyspnoea, agitation and then loss of consciousness with cardiovascular collapse. Blood pressure was unrecordable and heart rate 148 per minute on the pulse oximeter waveform. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was commenced with return of spontaneous circulation after 3 minutes and she is now intubated and ventilated with a pulse of 128 per minute and blood pressure 78/42 mmHg on adrenaline infusion.

She is oozing brisk fresh red blood from her venepuncture sites and from the vaginal delivery bed. Urgent bloods show haemoglobin 82 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L (150 to 400), prothrombin time 26 seconds (11 to 15), activated partial thromboplastin time 68 seconds (25 to 35), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0 to 4.0), D-dimer above 20 mg/L. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.14, PaO2 62 mmHg on FiO2 1.0, PaCO2 52 mmHg. There is no evidence of retained products, uterine rupture, cervical laceration or amniotic fluid still leaking. She has no known allergies and no comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 128 /min, blood pressure 78/42 mmHg on adrenaline, respiratory rate 16 /min (ventilated), SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0
data_table.Coagulation: Platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400), PT 26 s (11-15), APTT 68 s (25-35), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0), D-dimer >20 mg/L
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.14, PaO2 62 mmHg on FiO2 1.0, PaCO2 52 mmHg
data_table.Clinical: Fresh bleeding from venepuncture sites and vaginal bed; no retained products, no uterine rupture on inspection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol, give fibrinogen concentrate 4 g or cryoprecipitate 10 units and administer packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets in 1 to 1 to 1 ratio guided by ROTEM
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism causes early consumptive coagulopathy; rapid fibrinogen replacement (aim above 2 g/L) and 1 to 1 to 1 blood product resuscitation guided by ROTEM is the AU obstetric massive haemorrhage standard. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous heparin 5000 units bolus and infusion for disseminated intravascular coagulation with active thrombosis before considering any blood component transfusion or reversal of the coagulopathy
options.rationale: Heparin is contraindicated in obstetric disseminated intravascular coagulation with active haemorrhage; the phenotype is consumptive bleeding not thrombosis. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram per kg as first line treatment for the coagulopathy without first replacing fibrinogen or platelets or correcting acidosis prior to administration
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII carries a high thrombotic risk and requires baseline fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, platelets above 50 and pH above 7.2; it is not first line in amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 4 g bolus over 5 minutes as the only initial treatment and defer blood component transfusion until the tranexamic acid has been given time to exert its full anti-fibrinolytic effect
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is an adjunct but does not replace fibrinogen and platelet replacement in fulminant amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy; the standard dose is 1 g not 4 g bolus. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous atropine 1 mg, intravenous ondansetron 8 mg and intravenous ketorolac 30 mg (the A-OK protocol) as monotherapy and defer any blood product transfusion or additional resuscitation until reassessment at 30 minutes
options.rationale: A-OK is an adjunct protocol targeting vasoactive mediators; it does not replace haemorrhage resuscitation with blood products and coagulopathy correction. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare (2 to 8 per 100000 deliveries) but catastrophic obstetric emergency presenting with a triad of hypoxia, hypotension and consumptive coagulopathy occurring around labour or in the immediate postpartum period. Diagnosis is clinical and requires exclusion of alternatives (pulmonary embolism, sepsis, anaphylaxis, uterine rupture). Immediate management is high quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation with left uterine displacement (or perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if arrest before delivery), airway support, vasopressor support (noradrenaline or adrenaline), correction of coagulopathy with early fibrinogen (concentrate or cryoprecipitate) targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L, and balanced 1 to 1 to 1 blood component resuscitation guided by ROTEM or thromboelastography. Tranexamic acid 1 g is an adjunct. Recombinant activated factor VII is reserved for refractory bleeding after correction of pH, fibrinogen and platelets. Maternal mortality remains around 20 to 40 percent in Australia.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism triad: hypoxia, hypotension, consumptive coagulopathy peri-partum.
Early fibrinogen replacement (concentrate or cryoprecipitate) targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L.
1 to 1 to 1 packed cells to fresh frozen plasma to platelets, guided by ROTEM.
explanation.pearls: In suspected amniotic fluid embolism give fibrinogen concentrate 4 g or 10 units of cryoprecipitate early to target fibrinogen above 2 g/L; recombinant factor VII is reserved for refractory bleeding after fibrinogen, platelets and pH are corrected.

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic choice in a woman with chronic hypertension
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 32 year old G3P2 woman is 15 minutes into her third stage after a normal vaginal birth of a 3.8 kg baby at 40+1 weeks. She has essential hypertension on labetalol and asthma controlled on budesonide/formoterol.

She has soaked two large obstetric pads and continues to bleed briskly from the vagina. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Estimated blood loss is 1200 mL. The placenta was delivered intact and complete. On bimanual examination the fundus is soft and above the umbilicus, and there is no laceration visible on inspection.

She has already received oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly with delivery of the anterior shoulder and an intravenous infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution is running. The senior midwife asks which second-line uterotonic to give next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Uterine fundus soft and above the umbilicus, placenta intact, no visible laceration
data_table.Medications: Labetalol for hypertension, budesonide/formoterol for asthma; oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery plus oxytocin 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's IV infusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate second-line uterotonic?

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular, may repeat every 15 minutes to 8 doses maximum
options.rationale: Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma because of bronchospasm risk from prostaglandin F2 alpha; her budesonide/formoterol history rules it out (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; AMH).

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscular, may repeat every 2 hours to 5 doses maximum
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension; her chronic hypertension on labetalol rules it out and would risk hypertensive crisis (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; AMH).

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum single dose combined with bimanual compression
options.rationale: Misoprostol is the appropriate second-line uterotonic when both ergometrine (hypertension) and carboprost (asthma) are contraindicated; per rectum 800 mcg is the RANZCOG PPH dose (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement).

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes with no additional uterotonic given
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid should be given early in PPH but does not replace uterotonic therapy for uterine atony; both are needed (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; WOMAN trial).

options.text: Additional oxytocin 10 units intravenous bolus over 1 minute without changing the infusion
options.rationale: IV bolus oxytocin risks profound hypotension and adds little when a 40 unit infusion is already running; second-line uterotonic action is needed (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; AMH).

explanation.summary: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. First-line management combines uterine massage, bimanual compression, IV access, tranexamic acid and oxytocin. Second-line uterotonics escalate as needed: ergometrine, then carboprost, then misoprostol; contraindications drive the choice. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia and severe cardiac disease; carboprost is contraindicated in asthma; misoprostol has the fewest contraindications. Persistent bleeding needs balloon tamponade, uterine compression sutures, uterine artery embolisation or hysterectomy.
key_points: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of primary PPH
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma
Misoprostol 800 mcg PR is second-line when both are contraindicated
Give tranexamic acid early in addition to uterotonics
explanation.pearls: The WOMAN trial showed tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth reduces death from haemorrhage by nearly one third; give it early alongside uterotonics rather than as a substitute.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 38 year old primigravida is admitted at 34+2 weeks gestation with new blood pressure of 172/108 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart, and 3+ proteinuria on dipstick. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg and her pregnancy has otherwise been unremarkable. She reports a right upper quadrant heaviness and one episode of visual flickering this morning.

On examination her reflexes are brisk with no clonus and her fundi show no papilloedema. Vital signs are pulse 92, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg after 15 minutes rest, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148. Blood results show haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 78 U/L (5-45), AST 84 U/L (5-45), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), urine protein:creatinine ratio 250 mg/mmol (<30).

Intravenous labetalol is being drawn up. CTG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 168/104 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, FHR 148
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 78 U/L (5-45), AST 84 U/L (5-45), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), urine PCR 250 mg/mmol (<30)

lead_in: In addition to intravenous labetalol, what is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/h infusion
options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia to prevent eclampsia; loading is 4 g IV over 20 minutes with a 1 g/h maintenance infusion continued for 24 hours after birth or the last seizure (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous over 30 minutes as seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prevention as shown by the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial and is not the AU standard (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg intravenous over 1 minute for seizure prophylaxis and sedation
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are inferior to magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis and risk maternal respiratory depression and neonatal sedation (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular alone with delayed antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Betamethasone is indicated for fetal lung maturation but does not replace magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis or delay antihypertensive control in severe pre-eclampsia (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Immediate emergency caesarean section before further stabilisation of blood pressure
options.rationale: Blood pressure control and eclampsia prophylaxis must be established before delivery in stable maternal-fetal status; delivery is the definitive management but not immediate (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed with a systolic at least 160 or diastolic at least 110 with end organ involvement (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological). Management is a triad: control blood pressure to under 160/110 (IV labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine), give magnesium sulfate to prevent eclampsia, and plan timely delivery. Betamethasone accelerates fetal lung maturation if under 34+6 weeks; timing of delivery balances maternal deterioration against gestational age. Magnesium sulfate toxicity presents as loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression; monitor reflexes hourly and urine output.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia triad: BP control, MgSO4, plan delivery
Loading dose MgSO4 is 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/h maintenance
Continue MgSO4 for 24 hours after birth or last seizure
Betamethasone if under 34+6 for lung maturation
Toxicity: loss of reflexes then respiratory depression
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate toxicity is reversed with calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10 percent) IV over 3 minutes; keep an ampoule at the bedside during infusion.

subtopic_detail: OGTT threshold interpretation at 26 weeks
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar. A 34 year old G2P1 woman at 26+3 weeks gestation attends for review of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her previous baby weighed 4.4 kg at 39 weeks and was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; she had no formal diabetes testing in that pregnancy. She has a BMI of 33 and her mother has type 2 diabetes.

Her 75 g OGTT results are fasting 4.9 mmol/L (fasting under 5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (1 hour under 10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (2 hour under 8.5). Her booking HbA1c was 5.4 percent (under 5.7 percent), booking bloods otherwise normal. Her blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis shows no glycosuria and no proteinuria. Fetal growth on symphysis-fundal height measurement is on the 75th percentile.

She asks whether the results are normal, and what happens next.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): Fasting 4.9 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Examination: BP 118/72 mmHg, no glycosuria, no proteinuria, SFH on 75th centile

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Order fasting insulin and HbA1c today to distinguish gestational from pre-existing diabetes
options.rationale: Insulin measurement is not part of GDM diagnostic testing and adds no management value; the ADIPS OGTT thresholds define the diagnosis (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Reassure her the test is normal and continue routine antenatal care visits
options.rationale: Only her fasting and 2 hour values are under threshold; the 1 hour value of 10.6 mmol/L exceeds 10.0 mmol/L and diagnoses GDM under ADIPS criteria (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks at 30 weeks because only one value is abnormal
options.rationale: The ADIPS diagnosis needs only one abnormal value; repeat testing is not indicated and delays management that reduces macrosomia (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg orally twice daily now without further monitoring or education
options.rationale: Initial GDM management is lifestyle and blood glucose monitoring for 1 to 2 weeks; pharmacotherapy is added only if targets are not met and needs monitoring set-up first (Source: ADIPS GDM Management Statement).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer to the antenatal diabetes clinic for education
options.rationale: The ADIPS criteria diagnose gestational diabetes when any one value is met or exceeded; her 1 hour value of 10.6 mmol/L exceeds the 10.0 mmol/L threshold and requires referral to the antenatal diabetes clinic (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

explanation.summary: Australian universal screening at 24 to 28 weeks uses a 75 g OGTT with ADIPS diagnostic thresholds: fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L. A single value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM. Management starts with lifestyle (dietitian input, home glucose monitoring 4 times daily) with targets fasting under 5.0 and postprandial 1 hour under 7.4 or 2 hour under 6.7. Metformin then insulin are added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks. Delivery timing balances glycaemic control and fetal size, with induction at 38 to 39 weeks if insulin required or macrosomia identified.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L
A single abnormal value diagnoses GDM
First step is education, monitoring and lifestyle for 1 to 2 weeks
Metformin then insulin if targets are not met
Universal 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks in Australia
explanation.pearls: Early screening (14 to 20 weeks) is offered for BMI at least 35, prior GDM, prior macrosomic baby over 4.5 kg, first degree relative with diabetes, or high risk ethnicity.

sources.label: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic in a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 29 year old G3P1 woman presents at 6+4 weeks gestation by dates with 3 days of intermittent right sided lower abdominal ache and light spotting. She had a right salpingectomy 2 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic. She is trying to conceive and this is her first pregnancy since the surgery.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Vital signs are pulse 82, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Abdominal palpation reveals mild left iliac fossa tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with a 22 mm complex left adnexal mass adjacent to but separate from the left ovary, containing a small yolk sac with no fetal pole and no fetal cardiac activity; there is a small volume of anechoic fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

Beta hCG is 3200 IU/L, done today, with a value of 3150 IU/L 48 hours ago. She has normal renal, liver and full blood count results, and is very keen to preserve her fertility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no rebound
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterine cavity; left adnexal mass 22 mm with yolk sac, no fetal pole, no cardiac activity; small anechoic fluid in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 3200 IU/L today, 3150 IU/L 48 hours ago; renal, liver and FBC normal
data_table.Surgical history: Right salpingectomy 2 years ago for ruptured tubal ectopic

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscular with day 4 and day 7 beta hCG follow-up
options.rationale: Although this ectopic meets biochemical and imaging thresholds for methotrexate, its location in her only remaining tube swings the balance toward salpingostomy to preserve fertility if the tube is salvageable; methotrexate risks tubal damage from the same-tube treated ectopic (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with the intention to perform left salpingectomy of the affected tube
options.rationale: Salpingectomy in the setting of a prior contralateral salpingectomy renders her surgically infertile requiring IVF; when the tube is salvageable, salpingostomy preserves an option (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with the intention to perform salpingostomy on the affected tube
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; RANZCOG guidance in a fertility conserving context favours salpingostomy over salpingectomy when the tube is salvageable and future conception depends on it (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Repeat serum beta hCG in 48 hours and observation with no immediate intervention
options.rationale: Static beta hCG (below the 50 percent decline that suggests failing pregnancy) with a visible adnexal mass in the setting of prior tubal ectopic requires active treatment rather than surveillance (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Suction dilatation and curettage to confirm the pregnancy is not intrauterine before therapy
options.rationale: Ultrasound has already localised the pregnancy to the adnexa and a curettage risks disrupting a coexistent intrauterine pregnancy in a heterotopic case; imaging and beta hCG are sufficient here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

explanation.summary: Choice between methotrexate, salpingostomy, and salpingectomy in tubal ectopic pregnancy depends on haemodynamic stability, beta hCG level, tubal mass size, presence of cardiac activity, and the woman's fertility priorities. RANZCOG considers methotrexate when beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, and reliable follow-up. Above 5000 IU/L or with rupture, surgery is required. The salpingostomy versus salpingectomy decision hinges on the state of the contralateral tube: with a normal contralateral tube salpingectomy is often chosen because recurrence in the treated tube is common, but with prior contralateral salpingectomy the balance flips toward preserving the only remaining tube.
key_points: Methotrexate threshold: beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm
No cardiac activity and no significant pain are also required
Prior contralateral salpingectomy flips choice to salpingostomy
Beta hCG must fall over 15 percent between day 4 and day 7 after methotrexate
Rupture, haemodynamic instability, or heterotopic pregnancy needs surgery
explanation.pearls: Persistent trophoblast rates after salpingostomy are around 8 percent; weekly beta hCG follow-up is mandatory until below 5 IU/L to detect and treat with methotrexate if plateau or rise.

subtopic_detail: Threatened preterm labour at 30 weeks with contraindications to nifedipine
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 26 year old G2P1 woman at 30+1 weeks gestation presents with 4 hours of regular painful contractions and a small amount of clear vaginal discharge. This pregnancy has been complicated by placenta praevia diagnosed on the 19 week morphology scan and confirmed on 28 week rescan; the placenta covers the internal os by 32 mm.

Her previous baby was born at 34 weeks after preterm labour. On examination her contractions are palpable every 4 minutes, lasting 45 seconds. Vital signs are pulse 96, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 with reactive CTG. Speculum examination reveals no visible cervical dilation but the cervical os is open to 1 finger tip on transvaginal ultrasound with cervical length 12 mm. Amniotic fluid pooling test is negative. Fetal fibronectin is positive.

She has no penicillin allergy, no antihypertensive requirement and has never taken a calcium channel blocker.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, FHR 148 with reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: Contractions every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds; no vaginal bleeding; cervical length 12 mm on TVUS; fetal fibronectin positive
data_table.Antenatal history: Placenta praevia covering internal os by 32 mm, previous preterm birth at 34 weeks

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate tocolytic in addition to betamethasone and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection?

options.text: Atosiban intravenous loading dose then continuous infusion for up to 48 hours
options.rationale: Atosiban (oxytocin receptor antagonist) is preferred when nifedipine is contraindicated or undesirable; its neutral cardiovascular profile suits placenta praevia where haemodynamic changes could obscure obstetric haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 10 to 20 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours
options.rationale: Nifedipine is first-line tocolytic in AU practice but is not preferred here because it can drop blood pressure and mask the ongoing placenta praevia bleeding risk; another agent is preferred (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Salbutamol intravenous infusion titrated to reduce contraction frequency
options.rationale: Beta agonist tocolysis is no longer recommended in AU because of maternal cardiovascular adverse events including pulmonary oedema (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Indomethacin 100 mg per rectum then 25 mg orally every 6 hours for 48 hours
options.rationale: Indomethacin is avoided over 32 weeks and can cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus; at 30 weeks it is possible but the safety profile is inferior to atosiban with placenta praevia (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading as the primary tocolytic agent
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is used for fetal neuroprotection under 30 weeks, and no longer recommended as a tocolytic in isolation; her indication for magnesium is neuroprotection at the 30 week borderline (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm labour management aims for 48 hours of pregnancy prolongation to complete corticosteroids for lung maturation and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection under 30 weeks. Nifedipine is the AU first-line tocolytic, with atosiban preferred when nifedipine is contraindicated or where its vasodilator effect would obscure haemodynamic monitoring as in placenta praevia. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM at 0 and 24 hours delivers full lung maturation, while magnesium neuroprotection uses a 4 g load then 1 g/h to birth or 24 hours. Beta agonists are no longer used because of maternal cardiovascular events.
key_points: Aim of tocolysis is 48 h to complete steroids and neuroprotection
Nifedipine is AU first-line tocolytic
Atosiban is preferred with placenta praevia or nifedipine contraindication
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses, 24 hours apart
Magnesium neuroprotection under 30 weeks
explanation.pearls: Fetal fibronectin is a bedside vaginal swab; a negative result under 30 weeks has a strong negative predictive value (over 95 percent for delivery within 7 days) and often permits discharge without tocolysis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

subtopic_detail: Late onset FGR delivery timing with abnormal umbilical Doppler
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine registrar. A 30 year old G2P1 woman is at 36+4 weeks and has been under surveillance for a small for gestational age baby since a growth scan at 32 weeks showed estimated fetal weight on the 5th centile with a normal Doppler. Her first baby was born at term and weighed 3.4 kg.

Today her repeat scan shows estimated fetal weight on the 3rd centile with abdominal circumference on the less than 1st centile, umbilical artery pulsatility index at the 97th centile, and cerebroplacental ratio less than 1.0. Amniotic fluid volume is normal with a deepest vertical pocket of 3.2 cm. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is normal. CTG is reactive with a normal baseline of 138 beats per minute and no decelerations. Blood pressure today is 128/78 mmHg with no proteinuria; her booking blood pressure was 122/74 mmHg.

She has no other medical conditions and has completed her booking, morphology and antenatal blood tests without abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, no proteinuria, FHR 138 with reactive CTG
data_table.Ultrasound: EFW on 3rd centile, AC less than 1st centile, umbilical artery PI 97th centile, cerebroplacental ratio less than 1.0, AFI DVP 3.2 cm, MCA PSV normal
data_table.Antenatal history: Booking BP 122/74 mmHg, first baby term 3.4 kg, no medical conditions

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue outpatient twice weekly CTG and repeat Doppler in 7 days with no immediate change
options.rationale: A cerebroplacental ratio under 1.0 with rising umbilical artery PI reflects late onset placental insufficiency and is an indication for delivery beyond 36 weeks; conservative outpatient management risks stillbirth (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Deliver by induction of labour after a course of betamethasone commenced today
options.rationale: Late-onset FGR beyond 36 weeks with an abnormal Doppler (CPR under 1.0 or elevated umbilical artery PI) is an indication for delivery by induction of labour under RANZCOG; steroids can still be considered in some pathways though most deliver without further delay near term (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Elective caesarean section without a trial of labour for the small for gestational age foetus
options.rationale: Late-onset FGR with reactive CTG does not require caesarean by default; induction is the primary AU approach with intrapartum continuous CTG monitoring (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Admit for daily CTG and weekly Doppler and defer delivery until 39 weeks
options.rationale: Deferring delivery until 39 weeks in the presence of abnormal Doppler carries higher stillbirth risk than delivery near 37 weeks in this population; guidance recommends delivery from 36+0 (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Start aspirin 150 mg daily and continue to 39 weeks with weekly ultrasound review
options.rationale: Aspirin is preventive and started before 16 weeks for those at risk of pre-eclampsia and FGR; starting at 36 weeks provides no benefit and delays needed delivery (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

explanation.summary: Late-onset fetal growth restriction (after 32 weeks) is characterised by mild growth changes and subtle Doppler abnormalities and is associated with stillbirth risk. The Delphi consensus criteria (small for gestational age plus abnormal Doppler including a cerebroplacental ratio under 1.0 or umbilical artery pulsatility index above 95th centile) defines FGR versus constitutional smallness. RANZCOG recommends delivery by 37 weeks for late-onset FGR with abnormal Doppler; earlier if surveillance deteriorates. Route of delivery balances Doppler severity, CTG, and cervical favourability; induction with continuous CTG is appropriate with a reactive CTG and normal MCA PSV.
key_points: FGR needs SGA plus abnormal Doppler under Delphi consensus
CPR under 1.0 signals placental redistribution and stillbirth risk
Deliver at 36 to 37 weeks with abnormal Doppler
Induction with continuous CTG if surveillance and cervix allow
Aspirin is preventive before 16 weeks, not curative
explanation.pearls: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is used to screen for fetal anaemia rather than growth restriction; a value above 1.5 multiples of median suggests anaemia.

subtopic_detail: Severe OHSS after IVF requiring paracentesis versus admission
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman on day 9 after transvaginal oocyte retrieval. Her IVF cycle used a GnRH antagonist protocol with recombinant FSH 250 units daily; 32 oocytes were collected and she was triggered with hCG rather than a GnRH agonist because of a scheduling preference. She had a single fresh cleavage stage embryo transfer on day 3 and now presents with 4 days of progressive abdominal distension, breathlessness on climbing stairs, and reduced urine output.

On examination she is breathless at rest. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Abdominal examination shows a tense distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a palpable pelvic mass extending to the umbilicus. Bloods: haemoglobin 168 g/L (115-165), haematocrit 51 percent (36-46), white cells 18 x10^9/L (4-11), platelets 460 x10^9/L (150-400), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 24 g/L (35-50). Beta hCG is 320 IU/L; urine output over the last 6 hours is 60 mL.

Ultrasound confirms bilateral 12 cm enlarged ovaries with multiple follicular cysts and a moderate volume of free abdominal fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense distended abdomen, shifting dullness, palpable mass to the umbilicus
data_table.Ultrasound: Bilateral 12 cm ovaries with follicular cysts, moderate free abdominal fluid

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Immediate laparotomy and bilateral oophorectomy to remove the hyperstimulated enlarged ovaries
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for suspected ovarian torsion, cyst rupture with haemodynamic instability, or ectopic pregnancy; OHSS itself is medically managed and ovaries are preserved (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Outpatient monitoring with high protein oral fluids and daily blood tests as ambulatory care
options.rationale: Severe OHSS with haematocrit over 45 percent, oliguria, hypoxia and hyponatraemia is not managed as an outpatient because of VTE and renal failure risk (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Frusemide 40 mg intravenous bolus to increase urine output and reduce abdominal ascites volume
options.rationale: Diuretics in OHSS worsen intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration; the pathophysiology is third-spacing not fluid overload (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous crystalloid and human albumin, and arrange ultrasound guided paracentesis
options.rationale: This is severe OHSS with third-spacing (haematocrit 51 percent, oliguria, hyponatraemia, hypoxia, tense ascites) requiring inpatient management; RANZCOG-endorsed pathways use IV crystalloid then human albumin plus paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement; RCOG OHSS Guideline).

options.text: Repeat beta hCG in 48 hours before deciding any further intervention or admission arrangements
options.rationale: Delaying intervention in severe OHSS to await beta hCG risks renal failure, VTE and ARDS; treatment does not depend on confirming pregnancy (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

explanation.summary: OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of ART with fluid shift into the third space driven by VEGF-mediated capillary leak. The syndrome is classified mild (abdominal distension), moderate (ultrasound ascites, ovaries over 5 cm), severe (clinical ascites, haematocrit over 45 percent, hyponatraemia, oliguria, hypoproteinaemia), or critical (tense ascites, ARDS, thromboembolism, renal failure). Severe OHSS needs admission, cautious IV fluid resuscitation (100 to 150 mL/h crystalloid then albumin 25 percent for volume expansion), VTE prophylaxis, and paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia. Diuretics are avoided because they worsen intravascular depletion. Pregnancy exacerbates OHSS through endogenous hCG and often prolongs the illness.
key_points: Severe OHSS: HCT over 45, oliguria, hyponatraemia, hypoxia
Third-spacing pathophysiology, not fluid overload
Avoid diuretics; use crystalloid then human albumin
Paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia
VTE prophylaxis is mandatory during admission
explanation.pearls: GnRH agonist trigger (leuprolide) instead of hCG substantially reduces severe OHSS risk; freezing all embryos avoids endogenous hCG stimulation from an early pregnancy that would worsen the syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Second twin non-cephalic presentation management
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 28 year old G3P2 woman with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 38+1 weeks has delivered a cephalic first twin (2.9 kg) after a 45 minute second stage. Her previous births were both singleton uncomplicated vaginal deliveries.

Sixteen minutes after the first birth the CTG on the second twin shows recurrent variable decelerations to 90 beats per minute lasting 40 seconds, and the baseline is 155 beats per minute. Bedside ultrasound reveals the second twin lying transverse with the back down (dorsoinferior). The membranes are intact and the estimated fetal weight is 2.6 kg. Vaginal examination reveals the cervix is fully dilated with no presenting part palpable. There is no cord felt.

The operating theatre is 3 minutes away and an epidural is running well. Vital signs are pulse 92, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 155 with recurrent variable decelerations. The consultant obstetrician is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, FHR 155 with recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Ultrasound: Second twin transverse lie with back down (dorsoinferior); intact membranes; EFW 2.6 kg
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, no presenting part palpable, no cord felt
data_table.Setting: Epidural in situ, theatre 3 minutes away, consultant obstetrician present

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in delivering the second twin?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section with general anaesthesia for the second twin
options.rationale: Caesarean for a second twin after successful vaginal first twin birth increases combined maternal morbidity; a controlled internal podalic version with breech extraction achieves faster delivery when the operator is experienced (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: External cephalic version through the abdominal wall with tocolysis using intravenous salbutamol
options.rationale: ECV of the second twin has poor success in labour and delays delivery when the CTG is already non-reassuring; internal manoeuvres are preferred in this setting (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Internal podalic version with breech extraction under epidural top up in the birthing room
options.rationale: In dichorionic diamniotic twins with a dorsoinferior transverse second twin and non-reassuring CTG in an experienced hands setting with epidural in situ, internal podalic version and breech extraction is safer and faster than caesarean and preserves the vaginal delivery pathway; the manoeuvre grasps the fetal feet and delivers as an assisted breech (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Rupture membranes to allow the presenting part to descend then commence oxytocin
options.rationale: Rupturing membranes in a transverse lie risks cord prolapse and cannot achieve descent because no presenting part is engaged; the delivery pathway needs an actively directed fetal manipulation (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Await spontaneous rotation for 30 minutes before intervening if the CTG remains reassuring
options.rationale: The CTG shows non-reassuring recurrent variable decelerations already; waiting extends fetal compromise and adds no likelihood of spontaneous rotation in a dorsoinferior transverse (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

explanation.summary: The Twin Birth Study established vaginal delivery of the second twin as safe when the first is cephalic and the second is under 4 kg, regardless of the second twin's presentation. Non-cephalic second twins may be delivered by internal podalic version and breech extraction, by breech extraction directly if breech, or by caesarean if the operator lacks experience with internal manoeuvres. Dorsoinferior transverse lie is particularly amenable to internal podalic version. The team must be ready to convert to caesarean if extraction fails, if cord prolapse occurs, or if maternal or fetal status deteriorates. Continuous CTG and adequate anaesthesia (epidural top up or general anaesthesia if needed) are essential.
key_points: Vaginal birth of second twin safe with cephalic first and EFW under 4 kg
Dorsoinferior transverse suits internal podalic version
Internal podalic version + breech extraction is fast in experienced hands
Ready to convert to caesarean for failure or deterioration
Rupturing membranes in transverse lie risks cord prolapse
explanation.pearls: For a dorsosuperior transverse (back up) second twin, internal podalic version is much harder because the operator's hand must sweep past the fetal back to reach the feet; caesarean is often the safer choice.

subtopic_detail: Mode of delivery counselling after prior third or fourth degree perineal tear
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a birth planning clinic seeing a 32 year old woman at 34 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first birth 2 years ago was a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3800 g baby complicated by a 4a perineal tear (external anal sphincter over 50 percent thickness torn, internal anal sphincter intact) that was repaired by an experienced consultant obstetrician in theatre with an appropriate follow-up pathway.

Since the first birth she reports rare flatus incontinence around 2 to 3 times per month but no faecal incontinence or urgency, no dyspareunia, and no perineal pain. An endoanal ultrasound at 6 weeks postpartum from the first birth showed a healed but attenuated external anal sphincter defect at the 12 o'clock position spanning around 60 degrees. Anal manometry at 12 weeks postpartum showed a resting sphincter pressure of 42 mmHg (over 40) and squeeze pressure of 96 mmHg (over 60).

This pregnancy is uncomplicated. Fetal biometry today shows an estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile at 34 weeks, cephalic presentation, and anterior placenta. She asks for advice on mode of delivery in this pregnancy.

data_table.Previous obstetric history: Prior spontaneous vaginal delivery with 4a tear repaired in theatre by consultant obstetrician
data_table.Continence and imaging: Rare flatus incontinence 2 to 3 per month; no faecal incontinence or urgency; endoanal US showed healed sphincter with 60 degree defect at 12 o'clock; anal manometry resting 42 mmHg and squeeze 96 mmHg
data_table.Current pregnancy: 34 weeks; EFW 55th centile; cephalic; anterior placenta

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate recommendation for mode of delivery counselling?

options.text: Support planned vaginal birth after discussing recurrent tear risk with continence review in third trimester
options.rationale: RANZCOG and RCOG guidance recommends offering planned vaginal birth to women with prior third or fourth degree tear who are asymptomatic (or with only minor flatus incontinence) and have normal or adequate anal manometry, because absolute recurrent tear risk is around 5 to 7 percent, most women retain continence after a further vaginal birth, and elective caesarean carries its own morbidity and future pregnancy implications (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG; RCOG Green-top Guideline 29).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend planned elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the default subsequent mode of delivery
options.rationale: Elective caesarean is offered to women with significant faecal incontinence or urgency or symptomatic sphincter defect; it is not the default for an asymptomatic woman with preserved manometry, given the maternal morbidity and future-pregnancy implications (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend planned vaginal birth with prophylactic mediolateral episiotomy at all subsequent vaginal births
options.rationale: Routine mediolateral episiotomy has not been shown to reduce recurrent third or fourth degree tear risk in RCTs and is not the RANZCOG recommendation for women with prior tears; the decision on episiotomy is individualised (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend induction of labour at 38 weeks to limit fetal size and reduce risk of recurrent perineal tear
options.rationale: Induction of labour for the sole purpose of limiting fetal size and reducing tear risk in this indication is not supported by RCT evidence and has separate maternal and neonatal implications; it is not the RANZCOG recommendation (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Defer any decision on mode of delivery until labour has commenced and fetal size is confirmed on admission
options.rationale: Antenatal counselling and shared decision-making on mode of delivery is a RANZCOG standard for women with prior significant perineal trauma; deferring the discussion until labour commences forgoes the opportunity for informed choice (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

explanation.summary: Women with a prior third or fourth degree perineal tear (obstetric anal sphincter injury or OASI) are counselled antenatally on mode of delivery for subsequent pregnancies. RANZCOG guidance supports offering planned vaginal birth to women who are asymptomatic (or with only minor flatus incontinence) and have normal or adequate anal manometry, because the absolute recurrent tear risk is around 5 to 7 percent and most retain continence. Elective caesarean section is offered to women with significant faecal incontinence or urgency, symptomatic sphincter defect, or a strong preference to avoid recurrent perineal trauma. Assessment includes symptom review, anal manometry, and endoanal ultrasound where available. Routine mediolateral episiotomy in subsequent vaginal birth is not evidence-based for this indication and remains an individualised decision.
key_points: OASI prior tear: mode of delivery counselling in subsequent pregnancy
Asymptomatic with preserved manometry: offer planned vaginal birth
Elective caesarean for symptomatic incontinence or urgency
Recurrent tear risk around 5 to 7 percent overall
Routine prophylactic episiotomy not evidence-based
explanation.pearls: Anal manometry after OASI is the pivotal continence test in the RANZCOG algorithm because it discriminates functional sphincter reserve better than sonographic defect size alone; a preserved squeeze pressure above 60 mmHg with only minor flatus incontinence predicts a low probability of decompensation after a second vaginal birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis by 75 g OGTT
stem:
You are the antenatal shared care GP. A 31 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 27 weeks gestation returns for a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test result. She is well.

Her BMI at booking was 29 kg/m2 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. She has no polyuria or polydipsia and fetal movements are normal. Fetal biometry at 28 weeks last week was on the 60th centile with a normal umbilical artery Doppler.

The pathology report shows fasting plasma glucose 5.2 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L, and 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L. Her ferritin, thyroid function, and urinalysis at this visit were within normal limits.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): Fasting 5.2 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Booking: Nulliparous, 31 y, BMI 29 kg/m2, family history type 2 diabetes
data_table.Fetal growth: Biometry 60th centile at 28 weeks; UA Doppler within normal limits
data_table.Other labs: Ferritin, thyroid function, urinalysis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Reassure the woman that the results are within normal limits for the trimester and continue routine antenatal care
options.rationale: All three values are above the ADIPS thresholds; not diagnosing GDM leaves an at risk pregnancy without surveillance and lifestyle intervention (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks because only the 1 hour and 2 hour values met threshold and the fasting result was borderline
options.rationale: A single abnormal value on a 75 g OGTT diagnoses GDM under ADIPS; a repeat delays management and worsens perinatal outcomes (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg orally with breakfast immediately without a dietary trial or self monitoring interval
options.rationale: First line management of newly diagnosed GDM is medical nutrition therapy with self monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not achieved after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus).
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

options.text: Order HbA1c and only diagnose GDM if the result is 5.7% or greater as a confirmatory test in addition to the OGTT
options.rationale: HbA1c is not required as a confirmatory test after a diagnostic 75 g OGTT; ADIPS diagnoses on OGTT thresholds alone in the standard pathway (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer to the joint diabetes antenatal clinic for education and self monitoring
options.rationale: ADIPS 2014 diagnoses GDM if any single value is met or exceeded on a 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; all three are exceeded here, so multidisciplinary referral is next (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Under ADIPS 2014 any single 75 g OGTT value meeting or exceeding fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L diagnoses GDM. This woman meets all three. Management begins with education, dietary review, and self monitoring at a joint diabetes antenatal clinic. Pharmacotherapy is layered on if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 h 10.0, 2 h 8.5 mmol/L; any one diagnoses GDM.
Start with lifestyle plus SMBG before pharmacotherapy.
HbA1c is not a substitute for OGTT.
explanation.pearls: A single ADIPS OGTT threshold breach (fasting 5.1, 1 h 10.0, or 2 h 8.5 mmol/L) is enough to diagnose GDM without repeat or HbA1c confirmation.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy
RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

subtopic_detail: Second line uterotonic when hypertensive
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar. A 34 year old primipara has had a spontaneous vaginal birth 15 minutes ago at 40 weeks after augmentation for prolonged first stage. Estimated blood loss so far is 900 mL and continues to trickle.

Her booking blood pressure was 128/82. She developed gestational hypertension at 36 weeks and has been on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. Blood pressure in early labour was 152/98 and again 156/102 in second stage. She has no known allergies.

On examination the uterus feels boggy. The placenta appears complete on inspection. The perineum is intact. Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units was given with the anterior shoulder and a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1 L Hartmann is now running at 250 mL/hour. Uterine massage continues.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 156/98, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Uterine tone: Boggy on abdominal palpation despite massage
data_table.Uterotonics given: IM oxytocin 10 units at anterior shoulder; oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann infusion at 250 mL/hour
data_table.Blood pressure trend: Gestational hypertension on labetalol 200 mg BD; BP 152/98 then 156/102 in second stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to add?

options.text: Carboprost (15 methyl PGF2 alpha) 250 microgram intramuscular, up to 8 doses at 15 minute intervals
options.rationale: In PPH with atony and a hypertensive contraindication to ergometrine, carboprost 250 microgram IM is the appropriate second line uterotonic and can be repeated to a maximum of 8 doses; asthma is the main contraindication (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular immediately as a second line uterotonic
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disease because it can precipitate a severe surge in blood pressure and cerebrovascular events (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual as the second line uterotonic after oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a third line uterotonic in Australian PPH pathways; its onset is slower and it is often used only when parenteral options are exhausted or unavailable (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes and stop further uterotonics
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an important adjunct within 3 hours of onset per WOMAN and Australian guidance but does not replace ongoing uterotonic escalation while atony persists (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon before any further pharmacological escalation
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is a mechanical adjunct after pharmacological measures have failed to control atony; escalation of uterotonics with an appropriate agent takes priority now (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH continues despite oxytocin. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disease so the appropriate second line uterotonic is carboprost 250 microgram IM, repeated up to 8 doses. Tranexamic acid is a parallel adjunct. Balloon tamponade is a step later in the pathway.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension.
Carboprost 250 microgram IM up to 8 doses is the appropriate second line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours is an adjunct, not a substitute for uterotonics.
explanation.pearls: For PPH atony in a hypertensive woman, carboprost 250 microgram IM (up to 8 doses) is the second line uterotonic because ergometrine is contraindicated.

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment unit. A 28 year old woman presents at 6+3 weeks by her last menstrual period with left iliac fossa discomfort and light vaginal spotting for 2 days.

This is her first pregnancy. She has no significant medical history, no allergies, and takes only pregnancy multivitamins. She lives with her partner in the city, has reliable transport, and works from home for the next 4 weeks.

On examination her abdomen is soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness only. There is no rebound. Speculum shows a closed cervix with a small amount of dark blood. Bimanual is uncomfortable in the left adnexa without a definite mass.

Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7. Beta hCG is 2100 IU/L; a repeat 48 hours ago was 2280 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 8 mm and a 22 mm left tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity. Full blood count, renal, and liver function tests are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; endometrial thickness 8 mm; 22 mm left tubal mass; no fetal cardiac activity; no significant free fluid
