data_table.Blood tests: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits
data_table.Social: Reliable transport; works from home for next 4 weeks; lives with partner

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy today because any tubal ectopic requires surgical management once diagnosed
options.rationale: RANZCOG reserves surgery for bhCG 5000 IU/L or above, fetal cardiac activity, a mass 3.5 cm or larger, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or unreliable follow up; this case does not meet these thresholds (Source: RANZCOG GPS Ectopic Pregnancy).

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly beta hCG surveillance to day 7 and beyond until it is negative
options.rationale: This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG criteria for medical management: bhCG under 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, minimal pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, and no contraindications; single dose methotrexate is appropriate (Source: RANZCOG GPS Ectopic Pregnancy).

options.text: Serial beta hCG monitoring alone every 48 hours with expectant management for the next 2 weeks
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for suspected declining or resolving pregnancy of unknown location; a visualised 22 mm tubal mass warrants active treatment rather than watchful waiting (Source: RANZCOG GPS Ectopic Pregnancy).

options.text: Mifepristone 200 mg orally followed by misoprostol 800 microgram vaginally to complete a medical management pathway
options.rationale: Mifepristone plus misoprostol is a first trimester medical abortion regimen for intrauterine pregnancy and has no role in tubal ectopic management (Source: RANZCOG GPS Ectopic Pregnancy).

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve tubal patency for future fertility as a first line treatment
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is a fertility sparing surgical option but is not preferred over methotrexate in this stable candidate meeting all medical criteria (Source: RANZCOG GPS Ectopic Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Tubal ectopic meeting the RANZCOG medical criteria (bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no cardiac activity, mass below 3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow up, no contraindications) is treated with single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM. Weekly bhCG to day 7 and to negativity monitors response. Surgery is reserved for cases above these thresholds or unstable.
key_points: RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG 5000 IU/L or above.
Methotrexate is preferred when all medical criteria are met.
Expectant management is only for suspected resolving pregnancy of unknown location.
explanation.pearls: For tubal ectopic with bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, minimal pain and reliable follow up, single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM is the RANZCOG choice.

subtopic_detail: NCSP result triage
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a Cervical Screening Test result for a 32 year old woman. She had a self collected vaginal swab through the general practice 5 days ago and this is her first screening test.

She is well, has a regular sexual partner of 3 years, and uses combined oral contraceptive pills. Her last cervical screening prior to today was never; she was overseas during the transition from Pap smear to the NCSP renewed program. She has no dyspareunia and no post coital bleeding.

The report reads: HPV detected, other high risk type (not 16 or 18). Because the sample is self collected there is no liquid based cytology reported on this sample.

data_table.History: 32 y, first ever cervical screen; no post coital or intermenstrual bleeding
data_table.Sample: Self collected vaginal swab; no cytology reported on self collected sample
data_table.Result: HPV detected, non 16/18 high risk type

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step under the National Cervical Screening Program?

options.text: Repeat the self collected HPV test in 12 months without cytology and manage on the future HPV result
options.rationale: Repeat testing at 12 months without intervening cytology risks missing a prevalent high grade lesion; the NCSP requires cytology triage now (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Refer directly to colposcopy today because any HPV positive self collected sample requires colposcopy
options.rationale: Direct colposcopy from a self collected sample is only recommended for HPV 16 or 18 detected; non 16/18 types go via clinician collected cytology first (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Recall for a clinician collected cervical sample for reflex liquid based cytology and act on that cytology result
options.rationale: Under the NCSP, a self collected sample positive for HPV non 16/18 requires clinician collected liquid based cytology; if cytology is negative or low grade she returns for repeat HPV testing in 12 months, and high grade cytology triggers colposcopy (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Recall for a clinician collected sample to repeat HPV testing rather than proceed to cytology triage this cycle
options.rationale: Repeating HPV testing on a clinician sample does not add triage value; the NCSP pathway uses liquid based cytology at this step (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Reassure the woman that non 16 or 18 HPV clears spontaneously and rescreen at the routine 5 year interval
options.rationale: Rescreening at 5 years is only appropriate when HPV is not detected; any HPV detected result requires prompt triage rather than deferral (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: For a self collected NCSP sample with non 16/18 high risk HPV, the next step is clinician collected liquid based cytology to triage. Colposcopy is reserved for HPV 16 or 18 detected on self collection, or for high grade cytology. Rescreening at 5 years applies only when HPV is not detected.
key_points: Self collected HPV 16/18 detected: direct colposcopy.
Self collected non 16/18 HPV detected: clinician cytology triage.
Rescreen at 5 years only if HPV not detected.
explanation.pearls: Self collected non 16/18 HPV detected on the NCSP goes to clinician collected liquid based cytology triage, not straight to colposcopy.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines
RACGP Red Book preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: MgSO4 loading in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27 year old primigravida at 34+2 weeks who presented with headache and one episode of blurred vision.

Her booking blood pressure was 118/70 and 20 week anomaly ultrasound was reported as normal. Since 32 weeks she has been reviewed weekly for a rising blood pressure trend and was commenced on labetalol 200 mg twice daily 3 days ago.

On arrival tonight she is clinically well but reports a persistent frontal headache and one flash of blurred vision that has settled. There are no visible papilloedema, no epigastric tenderness, and no clonus. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the lower limbs. Fetal cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145, moderate variability, and accelerations without decelerations.

Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 178/112 (repeat 172/108 after 15 minutes), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. Full blood count, platelets 145, liver function tests within normal limits, urea 4.2, creatinine 68.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 178/112 then 172/108, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Fetal CTG: Baseline 145, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Examination: Frontal headache; one settled visual disturbance; brisk reflexes; no clonus, no papilloedema, no epigastric tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick 3+ protein; platelets 145 x10^9/L; LFTs within normal limits; UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediately as the initial antihypertensive with reassessment every 5 minutes
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is not recommended in pregnancy because of unpredictable rapid falls in blood pressure; oral immediate release nifedipine or IV labetalol or hydralazine is preferred (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Increase oral labetalol from 200 mg twice daily to 400 mg three times daily and reassess her blood pressure in 60 minutes
options.rationale: Oral titration is inadequate for a persistent systolic 170 mmHg or above with neurological symptoms; intravenous antihypertensive plus MgSO4 is required (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular for fetal lung maturation and defer any other intervention for 24 hours
options.rationale: Betamethasone is appropriate for a 34+2 weeks pregnancy but does not replace urgent MgSO4 and antihypertensive; delay risks eclampsia and stroke (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, alongside intravenous antihypertensive
options.rationale: This is severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms; the SOMANZ Australian pathway loads magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour to prevent eclampsia while urgent BP control is initiated (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Proceed straight to caesarean section within 30 minutes without magnesium sulfate loading or antihypertensive control first
options.rationale: Stabilisation with MgSO4 and BP control precedes delivery except in acute maternal compromise or unreassuring CTG; the CTG is reassuring so stabilisation is first (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms at 34+2 weeks requires MgSO4 for eclampsia prevention (4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour) alongside urgent intravenous BP control. Betamethasone is worth giving but does not replace stabilisation. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided. Delivery is planned after stabilisation.
key_points: SOMANZ MgSO4 load 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour.
Intravenous labetalol or hydralazine or oral IR nifedipine, not sublingual nifedipine.
Betamethasone given but does not defer treatment.
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms, MgSO4 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour is the SOMANZ eclampsia prophylaxis regimen alongside IV antihypertensive.

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Obstetric cholestasis surveillance
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar. A 29 year old woman at 34+4 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy presents with 10 days of generalised itch that is worse on her palms and soles at night.

Her first pregnancy 3 years ago was complicated by cholestasis diagnosed at 35 weeks and induced at 37 weeks; the baby was well. Her booking bloods, morphology, and glucose tolerance were within normal limits.

On examination she is well with no rash and no jaundice. Fetal movements are normal. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 138 with moderate variability, accelerations, and no decelerations.

Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7. Bloods this morning show ALT 118 U/L (5-40), ALP 320 U/L (30-120, elevated in pregnancy), GGT 92 U/L (5-40), bilirubin 12 micromol/L, fasting bile acids 62 micromol/L, INR 1.0, platelets 240.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Fetal CTG: Baseline 138, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Liver panel: ALT 118 U/L (5-40); GGT 92 U/L (5-40); bilirubin 12 micromol/L; fasting bile acids 62 micromol/L; ALP 320 U/L (elevated in pregnancy expected)
data_table.Past obstetric: Cholestasis in prior pregnancy at 35 weeks, induced at 37 weeks with well infant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure the woman that her pruritus is due to normal pregnancy skin changes and manage with emollients only
options.rationale: Fasting bile acids 62 micromol/L with elevated transaminases confirms cholestasis and requires structured surveillance and pharmacotherapy (Source: RCOG Green top 43 Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily and continue expectant management to spontaneous labour beyond 40 weeks
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk rises with gestation and bile acid concentration; expectant management beyond 40 weeks is inconsistent with Australian centre practice at this bile acid level (Source: RCOG Green top 43 Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Commence oral vitamin K 10 mg daily, chlorpheniramine 4 mg at night, and repeat liver and bile acid bloods in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin K is only indicated if the INR is prolonged; her INR is normal and delaying escalation to definitive management is inappropriate (Source: RCOG Green top 43 Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Deliver immediately by category one caesarean section because bile acids above 40 micromol/L mandate expedited birth today
options.rationale: Bile acids in the 40 to 99 range warrant birth by 35 to 36 weeks and not immediate delivery, so vaginal induction is preferred when there is no other indication for caesarean (Source: RCOG Green top 43 Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily, weekly bile acids, and plan delivery by 36 weeks given peak bile acids of 62
options.rationale: RCOG and Australian centres bring forward delivery to 35 to 36 weeks when peak fasting bile acids are 40 to 99 micromol/L because of a threefold rise in stillbirth risk from 37 weeks onward; UDCA relieves pruritus and biochemistry (Source: RCOG Green top 43 Obstetric cholestasis; Ovadia meta-analysis Lancet 2019).

explanation.summary: This is obstetric cholestasis with peak fasting bile acids in the 40 to 99 micromol/L band. Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for pruritus and biochemistry, and delivery is brought forward to 35 to 36 weeks because stillbirth risk rises steeply beyond that with these bile acid values. Vitamin K only substitutes when the INR is prolonged and expectant management to 40 weeks is not consistent with current Australian practice.
key_points: Peak fasting bile acids 40-99 micromol/L: aim delivery by 35-36 weeks.
Peak fasting bile acids over 100 micromol/L: consider birth by 34-35 weeks.
UDCA relieves symptoms; vitamin K only if INR prolonged.
explanation.pearls: In obstetric cholestasis, peak fasting bile acids 40 to 99 micromol/L bring the delivery target forward to 35 to 36 weeks; above 100 micromol/L consider 34 to 35 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Placenta praevia bleed at 32 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 33 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 32+1 weeks presents with a painless bright red vaginal bleed that soaked a pad over the last hour. She has had two prior lower segment caesarean sections.

Her morphology scan at 20 weeks and repeat scan at 28 weeks showed a placenta covering the internal cervical os (grade 4). She has been abstaining from intercourse and vaginal examinations since. She has known blood group O negative.

On assessment she looks alert with warm peripheries. Abdomen is soft and non tender; presenting part is high and mobile. Speculum examination is deferred. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140, moderate variability, accelerations, and no decelerations.

Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8. Ongoing bleeding is estimated at 250 mL over the last 30 minutes. Two large bore intravenous cannulas are sited, full blood count, group and hold, and coagulation are drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/64, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Blood loss: 250 mL ongoing over 30 minutes; bright red painless
data_table.Fetal CTG: Baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Prior imaging: 20 and 28 week scans: placenta covering internal os (grade 4)
data_table.Obstetric history: Two prior lower segment caesareans; group O negative
data_table.Access: Two large bore IV cannulas; FBC, group and hold, coags drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give IM betamethasone 11.4 mg, cross match blood, Anti D 625 IU, and prepare for possible category one caesarean
options.rationale: At 32+1 weeks with a grade 4 praevia and ongoing bleed, RANZCOG recommends corticosteroids for lung maturity, cross matched blood, Anti D for a Rh negative woman, and prompt caesarean if maternal or fetal compromise occurs (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Proceed to a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and confirm the source of bleeding before any imaging
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in known or suspected placenta praevia because it can precipitate massive haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery with a controlled artificial rupture of membranes to compress the placental edge
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is not appropriate in grade 4 praevia because the placenta covers the internal os; caesarean is mandatory for these women (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient follow up in the antenatal clinic in 48 hours once the bright red bleeding has slowed
options.rationale: Any antepartum haemorrhage at this gestation with grade 4 praevia mandates inpatient admission for surveillance because rebleeding is common (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and defer betamethasone corticosteroids until the visible bleeding has settled
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid can be considered as an adjunct in antepartum haemorrhage but does not replace corticosteroids, which should be given without delay at this preterm gestation (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

explanation.summary: This is a preterm bleed with a grade 4 placenta praevia at 32+1 weeks. Priorities are corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, Anti D for a Rh negative woman, cross matched blood, and readiness for category one caesarean if maternal or fetal compromise develops. Digital vaginal examination and any attempt at vaginal delivery are contraindicated.
key_points: No digital vaginal examination in praevia.
Grade 4 praevia is a caesarean delivery.
Give betamethasone, cross match, and Anti D 625 IU if Rh negative.
explanation.pearls: In known grade 4 placenta praevia bleeding at 32 weeks, give betamethasone, cross match blood, Anti D if Rh negative, and prepare for category one caesarean; digital vaginal examination is forbidden.

subtopic_detail: Breech delivery route counselling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit. A 32 year old primigravida at 36+5 weeks has a persistent frank breech presentation on ultrasound today after an unsuccessful external cephalic version 2 hours ago.

Estimated fetal weight is 3.2 kg with an amniotic fluid index of 12 cm and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. She has no cephalopelvic disproportion on examination and no hyperextension of the fetal neck. She has had no antepartum complications.

She asks about mode of birth. She has read that vaginal breech birth can be attempted at experienced units and wants an honest discussion. Her partner is supportive of either option. The senior obstetrician has agreed to be available.

data_table.Fetal parameters: Frank breech; EFW 3.2 kg; AFI 12 cm; UA Doppler within normal limits; no neck hyperextension
data_table.Maternal: 36+5 weeks; primigravida; no obstetric complications; adequate maternal pelvis on examination
data_table.Care: Senior obstetric team on call; woman wants an evidence based discussion

lead_in: What information best reflects the evidence base to guide her decision?

options.text: Planned vaginal breech birth has equivalent or lower perinatal morbidity than caesarean section in selected primigravidae
options.rationale: Contemporary meta-analyses of selected planned vaginal breech births at experienced units suggest closer outcomes than the Term Breech Trial but do not show lower morbidity than planned caesarean (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: Planned caesarean has a lower composite of perinatal mortality and serious morbidity than planned vaginal breech
options.rationale: The Term Breech Trial and subsequent RANZCOG position support planned caesarean as lower risk for the composite of perinatal death and serious neonatal morbidity in singleton term breech; long term outcomes at 2 years show no difference (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: Planned caesarean increases the risk of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage relative to a planned vaginal breech birth
options.rationale: Planned caesarean reduces, not increases, the risk of intracranial haemorrhage and other serious neonatal morbidity in term breech (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: A trial of vaginal breech is only reasonable if a second attempt at external cephalic version fails at 39 weeks under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: A second ECV attempt is not mandated by Australian pathways; the discussion at this gestation is between planned caesarean and planned vaginal breech at experienced units (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version).

options.text: Estimated fetal weight above 3 kg alone contraindicates any attempt at planned vaginal breech birth at term
options.rationale: Australian units typically consider EFW between 2.5 and 4 kg for planned vaginal breech; 3.2 kg is not itself a contraindication (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

explanation.summary: For singleton term breech, the Term Breech Trial and RANZCOG position support planned caesarean as lower risk than planned vaginal breech for the composite of perinatal death and serious neonatal morbidity. Long term outcomes at 2 years are similar. Vaginal breech remains an option at experienced units after careful counselling and case selection.
key_points: Planned caesarean reduces perinatal composite risk versus planned vaginal breech.
EFW between 2.5 and 4 kg and no neck hyperextension are typical selection criteria.
Long term outcomes at 2 years are similar.
explanation.pearls: Evidence based counselling for term breech at Australian units: planned caesarean lowers perinatal composite risk relative to planned vaginal breech, with equivalent long term outcomes at 2 years.

sources.label: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term
Term Breech Trial (Hannah et al. Lancet 2000)

subtopic_detail: Severe cyclical irritability with full remission after menstruation in a woman seeking treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who says that for about a week before each period she becomes so irritable and tearful that she has twice considered resigning from her job. She describes feeling entirely herself again within two days of her period starting.

She has had this pattern for three years and it has worsened since stopping the combined oral contraceptive pill eighteen months ago. Her cycles are regular at 29 days. She sleeps and functions normally in the fortnight after menstruation, denies any low mood or anxiety at those times, and has never had a period of persistent low mood lasting more than two weeks. She uses condoms, does not smoke, and her thyroid function and full blood count taken by a colleague last month were normal. She has kept no record of her symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask her to complete a daily symptom rating record across two consecutive menstrual cycles
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles showing symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free interval after menstruation, because retrospective recall substantially overestimates cyclicity. Around forty percent of women referred with this history turn out on prospective rating to have a continuous mood disorder that worsens premenstrually, and that distinction changes treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at low dose taken continuously and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic treatment is genuinely effective here and can be given continuously or only in the luteal phase, but committing to it before the pattern is documented risks treating a continuous mood disorder as a cyclical one. Prospective rating costs two cycles and prevents that error. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Measure serum oestradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase to confirm a hormonal imbalance
options.rationale: Circulating oestradiol and progesterone concentrations are normal in this condition, which reflects an abnormal central response to ordinary cyclical hormone change rather than abnormal hormone levels. Measuring them generates uninterpretable results and false reassurance. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Refer for consideration of a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is a later step for severe disease that has not responded to first line measures, and it requires add back therapy and bone density monitoring. Escalating to it before the diagnosis is even established is disproportionate. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Refer for psychological therapy addressing the workplace stressors that appear to precipitate symptoms
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy has a genuine role in management, but framing the problem as workplace stress ignores a timing pattern that is tied to the cycle rather than to external events. Therapy is offered alongside a confirmed diagnosis, not instead of making one. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is defined by affective and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free interval in the follicular phase and demonstrable interference with function. Because retrospective reports of cyclicity are unreliable, the diagnosis formally requires prospective daily ratings across at least two consecutive cycles, most often using a validated instrument such as the daily record of severity of problems. The commonest alternative explanation is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying continuous mood or anxiety disorder, which prospective rating exposes immediately because symptoms never fully remit. Hormone concentrations are normal and measuring them does not assist. Once confirmed, effective options include serotonergic antidepressants given continuously or in the luteal phase only, combined hormonal contraception used in an extended regimen, cognitive behavioural therapy, and ovarian suppression for refractory disease.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily rating are required before the diagnosis is made
A symptom free follicular phase is the defining feature
Premenstrual exacerbation of a continuous mood disorder is the main alternative
Oestradiol and progesterone levels are normal and are not measured
Serotonergic agents work within days and may be given in the luteal phase alone
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants act within one to two days in this condition rather than the two to four weeks expected in major depression, which is why luteal phase only dosing from ovulation to the onset of menstruation is effective and is often preferred by women who dislike continuous medication.

subtopic_detail: Inability to tolerate vaginal penetration with involuntary muscle guarding on attempted examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse with her partner of two years. She says that whenever penetration is attempted her body tightens up and she feels she is being torn, and she has begun avoiding intimacy altogether.

She has never used tampons for the same reason. She describes her relationship as loving and reports no history of sexual assault or coercion. She has regular periods without pain and no vaginal discharge, itching or postcoital bleeding. On attempting examination she withdraws and her thighs adduct before you make contact with the introitus, and you are able to inspect the vulva only briefly. The visible vulval skin is normal with no fissuring, no pallor and no architectural change.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulval skin with no fissures, pallor or architectural change, involuntary pelvic floor and thigh adductor contraction on approach to the introitus, internal examination not tolerated

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Prescription of vaginal oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks to improve introital tissue elasticity
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary changes of oestrogen deficiency, which produce pale thin tissue and are seen after menopause or with prolonged lactation or ovarian suppression. This woman is cycling normally with normal appearing vulval skin. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation and pelvic floor down training
options.rationale: Involuntary pelvic floor contraction preventing penetration, with normal vulval skin and no other pain condition, is treated first with pelvic floor physiotherapy using graded exposure, dilator work and techniques to release rather than strengthen the muscle. This has the strongest evidence of any single intervention and works through the involuntary guarding that is the core of the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Prescription of topical lidocaine gel applied to the introitus for twenty minutes before intercourse
options.rationale: Topical anaesthesia targets a localised nociceptive trigger at the vestibule and is useful in provoked vestibulodynia, where touch to a specific point reproduces burning pain. It does not address involuntary muscle contraction and can be used as an adjunct rather than as the primary treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Examination under general anaesthesia to exclude an obstructing vaginal septum or other anomaly
options.rationale: Structural anomaly is worth considering but is unlikely with regular painless menstruation and no history of obstructed flow, and anaesthesia removes the very muscle response that defines the condition. It is reserved for cases where anatomy genuinely cannot be assessed after treatment has begun. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Referral for botulinum toxin injection into the levator ani muscles under sedation as definitive therapy
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is a second line option for women who have not responded to physiotherapy and psychological treatment, and evidence remains limited with effects that wear off over months. Offering it first exposes her to an invasive procedure ahead of a conservative approach that usually succeeds. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

explanation.summary: Persistent difficulty with vaginal penetration accompanied by marked involuntary tensing of the pelvic floor and adductors, and by fear or anxiety about penetration, is classified within genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder. Assessment must exclude dermatological causes such as lichen sclerosus, infection, and structural anomaly, and must ask sensitively about prior trauma without assuming it. The single most effective intervention is pelvic floor physiotherapy, which teaches awareness and voluntary release of the muscle, combines graded dilator exposure with relaxation, and is typically paired with psychosexual therapy and partner involvement. Topical anaesthetics, oestrogen and botulinum toxin all have narrower indications and are adjuncts or second line. Progress is measured by tolerance of graded insertion rather than by achievement of intercourse, which reduces the performance pressure that maintains the cycle.
key_points: Involuntary muscle guarding, not tissue pathology, is the core mechanism
Exclude lichen sclerosus, infection and structural anomaly before attributing to muscle
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded dilators is the highest yield first intervention
Psychosexual therapy and partner involvement improve outcomes and are offered alongside
Botulinum toxin and surgery are later options after conservative treatment fails
explanation.pearls: Set the treatment goal as comfortable tolerance of a graded dilator or a tampon rather than as intercourse, because making penetration the measure of success reinstates the anticipatory anxiety and reflex guarding that the physiotherapy programme is designed to unlearn.

subtopic_detail: Smooth cervical lesion found at screening in a woman reporting bleeding after intercourse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a routine cervical screening test on a 41 year old woman who mentions that she has bled a few times after intercourse over the past three months.

On speculum examination there is a smooth, bright red, pedunculated lesion about 12 mm long protruding from the cervical os on a narrow stalk. The surrounding ectocervix looks healthy with no ulceration, no friable irregular tissue and no induration on palpation. Her previous screening test two years ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Her periods are regular and she has no intermenstrual bleeding, no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. Her result returns today as negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated bright red cervical lesion 12 mm on a narrow stalk arising from the os, healthy surrounding ectocervix, no ulceration or induration, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not tender
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, previous test two years ago also negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to gynaecological oncology given that postcoital bleeding with a cervical lesion is present
options.rationale: Urgent oncology referral is driven by a hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix, contact bleeding from an abnormal looking surface, or a cervix that feels indurated on palpation. A smooth pedunculated lesion on a narrow stalk with a healthy surrounding cervix does not meet that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Cervical cancer)

options.text: Prescribe a course of doxycycline and metronidazole for presumed cervicitis and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antimicrobial treatment addresses infective cervicitis, which presents with mucopurulent discharge and a friable inflamed cervix rather than a discrete pedunculated lesion. Treating empirically leaves the visible lesion in place and the bleeding unexplained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Remove the lesion in clinic by twisting the stalk and send the tissue for histological examination
options.rationale: A benign appearing pedunculated cervical polyp causing postcoital bleeding is removed by avulsion of the stalk in the clinic, which both stops the bleeding and provides tissue. Histology is mandatory because a small proportion harbour unexpected pathology and because polypoid appearance alone cannot exclude it. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

options.text: Reassure her that a negative screening test excludes significant pathology and repeat testing in five years
options.rationale: A negative human papillomavirus result reduces the risk of squamous disease but does not investigate a visible cervical lesion or exclude adenocarcinoma, which is less reliably detected by screening. Any symptomatic or suspicious visible lesion is assessed on its own merits regardless of the screening result. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling before any attempt is made at removal
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding and at risk factors for endometrial pathology, and this woman has neither. Imaging is added when the polyp appears to arise from higher in the canal or when bleeding continues after removal. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

explanation.summary: Cervical polyps are common benign lesions arising from the endocervical canal or ectocervix and are a frequent cause of postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. The essential clinical task is to distinguish a benign pedunculated polyp with a healthy surrounding cervix from a malignant lesion, which typically appears as a hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix. A negative human papillomavirus screening result is reassuring for squamous disease but must never be used to dismiss a visible lesion or a symptom such as persistent postcoital bleeding, since adenocarcinoma arises higher in the canal and is less reliably captured. Symptomatic polyps are removed by avulsion of the stalk in the clinic, with the specimen sent for histology because a small minority contain unexpected pathology. Persistent bleeding after removal, or a polyp whose base cannot be seen, prompts imaging and hysteroscopic assessment for an endometrial origin.
key_points: Smooth pedunculated lesion with a healthy surrounding cervix suggests a benign polyp
A hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix warrants urgent oncology referral
A negative human papillomavirus result never overrides a visible or symptomatic lesion
Avulsion in clinic treats the bleeding and provides tissue for histology
Bleeding persisting after removal prompts imaging and hysteroscopy for an endometrial source
explanation.pearls: Send every avulsed polyp for histology even when it looks unequivocally benign, because a small number contain endometrial or endocervical adenocarcinoma or high grade dysplasia, and discarding the specimen removes the only opportunity to detect a lesion whose visible appearance was reassuring.

subtopic_detail: Device stem palpable at the external os on routine check after insertion
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman six weeks after insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device. She reports cramping and irregular bleeding since insertion and says her partner can feel something hard during intercourse.

She has been using no other method of contraception since insertion and had unprotected intercourse four days ago. Her last menstrual period began nine days ago. On speculum examination the threads are visible but the firm white stem of the device is protruding about 1 cm through the external os. The uterus is anteverted, normal in size and non tender, with no cervical excitation and no adnexal tenderness. She is afebrile and there is no offensive discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Device stem visible protruding approximately 1 cm through the external os with threads present, uterus anteverted and non tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass or tenderness, no offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to confirm the device position before deciding on any intervention
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when threads are absent and the device cannot be seen, to distinguish complete expulsion from perforation or a high lying device. Here the stem is directly visible in the canal, so imaging adds delay without changing the plan. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Reassure her that irregular bleeding settles by six months and review the device position in three months
options.rationale: Unscheduled bleeding in the first six months is indeed expected and usually settles, but that counselling applies to a correctly positioned device. Leaving a displaced device in place exposes her to unintended pregnancy for three months. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Take endocervical swabs and treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease before removing the device
options.rationale: Pelvic infection is suggested by fever, pelvic tenderness, cervical excitation or offensive discharge, none of which are present. Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea remains reasonable on risk grounds but empirical treatment and delay are not warranted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Remove the device now, provide emergency contraception cover and arrange a replacement insertion
options.rationale: A device whose stem sits within the cervical canal is partially expelled and no longer provides reliable contraception, so it is removed rather than pushed back up, and a new device is inserted. Because she had unprotected intercourse four days ago while the device was already displaced, emergency contraception is required alongside the removal. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Reposition the device upwards into the uterine fundus using an instrument under direct vision
options.rationale: Pushing a partially expelled device back through the internal os is not recommended because it damages the device and the endometrium and the expulsion usually recurs. The correct action is removal and reinsertion of a new device. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

explanation.summary: Expulsion of an intrauterine device occurs in roughly two to ten percent of users and is most likely in the first three months, with heavy menstrual bleeding, insertion immediately postpartum and a history of previous expulsion increasing the risk. Partial expulsion, where the stem lies within the cervical canal, removes contraceptive reliability even though threads remain visible, and it presents with cramping, unscheduled bleeding or a partner feeling the device. Management is removal and insertion of a new device rather than repositioning, since repositioning damages the device and expulsion recurs. Contraceptive cover must be considered because the device may have been displaced for some time, so emergency contraception is offered when there has been recent unprotected intercourse and a pregnancy test is performed. Ultrasound is reserved for missing threads, where the alternatives are complete expulsion, a high lying device or uterine perforation.
key_points: Partial expulsion means the device stem lies in the cervical canal and is no longer reliable
Expulsion risk is highest in the first three months after insertion
Remove and replace rather than reposition a partially expelled device
Consider emergency contraception because the device may have been displaced for days
Ultrasound is for absent threads, to separate expulsion from perforation or high position
explanation.pearls: The copper device is the more effective emergency contraceptive but is unsuitable in this situation, so if a new hormonal device is inserted at the same visit, cover the preceding episode of unprotected intercourse with oral ulipristal or levonorgestrel and remember that ulipristal reduces the effectiveness of a hormonal method started in the following five days.

subtopic_detail: Couple asking when to stop other contraception after male surgical sterilisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38 year old woman and her 41 year old partner for a joint appointment about contraception. He had a vasectomy eleven weeks ago and they want to know whether she can now have her hormonal implant removed.

He reports that the wound healed without incident and that he has ejaculated well over thirty times since the procedure. He has not yet provided any semen sample, saying the clinic gave him a form but he did not get around to it. They have three children and are certain their family is complete. She has tolerated the implant well and is keen to stop it as soon as it is safe to do so. Neither has any other medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well healed scrotal incisions, no haematoma, no tenderness, testes normal to palpation
data_table.Investigations: No post procedure semen analysis performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Advise that the implant can be removed now because more than twenty ejaculations have occurred
options.rationale: Ejaculation count was historically used as a proxy but is unreliable, since a proportion of men still have motile sperm after twenty or more ejaculations. The reason the analysis exists is precisely that this proxy fails in a minority. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Advise that the implant can be removed once sixteen weeks have elapsed from the date of the procedure
options.rationale: A fixed interval without testing does not establish clearance, because clearance depends on the individual rate at which residual sperm are cleared rather than on the calendar. Some men take considerably longer and a small number never clear. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Arrange scrotal ultrasound to confirm that the vas has been successfully divided on both sides
options.rationale: Imaging does not assess whether sperm are still present in the ejaculate and is used for suspected haematoma, abscess or chronic scrotal pain after the procedure. The functional question is answered by semen analysis alone. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Remove the implant and advise condom use for a further three months as a precautionary measure
options.rationale: Substituting a highly effective long acting method for condoms increases typical use failure substantially during the very window when the outcome is still uncertain. The precaution should be maintaining the existing effective method rather than downgrading it. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Continue the implant until a semen sample confirms clearance, and arrange that analysis now
options.rationale: Sterility is confirmed only by post procedure semen analysis, usually collected from around twelve weeks and after a sufficient number of ejaculations, because residual sperm persist in the distal vas for a variable period. Time elapsed and ejaculation count alone are not accepted as proof, so existing contraception continues until a clearance result is issued. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

explanation.summary: Vasectomy does not produce immediate sterility because sperm persist in the vas deferens distal to the point of division, and clearance is confirmed only by post procedure semen analysis. Australian practice is to test from around twelve weeks after the procedure, and existing contraception is continued until a clearance result is issued. A result showing azoospermia confirms success, while persistent non motile sperm in low concentration may permit clearance at the operating surgeon's discretion, and persistent motile sperm indicates failure requiring repeat testing or a repeat procedure. Early recanalisation occurs in roughly one in two hundred to five hundred men and late recanalisation is rarer still, so couples are counselled that no method is absolutely permanent. Counselling before the procedure should also confirm that the decision is regarded as permanent, since reversal is expensive, not funded and has variable success.
key_points: Residual sperm in the distal vas mean sterility is not immediate
Semen analysis from around twelve weeks is the only accepted confirmation
Ejaculation count and elapsed time are unreliable proxies for clearance
Continue existing contraception until a clearance result is issued
Late recanalisation occurs rarely, so no method is presented as absolute
explanation.pearls: Persistent low concentrations of non motile sperm on repeat testing can be accepted as special clearance by the operating surgeon rather than triggering a second operation, but any motile sperm at three months means the procedure has failed and the couple must keep using contraception while a repeat is arranged.

subtopic_detail: Cyclical lower abdominal pain with absent menarche and normal secondary sexual development
stem:
You are the paediatric and adolescent gynaecology registrar seeing a 14 year old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period and has had monthly lower abdominal pain for six months.

The pain lasts three to four days each month and is now severe enough that she has missed school on several occasions. Her mother says her daughter has recently started complaining of difficulty passing urine on the worst days. Breast development began at eleven and both breast and pubic hair development are at the adult stage. She is on the 60th centile for height, has no headaches or visual symptoms, and has a normal sense of smell. Abdominal examination reveals a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus, and she is not sexually active.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, smooth non tender suprapubic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, external genitalia otherwise not yet inspected
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inspect the external genitalia with the parent present and arrange pelvic ultrasound the same day
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea, normal secondary sexual characteristics and a suprapubic mass indicates outflow obstruction with accumulating menstrual blood, and inspection of the introitus will show a bulging bluish membrane if the obstruction is at the hymen. Ultrasound confirms the level of obstruction and the presence of a normal uterus and ovaries, which together determine whether a simple incision or complex reconstruction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and oestradiol before performing any examination
options.rationale: Gonadotrophin measurement is the correct pathway when secondary sexual characteristics are absent or incomplete, because it separates gonadal failure from hypothalamic causes. Fully developed secondary characteristics with cyclical pain indicate a functioning axis and shift the question to outflow. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone to investigate a disorder of sexual development in this girl
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement are directed at complete androgen insensitivity, in which pubic hair is characteristically sparse or absent and there is no uterus, so no menstrual blood accumulates and cyclical pain does not occur. Adult pubic hair with cyclical pain argues against it. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the cycle and relieve the monthly pain she describes
options.rationale: Cycle suppression would reduce further accumulation but leaves an obstructed collection and its complications untreated, including retrograde flow and urinary retention. Hormonal suppression is a holding measure only after the anatomy is known. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis as the initial imaging test to define the anatomy
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex obstructive anomalies and for planning reconstruction, but ultrasound is the appropriate first test and is quicker and more accessible. Imaging by magnetic resonance is added when ultrasound shows a complex or higher level obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is approached first by asking whether secondary sexual characteristics are present, because that single question splits the differential. Absent or incomplete development points towards gonadal failure or hypothalamic pituitary causes and is investigated with gonadotrophins, oestradiol and karyotype. Normal development with cyclical pain points instead to an obstructed outflow tract, in which menstrual blood accumulates and produces a suprapubic mass, and pressure effects such as urinary retention or constipation. Imperforate hymen is the commonest such obstruction and is recognised at inspection as a tense bluish bulging membrane, while transverse vaginal septum and cervical agenesis sit higher and need magnetic resonance imaging and specialist reconstruction. Definitive treatment of an imperforate hymen is surgical incision with drainage, performed by a gynaecologist rather than at the bedside, after which menstruation and fertility are typically normal.
key_points: Presence of secondary sexual characteristics divides the differential in primary amenorrhoea
Cyclical pain with a suprapubic mass indicates accumulating obstructed menstrual blood
Urinary retention and constipation are pressure complications of a large collection
Inspection of the introitus is the diagnostic step for imperforate hymen
Higher obstructions such as transverse septum need magnetic resonance imaging and reconstruction
explanation.pearls: Never incise or aspirate a bulging obstructing membrane at the bedside or in the emergency department, because inadequate drainage through a small opening allows ascending infection of a large blood collection under pressure, and definitive hymenotomy with full drainage in theatre is the operation that preserves subsequent reproductive function.

subtopic_detail: Vaginal bulge in an older woman with significant comorbidity declining an operation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 78 year old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a lump she can feel at the vaginal entrance by the end of each day. It has been present for a year and now interferes with her gardening.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home oxygen at night, and her cardiologist has documented an ejection fraction of 35 percent. She has been told she is a poor anaesthetic candidate and says clearly that she does not want an operation. On examination there is descent of the anterior vaginal wall to 1 cm beyond the hymen on straining, with a well oestrogenised appearance following six weeks of topical oestrogen prescribed by her general practitioner. She empties her bladder completely and has no incontinence, no bleeding and no ulceration of the vaginal skin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descent to 1 cm beyond the hymen on Valsalva, vaginal epithelium well oestrogenised, no ulceration, post void residual volume 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 30 mL on bladder scan, urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Referral for colpocleisis as an obliterative procedure carrying lower operative risk than reconstruction
options.rationale: Colpocleisis is a legitimate option for frail women who no longer wish to be sexually active and does carry lower risk than reconstruction, yet it remains an operation that she has declined. It becomes relevant only if conservative management fails and she reconsiders surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Fitting of a vaginal support pessary with a planned review to check fit and vaginal skin condition
options.rationale: A pessary is the appropriate first line for symptomatic prolapse in a woman who declines surgery or is a poor operative candidate, and it can relieve the bulge symptom immediately without anaesthetic risk. Her vaginal epithelium is already well oestrogenised, which improves tolerance, and scheduled review detects erosion early. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Referral for anterior colporrhaphy under regional anaesthesia to minimise the perioperative risk involved
options.rationale: Regional technique reduces but does not remove the risk in a woman with severe airways disease and impaired ventricular function, and she has clearly declined an operation. Her stated preference is a decisive part of the decision rather than an obstacle to work around. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: A supervised pelvic floor muscle training programme alone as definitive management of the bulge symptom
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training helps mild prolapse and is a valuable adjunct, but descent beyond the hymen is unlikely to be reversed by muscle training alone. It is offered alongside a pessary rather than instead of one at this stage. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Continuation of topical vaginal oestrogen alone with review of her symptoms again in six months time
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves epithelial quality and comfort and supports pessary use but does not provide mechanical support for a descended wall. Six months of an ineffective single measure leaves her symptomatic and limits her activity further. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

explanation.summary: Management of pelvic organ prolapse is driven by symptoms rather than by the stage seen on examination, and the three broad options are observation, conservative treatment with pessary and pelvic floor training, and surgery. A pessary is first line for any woman who declines surgery, is awaiting it, is a poor operative candidate or is pregnant or planning further pregnancy, and it can relieve the bulge sensation immediately. Ring pessaries are usually tried first for anterior and apical descent, with Gellhorn or other space filling types used when a ring will not retain. Topical vaginal oestrogen improves epithelial quality and reduces erosion, and regular review is essential because a neglected pessary can ulcerate or become embedded. Pelvic floor muscle training is a useful adjunct and is most effective for milder degrees of descent.
key_points: Prolapse is treated for symptoms, not for the stage recorded on examination
Pessary is first line for women declining surgery or unfit for anaesthesia
Topical vaginal oestrogen improves epithelial quality and pessary tolerance
Scheduled review is mandatory to detect erosion or an embedded device
Pelvic floor training is an adjunct and works best for mild descent
explanation.pearls: Book the first pessary review within two to four weeks and then at least six monthly, because an unreviewed device can erode into the bladder or rectum and produce a fistula, and a woman who moves into residential care or develops cognitive impairment is the classic patient in whom a forgotten pessary is found years later.

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive coarse hair growth with clitoral change in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman with coarse dark hair on her chin, upper lip and lower abdomen. She says the change began about eight months ago and has accelerated, and that she now shaves daily when previously she needed nothing.

Her periods were regular every 28 days until six months ago and she has had none for the past three months. She has noticed her voice sounding deeper on recordings and that her hairline has receded at the temples. She takes no medications, no supplements and no androgenic preparations, and there is no family history of excess hair growth. Her body mass index is 23 kg per square metre and there are no violaceous striae, no proximal weakness and no facial rounding. On examination the clitoris measures 9 mm in transverse diameter.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse terminal hair on chin, upper lip and lower abdomen, temporal hairline recession, clitoral transverse diameter 9 mm, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, no striae or proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 340 mIU/L (less than 500)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for laser hair reduction and reassure her that this pattern is a common familial variation
options.rationale: Idiopathic and familial hirsutism develops gradually, does not cause voice change or clitoromegaly, and is not accompanied by new amenorrhoea. Cosmetic treatment without investigation would leave a potentially serious cause unexamined. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Measure early morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone alone to investigate for non classical adrenal hyperplasia
options.rationale: This measurement is a sensible part of the workup of hirsutism with menstrual disturbance, and non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a genuine cause. It does not on its own address a virilising picture, in which the priority is to identify or exclude a tumour. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Measure total testosterone with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and arrange pelvic and adrenal imaging
options.rationale: Rapid onset hirsutism over months with voice deepening, temporal recession and clitoromegaly is virilisation, which signals a marked androgen excess and raises the possibility of an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour. Measuring testosterone alongside the adrenal androgen indicates the likely source, and imaging of both ovaries and adrenals follows without delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill with an antiandrogenic progestogen and review after six months
options.rationale: This is appropriate treatment for the gradual hirsutism of polycystic ovary syndrome, which develops slowly from adolescence without virilising features. Suppressing symptoms in a woman with rapidly progressive virilisation risks masking a tumour for six months. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

options.text: Arrange an overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the first investigation of the androgen excess
options.rationale: Cortisol excess is suggested by violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, facial rounding and easy bruising, and none of these are present in a woman with a normal body mass index. It is a reasonable later test but not the first line of enquiry for virilisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Hirsutism and virilisation)

explanation.summary: Hirsutism describes excess terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution, and the overwhelming majority of cases are polycystic ovary syndrome or idiopathic, both of which evolve slowly from around puberty. Virilisation is a different clinical category and is defined by deepening of the voice, temporal balding, clitoromegaly, increased muscle bulk and breast atrophy, which together indicate a much higher circulating androgen concentration. Rapid onset over months with virilising features shifts the concern towards an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour, and to ovarian hyperthecosis in postmenopausal women. Investigation is with total testosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate to indicate the source, with early imaging of the ovaries by transvaginal ultrasound and of the adrenals by computed tomography. Cosmetic and hormonal suppressive treatments are correct for the common causes but must not be started before a virilising presentation has been investigated.
key_points: Slow hirsutism from puberty suggests polycystic ovary syndrome or an idiopathic cause
Voice change, temporal recession and clitoromegaly define virilisation
Rapid onset over months raises concern for an androgen secreting tumour
Testosterone with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate indicates ovarian versus adrenal source
Image ovaries and adrenals early rather than starting suppressive treatment
explanation.pearls: A markedly raised dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate points towards an adrenal source while a very high testosterone with a normal adrenal androgen points towards the ovary, and a normal transvaginal ultrasound does not exclude a small androgen secreting ovarian tumour, so persistent virilisation with high testosterone warrants specialist review and consideration of selective venous sampling.

subtopic_detail: Three first trimester losses with a uterine cavity abnormality seen on two dimensional imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 31 year old woman referred after three consecutive first trimester miscarriages, each at around nine weeks with fetal heart activity previously seen.

Her partner is the same for all three pregnancies and she has no living children. Her cycles are regular, she has never had pelvic infection or uterine instrumentation apart from one suction curettage, and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. Two dimensional transvaginal ultrasound reports a possible partition within the uterine cavity, and the sonographer notes that the external uterine contour could not be clearly assessed on that view. Antiphospholipid antibodies measured twelve weeks apart are negative, both parental karyotypes are normal, and her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin are within the reference range.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, no adnexal masses, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant negative, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, parental karyotypes normal, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.1 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Hysterosalpingography to outline the uterine cavity and to confirm that both fallopian tubes are patent
options.rationale: This outlines the cavity and shows tubal patency but is equally unable to demonstrate the external fundal contour, producing the same ambiguity. Tubal patency is also not the question in a woman who conceives readily. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Endometrial biopsy with culture to investigate chronic endometritis as a contributor to the losses
options.rationale: Chronic endometritis is an area of active research in recurrent loss but testing and treating it is not established practice, and it does not explain a structural finding already visible on imaging. The abnormality identified should be characterised first. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Products of conception karyotyping arranged prospectively should a further pregnancy loss occur
options.rationale: Cytogenetic testing of pregnancy tissue is informative and is offered in recurrent loss, but it requires another miscarriage to happen and answers a different question from the one raised by an abnormal cavity. It complements rather than replaces defining the anomaly now. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound to define the cavity outline together with the fundal contour
options.rationale: Distinguishing a septum from a bicornuate uterus depends on the external fundal contour, which two dimensional imaging cannot reliably show, and three dimensional coronal reconstruction visualises the cavity and the serosal outline in a single non invasive test. The distinction is decisive because a septum is treated hysteroscopically while a bicornuate uterus is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy under general anaesthesia to inspect and record the appearance of the cavity
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy shows two horns from the inside whether the cause is a septum or a bicornuate uterus, so it cannot make the distinction alone and would need laparoscopy alongside it. It becomes the operative step once imaging has established that a septum is present. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: A septate uterus is the congenital anomaly most consistently associated with recurrent first trimester loss, because implantation on the poorly vascularised fibrous septum leads to failure once the pregnancy demands greater perfusion. The essential distinction is from a bicornuate uterus, and it rests entirely on the external fundal contour, which is smooth or minimally indented in a septum and deeply cleft in a bicornuate uterus, while the internal view is identical. Two dimensional ultrasound and hysterosalpingography both image only the cavity and therefore cannot separate the two, whereas three dimensional coronal reconstruction shows cavity and serosal outline together and has become the investigation of choice. The distinction matters clinically because hysteroscopic septum resection is a straightforward day procedure associated with improved live birth rates in observational series, whereas a bicornuate uterus is not amenable to that operation. Renal tract anomalies coexist with Mullerian anomalies often enough that renal imaging is arranged when one is confirmed.
key_points: External fundal contour is the only feature separating septate from bicornuate uterus
Two dimensional ultrasound and hysterosalpingography image the cavity alone
Three dimensional coronal reconstruction shows cavity and serosal outline together
Hysteroscopic resection applies to a septum but not to a bicornuate uterus
Arrange renal tract imaging once a Mullerian anomaly is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Arrange renal tract ultrasound whenever a Mullerian anomaly is confirmed, because the paramesonephric and mesonephric systems develop together and unilateral renal agenesis accompanies a meaningful proportion of uterine anomalies, most classically in the obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Bone protection choice in a woman with ovarian failure well before the usual age
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman who stopped menstruating eighteen months ago and has had hot flushes and vaginal dryness since. Follicle stimulating hormone measured twice more than four weeks apart was elevated on both occasions with a low oestradiol.

Her bone density scan shows a lumbar spine Z score of minus 2.3. She has never had a fragility fracture, does not smoke, drinks minimal alcohol and walks daily. She has completed her family and uses condoms. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no history of venous thrombosis, and her blood pressure and lipids are normal. She has read online that hormone therapy causes breast cancer and asks whether she should take a bone medication instead.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 62 IU/L then 58 IU/L more than four weeks apart (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 42 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 74 nmol/L (greater than 50), lumbar spine Z score minus 2.3

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her bone health?

options.text: Weekly oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and repeat densitometry in two years
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half life and are avoided in young women of potentially reproductive age given uncertainty about fetal effects in a later pregnancy. They also leave the vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and cardiovascular consequences of oestrogen deficiency untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Six monthly subcutaneous denosumab with calcium and vitamin D and monitoring of bone turnover markers
options.rationale: Denosumab requires uninterrupted continuation because stopping it produces rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures, a poor commitment for a woman of 34 with decades ahead. It is also directed at the bone alone and does not address the underlying hormone deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation with a resistance exercise programme and repeat scanning in five years
options.rationale: Nutritional and exercise measures are worthwhile adjuncts but cannot compensate for absent oestrogen, and her vitamin D and calcium are already adequate. Deferring definitive treatment for five years allows further bone loss during the years of peak consolidation. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress symptoms and to maintain bone density
options.rationale: Combined contraception is an acceptable alternative when a woman prefers it or needs contraception, but the ethinyloestradiol dose is supraphysiological and it appears less favourable than replacement therapy for bone density and blood pressure. It is second choice rather than first recommendation here. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Systemic oestrogen with a progestogen for endometrial protection, continued until the average age of menopause
options.rationale: Ovarian insufficiency before forty is treated with physiological hormone replacement continued at least until the average age of natural menopause, because these women are oestrogen deficient for decades and face excess fracture and cardiovascular risk without it. In this age group the therapy replaces what her ovaries should be producing and the breast cancer risk seen in older postmenopausal users does not transfer to her situation. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is diagnosed before the age of forty on the basis of amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea with elevated follicle stimulating hormone on two occasions at least four weeks apart. It differs fundamentally from menopause at the usual age because these women face several additional decades of oestrogen deficiency, with consequences for bone density, cardiovascular risk, urogenital health, sexual function and possibly cognition. Hormone therapy is therefore replacement of a physiological deficiency rather than treatment of an age related change, and it is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause unless contraindicated. The breast cancer signal observed in older postmenopausal users does not apply to replacement in this age group, and this reassurance is central to the consultation. Bone specific agents such as bisphosphonates and denosumab are reserved for women who cannot take oestrogen, with bisphosphonate use in young women complicated by the long skeletal half life.
key_points: Diagnosis needs elevated follicle stimulating hormone twice, at least four weeks apart, under forty
Hormone therapy here replaces a deficiency and continues to the average age of menopause
The breast cancer risk of later postmenopausal therapy does not transfer to this group
Bisphosphonates are avoided in young women because of the long skeletal half life
Use the Z score rather than the T score to interpret density in women under fifty
explanation.pearls: Counsel explicitly that hormone therapy is not contraception, because spontaneous ovarian activity returns intermittently in around five to ten percent of women with premature ovarian insufficiency and pregnancies do occur, so a woman who wishes to avoid conception needs a separate reliable method alongside her replacement therapy.

subtopic_detail: Milky nipple discharge with a modestly raised hormone level in a woman on antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman referred with milky discharge from both nipples for four months and periods that have become infrequent, with the last one nine weeks ago.

She has schizophrenia treated with risperidone 4 mg daily for the past year with good symptom control, and takes no other medication. She has no headache, no visual field disturbance and no galactorrhoea on only one side. Her thyroid function is normal and a pregnancy test is negative. Her prolactin measured on a single unstressed morning sample is 2100 mIU/L. She tells you that her mental state has been the most stable it has ever been and that she is fearful of any change to her treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2100 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), urine pregnancy test negative, urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss a change of antipsychotic with her treating psychiatrist and review her prolactin afterwards
