options.rationale: A prolactin in this range with symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia in a woman on a strongly prolactin raising antipsychotic is best explained by the drug, and the diagnostic and therapeutic step is a supervised switch to a prolactin sparing agent such as aripiprazole or quetiapine with the level rechecked afterwards. The change is negotiated with her psychiatrist because relapse risk is the competing harm and she is currently stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa before making any change to her medication
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the level is very high, when there are mass effect symptoms such as headache or visual field loss, or when the elevation persists after the offending drug is changed. Scanning first exposes her to an investigation whose most likely result is a normal gland. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cabergoline at low dose and titrate according to prolactin response with monthly measurements
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists antagonise the very receptor blockade that controls her psychosis and can precipitate relapse, so they are used with great caution and only under specialist supervision in this setting. Changing the causative drug is safer and addresses the mechanism directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Request macroprolactin measurement on the existing sample to identify a biologically inactive complex
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is the right consideration when a raised level is found in a woman with no symptoms, since the complex is biologically inactive. This woman has genuine galactorrhoea and oligomenorrhoea, which indicates that the excess prolactin is biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeding and protect her bone density
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement is a legitimate strategy when the causative drug genuinely cannot be changed, since it protects bone and restores cycles. Offering it first accepts the hyperprolactinaemia and its galactorrhoea rather than removing the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia results from blockade of dopamine receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, and risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin far more than aripiprazole, quetiapine or clozapine. Levels are typically modestly elevated, and the practical rule is that concentrations in the range seen here are compatible with drug effect while much higher values, particularly above about 5000 mIU/L, suggest a prolactinoma and warrant pituitary imaging. The consequences of untreated hyperprolactinaemia are galactorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and, through hypo oestrogenism, reduced bone density over time. Management options are a supervised switch to a prolactin sparing antipsychotic, dose reduction, addition of aripiprazole as a partial agonist, or oestrogen replacement if the drug cannot be changed, with dopamine agonists used only cautiously because they may precipitate psychotic relapse. Every step is taken jointly with the treating psychiatrist because relapse of psychosis is the competing harm.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are the strongest prolactin raising agents
Modest elevations fit drug effect; markedly higher levels suggest a prolactinoma
Symptomatic galactorrhoea and oligomenorrhoea indicate biologically active prolactin
Switch to a prolactin sparing agent is preferred over a dopamine agonist
Untreated hypo oestrogenism carries a long term bone density cost
explanation.pearls: Request macroprolactin testing when a raised prolactin is an incidental finding in a woman with normal cycles and no galactorrhoea, because up to a quarter of such results reflect a biologically inactive immunoglobulin bound complex and reporting it prevents an unnecessary pituitary scan and a needless change of effective antipsychotic treatment.

subtopic_detail: Scant or absent menstruation with cyclical pain following instrumentation of the uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30 year old woman whose periods have become barely a smear on a pad since she had a suction curettage for retained products of conception seven months ago, complicated by endometritis treated with antibiotics.

Before that pregnancy her periods were heavy and lasted five days. She now has cramping lower abdominal pain each month at the time she expects to bleed, but almost nothing appears. She has been trying to conceive for four months without success. A pregnancy test is negative, her follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol are consistent with normal ovarian function, prolactin and thyroid function are normal, and transvaginal ultrasound reports a thin irregular endometrial echo with some bright linear areas within the cavity.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, mild suprapubic tenderness, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 310 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), transvaginal ultrasound showing a thin irregular endometrial echo with bright linear intracavity areas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation given four months of trying to conceive without success
options.rationale: Assisted reproduction cannot succeed while the cavity is obstructed by adhesion, since an embryo requires receptive endometrium to implant. The structural problem is corrected first, and four months of trying would not by itself meet the usual threshold for referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis and a strategy to prevent adhesions reforming
options.rationale: Loss of menstrual flow with cyclical pain after uterine instrumentation complicated by infection, alongside normal ovarian hormones and a thin irregular cavity echo, indicates intrauterine adhesions, and hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment. Division under direct vision is combined with a measure to keep the walls apart afterwards, because reformation is the principal problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Prescribe a three month course of cyclical oestrogen and progestogen and reassess her bleeding pattern
options.rationale: Cyclical hormones cannot generate bleeding from endometrium that has been replaced by fibrous adhesion, and her own oestradiol is already in the normal range. Oestrogen has a role after adhesiolysis to encourage re epithelialisation rather than as a stand alone treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Arrange repeat pelvic ultrasound in the luteal phase to reassess the thickness of the endometrium
options.rationale: Repeating the same test in a different phase adds little when the cavity already appears irregular with bright intracavity areas and the clinical picture is characteristic. Saline infusion sonohysterography would add more than a plain repeat, but hysteroscopy remains the definitive assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Commence a further course of doxycycline and metronidazole to treat persisting chronic endometritis
options.rationale: The infection was treated seven months ago and there is no fever, discharge or cervical excitation to suggest active infection now. Repeat antibiotics do not reverse fibrous adhesion that has already formed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Intrauterine adhesions form when the basal endometrium is damaged, most often by curettage performed on a recently pregnant uterus and particularly when infection complicates the procedure. The clinical hallmark is a change in menstrual pattern to scant flow or amenorrhoea, frequently with cyclical pain as retained blood cannot escape, together with subfertility and recurrent pregnancy loss. Ovarian function is normal, which is why gonadotrophins, oestradiol, prolactin and thyroid function are unremarkable and why cyclical hormone therapy alone fails to restore bleeding. Ultrasound may show a thin or irregular endometrial echo with bright intracavity areas, and saline infusion sonohysterography improves detection, but hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the treatment. Adhesiolysis is combined with a strategy to prevent reformation and with postoperative oestrogen to promote re epithelialisation, and a second look procedure is often planned because recurrence is common in severe disease.
key_points: Curettage on a recently pregnant uterus, especially with infection, is the classic antecedent
Scant flow or amenorrhoea with cyclical pain and normal ovarian hormones is the pattern
Cyclical hormones alone cannot produce bleeding from adhesion replaced endometrium
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the definitive treatment
Adhesion reformation is the main problem, so prevention and second look are planned
explanation.pearls: Prefer medical management or ultrasound guided gentle evacuation over sharp curettage for retained products where the clinical situation allows, because the single most effective way to treat intrauterine adhesions is to avoid creating them, and the risk rises sharply with repeated instrumentation and with concurrent endometritis.

subtopic_detail: Diffusely enlarged tender uterus with heavy painful bleeding in a woman wanting to conceive
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over four years, now soaking through protection hourly on the worst two days. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eight months.

She describes deep pelvic pressure and pain that begins several days before bleeding starts and continues throughout. On bimanual examination the uterus is diffusely enlarged to about the size of a ten week pregnancy, globular, softer than expected and tender to palpation, with no separate palpable lump and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports asymmetrical myometrial thickening with the posterior wall measuring twice the anterior wall, small myometrial cysts and indistinct borders between the endometrium and the myometrium, and no discrete mass with a surrounding rim.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Globular tender uterus enlarged to approximately ten week size, no discrete mass, no rectovaginal nodularity, cervix normal, adnexae free
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), transvaginal ultrasound showing asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and an indistinct endometrial myometrial junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange endometrial ablation to destroy the endometrium and to reduce the volume of menstrual loss
options.rationale: Ablation is contraindicated for any woman who may wish to conceive, and it also performs poorly in adenomyosis because the disease lies deep within the myometrium beyond the reach of the treatment. Pregnancy after ablation carries serious complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months with add back hormone therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression shrinks adenomyotic tissue and controls symptoms effectively but induces a temporary menopause and prevents conception throughout, which is unacceptable to a woman of 38 with declining fertility. It is used before surgery or when other options have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Treat the iron deficiency and offer a non hormonal option for bleeding and pain while she conceives
options.rationale: The ultrasound and examination findings describe adenomyosis, and every hormonal treatment for it works by suppressing ovulation or the endometrium, which is incompatible with her wish to conceive now. Iron replacement corrects the anaemia driving her fatigue, and tranexamic acid with a non steroidal anti inflammatory taken during menstruation reduces both loss and pain without preventing conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device as the most effective treatment for her bleeding and pain
options.rationale: This device is genuinely the most effective medical treatment for the bleeding and pain of adenomyosis, but it is a contraceptive and would prevent the pregnancy she is actively seeking. It becomes the treatment of choice once her family is complete. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce the uterine volume and to control the heavy bleeding
options.rationale: Embolisation reduces bleeding but carries a risk of diminished ovarian reserve and adverse effects on subsequent pregnancy, so it is not offered to a woman actively seeking conception. It is considered for women who have completed childbearing and wish to avoid hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium and typically presents in the later reproductive years with progressive heavy bleeding, dysmenorrhoea that starts before the flow, and pelvic pressure. Examination shows a diffusely enlarged globular tender uterus, in contrast to the firm irregular asymmetrically enlarged uterus of fibroids, and the ultrasound features are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, echogenic subendometrial lines and an indistinct junctional zone without the discrete mass and pseudocapsule of a fibroid. The therapeutic difficulty is that the most effective treatments all suppress ovulation or the endometrium and are therefore unusable in a woman trying to conceive. In that situation the practical plan is to correct iron deficiency and to use tranexamic acid with a non steroidal anti inflammatory during menstruation, both of which reduce loss and pain without preventing conception. Adenomyosis itself is associated with reduced implantation and increased miscarriage, so referral for fertility assessment is reasonable if conception does not occur.
key_points: Globular tender uterus with pain preceding the flow suggests adenomyosis over fibroids
Ultrasound shows asymmetrical thickening and myometrial cysts without a discrete mass
The levonorgestrel device is the most effective medical treatment but is contraceptive
Ablation and embolisation are unsuitable for women seeking future pregnancy
Tranexamic acid and a non steroidal anti inflammatory reduce loss without blocking conception
explanation.pearls: Treat the ferritin of 8 micrograms per litre as a diagnosis in its own right rather than a footnote to the bleeding, because iron deficiency at this level causes fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance well before the haemoglobin falls far, and an intravenous infusion restores stores in a single visit when oral iron is poorly tolerated or when conception is being actively sought.

subtopic_detail: Burning pain reproduced by light touch at the vestibule with normal vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 24 year old woman with two years of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever anything touches it, including tampons, tight jeans and intercourse. She says the pain begins the instant there is contact and lasts for hours afterwards.

She has been treated with four courses of topical and oral antifungals over the past year, each prescribed for presumed thrush, without any benefit. She has no discharge, no itch and no odour. On examination the vulval skin is entirely normal with no erythema, no fissuring, no pallor, no loss of architecture and no lesions. Light contact with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain sharply and reproducibly, while the same touch on the labia majora and the inner thigh causes nothing. A high vaginal swab and culture taken last month were negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture and colour, no fissures, erosions or lesions, cotton bud testing sharply positive at the posterior vestibule and negative on labia majora and thigh, pelvic floor muscles tender and hypertonic on gentle digital assessment
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab with fungal culture negative, no other tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform a vulval punch biopsy of the vestibule to establish the histological diagnosis before treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated when the skin looks abnormal, when a dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus or lichen planus is suspected, or when malignancy must be excluded. Normal skin with a purely sensory abnormality yields nothing on histology and adds a painful procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Refer for vestibulectomy to excise the painful tissue as the definitive surgical treatment of her pain
options.rationale: Vestibulectomy has reasonable success rates but is reserved for women with localised provoked pain who have failed conservative treatment including physiotherapy and medical therapy. Operating before those measures have been tried is not justified in a woman of 24. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment nightly for three months to settle vulval inflammation
options.rationale: Potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for an inflammatory vulval dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus, recognised by pallor, fissuring and loss of architecture. Prolonged application to normal skin causes atrophy without treating a neuropathic pain process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop all antifungal treatment and refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy with psychosexual support alongside
options.rationale: Reproducible burning provoked by light touch confined to the vestibule with entirely normal skin is localised provoked vulvodynia, a pain disorder rather than an infection, and repeated antifungals maintain an irritant contact dermatitis that worsens it. Pelvic floor physiotherapy addressing the associated muscle hypertonicity, combined with psychological and sexual therapy, has the strongest evidence base in this condition. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Prescribe a six month course of weekly oral fluconazole for chronic recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is appropriate for culture confirmed recurrent candidiasis, which presents with itch and discharge and responds at least partially to treatment. Negative cultures and four failed courses point away from a fungal cause entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable cause on examination, and the commonest form is localised provoked pain at the vestibule, in which light touch produces sharp burning that outlasts the stimulus. The cotton bud test is the central examination finding, reproducing pain at the vestibule while adjacent skin is unaffected, and the skin itself must be normal for the diagnosis to be made. Coexisting pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity is very common and is a major contributor to the pain cycle. The most frequent clinical error is repeated empirical antifungal treatment, which not only fails but produces an irritant dermatitis that amplifies the symptom. Management is multimodal, with pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy as the core, topical local anaesthetic and vulval care measures as adjuncts, neuromodulator medication for some, and vestibulectomy reserved for refractory localised disease.
key_points: Normal skin with reproducible vestibular pain on cotton bud testing defines the condition
Repeated empirical antifungals fail and cause irritant dermatitis that worsens pain
Pelvic floor hypertonicity is a common and treatable contributor
Physiotherapy with psychosexual therapy has the strongest evidence base
Biopsy and surgery are for abnormal skin and for refractory disease respectively
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the pain is provoked only by contact or is also present unprovoked while sitting or resting, because unprovoked generalised vulvodynia responds better to neuromodulator medication such as amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid, while the provoked localised form responds best to physiotherapy and local measures, and the two are frequently managed as if they were one condition.

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe unilateral pain in early pregnancy after ovarian stimulation with enlarged ovaries
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department at 2 am to see a 32 year old woman at 6 weeks gestation after a single embryo transfer, her fourth cycle of treatment and her first pregnancy.

She woke four hours ago with sudden severe right sided pain that comes in waves, and has vomited five times. She was reviewed three days ago for abdominal distension and was told her ovaries were enlarged from the stimulation. Transvaginal ultrasound now shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a fetal pole and cardiac activity, a right ovary measuring 82 mm with multiple peripherally displaced follicles and stromal oedema, a left ovary measuring 74 mm, moderate free fluid, and preserved arterial flow with absent venous flow in the right ovary. Her haemoglobin is 158 g/L with a haematocrit of 0.48 and her albumin is 29 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, severe right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, cervix closed, no vaginal bleeding, urine output 20 mL in the last two hours
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 158 g/L (115-155), haematocrit 0.48 (0.35-0.45), white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), transvaginal ultrasound showing viable intrauterine pregnancy, right ovary 82 mm with peripheral follicles and stromal oedema, absent venous flow with preserved arterial flow on the right, moderate ascites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid, analgesia and serial review, deferring surgery while the pregnancy is early
options.rationale: Conservative management is correct for the pain of hyperstimulation without torsion, but a twisted ovary infarcts within hours and delay converts a salvageable organ into a necrotic one. Early pregnancy is not a reason to withhold laparoscopy, which is safe in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy and perform right salpingo oophorectomy because a torted ovary is not salvageable
options.rationale: Removing the adnexa was historical practice based on fear of releasing thromboembolism, which evidence has not supported, and function recovers in most ovaries that look black at the time of untwisting. Oophorectomy in a woman with a hard won pregnancy and possible future cycles destroys reserve unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Perform ultrasound guided paracentesis of the ascites to relieve pressure and improve her urine output
options.rationale: Drainage of ascites genuinely relieves severe hyperstimulation and improves renal perfusion and respiratory function, and she will likely need it. It does nothing for a twisted pedicle and treating only the hyperstimulation would leave the torsion to progress to infarction. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before operative treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is safe in pregnancy and can demonstrate torsion, but arranging it overnight introduces a delay of hours in a time critical ischaemic process. The diagnosis here is clinical and the operation is both confirmatory and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Resuscitate with intravenous fluid and proceed to laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary
options.rationale: Absent venous flow with preserved arterial flow in a massively enlarged stimulated ovary alongside sudden severe pain and vomiting is torsion, and preserved arterial signal never excludes it because the dual blood supply and the sequence of venous then arterial occlusion make Doppler unreliable. Untwisting rather than removing the adnexa preserves ovarian function and is safe even when the ovary looks dusky, while the intravascular depletion from hyperstimulation is corrected before and during anaesthesia. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and ovarian torsion are linked because stimulated ovaries become heavy and mobile, and torsion complicates a meaningful minority of moderate to severe cases, with the risk rising further once pregnancy occurs and human chorionic gonadotrophin sustains the enlargement. The diagnostic trap is Doppler: the ovary has a dual arterial supply and venous flow is lost before arterial flow, so preserved arterial signal is common in confirmed torsion and must never be used to exclude it. This patient simultaneously has severe hyperstimulation, evidenced by haemoconcentration, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites, oliguria and rising creatinine, which raises anaesthetic and thromboembolic risk and requires fluid resuscitation and thromboprophylaxis planning around the operation rather than instead of it. Management is prompt laparoscopic detorsion with conservation, since even a black ovary recovers function in the great majority and oophorectomy is rarely justified. Ongoing care includes continued management of the hyperstimulation, which will persist and may worsen for days as the pregnancy advances.
key_points: Preserved arterial Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion
Pregnancy after assisted reproduction prolongs and worsens hyperstimulation
Haemoconcentration, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites and oliguria mark severe hyperstimulation
Detorsion with conservation is preferred; a dusky ovary usually recovers function
Resuscitate and plan thromboprophylaxis around the operation rather than delaying it
explanation.pearls: Prescribe thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin and graduated compression around the operation, because severe hyperstimulation combines haemoconcentration, immobility, pregnancy and an operative insult, and the thrombotic events that characterise this syndrome occur in unusual sites such as the internal jugular and subclavian veins and can present weeks after the ovaries have settled.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose for a sensitising event falling just beyond the twelve week threshold
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 13 weeks and 2 days. She reports fresh vaginal bleeding that soaked one pad over the past four hours, with no pain and no tissue passed.

Her booking bloods show blood group O RhD negative with a negative red cell antibody screen. A bedside ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity and a crown rump length consistent with dates, and no retroplacental clot. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination with a small amount of blood in the vault. She has had no previous pregnancy and has never received a blood transfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus non tender, cervix closed, small volume fresh blood in the posterior fornix
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), ultrasound showing a viable single intrauterine pregnancy at 13 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and rely on the routine prophylactic dose scheduled at twenty eight weeks
options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks covers silent foetomaternal transfusion, but it does not retrospectively cover a recognised sensitising event fifteen weeks earlier. Event based and routine prophylaxis are additive, not alternatives. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 250 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
options.rationale: The 250 international unit dose covers sensitising events before 12 completed weeks, such as miscarriage, termination or ectopic pregnancy managed in the first trimester. At 13 weeks that dose may be insufficient for the foetomaternal bleed possible at this placental mass. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and repeat the red cell antibody screen in four weeks to look for sensitisation
options.rationale: Waiting to detect anti-D antibodies means waiting for the sensitisation that prophylaxis exists to prevent, and once alloimmunisation occurs it cannot be reversed for this or any future pregnancy. Antibody screening is surveillance, not prophylaxis. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)

options.text: Give 625 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
options.rationale: Vaginal bleeding after 12 weeks is a sensitising event, and the Australian dose changes at that gestation because the volume of fetal red cells in the circulation rises with placental mass. From 12 weeks onward the dose is 625 international units, given as soon as possible and within seventy two hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Perform a Kleihauer test first and give anti-D immunoglobulin only if a fetal bleed is quantified
options.rationale: Quantification of foetomaternal haemorrhage is used from 20 weeks to decide whether additional doses beyond the standard one are needed, not to decide whether to treat at all. Delaying the dose while awaiting the result risks breaching the seventy two hour window. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)

explanation.summary: RhD negative women who have not already formed anti-D antibodies need immunoglobulin after any potentially sensitising event so that fetal red cells entering the maternal circulation are cleared before an immune response develops. The Australian dose is gestation dependent: 250 international units before 12 completed weeks and 625 international units from 12 weeks onward, reflecting the larger possible foetomaternal bleed as the placenta grows. The dose should be given within seventy two hours, and giving it late is better than not giving it at all. Kleihauer or flow cytometry quantification is added from 20 weeks to identify the minority of women who need more than one dose. Event based prophylaxis does not replace the routine doses at 28 and 34 weeks.
key_points: Sensitising events before 12 completed weeks attract 250 international units
From 12 weeks onward the dose is 625 international units
Give within seventy two hours of the event, and still give it if late
Quantify foetomaternal haemorrhage from 20 weeks to detect the need for extra doses
Event based doses are additional to routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Check the antibody screen result before ordering anti-D, because a woman who already has immune anti-D gains nothing from prophylaxis and instead needs referral for titres and middle cerebral artery Doppler surveillance; passively acquired anti-D from a dose given within the last twelve weeks usually titres at 4 or less and should not be mistaken for immune sensitisation.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose reassessment after insulin treated gestational diabetes once the baby is born
stem:
You are the obstetric resident doing a day two postnatal round on a 33 year old woman who had a normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks and required isophane insulin at night from 31 weeks for fasting readings above target.

Her insulin was ceased after birth and her capillary glucose readings since delivery have all been between 4.4 and 6.1 mmol/L while eating normally. She is breastfeeding without difficulty and the baby's blood glucose screening was normal. She asks what happens next with her diabetes and whether she should stay on a monitor at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.4 to 6.1 mmol/L off insulin, booking body mass index 29 kg/m2, antenatal 75 g oral glucose tolerance test fasting 5.4 mmol/L and two hour 9.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for reassessing her glucose tolerance?

options.text: Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test before discharge from hospital, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Testing in the first days after birth measures a rapidly changing physiological state as placental hormones fall, so results neither confirm nor exclude persisting diabetes. The reclassification window deliberately waits for that transition to finish. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a fasting venous glucose level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: A fasting sample alone is the least sensitive option after gestational diabetes, because post load hyperglycaemia commonly persists while fasting values normalise. Using it as the reclassification test underdiagnoses impaired glucose tolerance. (Source: RACGP: Management of type 2 diabetes)

options.text: Continue home capillary glucose monitoring for six weeks and arrange further testing only if readings exceed target
options.rationale: Self monitoring after birth is not a diagnostic pathway and produces scattered postprandial values that cannot be mapped onto diagnostic thresholds. Women whose home readings look acceptable still turn out to have impaired glucose tolerance on formal testing. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a glycated haemoglobin level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin reflects the preceding two to three months, which in this window still includes the pregnancy itself and is further distorted by delivery related blood loss and red cell turnover. It is a reasonable interval test later, not the reclassification test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Postnatal reclassification uses a full oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks, once the insulin resistance of pregnancy has resolved, because a proportion of women have persistent diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance that fasting testing alone misses. Lifelong periodic screening follows because the risk of type 2 diabetes remains elevated. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes identifies a woman whose pancreatic reserve was unable to meet the insulin resistance of late pregnancy, and roughly half go on to develop type 2 diabetes within a decade. Insulin is stopped at delivery because that resistance disappears with the placenta, but the underlying tendency does not. The Australian pathway is a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum, which is early enough that women are still engaged with maternity services and late enough that the physiology has settled. Women who test normal then need repeat screening every one to three years, and sooner if they are planning another pregnancy. Needing insulin antenatally, as here, marks a higher risk group in whom the follow up test is most often abnormal.
key_points: Stop insulin at delivery; the insulin resistance of pregnancy resolves with the placenta
Reclassify with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin are less sensitive in this window
Repeat screening every one to three years lifelong after a normal result
Test before any subsequent pregnancy, not just at the next booking visit
explanation.pearls: Write the six to twelve week oral glucose tolerance test request before she leaves the ward and copy it to her general practitioner, because completion rates in Australia sit near half and the commonest reason given is that nobody handed over the test; a woman who needed insulin antenatally has roughly a one in five chance of an abnormal result at that first visit.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

subtopic_detail: Referral pathway when a self collected screening sample returns the higher risk oncogenic genotypes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing results for a 41 year old woman who has never attended for cervical screening and who chose a self collected vaginal sample at her last visit. She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she has two children born vaginally.

Her sample returns positive for human papillomavirus type 16. The laboratory comment notes that liquid based cytology was not performed on this specimen. She is not pregnant, her last menstrual period was two weeks ago, and she has no immunosuppression and no history of a previous abnormal result.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdominal examination normal, no speculum examination performed at the screening visit
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal sample positive for oncogenic human papillomavirus type 16, no cytology performed on the specimen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and refer for colposcopy if the same genotype persists
options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to intermediate risk results, meaning oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 with negative or low grade cytology. Applying it to type 16 leaves prevalent high grade disease untreated for a year. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Refer her directly for colposcopy at this visit, without taking any further sample beforehand
options.rationale: Detection of type 16 or 18 carries a high enough risk of high grade disease that referral is immediate regardless of cytology, and a self collected sample cannot be used for cytology because it does not sample the transformation zone. Adding a clinician collected test first only delays the colposcopy that is already indicated. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the genotype before making any referral for colposcopy
options.rationale: Self collected polymerase chain reaction testing performs equivalently to clinician collection for detecting oncogenic human papillomavirus, so a confirmatory repeat adds no information. Treating the first positive as provisional is a common reason these women are lost to follow up. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Take a clinician collected sample for cytology and refer for colposcopy only if it shows a high grade change
options.rationale: This is the pathway for oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 found on a self collected sample, where cytology triages who needs colposcopy. With type 16 the referral threshold is already met and cytology cannot lower it. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and rescreen in five years in line with the routine interval
options.rationale: Vaccination does not clear an established infection or treat existing disease, and returning her to the routine interval ignores a result that already meets the referral threshold. Vaccination is a separate conversation after the colposcopy pathway is under way. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Human papillomavirus)

explanation.summary: The renewed Australian program screens primarily for oncogenic human papillomavirus, with management determined by genotype and, where available, reflex cytology. Types 16 and 18 account for most cervical cancer and carry a substantially higher immediate risk of high grade disease than the other oncogenic types, so their detection means direct colposcopy referral whatever the cytology shows. Self collection was extended to all screening participants to reach under screened and never screened women, who make up the majority of cervical cancer cases in Australia. A self collected vaginal sample is valid for the human papillomavirus test but cannot yield useful cytology, which is why type 16 or 18 on such a sample goes straight to colposcopy while other oncogenic types require a clinician collected sample for triage.
key_points: Types 16 and 18 trigger direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types on a self collected sample need clinician collected cytology to triage
Self collection is not valid for cytology because it misses the transformation zone
Never screened and under screened women account for most cervical cancers in Australia
Vaccination does not alter management of an existing positive result
explanation.pearls: When a never screened woman accepts self collection, book the colposcopy or the follow up sample during the same consultation rather than waiting for the result to arrive, because the group most likely to accept self collection is also the group most likely to be lost between a positive result and the referral that follows it.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choice of latency antibiotic after membranes rupture in the early third trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 30 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid two hours ago followed by continuing dampness, and she has no contractions and no bleeding.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix. Her temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius, the uterus is soft and non tender, and cardiotocography shows a baseline of 145 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations. Her low vaginal swab from 28 weeks grew no group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. The first dose of betamethasone has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Clear liquor pooling in the posterior fornix, cervix closed and uneffaced, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), low vaginal swab at 28 weeks negative for group B streptococcus

lead_in: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral erythromycin given for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs the interval to delivery, reduces neonatal infection and reduces the need for surfactant without the bowel injury seen with clavulanate containing regimens. Ten days, or until labour begins if sooner, is the standard course. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin in labour only, with no antibiotic while she remains undelivered
options.rationale: Intrapartum penicillin addresses group B streptococcal transmission at birth but does nothing for the ascending infection that shortens latency after membranes rupture. It is given in addition to the latency course when labour starts, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: No antibiotic now, with cultures repeated in forty eight hours and treatment if they are positive
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics forfeits a proven reduction in neonatal morbidity, and surveillance cultures identify colonisation rather than the subclinical chorioamnionitis that drives preterm labour here. The benefit of the latency course does not depend on a positive culture. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Oral metronidazole given for seven days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and bacterial vaginosis organisms but has not been shown to prolong latency or improve neonatal outcomes in this setting. It is not part of the standard regimen when membranes rupture preterm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: This combination prolonged latency but was associated with a significantly higher rate of necrotising enterocolitis in the neonates, which is why it is specifically avoided in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. The harm outweighed the latency benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes precedes about a third of preterm births and exposes the foetus to ascending infection from the moment the barrier is lost. Antibiotics given for latency prolong the interval to delivery, reduce chorioamnionitis and reduce neonatal infection and surfactant requirement. Erythromycin is the agent of choice because the large randomised comparison found amoxicillin with clavulanic acid raised necrotising enterocolitis rates despite similar latency benefit. The course runs ten days or until labour establishes. Corticosteroids are given for lung maturity, magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection if birth before 30 weeks is imminent, and surveillance for chorioamnionitis by maternal observations, fetal heart rate and inflammatory markers continues throughout.
key_points: Erythromycin for ten days or until labour is the latency antibiotic of choice
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Intrapartum group B streptococcal prophylaxis is additional, not a substitute
Corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 30 weeks
Monitor for chorioamnionitis with observations, cardiotocography and inflammatory markers
explanation.pearls: A rising baseline fetal heart rate is often the earliest sign of chorioamnionitis and precedes maternal fever, so a baseline that has climbed from 145 to above 160 beats per minute between daily traces should prompt review for delivery even when the temperature and C reactive protein are still normal.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Choosing emergency contraception at day five when body weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who had unprotected intercourse five days ago, on day 11 of a regular 28 day cycle. She has taken no contraception for the past year and does not wish to be pregnant.

She weighs 96 kg with a body mass index of 34 kg/m2. She has no pelvic pain, no abnormal discharge and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, and a urine pregnancy test today is negative. She tells you she would like reliable ongoing contraception as well, and she is willing to consider any option including a procedure today.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, body mass index 34 kg/m2, last menstrual period eleven days ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
options.rationale: The hormonal device does not reliably prevent implantation after intercourse has already occurred, so it is not an emergency method despite being excellent ongoing contraception. It can be placed once this cycle is shown not to be a pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
options.rationale: The copper device remains effective up to five days after intercourse, is far more effective than any oral option, and its performance is unaffected by body weight. It also provides the ongoing contraception she is asking for, and swabs are taken at insertion rather than waiting for results. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A single oral dose of levonorgestrel today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only to seventy two hours and its efficacy declines above about 70 kg, so at five days and at this weight it offers little protection. Doubling the dose is sometimes used but the evidence for that practice is weak. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: No emergency contraception because five days have elapsed, with a pregnancy test arranged in three weeks
options.rationale: Day five is within the window for the copper device, and intercourse on cycle day 11 sits squarely in the fertile period so the risk is real. Declining to act converts a preventable exposure into a wait and see. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A single oral dose of ulipristal acetate today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit
options.rationale: Ulipristal is licensed to five days and outperforms levonorgestrel, but its efficacy falls with increasing body weight and it is substantially less effective than a copper device at this point in the cycle. It also delays rather than provides ongoing contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception choice turns on three variables: time since intercourse, where the woman is in her cycle, and her body weight. The copper intrauterine device is the most effective option by a wide margin, with a failure rate below one in a thousand, and it works up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation. Oral methods act by delaying ovulation, so they fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, and both levonorgestrel and ulipristal lose efficacy as body weight rises. Ulipristal is licensed to five days and levonorgestrel to three. A woman who accepts a device gains both the emergency effect and long acting contraception in a single visit, which is why it is offered first rather than mentioned as an alternative.
key_points: Copper device is effective to five days and is unaffected by body weight
Levonorgestrel is licensed to seventy two hours and weakens above about 70 kg
Ulipristal is licensed to five days but efficacy also falls with rising weight
Oral methods work by delaying ovulation and fail once the surge has started
The hormonal intrauterine device is not an emergency method
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal blocks progesterone receptors, so starting a progestogen contraceptive within five days of taking it reduces its effect and can also reduce the contraceptive cover of the pill being started; if a woman takes ulipristal and wants to begin an oral contraceptive, wait five days and use condoms in between.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

subtopic_detail: Sudden urge with leakage on the way to the toilet and three voids a night in a woman of sixty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old retired teacher with twelve months of a sudden desperate need to pass urine, with leakage before she reaches the toilet about three times a week. She gets up three times a night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and she has no sensation of anything coming down. She had two vaginal births in her thirties. She drinks six cups of tea and two cans of diet cola a day and takes no diuretic. Her last period was eleven years ago and she uses no hormone therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, pale thin vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae, no descent of the anterior or posterior wall beyond the hymen on straining, no leak demonstrated on cough, voluntary pelvic floor contraction present but weak
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes, blood and glucose, post void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, glycated haemoglobin 38 mmol/mol, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before starting any treatment for these symptoms
options.rationale: Urodynamic testing is reserved for symptoms that fail conservative treatment, for mixed or unclear patterns, and before surgery for stress incontinence, because in a clear storage pattern with a negative dipstick and a normal residual it does not change the first line plan. It also carries cost, discomfort and a risk of infection. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic treatment is second line after behavioural measures, and oxybutynin in particular is the agent most associated with dry mouth, constipation and cognitive impairment in older women, with accumulating evidence linking long term anticholinergic load to dementia. If a drug is needed later, a more selective agent or a beta 3 agonist is preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for a midurethral sling procedure and review her six weeks afterwards
options.rationale: A sling treats leakage on effort by supporting the urethra, and she has none: no leak on coughing, sneezing or lifting, and none demonstrable on examination. Operating on the wrong mechanism can worsen urgency and cause voiding difficulty. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start mirabegron 25 mg daily and review her symptoms in three months time
options.rationale: A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a good second line choice in this age group, but drug treatment still follows a proper trial of behavioural measures because roughly half of women improve substantially without any medication. Blood pressure also needs monitoring on this agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology)

options.text: Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises
options.rationale: Urgency with urge leakage and nocturia, with no stress component, no prolapse, a negative dipstick and a normal residual, is an overactive bladder, and first line treatment is behavioural: a bladder diary, timed voiding with progressively lengthened intervals, reduction of caffeine and of evening fluids, weight loss, and supervised pelvic floor muscle training which suppresses detrusor contractions as well as supporting the urethra. Eight cups of caffeinated drinks a day is a directly modifiable contributor. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence in women is separated first into stress, urgency and mixed patterns, because the treatments diverge completely: stress incontinence responds to pelvic floor training and, if that fails, to a continence procedure, while urgency incontinence responds to bladder retraining and then to drug treatment. The initial assessment needs only a history, a bladder diary, an examination for prolapse and pelvic floor function, a urine dipstick to exclude infection, haematuria and glycosuria, and a post void residual. Behavioural treatment achieves substantial improvement in around half of women with an overactive bladder and carries no adverse effects, so it precedes any prescription. When drug treatment is needed, antimuscarinics and beta 3 agonists are roughly equivalent in efficacy, and the choice turns on adverse effects, with anticholinergic load a genuine concern in older women. Vaginal oestrogen is a useful adjunct where there is urogenital atrophy, and refractory cases proceed to specialist options including intravesical botulinum toxin and sacral neuromodulation.
key_points: Separate stress from urgency first because the treatments diverge completely
Dipstick, bladder diary, prolapse assessment and post void residual are the initial workup
Behavioural treatment helps around half of women and precedes any drug
Oxybutynin carries the highest anticholinergic burden and is a poor choice in older women
Urodynamics is for treatment failure, unclear patterns or before continence surgery
explanation.pearls: Topical vaginal oestrogen is worth adding here alongside the bladder training: atrophic changes of the urethra and trigone contribute to urgency and frequency after menopause, and low dose vaginal preparations produce negligible systemic absorption, so they are usable even in women for whom systemic hormone therapy is not appropriate.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Coarse facial and chest hair developing gradually over two years with testosterone 3.2 at twenty four
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old retail manager who has been shaving her chin and upper lip daily for the past year and has noticed coarse dark hairs appearing between her breasts. The change has come on gradually over about two years.

Her periods come every forty to sixty days and have done so since she was sixteen. Her voice has not changed, she has no increase in muscle bulk and she has not noticed any change in her external genitalia or thinning at her temples. She is not trying to conceive, uses condoms, and has no personal or family history of migraine, thrombosis or breast cancer. She does not smoke.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, coarse terminal hair over the chin, upper lip, periareolar area and linea alba, no clitoromegaly, no temporal recession, no abdominal or pelvic mass, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 3.2 nmol/L (0.3-1.8), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate within normal limits, early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits, prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), pelvic ultrasound shows multifollicular ovaries with normal volume and no adnexal mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for the hair growth?

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and review her hair growth in six months
options.rationale: Metformin improves insulin resistance, menstrual regularity and ovulation in this condition and has a place, but its effect on hair growth is minimal and it is not recommended as treatment for hirsutism. It would be the right choice if the target were cycle regulation or metabolic risk. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Start spironolactone 100 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months
options.rationale: Androgen receptor blockade is effective and is added after six months if the first line treatment has not achieved enough, but used alone in a woman of reproductive age it requires reliable contraception because of the risk of undervirilisation of a male foetus. The sequence, not the drug, is what is wrong here. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Refer for computed tomography of the adrenal glands and pelvic ultrasound
options.rationale: Imaging for an androgen secreting tumour is warranted with rapid onset over months, virilisation such as clitoromegaly, deepening voice or temporal balding, or a testosterone above about 5 nmol/L, and none of those apply to a gradual two year history with a modest elevation. Her pelvic ultrasound has already been done and shows no mass. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive and review the hair at six months
options.rationale: Gradual hirsutism with oligomenorrhoea since adolescence, a modestly raised testosterone, normal adrenal androgens and normal 17 hydroxyprogesterone is polycystic ovary syndrome, and combined hormonal contraception is first line for the hair because it suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone binding globulin. Six months is the minimum interval for assessing response because the hair growth cycle takes that long to turn over. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Start finasteride 5 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months time
options.rationale: Five alpha reductase inhibitors have some efficacy for hirsutism but are not approved for this use in women, carry the same teratogenic risk to a male foetus as other antiandrogens, and are not recommended ahead of the established options. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Hirsutism means coarse terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution and is quantified with the modified Ferriman Gallwey score, with a threshold around four to six in most populations. The critical triage is between the common causes, overwhelmingly polycystic ovary syndrome and idiopathic hirsutism, and the rare serious ones: an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour, non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome. Red flags for a tumour are rapid progression over months rather than years, frank virilisation with clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice or temporal balding, onset well after adolescence, and a total testosterone above roughly 5 nmol/L or twice the upper limit of normal. Non-classical adrenal hyperplasia is screened for with an early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase. Treatment of the hair itself is combined hormonal contraception first, with an antiandrogen added after six months if the response is insufficient, alongside mechanical or laser hair removal, and any assessment of response requires at least six months because of the length of the hair growth cycle.
key_points: Rapid onset, virilisation or testosterone above about 5 nmol/L suggests a tumour
Early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone screens for non-classical adrenal hyperplasia
Combined hormonal contraception is first line for hirsutism in polycystic ovary syndrome
Antiandrogens are added after six months and require reliable contraception
Assess response no earlier than six months because of the hair growth cycle
explanation.pearls: Warn her that the contraceptive will stop new terminal hairs developing but will not remove the ones already there, since existing terminal hair does not revert to fine vellus hair, which is why laser or electrolysis is offered alongside rather than after the hormonal treatment and why unrealistic expectations are the usual reason women abandon it at three months.

sources.label: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic positive chlamydia nucleic acid test on routine antenatal screening at twelve weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 24 year old woman in her first pregnancy at twelve weeks and two days. Her booking investigations included a self collected vaginal swab, which has returned positive for Chlamydia trachomatis on nucleic acid amplification testing.

She has no discharge, no pelvic pain, no bleeding and no urinary symptoms. Testing for gonorrhoea on the same swab was negative, and her syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology were all non-reactive. She has had one regular partner for eighteen months and reports no other partners in that time. She has no drug allergies and is taking only pregnancy multivitamins.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, abdomen non-tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology non-reactive, haemoglobin 122 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), midstream urine shows no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days with a test of cure in four weeks
options.rationale: A seven day tetracycline course is the preferred regimen outside pregnancy because it has higher cure rates, particularly for rectal infection, but tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy because of deposition in developing teeth and bone. The duration is not the issue; the class is. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose with a test of cure in four weeks
options.rationale: A single dose macrolide is the recommended treatment for genital chlamydia in pregnancy, being effective and safe in all trimesters, and a test of cure is performed at four weeks specifically because pregnancy is one of the situations where confirming eradication matters, given the risks of preterm birth and of neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia. Her partner is treated at the same time to prevent reinfection. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for seven days with no test of cure
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is a recognised alternative in pregnancy when a macrolide cannot be used, but it has lower microbiological cure rates and there is concern about driving latent infection, so it is second line rather than the default. Omitting the test of cure compounds the problem. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Defer treatment until after delivery and repeat the swab in the third trimester
options.rationale: Untreated infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes and low birth weight, and with neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia acquired during vaginal birth, so deferral exposes both mother and baby to preventable harm. Asymptomatic infection is treated exactly as symptomatic infection is. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once with a test of cure in four weeks time
options.rationale: A cephalosporin injection is the treatment for gonorrhoea, which her swab specifically excluded, and it has no useful activity against this intracellular organism. The pairing of the two infections in practice makes this an easy substitution to make by reflex. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: Chlamydia is the most frequently notified sexually transmitted infection in Australia, with the highest rates in people aged fifteen to twenty nine, and it is asymptomatic in about three quarters of infected women, which is why antenatal screening and annual screening of sexually active people under thirty are both recommended. Treatment differs by setting: outside pregnancy the preferred regimen is doxycycline for seven days, reflecting evidence of superior cure rates particularly at rectal sites, while in pregnancy a single dose of azithromycin is used because tetracyclines are contraindicated. A test of cure is not routine for uncomplicated genital infection but is recommended in pregnancy, after rectal infection, where adherence is uncertain and where an alternative regimen was used, and it is performed at four weeks because nucleic acid tests detect residual non-viable organism before then. Partner notification covering sexual contacts from the preceding six months is an integral part of management, and retesting for reinfection at three months is advised because reinfection from an untreated partner is common. Untreated maternal infection risks preterm birth and neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.
key_points: Around three quarters of infections in women are asymptomatic, hence routine screening
Doxycycline for seven days outside pregnancy; single dose azithromycin in pregnancy
Test of cure at four weeks is recommended in pregnancy, not routinely otherwise
Partner notification covers contacts from the preceding six months
Retest for reinfection at three months regardless of the initial cure
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis presents between five and fourteen days after birth, later than the gonococcal form which appears in the first two to five days, and it is treated with oral rather than topical erythromycin because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause an afebrile pneumonia at four to twelve weeks of age.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Choosing the follow up test after mifepristone and misoprostol for an eight week intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman in her second pregnancy who has decided, after two discussions and a week to think about it, to end this pregnancy. She has one child and is clear and settled about her decision.

Her dating ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length corresponding to eight weeks and one day, with cardiac activity present. She has no abdominal pain and no bleeding. Her blood group is O negative with no preformed antibodies. She lives forty minutes from the regional hospital, has her own car, and a friend has agreed to stay with her overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, uterus not palpable abdominally, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length of 8 weeks 1 day and cardiac activity present, blood group O negative with negative antibody screen, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with anti-D immunoglobulin and a review in two weeks
options.rationale: This was long standing practice, but current Australian guidance no longer recommends anti-D immunoglobulin for spontaneous or induced abortion before ten weeks gestation, because the volume of fetal red cells at that gestation is below the threshold needed to cause sensitisation. Giving it exposes her to a blood product she does not need. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a low sensitivity pregnancy test in two weeks
options.rationale: The combination regimen is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and she is within that window, and confirmation of success uses a low sensitivity urine test that turns negative once the hormone falls below about 1000 IU/L, at two weeks. This avoids the false positives of a standard high sensitivity test, which remains positive for weeks after a completely successful treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Misoprostol alone repeated as needed, with a serum hCG measurement in two weeks
options.rationale: Prostaglandin alone has a complete abortion rate around eighty per cent compared with more than ninety five per cent for the sequential combination, so it is reserved for settings where the antiprogestogen is unavailable. A single hormone measurement without a baseline for comparison is also uninterpretable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Refer for surgical aspiration as her blood group makes medical treatment unsuitable
options.rationale: Being rhesus negative is not a contraindication to medical treatment, and surgical aspiration is an equally valid option chosen for patient preference, gestation beyond the approved window, or contraindications such as suspected ectopic pregnancy, an intrauterine device in place, chronic adrenal failure or long term corticosteroid use. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a routine pelvic ultrasound in two weeks time
options.rationale: Routine scanning after medical abortion is specifically discouraged because retained blood and debris in the cavity look abnormal on ultrasound in many women who are entirely well, and acting on that appearance leads to unnecessary surgical intervention. Scanning is reserved for continuing symptoms, heavy bleeding, or a persistently positive test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Medical abortion with sequential mifepristone and misoprostol is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and can be provided in general practice by a prescriber who has completed the required training, including by telehealth with local pathology and ultrasound. The woman needs to know that bleeding is typically heavier than a period with clots and cramping over several hours, that it usually settles over one to two weeks, and that she should present for bleeding soaking two pads an hour for two hours, fever, or severe pain not relieved by simple analgesia. Confirmation of success matters because around two to five per cent of treatments fail or leave retained tissue, and the ongoing pregnancy rate is under one per cent; the standard confirmation is a low sensitivity urine pregnancy test at two weeks or a fall in serum hormone of more than eighty per cent at one week from a pre-treatment baseline. Routine ultrasound is avoided because it detects clinically irrelevant intrauterine echoes and drives unnecessary surgery. Contraception is discussed at the same visit and can be started immediately, including insertion of an intrauterine device once the abortion is confirmed complete.
key_points: The combination regimen is approved in Australia to sixty three days of gestation
Confirm success with a low sensitivity urine test at two weeks or an eighty per cent hormone fall at one week
Routine post-treatment ultrasound drives unnecessary surgical intervention
Anti-D immunoglobulin is not required before ten weeks gestation
