Contraception can be started immediately, with device insertion once completion is confirmed
explanation.pearls: A standard high sensitivity urine pregnancy test detects down to about 25 IU/L and can stay positive for four weeks or more after a completely successful medical abortion, which is why the low sensitivity test with a threshold near 1000 IU/L is used instead and why a positive standard test at two weeks causes avoidable alarm.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: A globular tender uterus with myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old administrator with three children who describes three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She passes clots the size of fifty cent pieces and changes a super tampon and a pad hourly on her two worst days.

The pain now begins two days before the bleeding starts and continues throughout, and she has deep pain with intercourse in the week before a period. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. She has completed her family and does not want an operation if it can be avoided. On examination her uterus is uniformly enlarged to about ten weeks size, globular, mobile and tender, with no separate adnexal mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uniformly enlarged globular uterus of about ten weeks size, mobile and tender on bimanual examination, no adnexal mass, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globular uterus with asymmetrical anterior myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts, an indistinct endometrial to myometrial junction and no discrete fibroid; endometrial thickness 6 mm; both ovaries normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and review her bleeding in six months
options.rationale: Embolisation has reasonable results in this condition and is a genuine option, but it is a radiological intervention with a significant post-procedural pain syndrome and is reserved for women who have failed medical management. It is more established for discrete fibroids, which her scan specifically excludes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer for total hysterectomy and review her in the clinic before the operation
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the only definitive cure and is entirely appropriate for a woman who has completed her family and failed medical treatment, but she has had no medical treatment at all and has asked to avoid an operation. Offering surgery first inverts the usual ladder. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and review her in six months
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression shrinks the uterus and stops the bleeding effectively but causes vasomotor symptoms and bone loss, so it is limited to six months without add back therapy and is generally used to prepare for surgery rather than as ongoing treatment. It is a bridging agent, not a first line one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system and review in six months
options.rationale: A globular tender uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and loss of the junctional zone on ultrasound is adenomyosis, and the intrauterine progestogen is first line because it treats both the heavy bleeding and the pain by producing endometrial and adenomyotic decidualisation and atrophy, with typical reductions in blood loss above eighty per cent. It also provides contraception and preserves the uterus, which is what she has asked for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start tranexamic acid during menses only and review her bleeding in six months
options.rationale: An antifibrinolytic reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a useful non-hormonal option for a woman who wants to conceive or declines hormones, but it does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia that are half her problem here. The difference from the correct answer is that one treats both symptoms and one treats a single symptom partially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it typically presents in women in their late thirties and forties with progressively heavier and more painful periods, often with deep dyspareunia and a chronically enlarged tender uterus. Its distinguishing examination finding is a uniformly enlarged globular uterus that is tender, as opposed to the irregular firm contour of fibroids or the fixed retroverted nodular uterus of deep endometriosis. Transvaginal ultrasound has largely replaced the old idea that it can only be diagnosed after hysterectomy, and the features to look for are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, a globular shape, subendometrial echogenic lines and an interrupted or indistinct junctional zone. Iron deficiency is very common and needs treating in its own right alongside the bleeding. Treatment is stepwise: the intrauterine progestogen first, then combined hormonal or oral progestogen options, with antifibrinolytics and anti-inflammatories as adjuncts, then embolisation or ablation, and hysterectomy as the definitive cure for women who have completed their family.
key_points: A uniformly enlarged, globular, tender uterus distinguishes it from fibroids on examination
Ultrasound features include myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone
The intrauterine progestogen is first line and treats both bleeding and pain
Antifibrinolytics reduce bleeding by about a third but do not help the pain
Iron deficiency accompanies it commonly and is treated in parallel
explanation.pearls: Treat the iron deficiency as a separate problem rather than assuming it will correct once the bleeding is controlled: a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L means stores are exhausted, oral iron on alternate days is better absorbed than daily dosing because of the hepcidin response, and symptoms of fatigue often improve before the haemoglobin does.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

subtopic_detail: A lumbar spine T score of minus 2.6 in a woman whose periods stopped at the age of forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 47 year old librarian whose periods stopped five years ago. Two follicle stimulating hormone measurements taken a month apart at the time were both in the postmenopausal range and a chromosomal and autoimmune screen found no cause.

She declined hormone therapy at the time because she did not like the idea of taking hormones, and she has taken nothing since. Her bone density scan has now been done and is reported below. She has never fractured a bone, does not smoke, drinks two standard drinks a week, and has about one serve of dairy food a day. Her coeliac serology, thyroid function, parathyroid hormone and calcium are all normal. She has no history of thrombosis, breast cancer, liver disease or migraine with aura.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 116/72 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, no kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height at age thirty, no proximal muscle weakness
data_table.Investigations: Bone mineral density T score minus 2.6 at the lumbar spine and minus 2.1 at the femoral neck, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 48 nmol/L (50-150), parathyroid hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for her bone density?

options.text: Start weekly alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and exercise
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are first line for postmenopausal osteoporosis at the usual age, but in women with early menopause they are second line because they do not replace the oestrogen deficiency that is causing the loss, and long term use in a woman who may need treatment for four decades raises concerns about atypical femoral fracture. They become appropriate if oestrogen is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Start denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Denosumab is effective but commits the patient to indefinite six monthly injections, because stopping it causes a rebound loss of bone density with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures unless another agent is substituted immediately. That is a poor commitment to make at forty seven when a physiological alternative exists. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Start menopausal hormone therapy with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Menopause before forty five is treated as replacement of a hormone she should still be producing rather than as optional symptom relief, and hormone therapy is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause around fifty one, for bone density, cardiovascular and cognitive protection. The usual risk calculus from trials in women over sixty does not apply, and she has no contraindication. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Start raloxifene daily with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: A selective oestrogen receptor modulator increases spinal density and reduces vertebral fracture but not hip fracture, raises the risk of venous thrombosis, and causes or worsens hot flushes, which is a particular problem in a woman who is already oestrogen deficient. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Advise weight bearing exercise and repeat her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D repletion are necessary for everyone and will be part of her plan, but as the entire treatment for established osteoporosis in a woman with five years of untreated oestrogen deficiency ahead of her, they allow avoidable further loss. Lifestyle alone is the answer for osteopenia without other risk factors. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Menopause before the age of forty is premature ovarian insufficiency and between forty and forty five is early menopause, and both are managed differently from menopause at the usual age. The central principle is that these women are deficient in a hormone their peers still produce, so treatment is framed as replacement until at least the average age of natural menopause, around fifty one, rather than as a short course weighed against the risks described in trials of older women. Untreated, they face accelerated bone loss with a high lifetime fracture risk, increased cardiovascular disease, and probably increased cognitive decline, which is why hormone therapy is first line for their bone protection ahead of bisphosphonates. Either standard menopausal hormone therapy or a combined oral contraceptive can be used, with the contraceptive preferred where pregnancy is still possible, which it occasionally is. Investigation at diagnosis includes karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and adrenal and thyroid autoantibodies, and bone density is measured at diagnosis and repeated every few years. Calcium intake of around 1300 mg a day and vitamin D sufficiency support whichever agent is chosen.
key_points: Menopause before forty five is replacement, not optional symptom relief
Hormone therapy is continued until at least the average age of menopause
It is first line for bone protection in this group, ahead of bisphosphonates
Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures
Karyotype, fragile X premutation and autoantibody testing belong in the initial workup
explanation.pearls: Her vitamin D of 48 nmol/L sits just below the target of at least 50 nmol/L year round, and correcting it matters before starting any antiresorptive agent, because giving a potent bisphosphonate or denosumab to a vitamin D deficient patient can precipitate symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Aftercare and future birth counselling on day one after theatre repair of a 3b anal sphincter injury
stem:
You are the obstetrics resident on the postnatal ward seeing a 29 year old woman on the first day after the birth of her first baby. She had a forceps birth with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage, and the baby weighed 3.9 kg.

The consultant repaired a tear involving more than half the thickness of the external anal sphincter in theatre under regional anaesthesia. The urinary catheter has been removed and she is voiding normally with good volumes. She has no incontinence of flatus or faeces and her pain is controlled on regular paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory. She asks what happens now and whether she will have to have a caesarean next time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Perineal repair intact with mild bruising and no haematoma, no cellulitis or discharge, uterus well contracted at the umbilicus, lochia normal, voiding residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate postnatal plan?

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and review at three months
options.rationale: Repair of an anal sphincter injury is followed by a course of broad spectrum antibiotics to reduce wound infection and breakdown, a stool softening laxative so that the first motions do not strain the repair, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with review in a dedicated clinic at around three months where continence is assessed and endoanal ultrasound and manometry are considered. That review, rather than a decision made now, determines the advice about the next birth. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics and laxatives, with review only if symptoms develop
options.rationale: The immediate measures are right but waiting for symptoms misses the women who will benefit most, since occult sphincter defects and reduced squeeze pressures are common while continence is preserved in the early months and deteriorates years later. Structured follow up is what allows the next birth to be planned properly. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Laxatives and physiotherapy, with a planned caesarean section for any next birth
options.rationale: Committing her to abdominal birth on the day after the injury pre-empts the assessment that should decide it: a woman who is fully continent with normal investigations at review can be supported to birth vaginally, and elective caesarean is reserved for those who are symptomatic or have abnormal studies. Omitting antibiotics also increases wound breakdown. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Antibiotics and physiotherapy, with a constipating agent to protect the repair
options.rationale: This gets the bowel management exactly backwards. Constipating the patient produces a hard bolus that has to be passed eventually and is far more likely to disrupt the repair than soft regular motions, which is why a stool softener and not a constipating agent is prescribed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Physiotherapy alone, with endoanal ultrasound and manometry before discharge
options.rationale: Imaging and pressure studies belong at the specialist review months later, when oedema has resolved and the findings reflect the healed anatomy rather than acute swelling, and doing them now would be uninterpretable. Physiotherapy alone also omits the antibiotics and laxatives that protect the repair. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are classified as third degree when the anal sphincter complex is involved, subdivided into less than half of the external sphincter torn, more than half torn, and involvement of the internal sphincter, and fourth degree when the anal epithelium is breached. Risk factors are a first vaginal birth, forceps delivery, a birth weight above 4 kg, a prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia and occipitoposterior position. Repair is performed in theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia and good lighting, by an appropriately trained clinician, using either overlap or end to end technique for the external sphincter, with the internal sphincter repaired separately end to end when torn. Aftercare is a course of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives rather than constipating agents, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with specialist review at around three months. The risk of recurrence at a subsequent vaginal birth is around five to seven per cent, and elective caesarean is offered to women who have persisting symptoms or abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, while asymptomatic women with normal studies may plan a vaginal birth.
key_points: Third degree tears are subdivided by how much of the external sphincter is torn
Antibiotics and laxatives, not constipating agents, protect the repair
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and specialist review at around three months are standard
Recurrence risk at a subsequent vaginal birth is roughly five to seven per cent
Elective caesarean is offered for persisting symptoms or abnormal investigations
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about incontinence of flatus and about faecal urgency at every review rather than about faecal incontinence alone, because loss of control of wind and an inability to defer a motion for more than a few minutes are the earliest and commonest symptoms of a sphincter defect, and women very rarely volunteer them.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care

subtopic_detail: Fifteen hot flushes a day in a woman taking tamoxifen after receptor positive early breast cancer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 49 year old graphic designer fourteen months into tamoxifen, prescribed after breast conserving surgery and radiotherapy for a grade 2 oestrogen receptor positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative early breast cancer.

She counts fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and wakes four times most nights drenched. She is falling asleep at her desk, has taken three days off this month, and tells you she is close to stopping the tablets because she cannot go on like this for another four years. Her mood is not low and she is enjoying her work when she is rested. She is still having periods and takes no other medication. Her oncologist has written asking you to manage the symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Surgical scar well healed with no mass in either breast, no axillary lymphadenopathy, no chest wall nodules, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and liver function within normal limits, most recent mammogram and ultrasound reported as no evidence of recurrence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for her flushes?

options.text: Start transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone for symptom control
options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and is contraindicated after a receptor positive breast cancer, where trial evidence showed an increase in new breast cancer events. The transdermal route changes the thrombotic risk profile but not the hormonal one. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Start paroxetine 20 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: This class does reduce flushes, but paroxetine and fluoxetine are potent inhibitors of the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, and using them together lowers that metabolite substantially with observational evidence of increased breast cancer mortality. The drug class is right and this particular member is the one to avoid. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Stop the tamoxifen and switch to an aromatase inhibitor for the remaining years
options.rationale: Aromatase inhibitors do not work in a woman who is still menstruating unless ovarian function is suppressed, and adding ovarian suppression would deepen the oestrogen deficiency and make the flushes considerably worse. It also changes her cancer treatment without her oncologist, when the request was to manage the symptoms. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

options.text: Start a vaginal oestradiol pessary and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: Low dose vaginal oestrogen is used cautiously for genitourinary symptoms in selected women after breast cancer, but systemic absorption is minimal by design, so it has no effect on hot flushes. It answers a different symptom from the one she has presented with. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Start venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the best studied non-hormonal option for vasomotor symptoms and typically reduces flush frequency by about sixty per cent, and venlafaxine is specifically preferred in women on tamoxifen because it is a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that generates the active metabolite. Treating the symptom effectively is also what protects five years of adjuvant endocrine therapy she is otherwise about to abandon. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: Vasomotor symptoms are the commonest reason women stop adjuvant endocrine therapy early, and non-adherence to tamoxifen translates directly into higher recurrence and mortality, so treating the flushes is oncological treatment rather than a comfort measure. Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen, its potent active metabolite, so strong inhibitors of that enzyme are avoided: paroxetine and fluoxetine are the ones to know, along with bupropion and quinidine, while venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram and citalopram are weak inhibitors and are considered safe. Effective non-hormonal options in order of evidence are the serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin at night where sleep disturbance dominates, clonidine, and cognitive behavioural therapy or hypnosis, which have good trial evidence and no interactions at all. Vaginal oestrogen is a separate question for genitourinary symptoms and is used cautiously and usually with oncologist involvement, particularly for women on aromatase inhibitors.
key_points: Untreated flushes drive early discontinuation of endocrine therapy and worsen outcomes
Systemic hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer
Tamoxifen requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to form its active metabolite
Avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion; venlafaxine and escitalopram are acceptable
Gabapentin at night and cognitive behavioural therapy are effective alternatives
explanation.pearls: If flushes at night are the dominant problem, gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime is worth knowing as an alternative to the antidepressants because it reduces night time flushes by a similar margin, has no interaction with tamoxifen at all, and its sedation is useful rather than a drawback when the symptom is waking her four times a night.

subtopic_detail: Gestational ceiling for fetal neuroprotection when birth is expected within hours
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 31 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 29 weeks and 4 days. She has been contracting every three minutes for two hours, her cervix is 6 cm dilated and the membranes are intact.

She received both doses of betamethasone eight days ago during an earlier admission for threatened preterm labour. The neonatal team has been called and the cot is confirmed. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, her reflexes are normal, her urine output has been 60 mL per hour, and her creatinine is within normal limits. Cardiotocography shows a normal trace. She has had no magnesium in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm dilated, membranes intact, vertex presenting at station minus 2, contractions every three minutes
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), patellar reflexes normal, urine output 60 mL per hour, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional treatment to start now?

options.text: A repeat course of intramuscular betamethasone as two doses given twenty four hours apart
options.rationale: A repeat course is considered when the first was given more than seven days earlier and birth is again threatened, but it cannot be completed in a woman delivering within hours and would delay the intervention that can be. Magnesium takes precedence when time is short. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate as a loading dose followed by an infusion until the birth
options.rationale: Antenatal magnesium given to women expected to give birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors, and this birth is imminent at 29 weeks and 4 days. The loading dose and infusion are started as soon as birth is anticipated rather than held back. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate withheld because the gestation has passed the threshold for neuroprotective benefit
options.rationale: The Australian threshold is birth before 30 completed weeks, and 29 weeks and 4 days sits inside it. Reading the threshold as 29 weeks or as 28 weeks is the commonest reason eligible women miss the treatment. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Intravenous nifedipine tocolysis as a loading dose followed by maintenance until 34 weeks
options.rationale: Nifedipine is an oral agent and tocolysis at 6 cm with regular contractions is very unlikely to stop labour. Its purpose is to buy time for steroids or transfer, both of which are already complete here. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin as a loading dose followed by four hourly doses until the birth
options.rationale: Group B streptococcal prophylaxis is reasonable in preterm labour of unknown carriage status and would usually be given, but it addresses neonatal sepsis rather than the neurological outcome that defines the window closing here. It is an addition, not the answer to what matters most now. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate given to the mother shortly before very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, with a number needed to treat of roughly 60 at gestations below 30 weeks. The Australian and New Zealand guideline sets the threshold at anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks, and treatment is given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion, ideally with at least four hours before birth although benefit is not abandoned if less time is available. Monitoring is clinical: respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output, with the infusion stopped if toxicity appears. Normal renal function matters because magnesium is renally cleared. Steroids and neuroprotection serve different endpoints and both are given when time permits.
key_points: Neuroprotective magnesium applies to anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks
Loading dose then infusion, ideally at least four hours before birth
Monitor respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output for toxicity
Renal impairment demands dose reduction because magnesium is renally cleared
Steroids reduce respiratory morbidity and do not replace neuroprotection
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest reliable sign of magnesium toxicity and appears well before respiratory depression, so check reflexes hourly and treat their disappearance as a reason to stop the infusion and recheck the level rather than waiting for the respiratory rate to fall below 12 breaths per minute.

sources.label: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Duration of postnatal thromboprophylaxis after caesarean in a woman with a previous unprovoked clot
stem:
You are the obstetric resident writing discharge medications for a 36 year old woman on day three after an emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m2.

She had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis in her left leg at the age of 28, treated with six months of anticoagulation, and she received prophylactic enoxaparin throughout this pregnancy. Thrombophilia screening after that event was negative. Her wound is clean, she is mobilising independently, her haemoglobin is 108 g/L and her platelet count is normal. She is breastfeeding and asks how long she needs to keep having injections.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Caesarean wound clean and dry, calves soft and non tender, mobilising independently
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: How long should her postnatal thromboprophylaxis continue?

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin until discharge only, with graduated compression stockings continued at home
options.rationale: Stopping at discharge leaves the highest risk weeks uncovered, since most postnatal events occur after the woman goes home. Stockings are an adjunct and do not substitute for pharmacological prophylaxis in a high risk woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Six weeks of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: A previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism places her in the high risk group, for whom prophylaxis continues six weeks postnatally rather than stopping at discharge. The postnatal period carries the highest daily thrombotic risk of the whole pregnancy, and the caesarean and body mass index add to it. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Six weeks of oral rivaroxaban from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended while breastfeeding because they are excreted in breast milk and infant safety data are lacking. Enoxaparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Six weeks of therapeutic dose enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Therapeutic dosing is for treating an acute event or for women on long term anticoagulation, not for prophylaxis after a remote treated thrombosis. It raises the risk of wound haematoma and secondary postpartum haemorrhage without added benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Ten days of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Ten days covers intermediate risk, such as an emergency caesarean with one or two minor risk factors and no thrombotic history. A previous unprovoked event moves her above that band. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the daily risk peaks in the first postnatal weeks rather than during pregnancy. Risk is scored from a combination of previous events, thrombophilia, mode of birth, body mass index, age, parity and immobility. A previous unprovoked thrombosis is a high risk marker in its own right and mandates prophylaxis antenatally and for six weeks postnatally, while intermediate risk combinations attract ten days. Prophylaxis is with low molecular weight heparin, which does not cross into breast milk in clinically relevant amounts. Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in breastfeeding women. The practical failure mode is not choosing the wrong drug but stopping it at discharge.
key_points: Previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism means six weeks of postnatal prophylaxis
Intermediate risk combinations attract ten days rather than six weeks
Most postnatal events occur after discharge, so the script must leave with her
Enoxaparin and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding, direct oral agents are not
Prophylactic dosing is used even when the previous event was unprovoked
explanation.pearls: Restart low molecular weight heparin at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and do not remove the catheter within twelve hours of a prophylactic dose, because spinal haematoma is the complication that turns a correct prophylaxis decision into a permanent injury.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

subtopic_detail: Operative plan when imaging suggests abnormal placental invasion over a previous scar
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal fetal medicine clinic reviewing a 34 year old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal birth, and this pregnancy was conceived spontaneously.

Ultrasound reports an anterior placenta reaching the internal os, with multiple placental lacunae, loss of the clear zone between placenta and myometrium, and bridging vessels crossing into the bladder wall on colour Doppler. She has had two small painless antepartum bleeds that settled without intervention. She has no pain now, the fetal growth is on the 45th centile, and she has been counselled in detail about the range of intrapartum possibilities by the consultant.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, no vaginal bleeding today, foetus in cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound showing anterior placenta praevia with multiple lacunae, loss of the clear zone and bridging vessels to the bladder, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), fetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left in situ, the uterus closed and methotrexate given afterwards
options.rationale: Expectant management leaving the placenta in situ is reserved for women who strongly desire uterine preservation and accept a high rate of delayed haemorrhage, sepsis and eventual hysterectomy. Methotrexate does not hasten placental involution and is not recommended as part of that strategy. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with manual removal of the placenta and uterine artery embolisation if bleeding follows
options.rationale: Manual removal is the specific manoeuvre that converts a controlled operation into torrential haemorrhage when the villi are invading myometrium, and embolisation cannot keep pace with that rate of loss. Interventional radiology has a role in planned balloon occlusion, not as a rescue after avoidable bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation
options.rationale: The imaging describes placenta accreta spectrum, where attempting to remove the placenta provokes catastrophic haemorrhage from vessels that cannot retract. Planned delivery before labour at a centre with the right team, with the placenta left in place and hysterectomy performed, gives the lowest maternal blood loss and morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging now, with the mode and timing of birth deferred until that result is available
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging helps define posterior placentation or the extent of parametrial spread, but it does not outperform good ultrasound for the diagnosis itself and adds nothing when the sonographic signs are this clear. Deferring the plan wastes the planning time that determines the outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 39 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation
options.rationale: Waiting to term in a woman who has already bled twice courts an emergency delivery out of hours without the assembled team, which is the setting in which most maternal deaths from this condition occur. The gestation is deliberately traded against that risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum follows implantation over a uterine scar where decidua is deficient, so villi anchor into or through myometrium. Incidence has risen in step with the caesarean rate, and the combination of placenta praevia with previous caesareans is the classic antenatal warning. Sonographic features are lacunae, loss of the hypoechoic clear zone, myometrial thinning, and bridging vessels extending towards the bladder. Outcomes are determined almost entirely by whether the diagnosis is made antenatally and the delivery planned: a scheduled operation at 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with blood bank support, experienced surgeons and critical care halves maternal morbidity compared with emergency delivery. The operative principle is to deliver the baby through an incision away from the placenta and not to attempt separation.
key_points: Praevia plus previous caesarean is the combination that should prompt the diagnosis
Plan birth at 34 to 36 weeks before labour or a large bleed forces the issue
Deliver through an incision away from the placenta and do not attempt separation
Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta in situ is the standard operation
Antenatal diagnosis and a planned team are the strongest predictors of outcome
explanation.pearls: Ask every woman with an anterior low placenta how many caesareans she has had, because the risk of accreta spectrum in the presence of praevia climbs from roughly 3 percent with one previous caesarean to more than 40 percent with three or more, and that single history question changes the ultrasound from routine to targeted.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

subtopic_detail: Delivery timing when serum bile acid concentration crosses the highest stillbirth risk band
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. For three weeks she has had intense itching of her palms and soles that keeps her awake, with no rash other than scratch marks.

Her total serum bile acids taken non fasting are 118 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase is 96 units/L, bilirubin is normal, and a liver ultrasound, hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are all unremarkable. Fetal growth is on the 60th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and a reassuring cardiotocograph. She has been taking ursodeoxycholic acid for two weeks with modest relief of itch. Her first pregnancy ended in a normal birth at term.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations on the forearms and shins, no primary rash, no jaundice, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 96 units/L (5-35), bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20), viral hepatitis serology negative, autoimmune screen negative, umbilical artery Dopplers normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Increase the ursodeoxycholic acid dose and defer any decision about birth until the bile acids have been rechecked
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves pruritus and lowers biochemistry modestly but the large randomised trial found no reduction in perinatal death, preterm birth or neonatal unit admission. Treating the number rather than the risk delays the intervention that does change outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of corticosteroids, with continued inpatient fetal monitoring meanwhile
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk in this condition is concentrated in women whose bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more, in whom the risk rises steeply from the mid thirties of gestation, so birth is brought forward to 35 to 36 weeks. Below that concentration the risk approximates background and delivery can wait until closer to term. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Repeat liver function tests and bile acids weekly and deliver only if alanine aminotransferase rises above 200 units/L
options.rationale: Transaminase level correlates poorly with perinatal risk in this condition, whereas the bile acid concentration is the variable that tracks stillbirth. Using the wrong marker as the trigger leaves an already high risk pregnancy undelivered. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Deliver by caesarean section within twenty four hours because of the height of the bile acid concentration
options.rationale: There is no evidence that abdominal birth improves outcome in this condition, and immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes prematurity without a corresponding gain over waiting the short interval to 35 to 36 weeks. Induction is the usual route once the decision to deliver is made. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 39 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography and growth scans every two weeks until then
options.rationale: Term delivery is appropriate for mild disease but not once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L. Surveillance is the deeper problem here: stillbirth in this condition is a sudden arrhythmic event and a normal trace does not predict the next few days. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus without a primary rash, classically on the palms and soles and worse at night, and is confirmed by raised serum bile acids once other liver disease is excluded. The important shift in the last decade came from pooled individual patient data showing that stillbirth risk is not uniform across the condition: it is essentially background when bile acids are below 40 micromol/L, slightly elevated between 40 and 99, and rises sharply above 100 micromol/L, particularly after 35 weeks. Management therefore stratifies by concentration, with birth at 35 to 36 weeks for severe disease and closer to term for milder disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid remains reasonable for symptom relief but the randomised evidence shows it does not prevent perinatal death, so it must not be used as a reason to delay delivery.
key_points: Bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more define the high stillbirth risk group
Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks for that group, later for milder disease
Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itch but does not reduce perinatal death
Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden fetal death seen in this condition
Diagnosis requires exclusion of viral, autoimmune and structural liver disease
explanation.pearls: Take the bile acid sample non fasting, because postprandial values run higher and the risk thresholds published from the pooled data were derived largely from non fasting samples; a fasting level reported as 85 micromol/L may sit above 100 micromol/L after a meal and place the woman in a different management band.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Obstetric cholestasis

subtopic_detail: Breathlessness three weeks after birth wrongly attributed to blood loss and deconditioning
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 38 year old woman three weeks after the birth of twins by caesarean section. She describes six days of breathlessness climbing the stairs, waking at night needing to sit up, and ankle swelling that has not settled.

She lost 700 mL at operation and was told her blood count was low afterwards. Her haemoglobin today is 118 g/L, having been 104 g/L on day two. She has bilateral basal crackles, a raised jugular venous pressure and pitting oedema to mid shin, with calves that are soft and equal. Her chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, and an electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic change. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy and today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure 6 cm above the sternal angle, bilateral basal crackles, pitting oedema to mid shin, calves soft and equal, caesarean wound healed
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion with outpatient review, on the basis that her symptoms date from the operative blood loss
options.rationale: Her haemoglobin has risen from 104 to 118 g/L, so anaemia is resolving while her symptoms are worsening, and anaemia does not raise the jugular venous pressure or produce upper lobe venous diversion. Attributing postnatal breathlessness to blood loss is the commonest reason this diagnosis is delayed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with doxycycline and discharge, treating the findings as an atypical community acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: She is afebrile with symmetrical basal crackles, oedema and a raised venous pressure, none of which fit infection, and the radiograph shows congestion rather than consolidation. Treating this as pneumonia sends home a woman in decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography with therapeutic enoxaparin started while awaiting the scan
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism deserves consideration in any breathless postnatal woman, but orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, bilateral crackles and cardiomegaly with venous diversion point to a congested circulation rather than an obstructed one. Echocardiography will answer both questions faster. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reassurance with graded exercise and a general practice review in two weeks, treating this as postnatal deconditioning
options.rationale: Deconditioning does not cause orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, hypoxaemia or an abnormal chest radiograph. Normalising these findings in a postnatal woman is precisely the pattern that turns a treatable cardiomyopathy into a late presentation. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Urgent transthoracic echocardiography with intravenous frusemide and admission under a physician
options.rationale: The clinical picture is pulmonary congestion with a raised venous pressure and radiographic changes, which requires imaging of ventricular function now and treatment of the congestion while that is arranged. Peripartum cardiomyopathy characteristically declares itself in the first month after birth and carries significant mortality if missed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after birth in a woman with no previously known cardiac disease. Multiple pregnancy, older maternal age, hypertensive disease and multiparity all increase risk. The presentation overlaps almost completely with normal late pregnancy and early postnatal symptoms, which is why the median time to diagnosis is measured in weeks, and the discriminating features are orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a raised jugular venous pressure and hypoxaemia. Echocardiography confirms a reduced ejection fraction and excludes valvular and pericardial causes. Treatment follows standard heart failure principles adapted for breastfeeding, using frusemide, beta blockade and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor postnatally, with anticoagulation considered when the ejection fraction is severely reduced.
key_points: Presents from the last month of pregnancy to five months after birth
Orthopnoea and a raised jugular venous pressure separate it from deconditioning
Twins, older maternal age and hypertensive disease raise the risk
Echocardiography is the diagnostic test and should not wait for outpatient booking
Postnatal treatment uses agents compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Captopril, enalapril and quinapril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best breastfeeding safety data and should be chosen over perindopril or ramipril in a woman who wants to keep feeding, because being told to wean is a common reason women stop taking the drug that most improves their ejection fraction.

sources.label: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

subtopic_detail: A fourth culture confirmed episode of vulval itch and thick discharge within twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old physiotherapist with her fourth episode this year of intense vulval itch, burning on passing urine and thick white discharge. Each previous episode was confirmed on swab and settled within days of a single antifungal capsule, then returned six to eight weeks later.

She is not pregnant, has taken no antibiotics or corticosteroids, and has had the same partner for three years. Her glycated haemoglobin last month was 33 mmol/mol and a human immunodeficiency virus test six months ago was negative. Today's high vaginal swab has grown Candida albicans, reported as sensitive to fluconazole.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the vulva with two shallow fissures in the interlabial folds, thick adherent white discharge, no ulceration, no lichenification, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture grew Candida albicans sensitive to fluconazole with no bacterial pathogen, vaginal pH 4.2, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative, glycated haemoglobin 33 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A single fluconazole dose now and a further single dose at each recurrence
options.rationale: Treating each episode as it arises is exactly what has been happening and has produced four episodes in a year, because a single dose clears the symptomatic infection without altering the propensity to recur. Episodic treatment is the correct approach for isolated infections, not for a recurrent pattern. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: A single fluconazole dose now and the same treatment for her regular partner
options.rationale: This is not a sexually transmitted infection and randomised trials of treating the male partner show no reduction in recurrence for the woman, so partner treatment is reserved for a man with symptomatic balanitis. It also misses the need for a maintenance regimen. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Topical nystatin pessaries nightly for fourteen days and then as required
options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles against this organism and as required use leaves the same episodic pattern in place. Topical azoles are a reasonable alternative to oral treatment where tablets cannot be used, but the regimen rather than the route is the problem here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nystatin to decolonise the bowel and a single fluconazole dose now
options.rationale: The idea that recurrence comes from a gastrointestinal reservoir was tested and abandoned, since oral nystatin does not reduce vaginal recurrence. The organism persists in the vagina at low density between episodes rather than being reintroduced from the bowel. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Induction fluconazole then weekly fluconazole for six months as maintenance
options.rationale: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease, and the treatment that changes the pattern is an induction phase of three doses forty eight to seventy two hours apart followed by six months of weekly suppression, which keeps around ninety per cent of women free of symptoms while it is running. The culture confirming a fluconazole sensitive albicans species is what makes this regimen appropriate rather than a topical alternative. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as four or more episodes in twelve months and affects around five to eight per cent of women of reproductive age. Confirming the diagnosis by culture rather than treating on symptoms alone is essential at this point, because the differential includes bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and vulvodynia, and because species identification matters: Candida glabrata and Candida krusei are intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole and require boric acid pessaries or nystatin instead. Predisposing factors worth excluding are diabetes, immunosuppression, pregnancy, recent antibiotics and corticosteroid use, but most women with recurrent disease have none of them and it is better understood as an abnormal inflammatory response to normal vaginal colonisation. Treatment is an induction phase followed by six months of weekly suppression, which controls symptoms in around nine out of ten women during treatment, though roughly half relapse in the year after it stops and may need a further course. Partner treatment, bowel decolonisation and dietary sugar restriction have all been tested and do not work.
key_points: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease
Culture identifies non-albicans species that are intrinsically fluconazole resistant
Induction followed by six months of weekly suppression is the effective regimen
Around half relapse after treatment stops and may need a further course
Partner treatment and bowel decolonisation do not reduce recurrence
explanation.pearls: If the culture grows Candida glabrata rather than albicans, fluconazole will fail regardless of the regimen, and the usual next step is intravaginal boric acid 600 mg nightly for fourteen days, which is compounded rather than commercially available and is toxic if swallowed, so it must be labelled clearly and kept away from children.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: A dilated non-filling left tube on hysterosalpingogram in a couple accepted for in vitro fertilisation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 33 year old woman and her partner after three years of trying to conceive with no pregnancy. She has never been pregnant.

Her cycles are regular at twenty nine days and a mid luteal progesterone confirms ovulation, her anti-Mullerian hormone is normal for her age, and her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. She had a laparoscopic appendicectomy at nineteen and was treated for chlamydia at twenty two. Her hysterosalpingogram and a follow up ultrasound are reported below. The couple have been accepted for a funded cycle of in vitro fertilisation and would like to start with the next cycle.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a healed port site scar, uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Hysterosalpingogram shows free fill and spill on the right, with the left tube dilated along its length and no spill of contrast; transvaginal ultrasound confirms a 3 cm fluid filled tubular left adnexal structure with incomplete septa; both ovaries normal with an antral follicle count of 14; mid luteal progesterone 38 nmol/L; chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy before the first embryo transfer is performed
options.rationale: A fluid filled obstructed tube roughly halves implantation and live birth rates in assisted reproduction and about doubles the miscarriage rate, because the fluid refluxes into the cavity and is both mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo. Removing the tube, or occluding it proximally where adhesions make removal unsafe, restores pregnancy rates to those of women without the condition, and it is done before transfer rather than after a failed cycle. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Proceed directly to embryo transfer and reassess the tube only if it fails
options.rationale: Proceeding without treating the tube spends a funded cycle at roughly half the expected success rate and exposes her to a higher miscarriage risk, when the intervention that corrects it is a single day procedure. Waiting for failure means the cycle is lost before the problem is addressed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Aspirate the hydrosalpinx under ultrasound guidance at the time of oocyte collection
options.rationale: Needle aspiration at the time of collection is easy and appealing but the fluid reaccumulates within days to weeks in most cases, so the benefit does not last through the implantation window, and it carries a risk of introducing infection into the pelvis. It is a fallback where surgery is refused or unsafe. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Prescribe doxycycline for fourteen days and repeat the imaging afterwards
options.rationale: The tubal damage here is the healed structural consequence of an infection cleared eleven years ago, and her current test is negative, so antibiotics cannot reopen a scarred and dilated tube. Antibiotic cover is used around instrumentation of the tract rather than as treatment for the damage itself. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic tubal reconstructive surgery to restore its patency
options.rationale: Opening the distal tube gives poor live birth rates when the tube is dilated and its lining destroyed, and it leaves a functionally useless conduit with a high risk of ectopic implantation and of the fluid simply reaccumulating. Reconstruction is considered only for mild disease in a woman declining assisted reproduction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: A hydrosalpinx is a distally obstructed, dilated, fluid filled fallopian tube, most often the late consequence of pelvic inflammatory disease, and in Australia chlamydia is the usual antecedent, frequently asymptomatic at the time. It matters out of proportion to its size because the accumulated fluid intermittently refluxes into the uterine cavity, where it impairs implantation both mechanically and through its inflammatory and embryotoxic content, roughly halving live birth rates in assisted reproduction and approximately doubling miscarriage. Randomised evidence supports removing the affected tube, or occluding it proximally when dense adhesions make excision hazardous, before embryo transfer, and this restores success rates to those of comparable women without the condition. Surgical technique matters because dissection close to the tube preserves the mesosalpingeal blood supply to the ovary and avoids compromising ovarian reserve, which is a genuine concern when the woman will undergo ovarian stimulation afterwards. A hydrosalpinx large enough to be visible on ultrasound, rather than only on contrast imaging, appears to have the greatest adverse effect, and is the group in which the case for surgery is strongest.
key_points: A hydrosalpinx roughly halves live birth rates and doubles miscarriage in assisted reproduction
Fluid refluxing into the cavity is mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo
Salpingectomy, or proximal occlusion where adhesions prevent it, precedes embryo transfer
Aspiration gives only transient benefit because the fluid reaccumulates
Careful dissection close to the tube preserves the ovarian blood supply
explanation.pearls: The tube found to be diseased at surgery also carries a risk that outlasts the fertility question: women with tubal damage have a markedly increased chance that any future pregnancy is ectopic, so an early ultrasound at around six weeks is arranged for every subsequent pregnancy, including one conceived through assisted reproduction.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

subtopic_detail: A firm hyperkeratotic plaque persisting after three months of correctly applied ultrapotent corticosteroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64 year old woman who has had vulval lichen sclerosus for five years, controlled on maintenance clobetasol propionate ointment with only occasional itch.

Four months ago she noticed a persistently sore spot on the left labium majus. You confirmed at the last visit that she applies the ointment daily to the affected area and she has used two 30 g tubes in three months, so quantity and technique are not the problem. The pale atrophic skin elsewhere on her vulva has improved over the same period and the itch has settled everywhere except this one area. She has had no bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and negative and she has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: A 1.5 cm firm raised hyperkeratotic plaque with a central fissure on the left labium majus, unchanged since the last review, with surrounding pale atrophic skin and loss of the labia minora, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Swab of the fissure grew mixed skin flora with no Candida and no Staphylococcus aureus, glycated haemoglobin 36 mmol/mol, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the steroid to twice daily and review the area in eight weeks
options.rationale: Escalating the frequency is reasonable when the whole vulva is under-treated, but she has used adequate quantities and every other area has responded, so a single focal region that has not is behaving differently from the surrounding disease. A further eight weeks of topical treatment delays a diagnosis that is time critical. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Add a topical antifungal to the steroid and review the area in eight weeks
options.rationale: Superimposed candidiasis is a genuine cause of persistent symptoms in women on long term ultrapotent steroid to the vulva, and it presents with itch, erythema and satellite lesions rather than a firm hyperkeratotic plaque, and her swab grew no Candida. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Start topical tacrolimus ointment and review the area in eight weeks time
options.rationale: A calcineurin inhibitor is a recognised second line agent for lichen sclerosus that fails corticosteroid, but it is relatively contraindicated in this setting because of theoretical concern about local immunosuppression in skin already at risk of squamous malignancy, and using it would suppress the signal being investigated. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Take a punch biopsy of the plaque and review her with the histology report
options.rationale: Any area of lichen sclerosus that fails to respond to three months of adequately applied ultrapotent corticosteroid, or that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or eroded, must be biopsied, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma arise on this background and can look like resistant disease. A punch biopsy taken from the thickest part of the abnormal area is the appropriate technique. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer for laser vaporisation of the plaque and review her after treatment
options.rationale: Ablative treatment destroys the tissue without providing histology, so an early invasive cancer would be both inadequately treated and rendered unstageable. Laser has no established role in lichen sclerosus and this option repeats the error of treating before diagnosing. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval condition, commonest after menopause, that produces itch, pallor, fissuring and progressive architectural loss with resorption of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, applied daily for an induction period and then titrated to the lowest frequency that maintains control, with long term maintenance reducing both symptoms and, on cohort evidence, the risk of malignant progression. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma in women with this condition is around two to five per cent, and it arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is human papillomavirus independent, occurs in older women and is much more aggressive than the usual human papillomavirus related type seen in younger women. The practical rule is that any focal area which is fixed, thickened, ulcerated, eroded, bleeding or simply not responding to adequate treatment is biopsied rather than re-treated. Lifelong review is recommended, and patients are taught to self examine and to present with any new lump, ulcer or bleeding rather than waiting for a scheduled appointment.
key_points: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with long term maintenance
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around two to five per cent
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia is human papillomavirus independent and aggressive
Biopsy any area that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or unresponsive to adequate treatment
Adequate steroid use is confirmed by quantity used, not by the prescription alone
explanation.pearls: A useful adherence check in this condition is the quantity of ointment consumed: a 30 g tube should last roughly twelve weeks on maintenance and about four weeks during induction, so a patient whose disease is uncontrolled while a single tube has lasted a year is under-treated, whereas one who has used the expected amount and still has a focal lesion needs a biopsy.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: An incidental 5 cm unilocular ovarian cyst with a normal tumour marker eight years after the last period
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman referred after a computed tomography scan performed for renal colic showed a right ovarian cyst. Her last menstrual period was eight years ago and she has had no bleeding since.

She has no abdominal pain, no bloating, no early satiety and no change in bowel or urinary habit, and her weight is stable. No relative has had ovarian, breast, bowel or endometrial cancer. A dedicated transvaginal ultrasound has now been performed and is reported below, and her tumour marker has been measured.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no palpable mass and no shifting dullness, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, normal vulva and cervix on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a right ovarian cyst of 5.2 cm that is unilocular and anechoic with a thin smooth wall, no solid component, no papillary projections, no internal septations and no internal vascularity on Doppler; left ovary normal; no free fluid in the pelvis; CA125 18 kIU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for laparotomy and staging
options.rationale: Referral to a specialist centre is reserved for a high risk of malignancy index or for ultrasound features suggesting malignancy, and her index is at the bottom of the scale with a completely simple cyst and a normal marker. Staging surgery for a benign simple cyst carries all the morbidity and none of the benefit. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy at the local hospital within six weeks
options.rationale: Surgery is offered for symptomatic cysts, for cysts above about 5 cm that are enlarging or complex, or where the woman prefers it after discussion, and none of those apply to an asymptomatic simple cyst found incidentally. Oophorectomy also carries operative risk and is not required to make the diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound and the tumour marker in four to six months time
options.rationale: Simple unilocular anechoic cysts under about 5 to 10 cm in postmenopausal women carry a risk of malignancy well under one per cent, and with a normal marker the calculated risk index here is at the lowest level, so conservative surveillance is appropriate. Repeat imaging at four to six months confirms stability or resolution, and most such cysts resolve or remain unchanged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any other decision
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for characterising a lesion that is indeterminate on ultrasound, particularly for distinguishing endometriomas, dermoids and fibroids, and this cyst is not indeterminate: it has every feature of a simple benign cyst. Additional imaging adds cost and anxiety without changing the plan. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Discharge her with no further imaging as the tumour marker is normal
options.rationale: The marker is normal in around half of early stage ovarian cancers and is raised in many benign conditions, so it is never used alone to exclude malignancy and is interpreted only alongside the ultrasound morphology and menopausal status. One period of surveillance to confirm stability is what makes conservative management safe. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

explanation.summary: The assessment of an adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman rests on combining ultrasound morphology, the CA125 concentration and menopausal status, conventionally through the risk of malignancy index, which multiplies an ultrasound feature score by a menopausal score by the marker value. Ultrasound features that raise concern are multilocularity, solid areas, papillary projections, bilateral lesions, ascites and intra-abdominal metastases, and a cyst with none of these scores zero. Simple unilocular anechoic cysts are common after menopause, are found in roughly one in five women on transvaginal scanning, and carry a risk of malignancy well below one per cent, so they are managed conservatively with a repeat scan rather than operated on. CA125 is unreliable in isolation because it is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and raised by endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, heart failure, liver disease and any peritoneal irritation, which is why it is never used as a screening test in the general population. Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre is indicated for a high index, because operating within such a centre improves staging quality and survival.
key_points: The risk index combines ultrasound score, menopausal status and the marker value
Simple unilocular anechoic cysts carry a malignancy risk well under one per cent
CA125 is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and is never used alone
Conservative surveillance with a repeat scan at four to six months is standard
A high index warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgery
explanation.pearls: Tell her what to come back for rather than only when: persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal or pelvic pain and urinary urgency occurring on most days for more than a few weeks are the symptom cluster associated with ovarian cancer, and new symptoms of that kind matter more than the next scheduled scan.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: A request for permanent contraception from a woman of twenty six who has never been pregnant
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old electrician who asks to be referred for an operation to permanently prevent pregnancy. She has been with the same partner for four years, has never been pregnant, and says she has known since her teens that she does not want children.

She has taken the combined pill for eight years, forgets it two or three times a month and has troublesome breakthrough bleeding, and has twice used emergency contraception in the past year. She has seen two other general practitioners about this and was told each time that she would change her mind, which she found humiliating. She has no medical contraindication to any contraceptive method, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. Her partner supports whatever she decides.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
