data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no mass, no clinical evidence of anaemia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), urine pregnancy test negative, cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus twelve months ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer her directly for laparoscopic tubal occlusion without further discussion
options.rationale: Referral without a comparison of the options is not respect for autonomy but an incomplete consent process, since a decision can only be informed if she knows that reversible methods match or beat the procedure for effectiveness. Referral remains entirely appropriate once that conversation has happened and she still wants it. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Recommend a contraceptive implant or intrauterine device as the first option
options.rationale: Long acting reversible methods have failure rates of around 0.05 to 0.2 per cent a year, which equals or betters tubal occlusion, while avoiding a general anaesthetic and remaining reversible, and they solve the specific problem that is failing her now, which is a method requiring daily action. Recommending it is a clinical recommendation rather than a refusal: if she considers it and still wants a permanent procedure, she is referred. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Decline the request and advise her to return when she is over thirty five
options.rationale: There is no age threshold for permanent contraception in Australia and a competent adult may consent to it, so refusing on age alone is paternalistic and has already driven her from two practices. Younger age and nulliparity are associated with higher rates of later regret, which is a reason to counsel carefully rather than to refuse. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Recommend that her partner have a vasectomy instead of any procedure for her
options.rationale: Vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper than tubal occlusion and deserves discussion, but it is his decision to make in his own consultation, and a method that depends on the relationship continuing does not protect her if it ends. It cannot be recommended as her contraceptive plan. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Recommend the progestogen only pill and review her bleeding in three months
options.rationale: Switching to another daily tablet ignores the reason her current method is failing, which is that she cannot reliably take a pill every day, and the progestogen only pill is less forgiving of late doses than the combined pill. It also causes irregular bleeding in a substantial proportion of users. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: A request for permanent contraception from a young woman without children tests the difference between counselling and gatekeeping. A competent adult can consent to sterilisation at any age in Australia, and refusing on the basis of age or parity is not clinically defensible, yet the doctor still owes her an accurate comparison of the options before referral. The comparison genuinely favours long acting reversible methods on the numbers: the etonogestrel implant fails in roughly 0.05 per cent of users a year and intrauterine devices in about 0.1 to 0.8 per cent, against a cumulative ten year failure rate of around 1.9 per cent for tubal occlusion with the added risk that a pregnancy after the procedure is more likely to be ectopic. Regret after sterilisation is reported by around one in five women sterilised before the age of thirty compared with under one in twenty afterwards, and it is higher again after nulliparity and after a decision made around the time of a birth or a relationship change. Counselling covers permanence, the failure rate, the ectopic risk, the surgical risks and the alternatives including vasectomy, and if she still chooses the procedure after that, the referral is made without further obstruction.
key_points: A competent adult may consent to permanent contraception at any age in Australia
Implants and intrauterine devices match or beat tubal occlusion for effectiveness
Pregnancy occurring after tubal occlusion is more likely to be ectopic
Regret is higher when sterilisation occurs before thirty and after nulliparity
Counsel fully, then refer if she still chooses the procedure
explanation.pearls: If she proceeds to a tubal procedure, current Australian practice is complete removal of both tubes rather than clipping or ligation, because the distal tube is now understood to be the origin of most high grade serous ovarian cancers and salpingectomy at the time of another operation is the one accessible risk reducing step available to the general population.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Planning birth when unprotected fetal vessels are seen crossing the membranes below the presenting part
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman at 32 weeks in her first pregnancy, conceived after in vitro fertilisation. Her morphology scan reported a bilobed placenta and a repeat transvaginal scan today has been arranged because of that finding.

The scan shows fetal vessels running through the membranes across the internal os, 1 cm below the presenting part, confirmed as fetal in origin on colour and pulsed wave Doppler. She has had no bleeding and no contractions, the membranes are intact, fetal growth is on the 55th centile and the cardiotocograph is normal. She lives forty minutes from the hospital and has been counselled about the range of birth options by the consultant.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, no vaginal bleeding, cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing fetal vessels crossing the internal os within the membranes, bilobed placenta, fetal growth on the 55th centile, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and perform emergency caesarean only if bleeding or labour occurs
options.rationale: Waiting for bleeding means waiting for fetal haemorrhage, and even an immediate response in a fully staffed unit rarely reaches the baby in time because the total fetal blood volume at this gestation is only around 250 mL. Admission is to shorten the response time for the unexpected, not to be the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Manage as an outpatient, give corticosteroids at 36 weeks, and plan caesarean section at 39 weeks before labour
options.rationale: Around a third of women labour or rupture membranes before 37 weeks, and this condition gives no warning and no time to intervene once that happens. Waiting to 39 weeks trades a modest gain in maturity for the specific catastrophe the diagnosis predicts. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Manage as an outpatient, plan induction of labour at 38 weeks, and perform amniotomy under direct vision in theatre
options.rationale: Any plan involving labour exposes the vessels to spontaneous or artificial rupture, and controlled amniotomy does not protect vessels that tear with uterine activity or with the presenting part descending. Vaginal birth is not an option once these vessels are confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and plan caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks before labour
options.rationale: Unprotected fetal vessels overlying the os rupture when the membranes do, and the fetal blood volume is so small that exsanguination occurs within minutes. Planned abdominal birth before labour, with steroids and inpatient proximity to theatre, converts a condition with very high perinatal mortality into one with survival above 95 percent. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal scan at 36 weeks, and decide on the mode of birth only if the vessels still overlie the os
options.rationale: Unlike a low lying placenta, which migrates as the lower segment forms, vessels running within the membranes do not move away from the os. Building a plan around resolution that does not occur risks the woman labouring while the decision is still open. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes fetal vessels running unsupported through the membranes over the internal os, typically arising from a velamentous cord insertion or connecting the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta. In vitro fertilisation, a low lying placenta in the second trimester and multiple pregnancy all raise the risk, which is why targeted transvaginal colour Doppler is performed when those features appear. When the diagnosis is missed, membrane rupture tears the vessels and the foetus exsanguinates into the vagina, with perinatal mortality historically above half. When it is made antenatally and birth is planned by caesarean before labour, survival exceeds 95 percent. Australian practice is corticosteroids and inpatient admission from around 32 weeks with delivery at 34 to 36 weeks, balancing prematurity against the unpredictable timing of membrane rupture.
key_points: Velamentous cord insertion and bilobed or succenturiate placentas are the substrates
Diagnosis is by transvaginal colour and pulsed wave Doppler confirming fetal vessels
Planned caesarean before labour at 34 to 36 weeks is the management
These vessels do not migrate away from the os as gestation advances
Antenatal diagnosis is the single variable that determines survival
explanation.pearls: Painless vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture with an immediate fetal bradycardia or a sinusoidal trace is fetal blood until proven otherwise and calls for immediate delivery, not for maternal resuscitation, because the mother is haemodynamically well while the baby is the one bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Vasa praevia

subtopic_detail: Sudden fetal bradycardia with rising station during trial of labour after a previous caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to a 33 year old woman at 40 weeks having a trial of labour after one previous caesarean. She has an epidural in situ and is on a low dose oxytocin infusion for slow progress, and forty minutes ago she was 8 cm dilated with the vertex at station zero.

The cardiotocograph has fallen to a baseline of 80 beats per minute over the past four minutes with no recovery. Her pulse is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. She reports no pain but feels suddenly unwell and nauseated. On vaginal examination the presenting part is now at station minus 2 and there is fresh blood at the introitus. The uterus feels unusually soft between the infrequent contractions on the tocograph.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 80 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Presenting part risen from station zero to minus 2, fresh vaginal bleeding, uterus soft between contractions, epidural block to T10
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocography showing a prolonged deceleration to 80 beats per minute for four minutes, haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155) on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin, give a tocolytic and reassess the trace over the next ten minutes before deciding
options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is appropriate for a bradycardia caused by uterine hyperstimulation, but the tocograph shows infrequent contractions and a soft uterus, which is the opposite pattern. Spending ten minutes reassessing here uses up the interval in which the baby and the mother are salvageable. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Perform fetal scalp lactate sampling to establish whether the bradycardia reflects significant acidosis
options.rationale: Scalp sampling is invalid during a prolonged deceleration and requires several minutes that this situation does not have. It also answers the wrong question, since the maternal signs already indicate a surgical emergency independent of the fetal blood gas. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Attempt an instrumental birth in the room, since she is 8 cm dilated and the head was recently at station zero
options.rationale: She is not fully dilated and the presenting part has risen, so the prerequisites for instrumental birth are absent, and traction on a head that is being displaced by a ruptured uterus worsens the tear. The recent station is a trap because it describes where the head was before the event. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparotomy with the neonatal team called and major haemorrhage protocol activated
options.rationale: A prolonged bradycardia with loss of station, fresh bleeding, maternal tachycardia and hypotension during a trial of labour is uterine rupture until proven otherwise, and the only treatment is immediate surgical delivery and repair. Maternal and fetal survival both fall sharply with every ten minutes of delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Give a fluid bolus and reposition her to the left lateral, then repeat the vaginal examination in five minutes
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is correct for a bradycardia caused by aortocaval compression or hypotension after an epidural top up, neither of which explains fresh bleeding and a presenting part that has risen. These measures delay the laparotomy that is the actual treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates roughly one in 200 trials of labour after caesarean, and abnormal fetal heart rate patterns, usually a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia, are the presenting feature in the great majority. Classical teaching emphasises scar pain, but working epidurals mask it, so the reliable signs are fetal, haemodynamic and mechanical: sudden bradycardia, maternal tachycardia and hypotension out of proportion to visible loss, fresh vaginal bleeding, loss of the previously recorded station, and cessation of effective contractions. Recognition is the whole task, because the treatment is immediate laparotomy with delivery and repair or, occasionally, hysterectomy. Neonatal outcome deteriorates rapidly beyond about ten to twenty minutes from the onset of the bradycardia, so investigations that add minutes are themselves harmful.
key_points: Abnormal fetal heart rate is the commonest presenting sign of scar rupture
An epidural masks scar pain, so absence of pain is not reassuring
Loss of station and fresh bleeding with maternal tachycardia complete the picture
Immediate laparotomy is the treatment, not further fetal assessment
Contractions often become infrequent and the uterus feels soft after rupture
explanation.pearls: Recheck the station yourself rather than accepting the last documented value, because a presenting part that has risen between two examinations is close to specific for rupture and is the single finding most often missing from the notes of cases reviewed after a poor outcome.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Discordant liquor volumes in a shared placenta twin pregnancy at the mid second trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a maternal fetal medicine clinic reviewing a 26 year old woman at 20 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, confirmed by a single placental mass and a T sign at 11 weeks.

Today's scan shows the deepest vertical pocket in the first sac at 1 cm with the bladder not visible, and in the second sac at 9 cm with a distended bladder. The second twin has absent end diastolic flow in the umbilical artery and a normal ductus venosus a wave. Estimated weights are discordant by 18 percent. Both twins have normal anatomy and both have cardiac activity. Her cervix measures 34 mm and she has no contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus larger than dates, soft and non tender, cervix closed on ultrasound at 34 mm
data_table.Investigations: Monochorionic diamniotic twins at 20 weeks, deepest vertical pocket 1 cm in twin one with bladder not visualised and 9 cm in twin two with distended bladder, absent end diastolic flow in twin two umbilical artery, estimated weight discordance 18 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange fortnightly growth scans with umbilical artery Dopplers and intervene if the discordance exceeds 25 percent
options.rationale: Growth discordance surveillance is the pathway for selective fetal growth restriction, a different complication of a shared placenta in which liquor volumes stay normal. Here the liquor discrepancy with an absent and a distended bladder defines a condition that progresses over days. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform serial amnioreduction from the polyhydramniotic sac and repeat the scan at weekly intervals
options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves the pressure and prolongs the pregnancy but leaves the anastomoses intact, so the randomised comparison showed worse survival and more neurological injury than laser. It is reserved for gestations beyond the laser window or where laser is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Administer maternal corticosteroids and plan delivery of both twins within the next forty eight hours
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is below the threshold of viability and guarantees the loss of both twins, so it cannot be the response to a treatable condition. Steroids have no role at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the larger twin from injury
options.rationale: Selective reduction is considered when one twin is already severely compromised or has a lethal anomaly and the other is at risk, not as first line when both twins are alive with a treatable vascular imbalance. It forfeits one healthy twin unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Refer for foetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses at a specialist fetal therapy centre
options.rationale: Laser ablation treats the cause by dividing the vascular connections that drive the transfusion, and it gives higher survival and markedly lower neurological morbidity than drainage for disease at this stage and gestation. Australian practice is urgent referral to one of the small number of centres offering the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates about one in ten monochorionic pregnancies and arises from unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses within the shared placenta. Diagnosis rests on the liquor discrepancy alone, defined in Australia as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other, and staging then follows the Quintero system: stage one is the liquor discrepancy, stage two adds a non visible donor bladder, stage three adds critically abnormal Dopplers, stage four hydrops and stage five death of either twin. Foetoscopic laser ablation divides the offending anastomoses and is the treatment of choice from about 16 to 26 weeks, with survival of at least one twin above 80 percent. Untreated advanced disease carries mortality above 90 percent, so recognition and immediate referral matter more than any bedside intervention.
key_points: Deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other defines the condition
A non visible donor bladder and abnormal Dopplers mark advancing Quintero stages
Foetoscopic laser ablation is first line between about 16 and 26 weeks
Amnioreduction gives worse survival and more neurological injury than laser
Selective growth restriction differs because liquor volumes remain normal
explanation.pearls: Establish chorionicity at the first trimester scan and record it in the handheld notes, because a lambda sign at 11 weeks excludes this condition entirely while a T sign commits the woman to fortnightly scanning from 16 weeks, and chorionicity cannot be reliably determined once the second trimester is well advanced.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Tense ascites and haemoconcentration in the luteal phase after an assisted reproduction cycle
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar admitting a 31 year old woman nine days after oocyte retrieval and five days after a fresh embryo transfer. She has marked abdominal distension, breathlessness when lying flat, and has passed only 300 mL of urine in the past twelve hours.

Her pulse is 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Her abdomen is tensely distended with shifting dullness, and her calves are soft. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries measuring 11 cm bilaterally with gross ascites, and no ovarian torsion on Doppler. Her haematocrit is 0.52, white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, sodium 129 mmol/L and albumin 26 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tensely distended abdomen with shifting dullness, reduced air entry at both bases, calves soft and equal
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.52 (0.36-0.46), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), ultrasound showing 11 cm ovaries with gross ascites and normal Doppler flow

lead_in: Which combination of measures is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, fluid restriction to one litre daily and hypertonic saline for the low sodium level
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia here is dilutional and resolves with correction of the underlying leak, so hypertonic saline treats a number rather than the patient and risks overcorrection. Fluid restriction is directly contrary to the need to refill the intravascular space. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and laparoscopic ovarian cyst aspiration under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgery on friable enlarged ovaries risks haemorrhage and rupture and does nothing for the ascites that is driving her symptoms. Operative intervention is reserved for torsion, rupture with bleeding, or an unrelated surgical diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, broad spectrum antibiotics and computed tomography of the abdomen for the raised white cell count
options.rationale: Leucocytosis above 15 x10^9/L is characteristic of this syndrome itself and does not indicate infection in an afebrile woman with a clear ultrasound diagnosis. Antibiotics and further imaging delay the drainage and anticoagulation that change the course. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites
options.rationale: Diuresis in a woman who is intravascularly depleted worsens the haemoconcentration and the acute kidney injury, even though she looks overloaded. Frusemide is considered only after the intravascular compartment has been restored and oliguria persists. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites
options.rationale: The pathology is capillary leak with intravascular depletion despite total body fluid overload, so the circulation is refilled while the third space is drained to relieve pressure on the diaphragm and renal veins. Thromboprophylaxis is mandatory because haemoconcentration and high oestradiol make this one of the strongest acquired thrombotic states in gynaecology. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome follows gonadotrophin stimulation and is mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor released from luteinised granulosa cells, producing capillary leak with ascites, pleural effusions and intravascular depletion. Late onset disease appearing more than a week after retrieval is driven by endogenous human chorionic gonadotrophin from an implanting pregnancy and tends to be more severe and more prolonged than the early form. Severity is graded on symptoms, haematocrit, white cell count, renal function and the presence of tense ascites or hydrothorax. Management is supportive and rests on three pillars: intravascular volume replacement, thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin, and drainage of tense ascites, which relieves dyspnoea and often restores urine output by lowering intra abdominal pressure. Diuretics and surgery both make things worse in the absence of specific indications.
key_points: Capillary leak means intravascular depletion despite visible fluid overload
Late onset disease implies an implanting pregnancy and runs a longer course
Replace volume, anticoagulate, and drain tense ascites
Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and renal impairment
Leucocytosis is part of the syndrome and does not indicate infection
explanation.pearls: Thrombosis in this syndrome occurs characteristically in the internal jugular and subclavian veins rather than the legs, and can appear weeks after the ascites has resolved, so neck or arm swelling in a woman who had a stimulated cycle in the past two months warrants imaging even if she now feels well.

subtopic_detail: Breakthrough convulsions in the second trimester when the plasma drug concentration has fallen
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation, controlled on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and seizure free for three years before conception.

She has had two generalised convulsions in the past fortnight, one while driving her car into the driveway. She has taken every dose, confirmed by her partner and by a dispensing history, and she takes no other medication and no oral contraceptive. She has been on high dose folic acid since before conception. Her plasma lamotrigine concentration is 40 percent below her preconception value, her sodium, calcium, glucose and full blood count are normal, and she has no fever, no headache and no hypertension. Fetal growth and morphology are normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Fully alert between episodes, no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema, no hyperreflexia or clonus
data_table.Investigations: Plasma lamotrigine concentration 40 percent below the preconception value, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), glucose 4.6 mmol/L, haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), urine protein negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by repeated concentration measurements through the rest of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Oestrogen driven induction of glucuronidation increases lamotrigine clearance markedly from the first trimester, so the same dose produces falling concentrations and breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman. Dosing is adjusted upward against serial levels with a planned reduction in the days after birth as clearance returns to baseline. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Admit for magnesium sulfate and expedite delivery, managing this as an atypical eclamptic presentation
options.rationale: Eclampsia requires hypertension or proteinuria or other features of the disease, and her blood pressure, urinalysis and reflexes are all normal with a known seizure disorder to explain the events. Magnesium is not a treatment for epilepsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch her to levetiracetam over the coming weeks, with concentrations repeated after the change is complete
options.rationale: Changing agent mid pregnancy exposes the foetus to two drugs during the transition and risks further seizures while neither is at an effective level. Levetiracetam is a reasonable preconception choice but is not the response to a predictable fall in concentration. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue the current dose and add clobazam intermittently for clusters, with concentrations repeated each trimester
options.rationale: Adding a second agent increases fetal exposure and side effects without correcting the pharmacokinetic change that caused the breakthrough. The simpler and safer step is to restore the concentration that previously controlled her seizures. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Reduce the lamotrigine dose to limit fetal exposure and manage her seizures with sleep and trigger avoidance
options.rationale: Generalised convulsions carry maternal and fetal risks including trauma, hypoxia, placental abruption and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, all of which outweigh the risk of this drug, which has one of the lowest malformation rates in the class. Reducing the dose inverts the risk balance. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy alters the handling of most antiseizure medicines through increased volume of distribution, increased renal clearance, reduced protein binding and, for lamotrigine specifically, strong induction of uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase by rising oestrogen. Lamotrigine clearance can more than double by the third trimester, and the resulting fall in concentration is the commonest reason for seizure deterioration in an adherent woman. Australian practice is to establish a preconception target concentration in a woman who is seizure free, measure at least each trimester, and increase the dose to maintain that individual target rather than to a population range. Seizure control matters because convulsions carry risks of trauma, abruption, fetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and driving restrictions apply as they would outside pregnancy. Because clearance falls rapidly after birth, the dose must be brought back down over the first one to two weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity.
key_points: Oestrogen induced glucuronidation markedly increases lamotrigine clearance
Falling concentration is the usual cause of breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman
Set an individual preconception target and measure at least each trimester
Seizure risks to mother and foetus outweigh the risk of this drug
Reduce the dose over one to two weeks after birth as clearance falls
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum taper on the discharge plan at the time you increase the dose antenatally, because clearance returns towards baseline within days of delivery and a woman left on her third trimester dose typically presents at two weeks with ataxia, diplopia and vomiting from toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Counselling about mode of birth when anal sphincter symptoms persist after a previous severe tear
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32 year old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was a forceps delivery with a repaired tear extending through both parts of the anal sphincter.

Since then she has had urgency of the bowels most days and has lost control of wind and, on three occasions in the past year, of loose stool. Endoanal ultrasound shows a persistent defect across a quarter of the sphincter circumference and anorectal manometry shows reduced resting and squeeze pressures. She has had pelvic floor physiotherapy for six months with limited benefit. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile and the current estimated fetal weight is appropriate for gestation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Perineal scar with a thinned perineal body, reduced voluntary anal squeeze on digital examination
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound showing a persistent defect over 25 percent of the sphincter circumference, anorectal manometry showing reduced resting and squeeze pressures, fetal growth on the 50th centile

lead_in: What would you first recommend about the mode of birth?

options.text: Elective caesarean section, booked at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks of abdominal birth
options.rationale: A woman who remains symptomatic after a previous severe tear and who has both a structural defect and abnormal manometry faces a high risk of irreversible deterioration in continence with another vaginal birth. In that specific combination abdominal birth is the recommended option rather than one of several equivalents. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Vaginal birth with an elective mediolateral episiotomy, planned at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks
options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not protect a sphincter that is already deficient and adds its own morbidity, and the evidence for prophylactic episiotomy in this group is not supportive. It offers false reassurance in the highest risk situation. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Vaginal birth avoiding instrumental delivery, planned at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks of each route
options.rationale: Avoiding forceps lowers but does not remove the risk, and a further tear or simple stretching of a compromised sphincter can convert manageable urgency into daily faecal incontinence. This is reasonable counselling for a woman who is asymptomatic with normal tests, which she is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Secondary sphincter repair during this pregnancy, followed by vaginal birth planned at 39 weeks
options.rationale: Sphincter repair is not performed in pregnancy, and its results deteriorate over time so it is reserved for women with disabling incontinence who have completed their families. It cannot be used to make a vaginal birth safe. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Further pelvic floor physiotherapy with biofeedback, and a decision about the mode of birth deferred to 37 weeks
options.rationale: Six months of physiotherapy has already failed and nine further weeks will not repair a structural defect, while deferring the decision leaves her at risk of presenting in labour without a plan. Physiotherapy continues alongside the decision rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury complicates about 3 percent of vaginal births and up to 6 percent of first vaginal births, with forceps delivery the strongest modifiable risk factor. Counselling about a subsequent birth depends on two things: whether she has symptoms, and what the sphincter looks like and does on testing. A woman who is asymptomatic with a normal endoanal ultrasound and normal manometry can be supported to have a vaginal birth with a small risk of recurrence. A woman who is symptomatic, or who has a significant structural defect with abnormal pressures, should be advised that a further vaginal birth carries a substantial risk of worsening incontinence, and elective caesarean is recommended. All women with a previous severe tear should be assessed in a dedicated perineal clinic before the next birth rather than at the time of labour.
key_points: Forceps delivery is the strongest modifiable risk factor for sphincter injury
Symptoms plus an ultrasound defect and abnormal manometry favour abdominal birth
Asymptomatic women with normal tests may be supported for vaginal birth
Routine episiotomy does not protect a previously injured sphincter
Secondary repair is for completed families, not to enable a vaginal birth
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about loss of control of wind and about bowel urgency rather than about incontinence of stool, because women consistently under report this and the question phrased as faecal incontinence is answered no by the majority who in fact have symptoms that would change the birth plan.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Perineal care

subtopic_detail: Severe period pain in a teenager with a normal pelvic ultrasound and school absence
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old girl brought by her mother because of period pain that has kept her home from school for two or three days every month for the past eighteen months. She describes cramping that starts a day before bleeding and continues for three days, and pain with opening her bowels during her period.

She has tried paracetamol and has not used a regular anti inflammatory. She is not sexually active. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound arranged by another doctor was reported as normal with no endometrioma and no adenomyosis. Her periods are regular at 29 days, her haemoglobin and ferritin are normal, and her growth and development are normal. Her mother asks whether she needs an operation to find out what is wrong.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, mild suprapubic tenderness, no masses, no internal examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound normal, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), ferritin 46 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: A trial of regular non steroidal anti inflammatory medication with continuous hormonal treatment, reviewed in three months
options.rationale: Empirical medical treatment is first line in adolescents with symptoms suggesting endometriosis, because a normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal disease and a good response avoids surgery altogether. Continuous rather than cyclical dosing suppresses the menstruation that drives the pain. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to look for deep infiltrating disease before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is useful for mapping deep infiltrating disease before complex surgery, not for diagnosis in an adolescent who has not yet had medical treatment. A normal scan would not change the plan and an incidental finding could lead to unnecessary surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Referral for diagnostic laparoscopy to establish the diagnosis histologically before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is no longer required to make the diagnosis, and operating on a teenager before medical treatment has been tried exposes her to surgical risk and to a negative result that does not exclude the condition. Surgery follows failed medical management, not precedes it. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy, arranged through a gynaecology clinic
options.rationale: These agents are reserved for disease that has failed first line hormonal treatment, and in an adolescent they raise particular concern about bone mineral density during the years of peak accrual. Starting there skips several safer and effective steps. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Reassurance that this is primary dysmenorrhoea with paracetamol as needed and review if her symptoms worsen
options.rationale: Pain causing regular school absence and pain on defaecation during menstruation are the features that separate this from ordinary period pain, and normalising them is why Australian women wait years for a diagnosis. Reassurance without treatment leaves a modifiable problem untreated. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects roughly one in seven Australian women and the average delay from first symptom to diagnosis has historically been six to eight years, much of it spent being told that severe period pain is normal. The current Australian guideline explicitly abandons laparoscopy as the requirement for diagnosis: a clinical diagnosis can be made from the symptom pattern, and empirical treatment started, because a normal ultrasound excludes endometrioma and deep disease but says nothing about superficial peritoneal implants. First line treatment is a regular non steroidal anti inflammatory taken from before the pain begins, combined with continuous hormonal suppression using a combined pill, a progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. Symptoms that persist after three to six months of adequate treatment prompt gynaecology referral, at which point laparoscopy becomes both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: A normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal endometriosis
Clinical diagnosis and empirical treatment come before any surgery
Continuous rather than cyclical hormonal dosing suppresses symptom cycles
Non steroidal anti inflammatory taken before the pain starts works better than after
Refer when three to six months of adequate medical treatment fails
explanation.pearls: Pain on opening the bowels or on passing urine that occurs only during menstruation is far more specific for endometriosis than the severity of the cramping itself, and asking that single cyclical question separates the teenagers who need treatment now from the much larger group with primary dysmenorrhoea.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

subtopic_detail: Bleeding after the menopause in a woman taking an oestrogen receptor modulator for breast cancer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 61 year old woman who has had two episodes of vaginal bleeding in the past month. Her last menstrual period was nine years ago and she has taken tamoxifen for four years after surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer.

Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and several small cystic spaces, and a normal ovarian appearance. She takes no other hormonal treatment, has never used menopausal hormone therapy, and her cervical screening has been up to date and negative. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she has no hypertension or diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulva and vagina, cervix appears healthy, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing endometrial thickness 9 mm with cystic change, normal ovaries, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155), cervical screening negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Blind endometrial sampling with a suction device in the clinic, accepting the result if it shows benign endometrium
options.rationale: A blind sample misses focal lesions, and tamoxifen associated pathology is characteristically focal within polyps, so a benign result cannot be accepted as excluding carcinoma. Hysteroscopy allows the lesion to be seen and sampled directly. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

options.text: Reassurance and repeat ultrasound in three months, as the thickness is above the 4 mm threshold used generally
options.rationale: The 4 mm threshold applies to women not taking this drug, and in any case exceeding it is an indication for biopsy rather than for repeat imaging. Rescanning a woman who is bleeding delays diagnosis by a further three months. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

options.text: Cease the tamoxifen and observe whether the bleeding settles over the following three months before investigating
options.rationale: Stopping adjuvant endocrine therapy for a hormone sensitive breast cancer has real oncological consequences and must not be done on the basis of bleeding that has not been investigated. The drug is usually continued while the endometrium is assessed. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

options.text: Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy, arranged regardless of the measured endometrial thickness
options.rationale: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial cystic change and stromal oedema that inflate the measured thickness and make sonographic thresholds unreliable, so imaging cannot be used to triage. Direct visualisation with targeted biopsy is required because this drug raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma and of polyps. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

options.text: Reassurance and repeat ultrasound in three months, as the thickness is below the 10 mm threshold for this drug
options.rationale: No validated thickness threshold exists for women on this drug, and reporting a measurement as reassuring is the specific error the sonographic appearance invites. Bleeding after the menopause requires tissue whatever the number. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

explanation.summary: Bleeding after the menopause carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma and always requires assessment. In women not on tamoxifen, transvaginal ultrasound is a valid first test and an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has a high negative predictive value, allowing some women to avoid instrumentation. Tamoxifen changes that calculus completely: it acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, producing polyps, hyperplasia, subendothelial cystic change and stromal oedema that thicken the measurement without indicating malignancy, while also roughly doubling to trebling the risk of carcinoma. There is no reliable sonographic cut off in these women, and the pathology is typically focal, so hysteroscopy with directed biopsy rather than blind sampling is the appropriate investigation. Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound for the same reason.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries about a one in ten risk of endometrial cancer
The 4 mm sonographic threshold does not apply to women taking tamoxifen
Tamoxifen related pathology is focal, so blind sampling can miss it
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the investigation of choice
Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened by ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Keep the tamoxifen going while the endometrium is investigated, and involve the treating oncologist before any decision to switch to an aromatase inhibitor, because in a postmenopausal woman that switch removes the endometrial risk but brings bone loss and arthralgia that need their own management plan.

subtopic_detail: Endometrial thickness threshold triggering tissue sampling in postmenopausal bleeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman who reports two episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks, each lasting a day. Her last menstrual period was seven years ago and she has never used menopausal hormone therapy.

Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and a small amount of old blood in the vault, and her cervical screening test from last year was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrial echo measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion and normal ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows regular endometrial thickness 9 mm, no focal lesion, both ovaries normal, human papillomavirus screening negative last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her and arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in three months time
options.rationale: A thickness of 9 mm is already well above the threshold at which sampling is indicated, so repeating the same measurement cannot reclassify her. Interval imaging in this setting delays a diagnosis in which stage at presentation drives survival. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Commence a trial of cyclical oral progestogen and review the bleeding pattern in three months
options.rationale: Progestogen therapy is a treatment for confirmed hyperplasia without atypia and may mask bleeding from an undiagnosed carcinoma. Treating the symptom before establishing the histology removes the only warning sign the patient has. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test with reflex cytology and review the result in a month
options.rationale: Cervical screening looks for a different disease at a different site and a negative human papillomavirus result does not address the endometrium at all. Her cervix is visibly healthy, so the bleeding source needs to be sought above the internal os. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy under the care of a gynaecologist
options.rationale: An endometrial thickness above 4 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue diagnosis, and at 9 mm with obesity and diabetes her risk of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma is substantial. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation as well as sampling, which matters because focal lesions can be missed by blind biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Request serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the laboratory reference range
options.rationale: CA125 is used in the assessment of an adnexal mass rather than of endometrial bleeding, and it is neither sensitive nor specific for early endometrial carcinoma. Using a normal result as a gate to referral would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma and is the symptom that makes this the most curable of the gynaecological cancers, because it declares itself while disease is still confined to the uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is used as a triage tool rather than a diagnostic one: a thin regular endometrium at or below 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and permits observation, while anything above that threshold requires tissue. Obesity drives risk through peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrone in adipose tissue, producing unopposed oestrogen exposure, and diabetes and nulliparity compound it. Recurrent bleeding despite a reassuring initial assessment always warrants repeat investigation, because the negative predictive value applies to a single episode rather than to a pattern.
key_points: Endometrial thickness above 4 mm with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue sampling
A thickness at or below 4 mm with a single episode of bleeding permits observation
Obesity, diabetes, nulliparity and late menopause all raise endometrial cancer risk
Hysteroscopy adds direct visualisation and detects focal lesions that blind sampling misses
Recurrent bleeding after a reassuring scan mandates repeat assessment regardless
explanation.pearls: Around 90% of women with endometrial carcinoma present with abnormal bleeding, which is why any postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation within weeks, and why the 4 mm cut-off applies only to women not taking menopausal hormone therapy.

subtopic_detail: Follow-up requirement for an incidental simple ovarian cyst found in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 27-year-old woman who had an abdominal ultrasound last week for intermittent right-sided discomfort that has since settled completely. She has regular 29-day cycles, no intermenstrual bleeding and no change in bowel or bladder habit.

Her abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable mass, and a bimanual examination is unremarkable. She has no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. The ultrasound describes a 42 mm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid areas, no internal septations and no vascularity on Doppler, with a normal left ovary and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no palpable mass, bimanual examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Right ovary contains a 42 mm unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation, no Doppler flow; left ovary normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for consideration of laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy this year
options.rationale: Surgery on a physiological cyst removes normal ovarian cortex and reduces ovarian reserve for no benefit, and carries operative and adhesion risk. Cystectomy is reserved for persistent symptomatic cysts, suspicious features or acute complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the formation of further cysts
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception reduces the incidence of new functional cysts over time but does not hasten resolution of one already present. Prescribing it as treatment for this finding implies the cyst needs treating, which it does not. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to confirm that the cyst has resolved
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is reserved for simple cysts between 50 and 70 mm, which are followed yearly, and for any cyst with complex features. Scanning a 42 mm simple cyst generates incidental findings and anxiety without changing management. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Request serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding on referral
options.rationale: The risk of malignancy index is validated in postmenopausal women and performs poorly before menopause, where CA125 rises with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and pelvic inflammation. Applying it to a simple cyst in a young woman generates false positives and unnecessary surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Reassure her that no further imaging or gynaecology referral is required at this stage
options.rationale: A simple unilocular cyst under 50 mm in a premenopausal woman is a physiological finding that resolves spontaneously in the great majority of cases and carries no malignant potential. Australian and international guidance is explicit that cysts of this size and appearance need no follow-up imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cysts are found incidentally on a large proportion of pelvic scans in women of reproductive age, and most represent the normal physiology of follicular development or corpus luteum formation rather than disease. Sonographic characterisation does most of the diagnostic work: a unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation and no internal vascularity is described as simple and is effectively never malignant. Size then sets the follow-up, with the commonly used premenopausal thresholds being no follow-up below 50 mm, annual imaging between 50 and 70 mm, and further assessment with magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral above 70 mm where ultrasound cannot see the whole cyst. The important harm to avoid is overtreatment, since surgery on a young woman's ovary costs follicles permanently.
key_points: Simple premenopausal cysts under 50 mm need no follow-up imaging
Simple cysts of 50 to 70 mm are followed with yearly ultrasound
Cysts above 70 mm warrant magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral
The risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and misleads before menopause
Any solid component, thick septation or internal vascularity moves the cyst out of the simple category
explanation.pearls: A haemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst shows a characteristic lacy reticular internal pattern with no Doppler flow within the clot, and repeating the scan in the early follicular phase of the next cycle, around day 5 to 10, shows resolution and avoids an unnecessary referral.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Ovarian Cysts in Premenopausal Women

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dosing schedule for a low ferritin identified in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. She feels well, with no bleeding and normal fetal movements, and reports mild tiredness that she attributes to chasing a toddler.

She is vegetarian and her first child was born 14 months ago. Her booking bloods at 11 weeks were normal. Repeat bloods this week show haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100) and ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein and a normal white cell count and platelet count.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 148/min on Doppler, no pallor of the conjunctivae, no koilonychia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100), ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), white cell count and platelet count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose given as a single infusion in the day procedure unit
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when absorption is impaired, or when the gestation is too advanced for an oral response. At 20 weeks with no oral trial yet, it commits her to an infusion and its risks unnecessarily. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Dietary advice on iron rich foods alone with repeat full blood count at 28 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Diet cannot replete established deficiency within the timeframe of a pregnancy, and non-haem iron from a vegetarian diet is absorbed less efficiently than haem iron. Dietary advice belongs alongside supplementation rather than instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Oral elemental iron taken on alternate days on an empty stomach with vitamin C
options.rationale: A ferritin below 30 micrograms/L confirms depleted stores and oral iron is first line in the second trimester when there is time to respond before delivery. Alternate-day dosing produces greater fractional absorption than daily dosing because it avoids the hepcidin rise that a dose triggers for the following 24 hours. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Oral elemental iron taken three times daily with meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset
options.rationale: Divided daily dosing raises hepcidin and reduces the fraction absorbed from each subsequent dose, and taking iron with food further impairs uptake through phytate and calcium binding. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is dose frequency and timing rather than the drug itself. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Serum folate and vitamin B12 assay with treatment deferred until those results return
options.rationale: Folate and B12 deficiency cause macrocytosis rather than the microcytosis present here, and B12 is worth checking in a vegetarian but does not explain these indices. Deferring iron for a fortnight while a parallel test returns wastes treatment time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy to supply expanded maternal red cell mass, the foetus and the placenta, and a short interpregnancy interval means stores have had little chance to recover. Ferritin is the best single measure of iron stores but is an acute phase reactant, so a normal or raised value alongside a normal C-reactive protein is interpretable while a raised value with inflammation is not. Treatment matters beyond maternal symptoms, because antenatal iron deficiency is associated with low birth weight, preterm birth and reduced neonatal iron endowment that affects infant development. The hepcidin response to an oral dose suppresses absorption for around 24 hours, which is the physiological basis for alternate-day rather than divided daily dosing.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms/L indicates deficiency even when haemoglobin is only mildly reduced
Oral iron on alternate days is absorbed more efficiently than the same total dose split daily
Take iron away from food, tea, coffee and calcium, with vitamin C to aid absorption
Intravenous iron is for oral failure, intolerance, malabsorption or late gestation
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so interpret it alongside C-reactive protein
explanation.pearls: Expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L within 2 to 4 weeks of starting adequate oral iron, and treat failure to achieve that as a trigger to check adherence and reconsider the diagnosis rather than simply escalating the dose.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding when the uterine cavity is structurally normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon and a pad every hour on her two heaviest days, with clots the size of a twenty cent coin and two days off work each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days.

She has completed her family and would prefer not to become pregnant, though she is not seeking permanent contraception. Pelvic examination is normal with a normal sized mobile uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus with an endometrium of 6 mm, no fibroid and no polyp. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L (115-155) with ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200), and thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows normal uterus, endometrium 6 mm, no fibroid or polyp; haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155); ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: Which treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy started on the first day of each period
options.rationale: Non-steroidal agents reduce blood loss by around a fifth and help dysmenorrhoea, making them useful adjuncts, but they are the weakest of the medical options for volume. Used alone they are unlikely to correct bleeding severe enough to cause this degree of iron depletion. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Oral norethisterone taken from day five to day twenty six of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Long-course oral progestogen does reduce bleeding but requires daily tablets for three weeks of every cycle, is poorly tolerated and is less effective than an intrauterine device. Short luteal-phase courses are ineffective and should not be used at all. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Referral for endometrial ablation after counselling about future pregnancy implications
options.rationale: Ablation is effective but is a surgical procedure that mandates reliable contraception afterwards because pregnancy following ablation carries serious risk. It is considered after medical therapy has failed rather than before it has been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at her next convenient visit
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss more than any other medical therapy and is first line for heavy bleeding with a structurally normal cavity. It simultaneously provides the contraception she wants without committing her to a permanent procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Oral tranexamic acid taken during the heaviest days of each menstrual period only
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a reasonable option for a woman wanting non-hormonal treatment or trying to conceive, but the magnitude of benefit is smaller and it provides no contraception. It is the alternative when an intrauterine device is declined or unsuitable. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's physical, social and emotional quality of life rather than by a measured volume, so the history of flooding, clots and time off work is the diagnosis. The PALM-COEIN system separates structural causes, which are polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy, from non-structural ones including coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial and iatrogenic causes, and it directs the workup. A normal ultrasound with regular ovulatory cycles points to a primary endometrial disorder of haemostasis, which is the setting in which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system performs best. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of these women and must be treated alongside the bleeding rather than assumed to resolve with it.
key_points: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by quality of life impact, not by measured millilitres
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line when the cavity is structurally normal
Tranexamic acid and non-steroidal agents are non-hormonal options for women avoiding hormones or seeking pregnancy
Short luteal-phase progestogen courses are ineffective for heavy bleeding
Treat coexisting iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Around one in five women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche has an underlying bleeding disorder, most commonly von Willebrand disease, so bleeding that dates from the very first period warrants a coagulation screen and von Willebrand studies rather than empirical treatment alone.

subtopic_detail: Colposcopy pathway after human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 on a self collected screening sample
stem:
You are the general practitioner contacting a 41-year-old woman with her cervical screening result. She chose self collection because she had found previous speculum examinations distressing, and this was her first screening test in eleven years.

She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she is not pregnant. Her only previous screening results were normal cytology on two occasions in her twenties. The laboratory reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16, with a note that reflex cytology could not be performed on the self collected specimen.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test on a self collected vaginal sample: oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16; reflex liquid based cytology not performed on this specimen type

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months to see whether the infection clears
options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to women with oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 whose reflex cytology is negative or low grade. Applying it to a type 16 result in a woman screened once in eleven years risks allowing established high grade disease to progress. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Refer directly for colposcopy without arranging any further sampling beforehand
options.rationale: Detection of human papillomavirus type 16 or 18 leads straight to colposcopy regardless of cytology, because these two types account for the large majority of cervical cancers and confer the highest immediate risk of high grade disease. The absence of reflex cytology on a self collected sample does not alter that pathway. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and repeat screening in twelve months time
options.rationale: Vaccination is prophylactic and does not clear an infection that is already established or treat existing cervical disease. Offering it as an alternative to assessment misapplies a preventive intervention to a diagnostic problem. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the result before making any referral
options.rationale: Self collected samples tested with a polymerase chain reaction assay have equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease to clinician collected samples, so the result does not need confirmation. Repeating it duplicates a reliable test and postpones definitive assessment. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a clinician collected sample for liquid based cytology and refer if it is abnormal
options.rationale: Cytology triage determines management for the other oncogenic types, where a negative or low grade result allows a 12-month repeat, but types 16 and 18 bypass that triage entirely. Waiting on cytology here would delay colposcopy without any possibility of changing the destination. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary human papillomavirus testing every five years from age 25 to 74, with partial genotyping that separates types 16 and 18 from the other oncogenic types. That split exists because 16 and 18 cause around 70% of cervical cancers and carry a much higher risk of prevalent high grade disease, so they are referred to colposcopy immediately while the other types are triaged on cytology. Self collection is now available to every screening participant as a way of reaching women who have been under-screened, and its performance for high grade disease is equivalent to clinician collection. Reflex cytology cannot be performed on a self collected vaginal sample, so a woman needing cytology triage must return for a clinician collected specimen, but that requirement does not apply when the result is type 16 or 18.
key_points: Human papillomavirus 16 or 18 detected means direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types are triaged with reflex cytology and often repeated at 12 months
Self collection has equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease and is available to all participants
Reflex cytology is not possible on a self collected sample, so cytology triage needs a clinician collected one
Under-screened women carry the highest burden of cervical cancer in Australia
explanation.pearls: Cervical screening starts at 25 years or two years after first sexual activity if later, and in Australia any symptomatic woman with abnormal bleeding or postcoital bleeding needs a co-test with cytology and speculum examination regardless of when she last screened.

subtopic_detail: Where to operate on a complex adnexal mass with a high risk of malignancy index after menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar assessing a 64-year-old woman referred with four months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. She went through menopause at 51 and has never used hormone therapy.

Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and a firm irregular mass palpable in the right iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked internal vascularity, together with moderate ascites. Serum CA125 is 640 kU/L (<35). A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows omental thickening but no parenchymal liver or lung lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular right iliac fossa mass, no palpable supraclavicular nodes
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked vascularity, moderate ascites; CA125 640 kU/L (<35); computed tomography shows omental thickening without liver or lung metastases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to further characterise the adnexal mass
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when ultrasound findings are indeterminate and the mass could be a fibroid, an endometrioma or a dermoid, which is not the case here. Adding a fourth imaging study to an already convincing picture only delays referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: Arrange therapeutic paracentesis with cytology and review her again once the result returns
options.rationale: Ascitic cytology can be useful when neoadjuvant chemotherapy is being considered and a tissue diagnosis is needed without surgery, but that decision belongs to the oncology team. A negative cytology does not exclude malignancy, so a normal result would not change the referral. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for multidisciplinary assessment and surgery
options.rationale: Her risk of malignancy index is far above the threshold of 200 that mandates specialist referral, combining a postmenopausal score, a CA125 of 640 kU/L and multiple suspicious ultrasound features. Survival is measurably better when cytoreductive surgery for ovarian cancer is performed by a subspecialist in a centre with the full multidisciplinary team. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: Repeat the CA125 in six weeks and refer if the value has risen above the current level
options.rationale: Serial CA125 has a role in monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, not in deciding whether to investigate a suspicious mass. A six week delay in a woman with ascites and omental disease allows measurable progression. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy on the local gynaecology list within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Operating locally on a likely advanced ovarian malignancy risks incomplete staging, tumour rupture with upstaging, and port site seeding, and a general list cannot deliver the debulking these women need. Speed is valuable but does not compensate for the wrong operation in the wrong place. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer is the gynaecological malignancy with the poorest survival in Australia, largely because the early symptoms of bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency and abdominal pain are non-specific and commonly attributed to gastrointestinal causes for months. The risk of malignancy index multiplies a menopausal score, an ultrasound morphology score and the CA125 value, and a result above 200 is the accepted trigger for referral to a gynaecological oncology service. The reason the destination matters so much is that survival correlates strongly with the completeness of cytoreduction, which requires a surgeon able to perform bowel resection, splenectomy and diaphragmatic stripping as needed. Where disease is too extensive for primary debulking, neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval surgery is the alternative, and that decision is made by the multidisciplinary team rather than at the point of referral.
