key_points: A risk of malignancy index above 200 mandates gynaecological oncology referral
The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology score and CA125
Survival improves when surgery is performed by a subspecialist in a specialist centre
Bloating, early satiety and abdominal pain lasting weeks warrant investigation in women over 50
Completeness of cytoreduction is the strongest surgical determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Any woman diagnosed with high grade serous ovarian cancer in Australia should be offered germline and tumour BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing at diagnosis, because a pathogenic variant both opens access to PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy and triggers cascade testing of her relatives.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Reading a raised CA125 against a suspected endometrioma before menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with a raised tumour marker and a request for urgent oncology assessment. She has had severe period pain since her teens, deep pain with intercourse and pain on opening her bowels during menstruation.

She has been trying to conceive for 18 months. Her appetite and weight are stable and there is no bloating or early satiety. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid papillary projection and no internal vascularity, with the ovary tethered to the uterus on probe pressure. Serum CA125 is 118 kU/L (<35).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender nodularity palpable in the posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, right adnexal tenderness, no ascites, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid component, no internal vascularity, reduced ovarian mobility; CA125 118 kU/L (<35); full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: The finding requires tissue; arrange ultrasound guided cyst aspiration with fluid cytology
options.rationale: Aspiration of an endometrioma yields old altered blood that is unhelpful cytologically, and recurrence after aspiration alone approaches certainty. Puncturing a cyst that has not been excluded as malignant also risks peritoneal spill. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: The marker is raised by benign disease; plan fertility focused gynaecology management
options.rationale: CA125 is expressed by any inflamed coelomic epithelium, so endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, menstruation and pregnancy all raise it, and the risk of malignancy index is not validated before menopause. The ground glass appearance without vascularity and the fixed tender pelvis describe an endometrioma in a woman whose pressing clinical problem is subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

options.text: The marker is non-diagnostic; arrange serial measurement every six weeks for six months
options.rationale: CA125 fluctuates with the menstrual cycle and with disease activity in endometriosis, so serial values in this setting generate noise rather than information. There is no threshold or trajectory that would reclassify a sonographically benign endometrioma. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

options.text: The marker indicates likely malignancy; refer urgently to a gynaecological oncology centre
options.rationale: Subspecialist referral is driven by a high risk of malignancy index in a postmenopausal woman or by suspicious morphology such as solid papillary projections, thick septations, vascularity or ascites, none of which is present. Referring on the marker alone would subject a young woman to oncological surgery for benign disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: The finding needs suppression; start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months
options.rationale: Medical suppression reduces endometriosis-associated pain but induces a hypo-oestrogenic state that prevents conception, which directly opposes her goal of pregnancy. It also shrinks endometriomas only modestly and they recur on cessation. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

explanation.summary: CA125 is a glycoprotein shed by mesothelial and Mullerian epithelium under almost any inflammatory stimulus, so its specificity for ovarian cancer is poor in premenopausal women and good only after menopause, when the benign causes largely disappear. That difference is why the risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and why applying it to a young woman with endometriosis produces a false alarm. The sonographic appearance carries far more weight than the marker: an endometrioma shows homogeneous low level ground glass echoes with no solid component and no internal Doppler flow, and site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility on the probe add to the picture. Managing this woman well means addressing pain and subfertility together, since surgical excision of an endometrioma removes healthy cortex and can lower ovarian reserve, so the decision to operate is weighed against assisted reproduction.
key_points: CA125 rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation and pregnancy
The risk of malignancy index is validated after menopause and misleads before it
Ground glass internal echoes with no solid component or vascularity characterise an endometrioma
Site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility indicate adhesive pelvic disease
Endometrioma excision can reduce ovarian reserve, so weigh surgery against assisted reproduction
explanation.pearls: Ovarian endometriomas larger than 3 cm reduce antral follicle count in the affected ovary even before surgery, so an anti-Mullerian hormone level measured before any planned cystectomy gives the couple a realistic baseline for counselling about fertility outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Tumour based mismatch repair testing after endometrial carcinoma diagnosed before age fifty
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman two weeks after a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, reported as grade 1 with less than half myometrial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion.

She is recovering well with no complications. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2, she has had three pregnancies and she has never had diabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome. Her father had bowel cancer at 52 and a paternal aunt had a uterine cancer in her forties. She asks whether her two daughters need to do anything.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdominal wounds healing well, no collection, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Histology: grade 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma, myometrial invasion less than 50%, no lymphovascular space invasion, margins clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the family history is on the paternal side and carries no risk to daughters
options.rationale: Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted equally through the paternal line, so a father with early bowel cancer is as informative as a mother would be. This is a common misconception about gynaecological cancer risk that leads to missed diagnoses. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Request mismatch repair immunohistochemistry on the hysterectomy tumour specimen
options.rationale: Endometrial cancer is the sentinel malignancy in around half of women with Lynch syndrome, and her age under 50 with a father and aunt affected by Lynch spectrum cancers raises that possibility strongly. Immunohistochemistry for the four mismatch repair proteins on existing tumour tissue is the standard first triage test and requires no new sample. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Request germline gene panel testing on a blood sample from her before any tumour testing
options.rationale: Germline testing is the confirmatory step and is appropriate once tumour triage suggests mismatch repair deficiency or when family history alone is compelling enough to bypass triage. Going straight to a blood panel in every case tests many women whose tumours are mismatch repair proficient. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Arrange adjuvant vaginal vault brachytherapy and defer any genetic discussion until after it
options.rationale: Grade 1 disease with superficial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion is low risk and does not usually require adjuvant radiotherapy at all. The genetic question is independent of adjuvant treatment and should not be deferred behind it. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange colonoscopy for her and for both daughters within the next twelve month period
options.rationale: Colonoscopic surveillance is exactly what a confirmed diagnosis would trigger, but the interval and starting age depend on which gene is involved, and testing unaffected daughters before the family variant is known is uninformative. The sequence runs from tumour to germline to cascade testing. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome results from a germline pathogenic variant in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2, or in EPCAM, and it substantially raises lifetime risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial and other cancers. Endometrial cancer precedes the colorectal cancer in a large share of affected women, which makes the gynaecologist the person most likely to make the diagnosis for the whole family. Testing follows a sequence: immunohistochemistry or microsatellite instability testing on tumour tissue, then MLH1 promoter methylation analysis when MLH1 and PMS2 are both lost to distinguish sporadic epigenetic silencing from inherited disease, and finally germline testing. Identifying a variant changes management for the patient through colonoscopic surveillance and aspirin chemoprophylaxis, and for relatives through cascade testing and risk-reducing surgery.
key_points: Endometrial cancer is the sentinel cancer in about half of women with Lynch syndrome
Tumour mismatch repair immunohistochemistry is the first triage test and uses existing tissue
Loss of MLH1 and PMS2 needs promoter methylation testing to separate sporadic from inherited causes
Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted through either parent
Confirmation triggers colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin prophylaxis and cascade family testing
explanation.pearls: Regular aspirin reduces colorectal cancer incidence in Lynch syndrome by around half with the benefit emerging after several years of use, which is why it is offered to confirmed carriers alongside one to two yearly colonoscopy starting at 25 years for MLH1 and MSH2 carriers.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Switching from oral to intravenous iron in the third trimester after gastrointestinal intolerance
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She was started on oral iron at 22 weeks but stopped after ten days because of severe constipation and epigastric pain, and a second preparation caused the same problem.

She reports increasing breathlessness climbing stairs and has a placenta that was reported as low lying at her morphology scan, with a repeat scan booked for 34 weeks. Her bloods today show haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100) and ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein, normal B12 and folate, and a normal haemoglobin electrophoresis performed at booking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 C, fetal heart rate 145/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, cephalic presentation, pale conjunctivae, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits, haemoglobin electrophoresis normal at booking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Recombinant human erythropoietin given subcutaneously with oral iron supplementation
options.rationale: Erythropoiesis stimulating agents are used in anaemia of chronic kidney disease rather than in uncomplicated iron deficiency, where the limiting factor is substrate rather than erythropoietin. Giving it alongside oral iron she cannot absorb compounds the error. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: A third oral iron preparation taken with food to improve gastrointestinal tolerability
options.rationale: Two preparations have already failed for the same reason, and taking iron with food to reduce symptoms substantially reduces the fraction absorbed. Persisting orally spends weeks she does not have before delivery. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Transfusion of two units of packed red cells arranged as an elective admission this week
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia near delivery, active bleeding or haemodynamic compromise, and it carries alloimmunisation risk that matters in a woman who may have further pregnancies. She is stable, so iron replacement is the correct pathway. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the full blood count and ferritin in four weeks before committing to any treatment
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already secure with a microcytic anaemia, a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L and a normal C-reactive protein, so repeat testing adds nothing. Four weeks of observation takes her to 34 weeks with untreated severe anaemia and a possible placenta praevia. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged in the day unit within the coming week
options.rationale: She has documented intolerance of two oral preparations, a haemoglobin of 86 g/L and only ten weeks left, which is too little time for oral therapy to correct stores even if she could take it. Intravenous iron is safe from the second trimester onwards and raises haemoglobin faster and more completely than oral replacement. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Antenatal iron deficiency anaemia matters most for what it does to a woman's tolerance of blood loss at delivery, since postpartum haemorrhage is common and a woman entering labour with a haemoglobin of 86 g/L has no reserve. Intravenous iron preparations such as ferric carboxymaltose deliver a large replacement dose in a single short infusion and are established as safe after the first trimester, with the main issues being transient hypophosphataemia, infusion reactions and skin staining from extravasation. The threshold for moving from oral to intravenous therapy is set by intolerance, malabsorption, failure to respond, severity of the anaemia, and how much time remains before delivery. A low lying placenta adds weight to correcting the anaemia early, because it raises the probability of significant peripartum bleeding.
key_points: Intravenous iron is indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption, non-response or late gestation
It is considered safe from the second trimester onwards
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, active bleeding or severe symptomatic anaemia near delivery
Antenatal anaemia reduces tolerance of postpartum haemorrhage and increases transfusion need
Confirm the diagnosis with ferritin plus C-reactive protein before infusing
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes transient hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority of recipients, so a woman needing repeat infusions or reporting persistent bone pain or weakness afterwards should have a serum phosphate checked rather than being given more iron.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Operative approach to a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity in a woman wanting pregnancy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 36-year-old woman with two years of progressively heavier periods and two early miscarriages. She has been trying to conceive for a third pregnancy for the past year.

She has already completed a six month trial of tranexamic acid with only partial benefit and declines hormonal treatment because she wants to conceive. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 26 mm fibroid that appeared to indent the cavity, and a subsequent saline infusion sonohysterogram confirms a submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume within the cavity and a normal outer myometrial margin. Her haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115-155).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bulky uterus approximately 8 week size, mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Saline infusion sonohysterogram: 26 mm submucosal fibroid with more than 50% intracavitary component, remainder of cavity normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 11 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Hysteroscopic resection of the fibroid performed transcervically under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume in the cavity is accessible transcervically, and hysteroscopic resection removes it without any uterine incision, preserving the myometrium for a future pregnancy. Submucosal fibroids are the subtype with the clearest adverse effect on both bleeding and implantation, so removal addresses her two problems together. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist therapy for six months to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks fibroids and corrects anaemia before surgery, which is a legitimate adjunct, but the effect reverses on cessation and the drug prevents conception while it is given. It is preparation for an operation rather than a definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Laparoscopic myomectomy with layered closure of the resulting myometrial defect
options.rationale: Abdominal or laparoscopic myomectomy is the approach for intramural and subserosal fibroids that cannot be reached from the cavity, and it creates a myometrial scar that raises the small risk of uterine rupture in labour. Choosing it for a predominantly intracavitary fibroid imposes an unnecessary uterine incision. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Endometrial ablation with a second generation device following endometrial preparation
options.rationale: Ablation destroys the endometrium and is absolutely contraindicated in a woman planning pregnancy, since subsequent conception carries high rates of abnormal placentation and loss. It also performs poorly when the cavity is distorted by a submucosal fibroid. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation performed by interventional radiology as a day case procedure
options.rationale: Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms but is relatively contraindicated when future fertility is desired, because of effects on ovarian reserve and on placentation. A submucosal fibroid can also slough after embolisation and cause prolonged discharge or infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

explanation.summary: Fibroid management is driven by location far more than by size, which is why the submucosal, intramural and subserosal distinction and the degree of intracavitary extension determine the operation. Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity and disrupt the endometrium, producing heavy bleeding and interfering with implantation, and they are the group for which removal has the clearest fertility benefit. Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is needed to grade the intracavitary component because standard ultrasound often cannot tell an intramural fibroid indenting the cavity from a true submucosal one. Where more than half the fibroid lies within the cavity the lesion can usually be resected in a single hysteroscopic procedure, whereas a deeper lesion may need a staged approach to avoid perforation and excessive fluid absorption.
key_points: Location rather than size determines the operative approach to fibroids
Submucosal fibroids cause heavy bleeding and impair implantation
Saline infusion sonohysterography grades the intracavitary component before surgery
Hysteroscopic resection avoids a myometrial incision and preserves the uterus for pregnancy
Embolisation and ablation are both unsuitable when future fertility is desired
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit is monitored continuously during hysteroscopic resection because absorption of hypotonic distension medium causes dilutional hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema, and the procedure is stopped at a deficit of around 1000 mL with hypotonic fluid in a healthy woman.

subtopic_detail: Adnexal torsion where preserved Doppler arterial flow argues against the diagnosis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 24-year-old woman with eight hours of severe right iliac fossa pain that began abruptly while she was at the gym, with three episodes of vomiting. The pain has waxed and waned in intensity but has never fully settled.

Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago and a urinary pregnancy test is negative. She had a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid documented on a scan two years ago that she elected to leave alone. On examination she is tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged oedematous right ovary measuring 78 mm containing the known dermoid, with a small volume of free fluid, and the report notes that arterial and venous Doppler flow are both demonstrable within the ovary.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rebound, cervix closed with no bleeding, right adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), transvaginal ultrasound shows 78 mm oedematous right ovary containing a dermoid, free fluid present, arterial and venous Doppler flow both demonstrable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat the Doppler ultrasound in twelve hours
options.rationale: Waiting for arterial flow to disappear means waiting for the ovary to infarct, since loss of arterial signal is a late finding rather than the diagnostic threshold. The waxing and waning pain characteristic of intermittent torsion is precisely the window in which surgery preserves the ovary. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Request computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to exclude appendicitis first
options.rationale: Appendicitis is a reasonable differential given the right sided pain and mild inflammatory response, but the ultrasound has already identified an enlarged oedematous ovary containing a known mass, which explains the presentation. Imaging that irradiates a young woman while the ovary twists trades a small diagnostic gain for a large time cost. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before operating
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging can show ovarian oedema and a twisted pedicle, but obtaining it out of hours is slow and it changes nothing about the need for surgery in a patient with this history and these findings. No imaging result would make observation safe. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy with a view to untwisting and conserving the ovary
options.rationale: Preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because the ovary has a dual blood supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries and venous and lymphatic obstruction precede arterial compromise, producing the oedematous enlargement seen here. Torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis, and untwisting rather than removing the ovary is now standard because the great majority regain function even when the ovary looks dusky. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for presumed pelvic inflammatory disease and review tomorrow
options.rationale: Pelvic inflammatory disease typically produces bilateral pain with cervical motion tenderness, discharge and a more indolent onset rather than abrupt pain during exertion with vomiting. The mildly raised white cell count here reflects the stress response and tissue ischaemia rather than infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is the gynaecological emergency most often missed, and the single commonest reason is misplaced confidence in Doppler ultrasound. The ovary receives blood from both the ovarian artery and the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, so arterial flow is frequently still detectable in a torted ovary, and because the thin walled veins and lymphatics obstruct before the arteries do, the earliest and most reliable sonographic sign is unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema rather than absent flow. Most torsion occurs around a lead point, typically a benign cyst or dermoid between 5 and 10 cm, since very large masses are less mobile and small ovaries rarely twist. Management has shifted decisively towards conservative detorsion even when the ovary appears necrotic, because gross appearance correlates poorly with recoverable function and the risk of thromboembolism from untwisting has not been borne out.
key_points: Present Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because of the dual arterial supply
Unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema is the more reliable sonographic sign
Waxing and waning severe pain suggests intermittent torsion and should not reassure
A lead point mass of 5 to 10 cm is the usual precipitant
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy even for a dusky ovary
explanation.pearls: Oophoropexy is considered after detorsion when there is no lead point mass, when torsion is recurrent, or when the contralateral ovary has already been lost, since the underlying problem in those cases is an abnormally long utero-ovarian ligament rather than the mass itself.

subtopic_detail: Assessing bleeding on tamoxifen where the usual endometrial thickness cut-off is not applicable
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman with a single episode of vaginal spotting last week. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which she is due to continue for a further two years.

She went through menopause at 50 and has no other bleeding, no discharge and no pain. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a cystic heterogeneous appearance and poorly defined margins, and the sonographer comments that the endometrial-myometrial interface is difficult to resolve. The ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 11 mm, cystic heterogeneous appearance, indistinct endometrial-myometrial interface, ovaries normal, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contact her oncologist to switch tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor and rescan afterwards
options.rationale: Switching to an aromatase inhibitor removes the endometrial stimulus and may well be discussed once the histology is known, but changing adjuvant breast cancer therapy does not investigate the bleeding that has already occurred. The sequence is to obtain tissue first and involve the oncologist afterwards. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy irrespective of the measured endometrial thickness
options.rationale: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial stromal cystic change that inflates the sonographic measurement and blurs the interface, so the thickness threshold used in other postmenopausal women is not valid and cannot be used to triage her. Hysteroscopy allows the cavity to be seen directly and focal lesions to be sampled under vision, which blind sampling would miss. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to assess for myometrial invasion first
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging stages a carcinoma that has already been diagnosed histologically and cannot distinguish benign tamoxifen change from malignancy. Using it as a diagnostic filter ahead of tissue reverses the order of assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Reassure her that the appearance is a recognised drug effect and repeat the scan in six months
options.rationale: The sonographic appearance is indeed a recognised tamoxifen effect, but she has bled, and bleeding is the symptom that demands tissue regardless of how well the imaging is explained. Attributing a symptom to a known drug effect without excluding malignancy is the central error in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Arrange outpatient pipelle endometrial sampling and manage according to the histology
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling detects diffuse disease well but samples only a fraction of the cavity, and the lesions tamoxifen causes are characteristically focal polyps rather than a uniform process. A benign pipelle result would therefore not exclude a focal carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen acts as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, antagonising the receptor in breast tissue while behaving as a partial agonist in the endometrium, which is why it both reduces breast cancer recurrence and raises endometrial cancer risk several-fold in postmenopausal women. It characteristically produces subendometrial stromal hypertrophy with cystic change, endometrial polyps and adenomyotic change, all of which thicken and distort the sonographic endometrial stripe without any malignancy being present. The practical consequence is that the 4 mm triage threshold, which depends on a thin uniform endometrium having a high negative predictive value, breaks down entirely in these women, and ultrasound cannot be used to decide who needs sampling. Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound for the same reason, since it generates procedures without improving outcomes, but any bleeding is investigated promptly.
key_points: Tamoxifen is an endometrial partial agonist and raises endometrial cancer risk after menopause
It causes subendometrial cystic change that invalidates the usual thickness threshold
Any bleeding on tamoxifen requires hysteroscopy and directed biopsy, not ultrasound triage
Lesions are often focal polyps, so blind sampling can miss them
Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole do not carry the endometrial risk of tamoxifen because they lower oestrogen synthesis rather than acting at the receptor, which is one reason a postmenopausal woman who develops endometrial pathology on tamoxifen is often switched rather than simply monitored.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Booking microcytosis with replete iron stores requiring haemoglobinopathy evaluation of the couple
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing booking bloods for a 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. She feels well apart from mild nausea and has no bleeding.

She was born in Australia and her parents came from southern Italy. She was told as a teenager that she was anaemic and took iron tablets for a year without any change in her blood count. Today her haemoglobin is 103 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33) and red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), with ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), normal C-reactive protein and normal B12 and folate. Her partner was born in Cyprus and has not been tested.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No pallor, no jaundice, no splenomegaly, uterus not palpable abdominally
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 103 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her alone and test the partner only if hers is abnormal
options.rationale: Sequential testing is standard in many settings but costs weeks at exactly the point in pregnancy when chorionic villus sampling remains an option. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is timing: with ancestry pointing to risk on both sides, parallel testing preserves the full range of reproductive choices. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her and arrange testing of her partner now
options.rationale: A ferritin of 96 micrograms/L with a normal C-reactive protein excludes iron deficiency as the cause of a mean cell volume of 64 fL, and a raised red cell count with disproportionate microcytosis is the classic thalassaemia trait picture. Because both partners have ancestry from high prevalence regions, partner testing must happen in parallel so that prenatal diagnosis remains available within the first trimester if both carry a variant. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Request a blood film and reticulocyte count and defer further testing to the 28 week visit
options.rationale: A film showing target cells and basophilic stippling would support the suspicion but adds little to indices this characteristic, and reticulocytes do not discriminate. Deferring to 28 weeks removes every prenatal diagnostic option the couple might want. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Request non-invasive prenatal testing on maternal blood to assess the foetus for this condition
options.rationale: Non-invasive prenatal testing screens for common aneuploidies and does not detect haemoglobinopathies in routine Australian practice. Offering it here substitutes an unrelated screening test for carrier testing of the parents. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement and repeat the full blood count in four weeks to assess response
options.rationale: Her stores are replete, so giving iron cannot raise the haemoglobin and repeats the failed teenage trial she has already described. Continued supplementation in a thalassaemia carrier risks iron overload over time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia in pregnancy is so commonly due to iron deficiency that the diagnosis is often assumed, but ferritin with a concurrent C-reactive protein separates the two causes reliably, and a normal or high ferritin redirects the workup to haemoglobinopathy. Several features point that way here: the degree of microcytosis is out of proportion to the modest fall in haemoglobin, the red cell count is raised rather than reduced, the Mentzer index falls well below 13, and iron therapy previously failed. Beta thalassaemia trait carries little consequence for the woman herself, but if her partner also carries a beta variant each pregnancy has a one in four chance of transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia major. That is why partner testing is urgent rather than routine, since chorionic villus sampling is available from around 11 weeks and amniocentesis from 15 weeks, and the counselling that precedes either takes time.
key_points: Ferritin with C-reactive protein distinguishes iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait
Disproportionate microcytosis with a raised red cell count suggests a haemoglobinopathy
Previous failure of iron therapy is a strong historical clue
Partner testing is urgent because prenatal diagnostic options are time limited
Alpha thalassaemia may need DNA studies because electrophoresis can be normal in carriers
explanation.pearls: The Mentzer index, the mean cell volume divided by the red cell count, is below 13 in thalassaemia trait and above 13 in iron deficiency, and here it is about 11, which flags the diagnosis from the full blood count alone before any specialised test is ordered.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

subtopic_detail: Treatment regimen for trichomoniasis diagnosed in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her second pregnancy describes 3 weeks of a frothy yellow-green discharge with vulval itch and soreness during sex. She has a single regular partner of 4 years.

She has taken no antibiotics recently and has not douched. She is not diabetic and her oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks is not yet due.

On speculum examination there is an adherent frothy discharge with punctate haemorrhages visible across the ectocervix, and the vaginal pH measures 5.5. A vaginal nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Trichomonas vaginalis and negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Her syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology from booking were both negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Adherent frothy vaginal discharge, punctate haemorrhages across the ectocervix, vaginal pH 5.5
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal nucleic acid amplification test positive for Trichomonas vaginalis, negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; booking syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Tinidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
options.rationale: Tinidazole is effective against Trichomonas vaginalis but Australian product information advises against its use in pregnancy because human safety data are far thinner than for metronidazole. It is the acceptable alternative outside pregnancy when metronidazole fails. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, with no treatment for her partner
options.rationale: Clotrimazole treats candidiasis, which presents with a thick white discharge and a vaginal pH below 4.5 rather than the frothy discharge and pH of 5.5 here, and it has poor activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, with the same course given to her partner
options.rationale: A 7-day oral metronidazole course is the preferred Australian regimen because cure rates exceed those of single-dose therapy, particularly in women with human immunodeficiency virus and in pregnancy, and metronidazole is regarded as safe in all trimesters. Concurrent partner treatment is essential since reinfection is otherwise the rule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
options.rationale: Single-dose metronidazole is an accepted option where adherence is a concern, but randomised data show higher rates of treatment failure than the 7-day course, which is why the longer regimen is preferred. This is the near-pair worth distinguishing by cure rate rather than by safety. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Defer all antimicrobial therapy until after the birth, with a test of cure at 6 weeks postnatally
options.rationale: Deferring treatment leaves symptoms untreated and leaves the infection transmissible, and metronidazole has a long record of safe use across pregnancy including the first trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmissible protozoal infection that is far more common in remote and regional Australian communities than in metropolitan populations, and nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced wet mount microscopy because its sensitivity is much higher. In pregnancy it is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, although treatment has not been shown to reverse that risk, so the indication for treating is symptom relief and interruption of transmission. Metronidazole is the drug of choice in every trimester and while breastfeeding. Partner treatment without the need for the partner to be tested is standard, and patients should be advised to avoid sex until 7 days after both have completed therapy. A positive result should prompt a full sexually transmissible infection screen, since coinfection is common.
key_points: Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days is preferred over single-dose therapy because of higher cure rates
Metronidazole is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy and during breastfeeding
Treat partners empirically without waiting for their test results and advise no sex for 7 days after both finish
Tinidazole is a second-line alternative outside pregnancy, not a pregnancy option
A positive result should prompt screening for other sexually transmissible infections
explanation.pearls: Vaginal pH is the fastest bedside discriminator: candidiasis sits below 4.5, while trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis both run above 4.5, so a normal pH essentially excludes trichomoniasis.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Suppressive regimen for culture confirmed recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends your general practice frustrated by a fifth episode of vulval itch and a thick white discharge in the past 12 months. Each episode has settled with an over-the-counter antifungal cream and then returned within 6 to 8 weeks.

She uses condoms for contraception, has had the same partner for 6 years and has taken no antibiotics in the past year. She uses a plain soap-free wash and no vaginal products.

Her glycated haemoglobin is 5.2 per cent (below 6.0) and her human immunodeficiency virus serology is negative. A high vaginal swab taken during the current episode has grown Candida albicans on culture, with speciation confirmed and no resistance reported. On examination there is vulval erythema with fissuring in the natal cleft and a thick adherent white discharge. A pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with fissuring, thick adherent white vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture positive for Candida albicans with no resistance reported, glycated haemoglobin 5.2% (below 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4 and 7, then 150 mg weekly for 6 months
options.rationale: Four or more culture-proven episodes in a year defines recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, which is managed with an induction phase of three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart followed by weekly suppression for 6 months. Around 90 per cent of women remain free of symptoms while on suppression, although roughly half relapse after it stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose to be repeated with each further episode
options.rationale: Single-dose treatment of each episode is appropriate for sporadic candidiasis but does nothing to break the recurrence cycle, which is the actual problem once four or more episodes occur in a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Boric acid 600 mg vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms
options.rationale: Boric acid is reserved for non-albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, which is intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole; the culture here confirms Candida albicans, for which azoles remain the right class. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.text: Nystatin vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles for vulvovaginal candidiasis and, like any single course, treats the current episode without addressing recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, repeated in the week before each period
options.rationale: Topical suppression timed to the menstrual cycle is a second-line option when oral therapy is contraindicated or refused, but oral fluconazole suppression has better evidence and much better adherence. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined by four or more episodes in 12 months, and the diagnosis requires culture confirmation because up to half of women who self-treat for thrush have another cause such as dermatitis, lichen sclerosus or bacterial vaginosis. Speciation matters because Candida glabrata and Candida krusei respond poorly to fluconazole. The recognised contributors worth excluding are poorly controlled diabetes, immunosuppression, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and high-dose oestrogen exposure. Management is a fluconazole induction phase followed by 6 months of weekly suppression, with counselling that relapse after cessation is common. Partner treatment is not indicated for candidiasis, which distinguishes it clearly from trichomoniasis.
key_points: Four or more culture-confirmed episodes in 12 months defines the recurrent form
Induction with three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart, then weekly suppression for 6 months
Speciate before treating, since Candida glabrata needs boric acid or nystatin rather than fluconazole
Exclude diabetes, immunosuppression and recent antibiotics as contributors
Partner treatment is not indicated, unlike in trichomoniasis
explanation.pearls: Fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy at any dose above a single 150 mg exposure, so pregnant women with recurrent disease are suppressed with topical clotrimazole instead; check the pregnancy test before writing a 6-month oral script.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a first presentation Bartholin abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar on call. A 32-year-old woman presents with 4 days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina, now severe enough that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably.

She has never had a similar problem before. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, and has had no fever or rigors at home. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and was negative for human papillomavirus.

On examination there is a tense, fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior aspect of the introitus on the right, with overlying erythema but no spreading cellulitis into the labium or thigh. The swelling is exquisitely tender. There is no induration extending towards the ischiorectal fossa and no crepitus. Swabs have been taken for gonorrhoea and chlamydia nucleic acid amplification testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus, overlying erythema without spreading cellulitis, no induration towards the ischiorectal fossa, no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Nucleic acid amplification swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di-flucloxacillin with sitz baths and clinical review in 48 hours if no improvement
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone will not resolve a tense fluctuant collection, and the delay prolongs severe pain; antibiotics are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, immunosuppression or systemic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic with a loose dressing and no catheter
options.rationale: Simple incision relieves pain immediately but the incision seals within days and recurrence rates are in the order of 10 to 15 per cent or higher, which is precisely the problem the Word catheter was designed to solve. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.text: Excision of the entire Bartholin gland under general anaesthetic on the next available list
options.rationale: Gland excision carries risks of significant bleeding from the underlying venous plexus, dyspareunia and scarring, and is reserved for repeated failure of simpler measures or where malignancy is suspected in a woman over 40. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter under local anaesthetic today
options.rationale: A Word catheter is left in for 4 to 6 weeks so that the tract epithelialises and a permanent drainage channel forms, which reduces recurrence compared with simple incision while remaining a bedside procedure under local anaesthetic. It is the first-line definitive treatment for a first presentation abscess. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.text: Marsupialisation of the abscess cavity under general anaesthetic on the next available list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is comparably effective at preventing recurrence but requires theatre and general anaesthesia, so it is generally kept for recurrence after a Word catheter rather than used first. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts that can obstruct, producing a cyst that may then become infected. Most abscesses are polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora rather than being sexually transmitted, but gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing is still performed because they are recoverable in a minority. Definitive management aims to create a permanent drainage tract rather than simply emptying the cavity, which is why the Word catheter and marsupialisation outperform simple incision. A new Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 raises the possibility of a vulval or Bartholin gland carcinoma and warrants biopsy rather than blind drainage. Antibiotics are an adjunct, indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunosuppression or pregnancy.
key_points: Word catheter insertion after incision creates an epithelialised tract and is first-line for a first abscess
The catheter stays in place for 4 to 6 weeks; simple incision alone recurs frequently
Marsupialisation and gland excision are escalation options, not first-line choices
Antibiotics are adjunctive and indicated for cellulitis, systemic illness, immunosuppression or pregnancy
A new Bartholin mass after age 40 requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: Place the incision inside the hymenal ring on the mucosal surface rather than on the labial skin, since an external incision predisposes to a chronic draining fistula.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

subtopic_detail: Penicillin regimen for syphilis seroconversion detected on third trimester screening
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional antenatal clinic. A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy is recalled after her routine third trimester screening bloods.

Her booking serology at 10 weeks was negative for syphilis. The current sample is reactive on treponemal enzyme immunoassay, reactive on Treponema pallidum particle agglutination, and shows a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1:32.

She feels well and has no rash, no genital ulceration and no lymphadenopathy. She has had one new sexual partner in the past 5 months. She has never been treated for syphilis and has no allergies to any medication, including penicillin. Her human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology are negative and a detailed ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with normal growth and liquor volume.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, symphysis-fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin 1:32; booking syphilis serology at 10 weeks negative; human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound today shows normal fetal anatomy, growth and liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin titre in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin does not reliably cross the placenta, so it cannot be relied on to treat the foetus. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly, with a second identical dose one week later
options.rationale: A negative result at 10 weeks with a titre of 1:32 now establishes infection acquired within the past 18 weeks, which is early syphilis, and Australian guidance adds a second dose one week after the first when the woman is pregnant to reduce the risk of treatment failure and congenital infection. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the foetus as well as the mother. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly as a single dose, with no further injections
options.rationale: A single dose is the standard regimen for early syphilis outside pregnancy, but a second dose is added in pregnancy because of the higher stakes of treatment failure for the foetus. This is the near-pair to know by pregnancy status rather than by stage. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly weekly for three doses over three weeks
options.rationale: Three weekly doses is the regimen for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration; a documented negative test 18 weeks earlier dates this infection as early and makes the longer course unnecessary. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin at delivery
options.rationale: Doxycycline is the non-pregnant alternative for penicillin-allergic patients; it is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of effects on fetal teeth and bone, and it does not treat the foetus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Australia has seen a sustained resurgence of infectious syphilis, with congenital cases returning in several jurisdictions, which is why repeat third trimester screening has been reinstated in many antenatal programmes alongside booking and delivery testing. Staging determines the regimen: early syphilis, meaning primary, secondary or early latent infection acquired within the past 2 years, is treated with benzathine penicillin, while late latent disease or infection of unknown duration requires three weekly doses. A documented negative test within the previous 2 years is what allows infection to be staged as early. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably crosses the placenta at treponemicidal concentrations, so a woman with genuine penicillin allergy must be desensitised rather than given an alternative. Response is monitored by a fourfold fall in the rapid plasma reagin titre, and the neonate requires assessment and follow-up regardless of maternal response.
key_points: A negative test within the past 2 years stages the infection as early and shortens the regimen
Pregnant women with early syphilis receive a second benzathine penicillin dose one week after the first
Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the foetus; allergic women are desensitised rather than substituted
Three weekly doses are reserved for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration
Monitor treatment response with a fourfold fall in rapid plasma reagin titre and notify the case
explanation.pearls: Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of the first dose: in the third trimester it can provoke uterine contractions and transient fetal heart rate abnormalities, so treat where fetal monitoring is available.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacotherapy after a minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your general practice to discuss her bone density result. Six months ago she tripped on a garden step and fractured her left distal radius, which was managed in a cast.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has no vasomotor symptoms now and does not want to take hormone therapy. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week, and walks 30 minutes most days. She takes no corticosteroids and has no family history of hip fracture.

Bone densitometry reports a femoral neck T-score of -2.6 and a lumbar spine T-score of -2.2. Her corrected calcium is 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone is 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 90 mL/min/1.73m2 and coeliac serology is negative. She has no reflux symptoms and can sit upright after medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Femoral neck T-score -2.6, lumbar spine T-score -2.2, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, coeliac serology negative
data_table.History: Minimal trauma distal radius fracture 6 months ago, menopause at 51, no corticosteroid use, no reflux symptoms

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy is restricted on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme to severe established osteoporosis with a T-score of -3.0 or below plus two or more fractures, one of which must have occurred on antiresorptive therapy. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Calcium 1000 mg and colecalciferol 1000 IU daily alone, with repeat densitometry in 2 years
options.rationale: Supplements support antiresorptive therapy but do not substitute for it, and her vitamin D is already adequate at 78 nmol/L; leaving a woman with a minimal trauma fracture on supplements alone forgoes proven fracture reduction. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy with transdermal oestradiol and micronised progesterone daily
options.rationale: Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and is a reasonable choice for a woman under 60 who also wants vasomotor symptom relief, but she has no such symptoms and declines it, and it is not the first-line agent for established osteoporosis with a fracture. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: Denosumab is equally effective but is generally reserved for intolerance of or contraindication to oral bisphosphonates, largely because missing a dose produces rapid bone loss and a rebound risk of multiple vertebral fractures, which demands reliable 6-monthly adherence. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: A minimal trauma fracture after the age of 50 establishes osteoporosis irrespective of the T-score and meets Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria for antiresorptive therapy, and an oral bisphosphonate is first-line because it is effective, inexpensive and forgiving of an occasional missed dose. Her normal renal function and absence of reflux make alendronate suitable. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture, meaning one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, defines osteoporosis clinically in anyone over 50 regardless of what the bone density shows. Secondary causes are screened for before committing to long-term therapy, which is why calcium, vitamin D, thyroid function, renal function and coeliac serology were checked here. Oral bisphosphonates are first-line in Australia, with zoledronic acid or denosumab used where oral therapy is not tolerated or absorption is doubtful. Alendronate requires an upright posture for 30 minutes with plain water on an empty stomach, so reflux, oesophageal stricture and inability to sit up are the practical contraindications. Treatment is generally reviewed after 5 years of oral therapy, when a drug holiday may be considered for lower-risk patients, whereas denosumab must never simply be stopped without transitioning to another antiresorptive.
key_points: A minimal trauma fracture after age 50 defines osteoporosis irrespective of T-score and triggers therapy
Oral bisphosphonates are first-line; denosumab and zoledronic acid follow where oral therapy is unsuitable
Screen for secondary causes with calcium, vitamin D, thyroid, renal function and coeliac serology before starting
Stopping denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive causes rebound vertebral fractures
Anabolic therapy is reserved for severe established disease meeting strict Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria
explanation.pearls: Ask about jaw pain and dental plans before starting any antiresorptive: invasive dental work is best completed beforehand, since osteonecrosis of the jaw risk on osteoporosis doses is low but concentrated around extractions.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention
Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

subtopic_detail: Uterus conserving treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding with a thickened junctional zone
stem:
A 42-year-old woman attends your gynaecology clinic with 2 years of progressively heavier periods. She now changes a super tampon hourly on her worst two days, passes clots the size of a fifty cent coin, and has taken sick leave twice this year.

Her period pain has become worse over the same period and now starts 2 days before bleeding. She has two children and does not want further pregnancies, but she is clear that she does not want a hysterectomy.

On examination the uterus is bulky, about 10 weeks in size, symmetrically enlarged and tender on bimanual palpation. Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging reports a junctional zone thickness of 14 mm. An endometrial pipelle biopsy shows benign proliferative endometrium. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-155) and ferritin is 9 micrograms/L (30-200). Her cervical screening test is up to date and negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrically bulky tender uterus, approximately 10 weeks in size
data_table.Imaging: Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid, endometrial thickness 6 mm; magnetic resonance imaging junctional zone thickness 14 mm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-200), endometrial pipelle biopsy benign proliferative endometrium

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation by the interventional radiology service
options.rationale: Embolisation has a role in symptomatic adenomyosis, with reported symptom improvement in many women, but it is an invasive second-line option after medical therapy has failed rather than a first recommendation. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for the heaviest days of each period
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual loss by around a third and is a reasonable adjunct, but it does nothing for her worsening dysmenorrhoea and is less effective than the intrauterine system for bleeding of this severity. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at the next available appointment
options.rationale: A junctional zone of 12 mm or more on magnetic resonance imaging with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis, for which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective uterus-conserving treatment, reducing both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. It also provides contraception, which suits a woman who has completed her family and declines hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for endometrial ablation on the next available operating theatre list
options.rationale: Ablation destroys only the superficial endometrium, so it performs poorly where glandular tissue lies deep within the myometrium, and failure rates in adenomyosis are high with a real chance of later hysterectomy. The distinguishing point against the intrauterine system is depth of disease, not severity of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with tibolone add-back therapy
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue effectively but causes hypo-oestrogenic side effects and bone loss, so its role is short-term, usually to bridge to surgery, rather than as ongoing management at 42. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it is being diagnosed far more often now that magnetic resonance imaging and high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound are used to assess heavy menstrual bleeding. The classic combination is heavy bleeding with progressive dysmenorrhoea and a symmetrically bulky, tender uterus, which distinguishes it from the asymmetrical, non-tender enlargement of fibroids. A junctional zone of 12 mm or more is the accepted imaging threshold. Management in a woman who wants to keep her uterus starts with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, with tranexamic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or combined hormonal contraception as adjuncts. Iron deficiency is almost always present by the time a woman presents and should be treated in parallel, since correcting the bleeding alone will not restore her stores quickly.
key_points: A junctional zone of 12 mm or more with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first-line uterus-conserving treatment, helping both bleeding and pain
Endometrial ablation performs poorly in adenomyosis because the disease lies deep in the myometrium
Exclude endometrial pathology with a biopsy in women over 45, or younger with risk factors, before committing to medical therapy
Treat the accompanying iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre confirms iron deficiency regardless of haemoglobin, and oral iron taken on alternate days rather than daily achieves better absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose.

subtopic_detail: Investigating increased liquor volume when the glucose tolerance test and antibody screen are normal
stem:
You are the registrar in a tertiary antenatal clinic. A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is referred at 32 weeks because her symphysis-fundal height measures 38 cm and she feels uncomfortably stretched.

Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated and that baby weighed 3.4 kg at term. She has had no fever, no rash and no contact with unwell children. She takes no medications and does not drink alcohol.

Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks was normal at every time point. She is blood group O positive with a negative antibody screen. Today's ultrasound reports a single deepest vertical pocket of 9.5 cm with an amniotic fluid index of 28 cm, an estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, normal umbilical artery Dopplers, and no hydrops. The sonographer notes that the fetal stomach was not confidently visualised on any of three attempts.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 38 cm at 32 weeks, tense abdomen, fetal parts difficult to palpate
data_table.Imaging: Single deepest vertical pocket 9.5 cm, amniotic fluid index 28 cm, estimated fetal weight 55th centile, normal umbilical artery Dopplers, no hydrops, fetal stomach not confidently visualised
data_table.Investigations: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks normal at all time points; blood group O positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a tertiary level fetal morphology ultrasound directed at swallowing and the upper gut
options.rationale: With diabetes excluded by a normal glucose tolerance test and alloimmunisation excluded by a negative antibody screen, a structural cause of impaired fetal swallowing becomes the leading explanation, and a non-visualised stomach on repeated attempts points directly to an upper gastrointestinal obstruction. Detailed imaging changes the birth plan by identifying a baby who will need a paediatric surgical centre. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test now, since gestational diabetes can develop later
options.rationale: Repeat testing is occasionally done where polyhydramnios or macrosomia appear after a normal early test, but her estimated fetal weight is on the 55th centile and the non-visualised stomach demands a structural explanation first. (Source: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

options.text: Arrange maternal serology for cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis and parvovirus infection
options.rationale: Congenital infection is a recognised cause of increased liquor, but it characteristically produces hydrops, growth restriction or intracranial calcification, none of which is present, so serology is a reasonable parallel test rather than the priority. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Admit for amnioreduction to relieve her discomfort and reduce the risk of preterm labour
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is reserved for severe maternal respiratory compromise or intractable discomfort and carries risks of membrane rupture, abruption and infection; it treats a symptom without establishing the cause. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Continue two weekly growth scans with cardiotocography and review again at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Serial surveillance is appropriate once a cause has been sought and none found, but adopting it now would leave an unexplained structural finding undiagnosed until birth in a hospital that may lack paediatric surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm, and about half of cases are idiopathic. The three causes that must be actively excluded are maternal diabetes, fetal structural anomalies that impair swallowing, and congenital infection or anaemia producing hydrops. Impaired swallowing covers oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, neurological conditions with poor swallowing and any mass effect in the neck or chest. A stomach that cannot be visualised on repeated attempts alongside increased liquor is a specific pairing that should prompt tertiary imaging and planning for delivery where paediatric surgery is available. Polyhydramnios itself increases the risk of preterm labour, malpresentation, cord prolapse at membrane rupture and postpartum haemorrhage from uterine overdistension, so the birth plan is altered even when no cause is found.
key_points: Diagnostic thresholds are a deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more, or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm
Exclude maternal diabetes, fetal structural anomaly and congenital infection before accepting an idiopathic label
Increased liquor with a non-visualised fetal stomach suggests upper gastrointestinal obstruction
Anticipate malpresentation, cord prolapse at rupture of membranes and postpartum haemorrhage
Amnioreduction is symptomatic relief for severe maternal compromise, not a diagnostic step
explanation.pearls: Rupture membranes in a woman with polyhydramnios in a setting equipped for immediate caesarean, since the risk of cord prolapse is highest with a high presenting part and a sudden large fluid loss.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for isolated reduced liquor volume with normal growth and Dopplers
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 34 weeks, referred after a growth scan arranged because of a small symphysis-fundal height measurement.
