She reports normal fetal movements and denies any fluid loss, wetness or a gush at any point. She has no abdominal pain and no vaginal bleeding. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg and it remains in that range today, with no proteinuria on dipstick.

The ultrasound reports a single deepest vertical pocket of 1.6 cm, an estimated fetal weight on the 40th centile with growth tracking along the same centile from the 28-week scan, normal umbilical artery Dopplers with positive end diastolic flow, and a normal middle cerebral artery pulsatility index. A sterile speculum examination shows no pooling and a point of care test for amniotic fluid is negative. Cardiotocography today is reactive with normal variability and no decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Imaging: Single deepest vertical pocket 1.6 cm, estimated fetal weight 40th centile tracking from the 28-week scan, normal umbilical artery Dopplers with positive end diastolic flow, normal middle cerebral artery pulsatility index
data_table.Investigations: Sterile speculum with no pooling, point of care amniotic fluid test negative, urine dipstick negative for protein, cardiotocography reactive with normal variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Arrange delivery by caesarean section today given the reduced liquor volume around the foetus
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes the morbidity of late preterm birth on a foetus with normal growth, normal Dopplers and a reactive cardiotocograph, none of which indicates compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)

options.text: Increase maternal oral fluid intake and repeat the liquor volume assessment in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Maternal hydration produces a small transient increase in liquor volume but does not alter outcome, and a 4-week interval leaves a pregnancy with a recognised stillbirth risk unmonitored. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids now and plan delivery in 48 hours once the course is complete
options.rationale: A corticosteroid course is appropriate when preterm birth is genuinely planned or threatened within 7 days, which is not the case here; giving it now and delivering at 34 weeks repeats the error of unnecessary late preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Begin twice weekly fetal surveillance now with planned birth between 36 and 37 weeks
options.rationale: Isolated oligohydramnios with normal growth and normal Dopplers carries a modestly increased risk of stillbirth and intrapartum compromise without evidence of current placental insufficiency, so the balance is struck by surveillance now and birth in the late preterm to early term window rather than immediate delivery. Ruptured membranes and growth restriction have both been excluded, which is what makes this the isolated form. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Continue expectant care to 40 weeks with weekly cardiotocography and no change to the plan
options.rationale: Expectant management to term ignores the observed rise in stillbirth and intrapartum compromise associated with persistently reduced liquor, and weekly monitoring alone is less than the recommended surveillance intensity. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)

explanation.summary: Oligohydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm and the first task is always to establish whether it is isolated or a marker of another process. Ruptured membranes are excluded by history, speculum examination and a point of care test, and placental insufficiency is excluded by normal growth and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Renal tract anomalies and exposure to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or angiotensin blockade are the other causes to consider. Truly isolated oligohydramnios is associated with a modest increase in stillbirth, meconium-stained liquor and cord compression in labour, which is why surveillance is intensified and birth is planned in the 36 to 37 week window rather than at term. When the liquor is low because of growth restriction, the timing decision is driven by the Doppler findings instead, and delivery is often much earlier.
key_points: A single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm defines oligohydramnios
Exclude ruptured membranes and growth restriction before calling it isolated
Isolated oligohydramnios is managed with twice weekly surveillance and planned birth at 36 to 37 weeks
Where growth restriction coexists, Doppler findings rather than liquor volume drive the timing of birth
Ask about non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and renin-angiotensin drug exposure, and check the fetal renal tract
explanation.pearls: The single deepest vertical pocket is preferred over the amniotic fluid index for diagnosing oligohydramnios, because the index diagnoses more cases and leads to more inductions and caesareans without improving perinatal outcome.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

subtopic_detail: Immediate advice on an established antiepileptic drug at first presentation in early pregnancy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends your general practice having done a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 3 days ago and the pregnancy was not planned.

She has generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy and has been free of seizures for 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily. Lamotrigine was stopped 6 years ago after a widespread rash requiring admission, and levetiracetam was stopped 5 years ago because of severe irritability and mood disturbance that resolved on withdrawal.

She has read about the risks of her medication overnight and has brought a printout. She is still taking the valproate and asks whether she should stop it today. She drives to work and cares for a 3-year-old niece two days a week. She takes no other medications and has not been taking folic acid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.History: Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy, seizure free 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily, previous severe rash on lamotrigine and severe mood disturbance on levetiracetam
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no focal deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate advice?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose today and arrange review at the joint clinic within 4 weeks
options.rationale: An abrupt halving of the dose risks breakthrough seizures without meaningfully reducing teratogenic risk at this gestation, since organogenesis of the neural tube is already complete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Continue the valproate unchanged and arrange joint obstetric and neurology review this week
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by about 6 weeks of gestation, so stopping valproate now cannot undo that risk, while abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both of which are among the leading causes of maternal death in Australian reports. Any change of agent belongs to a specialist review arranged urgently, not to a single consultation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the valproate today, start folic acid 5 mg daily and review her again in 2 weeks
options.rationale: High-dose folic acid is indeed indicated and will be started, but coupling it with abrupt cessation of an effective anticonvulsant exposes her to seizure recurrence for no fetal benefit at 6 weeks. This is the most tempting option because half of it is correct. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch her to levetiracetam today at an equivalent dose and review her again in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is usually the preferred agent in pregnancy, but she has a documented history of severe mood disturbance on it, and any cross-taper in an established patient requires neurology supervision rather than a same-day switch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the valproate today and review the situation at her 12-week nuchal translucency scan
options.rationale: This combines abrupt withdrawal with a 6-week gap in supervision, which is the worst combination of seizure risk and lost opportunity to plan monitoring, fetal surveillance and delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiepileptic drugs, with major congenital malformation rates around 10 per cent and a dose-dependent risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and it should be avoided in women of childbearing potential wherever an alternative works. The clinical problem in this consultation is different: the exposure has already occurred and the neural tube closed weeks ago, so the decision is about seizure safety from here on. Uncontrolled generalised tonic-clonic seizures in pregnancy carry risks of maternal trauma, fetal hypoxia, status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and epilepsy consistently features among indirect causes of maternal death in Australian and United Kingdom mortality reports. Management therefore centres on urgent specialist review, high-dose folic acid, a detailed anomaly scan, monitoring of drug levels across pregnancy, and planning for the postnatal period including vitamin K and safe infant care advice.
key_points: Neural tube closure completes by about 6 weeks, so stopping valproate at that point does not reverse the risk already incurred
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both recognised causes of maternal death
Start folic acid 5 mg daily and refer urgently to a joint obstetric and neurology clinic
Arrange a detailed anomaly scan and monitor antiepileptic levels, which fall across pregnancy
Any change of agent is made by the specialist team with a supervised cross-taper, not same day in general practice
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine plasma concentrations can fall by more than half by the third trimester because of oestrogen-driven glucuronidation, so levels are checked each trimester and the dose is reduced again within 2 weeks of birth to avoid toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Selecting heart failure therapy in the early postpartum period while breastfeeding is continuing
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar asked to review a 33-year-old woman on day 5 after a normal vaginal birth of her third baby.

She was readmitted overnight with breathlessness lying flat and waking gasping at 2 am. She has no pleuritic pain, no calf swelling and no cough. She had no hypertension in pregnancy and no proteinuria at any visit.

Her chest radiograph shows upper lobe venous diversion with small effusions, and a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram performed overnight excludes pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiography today reports a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 32 per cent and no valvular lesion. Her N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide is 4100 ng/L (below 125) and her troponin is within normal limits. She is breastfeeding fully and is very keen to continue. The intern has charted frusemide and asks you what else to start.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasal crackles, mild ankle oedema, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide 4100 ng/L (below 125), troponin within normal limits, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with upper lobe venous diversion and small effusions; computed tomography pulmonary angiogram negative for embolism; echocardiogram dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 32 per cent and no valvular lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her frusemide?

options.text: Digoxin with ongoing frusemide, deferring other agents until an echocardiogram in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Digoxin is compatible with breastfeeding and may help rate control, but it does not modify remodelling, and deferring disease-modifying therapy for 6 weeks wastes the period in which recovery is most achievable. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Candesartan with spironolactone, advising her to suppress lactation and switch to formula
options.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers lack the breastfeeding safety data that older angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors have, and there is no need to stop breastfeeding when compatible alternatives exist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Sacubitril with valsartan and cabergoline to suppress lactation, with frusemide continued
options.rationale: Sacubitril with valsartan has no safety data in lactation and is not a first-line initiation agent in the puerperium, and routine lactation suppression is not required; cabergoline in peripartum cardiomyopathy remains an investigational adjunct rather than standard care. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Enalapril with metoprolol, continuing frusemide and supporting her to keep breastfeeding
options.rationale: Once the baby is born the teratogenic objection to renin-angiotensin blockade no longer applies, and enalapril and captopril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best data in lactation, passing into milk in negligible amounts. Adding a beta blocker completes the two agents that drive reverse remodelling, and recovery of ejection fraction in peripartum cardiomyopathy is best when therapy starts early. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Frusemide alone at a higher dose, avoiding all other agents for as long as she is breastfeeding
options.rationale: This reflects the common misconception that lactation blocks all heart failure therapy; diuresis relieves congestion but leaves the ventricle without any remodelling therapy during the window when recovery is most likely. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum without another identifiable cause, and it is a leading cardiac contributor to maternal mortality in Australia. Orthopnoea and waking gasping distinguish it from the ordinary breathlessness of late pregnancy and the early puerperium, and natriuretic peptide is a useful discriminator because it stays near normal in physiological breathlessness. Treatment after birth follows standard heart failure principles, with drug choice adjusted for lactation rather than abandoned because of it: enalapril, captopril, metoprolol, frusemide and hydralazine with nitrate are all usable. Anticoagulation is considered when the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, because the puerperium is already prothrombotic and mural thrombus is well described. Contraception counselling is essential, since a subsequent pregnancy carries a significant risk of relapse, particularly if ventricular function has not normalised.
key_points: Peripartum cardiomyopathy arises in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum with no other cause
After birth, enalapril and captopril are the preferred angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors during breastfeeding
Beta blockade with metoprolol is added for reverse remodelling; frusemide treats congestion only
Consider anticoagulation where the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, given puerperal thrombotic risk
Counsel about contraception and the risk of relapse in a future pregnancy, especially if function does not normalise
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine added to standard therapy has been studied in peripartum cardiomyopathy on the basis of the prolactin fragment hypothesis, but it requires lactation suppression and anticoagulation cover and is not routine Australian practice.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

subtopic_detail: First trimester anticoagulation choice for a mechanical mitral valve on a low warfarin dose
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic. A 31-year-old woman attends at 6 weeks in an unplanned first pregnancy.

She had rheumatic fever as a child in the Pacific and underwent mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis 7 years ago. She takes warfarin 3 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0 and has had no thromboembolic or bleeding events since surgery.

Her international normalised ratio today is 2.9 and her renal and liver function are normal. Echocardiography 3 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no regurgitation and normal ventricular function. She is in sinus rhythm. She is very anxious about the reports she has read about warfarin and asks whether she should be changed to injections for the rest of the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.9 on warfarin 3 mg daily, renal and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram 3 months ago with normally functioning bileaflet mitral prosthesis and normal ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Stop warfarin and use aspirin 100 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is grossly inadequate for a mechanical mitral prosthesis and would expose her to a high risk of valve thrombosis, which carries substantial maternal and fetal mortality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Stop warfarin and use rivaroxaban 20 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves in any patient after trials showed excess thromboembolism and bleeding, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue warfarin at her current dose with weekly international normalised ratio monitoring
options.rationale: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and falls to around 3 per cent or less at doses of 5 mg daily or under, so at 3 mg daily continuation offers the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis for a small fetal risk, and this is the recommended strategy for low-dose warfarin. Weekly monitoring accounts for the shifting warfarin requirement across pregnancy, and the switch to heparin is planned near term rather than now. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Stop warfarin and use therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily until 12 weeks, then resume warfarin
options.rationale: Substituting low molecular weight heparin through the first trimester avoids embryopathy but carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis, and it is the preferred strategy only when the warfarin dose needed exceeds 5 mg daily or the woman declines warfarin after counselling. This is the genuine near-pair, separated by the warfarin dose threshold. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Admit her for an unfractionated heparin infusion until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: An intravenous infusion for 6 weeks is impractical and carries risks of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, osteoporosis and line infection, and unfractionated heparin is reserved for the peripartum period when rapid reversibility matters. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation for a mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is one of the clearest examples of a decision that trades maternal against fetal risk, and no option is free of harm. Warfarin gives the best protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy, with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, when exposure occurs between 6 and 12 weeks. That risk is strongly dose dependent, which is why the 5 mg daily threshold has become the pivot of the decision: at or below it, continuation is recommended, and above it, a first trimester switch to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin with anti-Xa monitoring is offered. Warfarin is stopped and replaced with heparin from around 36 weeks so that the foetus is not anticoagulated at delivery, since fetal liver immaturity means the fetal international normalised ratio exceeds the maternal one. Care belongs in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic in a centre with cardiac surgical backup.
key_points: The warfarin dose threshold of 5 mg daily decides whether to continue warfarin or switch in the first trimester
Embryopathy risk is concentrated in exposure between 6 and 12 weeks and is dose dependent
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves and in pregnancy
Switch to heparin at around 36 weeks so the foetus is not anticoagulated at birth
Valve thrombosis carries high maternal and fetal mortality, which is why heparin strategies are not automatically safer
explanation.pearls: Monitor therapeutic low molecular weight heparin in mechanical valve pregnancies with peak anti-Xa levels 4 to 6 hours after a dose, targeting about 1.0 to 1.2 IU/mL, since weight-based dosing alone is unreliable as pregnancy alters clearance.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a negative oestrogen and progestogen challenge in secondary amenorrhoea after uterine instrumentation
stem:
A 31-year-old woman is referred to your gynaecology clinic because she has had no periods for 11 months and has been unable to conceive.

Fourteen months ago she had a surgical evacuation of retained products of conception for secondary postpartum bleeding, which was repeated a week later for persistent bleeding. She breastfed for 3 months and stopped 10 months ago. Her periods have never returned.

She has no hot flushes, no night sweats and no vaginal dryness. Her weight is stable and her exercise and eating patterns are unchanged. She has no headache, no galactorrhoea and no visual symptoms, and she takes no medication.

Her pregnancy test is negative. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone is 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol is 340 pmol/L, prolactin is 290 mIU/L and thyroid stimulating hormone is 1.6 mIU/L, all within the reference range for the follicular phase. She bled neither after a 10-day course of medroxyprogesterone acetate nor after a subsequent 21-day cycle of oestrogen followed by progestogen. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a thin irregular endometrial line with bright echogenic areas.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal secondary sexual characteristics, normal external genitalia and cervix, no galactorrhoea
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin 290 mIU/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L, all within the follicular phase reference range; pregnancy test negative
data_table.Challenge testing: No withdrawal bleed after 10 days of medroxyprogesterone acetate; no bleed after a subsequent 21-day oestrogen and progestogen cycle
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound with a thin irregular endometrial line and bright echogenic areas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange diagnostic hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis under direct vision
options.rationale: Ovulatory hormone levels with a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge locate the problem in the outflow tract rather than the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, and repeated instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment, since adhesions are divided under direct vision. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.text: Request an anti-Mullerian hormone level and repeat follicle stimulating hormone in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Ovarian reserve testing investigates premature ovarian insufficiency, which is excluded here by a normal follicle stimulating hormone and a clearly normal oestradiol, alongside the absence of any vasomotor symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa to exclude a pituitary lesion
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated with a raised prolactin, headache, visual field loss or hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, none of which is present; her gonadotrophins and oestradiol confirm an intact axis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to re-establish a regular withdrawal bleed pattern
options.rationale: This would provide exogenous hormone to an endometrium that has already failed to respond to a formal oestrogen and progestogen challenge, and it also frustrates her stated wish to conceive. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.text: Measure a 17-hydroxyprogesterone level and free androgen index for an androgen excess disorder
options.rationale: Androgen excess evaluation belongs to women with hirsutism, acne or a raised luteinising hormone to follicle stimulating hormone ratio, and it would not explain a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge whatever the result. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary and hypothalamus. The progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium and a patent outflow tract are present, and a negative result is followed by an oestrogen and progestogen challenge to separate an unresponsive endometrium from simple anovulation. Failure of both challenges in a woman with normal gonadotrophins and normal oestradiol points to the endometrium or the outflow tract, and intrauterine adhesions are the dominant cause when there has been recent uterine instrumentation, particularly repeated evacuation of a puerperal uterus or curettage in the presence of infection. Ultrasound may show a thin irregular endometrium with echogenic areas but cannot exclude adhesions, so hysteroscopy remains the definitive test. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, often with measures to prevent re-adhesion, and fertility outcomes depend heavily on the severity of disease at the time of diagnosis.
key_points: Work through secondary amenorrhoea by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary, hypothalamus
A failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge with normal gonadotrophins localises the problem to the endometrium or outflow tract
Repeated evacuation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment; ultrasound cannot exclude adhesions
Normal oestradiol with no vasomotor symptoms argues strongly against premature ovarian insufficiency
explanation.pearls: The risk of adhesions rises sharply when evacuation is performed on a postpartum or post-miscarriage uterus rather than a non-pregnant one, and repeat procedures within a fortnight carry the highest risk of all; this is a specific argument for expectant or medical management of retained products where it is safe.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

subtopic_detail: Surveillance plan after velamentous cord insertion is reported at the morphology scan
stem:
You are the resident in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 29-year-old woman attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her morphology scan.

The pregnancy was conceived spontaneously and has been uncomplicated. She takes pregnancy multivitamins and has no medical history. She has no bleeding, no pain and reports normal fetal movements for gestation.

The scan report describes a single foetus with growth on the 45th centile and normal anatomy. The placenta is posterior and its lower edge is 55 mm from the internal os. The umbilical cord is reported to insert into the membranes 40 mm from the placental edge, with vessels running through the membranes toward the placental disc. Colour Doppler over the internal os shows no vessels crossing it. Her blood pressure is 108/66 mmHg and urinalysis is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan at 20 weeks: single foetus, growth 45th centile, normal anatomy, posterior placenta with lower edge 55 mm from internal os, cord inserting into membranes 40 mm from placental edge, no vessels crossing the internal os on colour Doppler. Urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Arrange planned caesarean section at 35 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, with inpatient admission from 32 weeks
options.rationale: Early planned birth with admission is the pathway for confirmed vasa praevia, where unprotected vessels cross the internal os and can rupture at membrane rupture. It would be correct if colour Doppler had shown vessels over the os, which it specifically did not. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange repeat placental localisation at 32 weeks with continued routine antenatal care and no growth scans
options.rationale: Repeat localisation is the follow-up for a low-lying placenta, and this placenta sits 55 mm from the internal os, which is already well clear. Repeat localisation would be indicated if the lower edge were within 20 mm of the os. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for fetal karyotype and microarray, with continued routine antenatal care thereafter
options.rationale: An abnormal cord insertion in isolation with normal anatomy and normal growth is not an indication for invasive testing. Amniocentesis would be considered if structural anomalies or soft markers were also present on the morphology scan. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

options.text: Arrange serial growth ultrasound scans from the early third trimester with continued routine antenatal care
options.rationale: Velamentous cord insertion without vessels over the internal os is associated with fetal growth restriction rather than with vasa praevia, so serial growth surveillance is the intervention that changes management. Routine care otherwise continues because the mode and timing of birth are not altered by the insertion site alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange low dose aspirin from today with continued routine antenatal care and no additional growth scans
options.rationale: Aspirin is given for pre-eclampsia risk reduction and must be started before 16 weeks to be effective, so commencing at 20 weeks offers little benefit. It would be correct if started at the first visit in a woman with recognised pre-eclampsia risk factors, which are absent here. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Velamentous cord insertion describes the cord inserting into the membranes rather than the placental disc, so the vessels run unprotected by Wharton jelly for some distance before reaching the placenta. Its clinical significance splits into two quite separate problems that are frequently conflated. If those unprotected vessels happen to run across the internal cervical os the condition is vasa praevia, which is catastrophic if membranes rupture unrecognised and therefore demands planned preterm caesarean birth. If they do not cross the os, as here, the relevant association is with impaired placental transfer and fetal growth restriction, and the appropriate response is growth surveillance. Velamentous insertion is considerably more common in twin pregnancies and after assisted reproduction, and deliberately examining the os with colour Doppler whenever it is reported is what separates the two pathways.
key_points: Velamentous insertion means the cord inserts into membranes, leaving vessels without Wharton jelly
Colour Doppler over the internal os distinguishes vasa praevia from an isolated abnormal insertion
Isolated velamentous insertion is associated with fetal growth restriction and warrants serial growth scans
Vasa praevia requires antenatal corticosteroids and planned caesarean birth before labour
Incidence is higher in multiple pregnancy and after assisted reproductive technology
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is defined by fetal vessels running within 20 mm of the internal os, so ask explicitly for that measurement whenever a velamentous or marginal cord insertion is reported rather than accepting the insertion description alone.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum
RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

subtopic_detail: Management of nocturnal hand paraesthesia developing in the third trimester
stem:
You are the resident in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy describes 3 weeks of tingling and numbness in both hands that wakes her at night and is relieved by shaking them over the side of the bed.

She works as a hairdresser and says her grip has felt clumsy when holding scissors. She has gained 14 kg this pregnancy and has noticed swollen fingers and ankles in the evenings. Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated.

On examination there is sensory blunting over the palmar aspects of the thumb, index and middle fingers of both hands. Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling bilaterally. Thenar bulk is preserved and abductor pollicis brevis power is 5/5. Reflexes are normal. Blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein, and haemoglobin, thyroid function, liver function tests and platelets are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral sensory blunting over palmar thumb, index and middle fingers, percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling, thenar bulk preserved, abductor pollicis brevis power 5/5, reflexes normal, mild peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis no protein; haemoglobin, thyroid function, liver function tests and platelets within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the flexor retinaculum and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms with motor involvement or failure of conservative measures after birth, and thenar bulk and power are preserved here. Decompression would be indicated for thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction or symptoms persisting well beyond the postpartum period. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a local corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Injection is a reasonable second-line option but is not the initial step when a simple non-invasive measure has not been tried in a self-limiting condition. It would be appropriate if splinting failed and symptoms remained disabling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral frusemide to reduce the peripheral oedema and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Diuretics do not relieve this compression and reduce plasma volume in a pregnancy that depends on expansion for placental perfusion, so they are avoided for physiological oedema. Frusemide has a place in pulmonary oedema complicating severe pre-eclampsia, not in dependent swelling. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies of both upper limbs and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Electrophysiology is unnecessary when the distribution and provoking features are typical and management would be conservative regardless of the result. It would be worthwhile if the distribution were atypical, symptoms were unilateral with wasting, or surgery were being planned. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.text: Provide neutral position wrist splints for night-time use and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Pregnancy-related median nerve compression without motor loss is managed conservatively because fluid shifts reverse after birth and most women resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. Neutral wrist splinting worn overnight addresses the nocturnal flexion posture that provokes symptoms and is the first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist affects a substantial minority of pregnancies and is driven by the same fluid retention that produces peripheral oedema, with the carpal tunnel being a rigid compartment that tolerates little extra volume. The symptoms are worst at night because sleep tends to be spent with the wrist flexed, which further narrows the tunnel, and the classic history is waking to shake the hand out. The important clinical distinction is between sensory symptoms alone, which are self-limiting and managed conservatively, and motor involvement with thenar wasting, which risks permanent deficit and warrants escalation. Most cases resolve within weeks to a few months of birth as the fluid shift reverses, so the counselling message is as important as the splint. Symptoms persisting past 6 months postpartum should prompt reassessment, since the pregnancy explanation no longer holds.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history
Fluid retention narrows a rigid compartment, so the condition parallels peripheral oedema
Preserved thenar bulk and thumb abduction power indicate sensory-only involvement suitable for conservative care
Neutral position night splints are first-line; corticosteroid injection is second-line
Diuretics are not used, and nerve conduction studies are reserved for atypical or motor presentations
explanation.pearls: Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction converts this from a self-limiting nuisance into an indication for surgical referral during pregnancy, because axonal loss recovers poorly even after the oedema resolves.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose tolerance testing when booking body mass index is in the obese range
stem:
You are the resident at a first antenatal visit. A 33-year-old woman attends at 11 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her height is 1.62 m and her weight is 98 kg.

Her first child was born at term weighing 4350 g after a normal vaginal delivery 4 years ago. She was not tested for gestational diabetes in that pregnancy. She has no personal history of diabetes and her mother developed type 2 diabetes at 56.

She takes no regular medicines. Blood pressure today is 124/78 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein and no glucose. Booking bloods include a random glucose of 5.8 mmol/L and a glycated haemoglobin of 39 mmol/mol (<42). She asks when she will be tested for diabetes in this pregnancy, having been told she is high risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Anthropometry: Height 1.62 m, weight 98 kg, body mass index 37.3 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 5.8 mmol/L, glycated haemoglobin 39 mmol/mol (<42), urinalysis no protein and no glucose
data_table.History: Previous term infant 4350 g, untested for gestational diabetes in that pregnancy; mother with type 2 diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for glucose testing?

options.text: Perform an early oral glucose tolerance test now, repeated at 24 to 28 weeks if the early test is normal
options.rationale: A body mass index above 35 with a previous macrosomic infant places her in the group for whom early testing is recommended so that unrecognised pre-existing hyperglycaemia is not missed through the first trimester. A normal early result does not exclude gestational diabetes developing with rising insulin resistance, so the routine test at 24 to 28 weeks is still required. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Perform an oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks only, with no additional early testing
options.rationale: Testing only in the routine window is appropriate for women without risk factors, but it delays detection of hyperglycaemia already present in the first trimester in a high risk woman. It would be correct for a woman with a normal body mass index and no previous macrosomia or family history. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Rely on the glycated haemoglobin result now, repeated at 24 to 28 weeks if this early value is normal
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin falls in pregnancy because red cell turnover accelerates, so it lacks sensitivity for gestational diabetes and is not a diagnostic test in this setting. It is useful for detecting overt pre-existing diabetes at booking when clearly elevated, not for excluding milder hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange fasting capillary glucose monitoring at home now, with an oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
options.rationale: Home monitoring is a tool for managing diagnosed gestational diabetes rather than for making the diagnosis, and capillary meters lack the accuracy required for diagnostic thresholds. It becomes appropriate once a diagnosis has been established on a laboratory test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Perform an early oral glucose tolerance test now, with no further testing required if the early test is normal
options.rationale: Insulin resistance rises substantially through the second trimester under the influence of placental hormones, so a normal early result cannot substitute for the routine test. Omitting the later test would be reasonable only if the early test had already established the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Australian practice tests for hyperglycaemia in pregnancy with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks for everyone, and adds an early test for women whose risk profile makes previously unrecognised diabetes or very early gestational diabetes likely. Risk factors that trigger early testing include a body mass index above 30, previous gestational diabetes, previous macrosomia, a first-degree relative with diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds with high population prevalence. The most commonly misunderstood point is that a normal early test does not end the matter, because placental lactogen, progesterone and cortisol drive insulin resistance upward as pregnancy advances, and a woman who passes at 12 weeks may fail at 26. Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in pregnancy because accelerated erythrocyte turnover lowers it independently of glycaemia. Detecting and treating hyperglycaemia reduces macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and pre-eclampsia, which is why the testing schedule is worth getting right.
key_points: Everyone is offered a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Early testing is added for body mass index above 30, previous macrosomia, previous gestational diabetes or a first-degree relative with diabetes
A normal early test must still be followed by the routine 24 to 28 week test
Glycated haemoglobin is lowered by accelerated red cell turnover and is not diagnostic in pregnancy
Capillary home monitoring manages established disease and does not diagnose it
explanation.pearls: Australian diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g test in pregnancy are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above, and a single value reaching any one of them makes the diagnosis.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with cyclical pelvic pain, no menses and normal secondary sexual characteristics
stem:
You are the resident in a gynaecology clinic. A 14-year-old girl attends with her mother because she has never had a period, and for the past 8 months has had lower abdominal pain that comes for about 4 days roughly every month and then settles completely.

She has recently been getting up twice a night to pass small volumes of urine. She is otherwise well, plays netball and is doing well at school. She takes no medicines.

On examination her height is on the 60th centile and her weight on the 55th. Breast development is Tanner stage 5 and pubic hair is Tanner stage 5. The abdomen is soft with a smooth suprapubic mass palpable 4 cm above the symphysis pubis, which is not tender today. External genital inspection shows a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus that protrudes on Valsalva. Serum follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and prolactin are within normal limits, and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Height 60th centile, weight 55th centile, breast Tanner stage 5, pubic hair Tanner stage 5, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass 4 cm above the symphysis, bluish bulging membrane at the introitus protruding on Valsalva
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and prolactin within normal limits; urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any further examination or intervention is arranged
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement investigate a disorder of sex development, which typically presents with absent or discordant pubic hair and no cyclical pain from retained menstrual blood. They would be appropriate for absent uterus on imaging with a raised testosterone and absent pubic hair. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological surgeon for surgical incision and drainage of the obstructed outflow tract
options.rationale: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain, a palpable pelvic mass and a bulging bluish membrane indicate an obstructed but otherwise normal genital tract, and the treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction. Normal gonadotrophins confirm an intact hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis, so the problem is mechanical rather than endocrine. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress menstruation and review the symptoms in 3 months
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression relieves the pain by stopping endometrial shedding but leaves an obstructed tract with accumulated blood and risks ongoing retrograde flow and endometriosis. It would be reasonable for primary dysmenorrhoea with an unobstructed tract and normal menses. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Reassure that menarche can be delayed to 16 years and arrange gynaecology review in a further 12 months
options.rationale: Waiting is reasonable for absent menses with no other findings, but cyclical pain with a palpable mass indicates accumulating blood that will continue to distend the tract and compress the bladder. Observation would be correct for primary amenorrhoea at 14 with normal examination and no cyclical symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before deciding whether any intervention is required
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex or higher obstructions and duplicated systems, but the level of obstruction is already visible at the introitus here and imaging would delay treatment. It would be indicated if the introitus appeared normal and a higher transverse septum or duplication were suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is approached by asking first whether secondary sexual characteristics are present, because their presence establishes that oestrogen production and therefore the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis are intact. When puberty has proceeded normally but menses have never appeared, the problem lies in the uterus or the outflow tract, and cyclical pain is the clue that a functioning endometrium is shedding into an obstructed space. Accumulating blood distends the vagina and then the uterus, producing a palpable mass and often urinary frequency or retention from bladder compression, which is a commonly missed presenting complaint. The differential includes an imperforate hymen, a transverse vaginal septum and cervical agenesis, and they differ substantially in surgical complexity, which is why the examination finding of a bulging membrane at the introitus matters. Prompt relief prevents further retrograde menstruation, which is associated with later endometriosis.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea point to a uterine or outflow tract cause
Cyclical pain indicates functioning endometrium shedding into an obstructed space
Urinary frequency or retention arises from bladder compression by the distended vagina
Normal gonadotrophins exclude hypogonadism and confirm the problem is mechanical
Relieving obstruction limits retrograde menstruation and the associated endometriosis risk
explanation.pearls: A bluish bulging membrane that protrudes on Valsalva localises the obstruction to the hymen, which is a straightforward repair, whereas a normal introitus with the same cyclical picture suggests a transverse septum or cervical agenesis needing preoperative magnetic resonance imaging.

subtopic_detail: Choosing incision angle and site when performing an episiotomy at operative vaginal birth
stem:
You are the registrar conducting an assisted vaginal birth. A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is at full dilatation at 40 weeks with the vertex at station plus 2 in the direct occipito-anterior position.

She has been pushing for 2 hours and the cardiotocograph now shows recurrent late decelerations with a baseline of 150 beats per minute and reduced variability. The consultant has confirmed that a low forceps birth is appropriate and the theatre team has been notified. She has an effective epidural in situ and has consented to an assisted birth with perineal incision if required.

The perineum is short and the head is distending it with each contraction. You decide to perform an episiotomy at crowning.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 150/min
data_table.Examination: Full dilatation, vertex station plus 2, direct occipito-anterior, short perineum distending with contractions, effective epidural in situ
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph: baseline 150/min with reduced variability and recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: Which incision technique is most appropriate?

options.text: Midline incision beginning at the posterior fourchette directed vertically toward the anus at crowning
options.rationale: The midline incision heals well and is less painful but extends directly into the anal sphincter and rectum with substantially higher rates of third and fourth degree injury. It is used in some overseas settings for spontaneous birth but is not recommended in Australia, particularly at instrumental birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 25 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: An angle this shallow at crowning finishes close to the midline once the perineum retracts after birth and carries a sphincter injury risk approaching that of a midline cut. Twenty five degrees would be the measured angle of a correctly placed incision assessed after delivery, not the angle to cut at. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: Mediolateral incision directs the cut away from the anal sphincter complex and is the technique that reduces obstetric anal sphincter injury at operative vaginal birth. An angle near 60 degrees from the midline at the moment of crowning is required because the distended perineum straightens the incision, so a cut made at a shallower angle ends up close to the midline. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline before traction
options.rationale: Cutting before the perineum is distended produces more bleeding over a longer interval and misjudges the final angle because the tissue has not yet stretched into its delivery position. The correct timing is at crowning when the perineum is thinned and stretched over the presenting part. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Lateral incision beginning 2 cm lateral to the fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: Starting lateral to the fourchette divides the vestibular tissue and Bartholin duct region rather than the perineal body, causing bleeding and poor healing without protecting the sphincter. The incision must originate at the posterior fourchette itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Episiotomy has moved from routine to restricted use, and the remaining clear indication is to reduce severe perineal trauma at operative vaginal birth, particularly a first instrumental birth with a short perineum. The geometry of the incision matters more than whether one is performed at all. The perineum at crowning is stretched taut, so an incision that looks adequately angled at that moment straightens toward the midline once the tissue retracts after birth, and studies measuring post-delivery angles show that a cut made at 60 degrees ends up near the 45 degree mark associated with the lowest sphincter injury rates. Every incision should be followed by systematic examination including a digital rectal examination, because a proportion of sphincter injuries are recognised only when specifically sought. Repair technique, antibiotic cover and structured follow-up all influence long-term continence outcomes.
key_points: Mediolateral technique protects the anal sphincter complex; midline incision increases severe tears
Cut at crowning when the perineum is stretched, not before traction is applied
Incise at about 60 degrees from the midline so the healed angle sits near 45 degrees
Begin at the posterior fourchette rather than lateral to it
Perform a digital rectal examination after every operative vaginal birth to detect occult sphincter injury
explanation.pearls: A mediolateral episiotomy measured at 45 degrees or more from the midline after birth is associated with the lowest rate of obstetric anal sphincter injury, which is why the incision is made at around 60 degrees while the perineum is distended.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice for a febrile pregnant woman after high risk food exposure
stem:
You are the resident in an obstetric assessment unit. A 28-year-old woman at 27 weeks in her first pregnancy presents with 2 days of fever, muscle aches and mild diarrhoea.

She attended a work function 4 days ago and ate a soft cheese platter and a prepared rockmelon salad. She has had no urinary symptoms, no cough, no rash and no contact with anyone unwell. She has not travelled overseas.

On examination the uterus is soft and non-tender and the symphysis fundal height is 27 cm. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness and the chest is clear. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 160 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Urinalysis shows no nitrites and no leucocytes, and a midstream urine specimen has been sent. Two sets of blood cultures have been collected. White cell count is 15.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) and C-reactive protein is 68 mg/L (<5).

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 160/min
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, symphysis fundal height 27 cm, no costovertebral angle tenderness, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph baseline 160/min with normal variability and accelerations, no decelerations. Urinalysis no nitrites or leucocytes, midstream urine sent, two sets of blood cultures collected. White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone, adding azithromycin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: All cephalosporins lack intrinsic activity against Listeria monocytogenes, so this regimen would leave the organism untreated despite being a reasonable broad spectrum choice for other causes of sepsis. Ceftriaxone would be appropriate for pyelonephritis, where the urinalysis would typically show nitrites or leucocytes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin, adding intravenous cefazolin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin only achieves therapeutic concentrations in urine and cannot treat a bacteraemic illness, and the urinalysis gives no evidence of urinary infection. It would be correct for asymptomatic bacteriuria or uncomplicated cystitis in the second trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral doxycycline, adding intravenous ceftriaxone if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Tetracyclines are avoided after the first trimester because they bind to developing bone and teeth, and doxycycline lacks reliable listerial activity in any case. Doxycycline would be considered for suspected rickettsial illness in a non-pregnant patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin, adding gentamicin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: A febrile pregnant woman with a systemic illness after eating soft cheese and prepared melon must be treated empirically for Listeria monocytogenes, and benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is the agent with reliable activity against it. Gentamicin is added synergistically once infection is confirmed, particularly for invasive disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous aciclovir, adding benzylpenicillin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy treats disseminated herpes simplex or varicella, which present with vesicular lesions or hepatitis rather than a febrile diarrhoeal illness after a food exposure. Aciclovir would be indicated for a pregnant woman with varicella pneumonitis or disseminated herpes infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are roughly 10 to 20 times more susceptible to invasive listeriosis than the general adult population, because cell-mediated immunity is modulated to tolerate the foetus and Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular organism controlled by that arm of immunity. The maternal illness is often unimpressive, amounting to fever, myalgia and gastrointestinal upset that looks like a viral syndrome, while the fetal consequences include miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. The key pharmacological fact is that cephalosporins, which dominate empirical sepsis regimens, have no activity against Listeria, so a standard ceftriaxone-based approach fails precisely when the diagnosis is missed. Blood cultures are the principal diagnostic test since stool culture is insensitive and not routinely performed. High risk foods in Australia include soft and semi-soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and cut melon, cold cooked chicken, pate and smoked seafood, and dietary counselling is a standard part of antenatal care.
key_points: Pregnancy substantially increases susceptibility to invasive Listeria monocytogenes infection
Maternal illness is mild and non-specific while fetal loss and neonatal sepsis are the major risks
Cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria, so standard sepsis regimens can miss it
Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is first-line, with gentamicin added for synergy in invasive disease
Blood cultures are the main diagnostic test; stool culture is insensitive
explanation.pearls: Any febrile pregnant woman treated empirically with ceftriaxone alone has no listerial cover, so add benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin whenever the history includes soft cheese, pre-prepared salad, cut melon, pate or cold cooked chicken.

sources.label: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and food

subtopic_detail: Surveillance after maternal seroconversion to parvovirus B19 in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in a maternal fetal medicine clinic. A 30-year-old primary school teacher at 17 weeks in her second pregnancy was exposed to several children with a facial rash at work 3 weeks ago and developed joint aches in her hands 5 days ago.

She has had no fever and no rash herself. Fetal movements are not yet felt. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated.

Booking serology 8 weeks ago showed parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin G negative and immunoglobulin M negative. Repeat serology this week shows immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Rubella immunoglobulin G is positive from booking and her measles status is immune. An ultrasound today shows a single foetus with growth on the 50th centile, normal anatomy, an amniotic fluid index within the normal range, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and no skin oedema. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is 0.9 multiples of the median.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Booking parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M and G both negative; current immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Ultrasound today: growth 50th centile, normal anatomy, normal amniotic fluid index, no ascites, pericardial effusion or skin oedema; middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 0.9 multiples of the median

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that the foetus is unaffected and continue routine antenatal care with a growth scan at 34 weeks
options.rationale: A single normal scan performed days after seroconversion cannot exclude anaemia that typically develops over the following 2 to 8 weeks, so discharging surveillance now risks missing hydrops at its treatable stage. Routine care would be appropriate if booking serology had shown pre-existing immunoglobulin G immunity. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing and karyotype within the next week
options.rationale: Invasive testing carries procedure-related loss risk and confirming viral genome in amniotic fluid does not change management, which is driven by the Doppler findings. Amniocentesis has a role where maternal serology is equivocal and fetal infection must be established to guide counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Administer maternal intravenous immunoglobulin now and repeat the ultrasound scan in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Maternal immunoglobulin has no established role in preventing fetal parvovirus infection or anaemia and would delay the surveillance that actually detects deterioration. Immunoglobulin is used for chronic parvovirus infection in immunocompromised adults, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange fetal blood sampling with intrauterine transfusion at the earliest available operating list
options.rationale: Transfusion is the treatment for demonstrated severe fetal anaemia and carries significant procedural risk, so it is not undertaken while Doppler velocities remain normal. It becomes indicated when middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops develops. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Weekly ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment for the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: Confirmed maternal seroconversion requires serial Doppler surveillance because fetal anaemia develops silently and the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises before hydrops becomes visible. Surveillance is maintained for 8 to 12 weeks after infection, which is the interval within which almost all fetal complications appear. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitor cells, and in a foetus with a short red cell lifespan and rapidly expanding blood volume this can produce profound aplastic anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Risk is greatest with infection before 20 weeks and falls substantially thereafter, which places this pregnancy in the higher risk window. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the elegant non-invasive tool here: anaemic blood has lower viscosity and flows faster, so the velocity rises well before hydrops is visible, allowing intrauterine transfusion to be offered at a stage where survival is good. Maternal infection is frequently asymptomatic or presents only with arthralgia, and the classic slapped cheek rash is a childhood feature rather than an adult one, so exposure history and serology carry the diagnosis. Spontaneous resolution of fetal anaemia occurs in a meaningful proportion of cases, which is why surveillance rather than immediate intervention is the correct posture while velocities are normal.
key_points: Risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops is highest with maternal infection before 20 weeks
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises with anaemia before hydrops becomes visible
Serial weekly Doppler surveillance continues for 8 to 12 weeks after seroconversion
Intrauterine transfusion is indicated once velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops appears
Maternal infection is often asymptomatic or limited to arthralgia, with no rash in most adults
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median is the transfusion threshold for fetal anaemia from any cause, parvovirus and red cell alloimmunisation alike.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

subtopic_detail: Interpreting discordant cytomegalovirus avidity and immunoglobulin results in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 26-year-old childcare worker at 13 weeks in her first pregnancy had serology sent by her general practitioner after 10 days of fatigue and mildly tender neck glands that have now resolved.

She has a well 2-year-old nephew in her care 3 days a week. She has had no rash, no sore throat and no jaundice. She takes pregnancy multivitamins only.

Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M is positive, immunoglobulin G is positive, and immunoglobulin G avidity is reported as high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Liver function tests, full blood count and film are within normal limits. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M is negative. An ultrasound at 13 weeks shows a single foetus with crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, and no intracranial or abdominal abnormality identified.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M positive, immunoglobulin G positive, immunoglobulin G avidity high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M negative. Liver function tests, full blood count and film within normal limits. Ultrasound at 13 weeks: crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, no intracranial or abdominal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Infection occurred before conception; give hygiene advice and continue routine antenatal care with a morphology scan
options.rationale: High immunoglobulin G avidity in the first trimester indicates that infection occurred more than about 3 months earlier, which places it before conception and means the foetus is not at risk from that episode. Persistent immunoglobulin M is common for months after infection and is the reason avidity testing exists, so the discordance resolves in favour of past infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction after 21 weeks
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is the correct investigation for confirmed primary infection during pregnancy, but the high avidity result here excludes recent infection. It would be indicated if avidity were low or if seroconversion from a negative immunoglobulin G had been documented. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; commence oral valaciclovir and arrange serial fetal neurosonography
options.rationale: High dose valaciclovir is an emerging option to reduce vertical transmission after confirmed periconceptional or first trimester primary infection, which has not occurred here. Treatment would be considered only once recent primary infection were established by low avidity or documented seroconversion. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: The results are uninterpretable; repeat the full serology panel in 3 weeks before giving any advice or counselling
options.rationale: Paired testing is valuable when avidity is intermediate or unavailable, but a clearly high avidity result in the first trimester is already conclusive and repeating it delays reassurance. Repeat testing would be appropriate for an intermediate avidity index or an equivocal immunoglobulin G. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Reactivation has occurred in pregnancy; arrange monthly fetal growth ultrasound and neonatal hearing assessment only
options.rationale: Non-primary infection carries a much lower transmission risk than primary infection and does not warrant monthly growth surveillance in a structurally normal foetus. The described serology fits resolved past primary infection rather than active reactivation, which would not typically produce a symptomatic illness. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, so serology results generate considerable anxiety and are frequently misinterpreted. The central problem is that immunoglobulin M is neither sensitive nor specific for recent infection: it can persist for six to nine months after primary infection, can reappear during reactivation, and can be falsely positive through cross-reactivity with other herpesviruses. Avidity testing solves this by measuring how tightly immunoglobulin G binds antigen, which increases as the antibody response matures, so high avidity in early pregnancy places the infection before conception. Vertical transmission risk after primary infection is roughly 30 to 40 per cent and is highest with first trimester infection, whereas non-primary infection carries a risk closer to 1 to 2 per cent. Australia does not screen routinely, so hygiene counselling for women in contact with young children remains the main preventive strategy.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M persists for months and cross-reacts, so it cannot date an infection alone
High immunoglobulin G avidity indicates infection more than about 3 months earlier
Primary infection carries roughly 30 to 40 per cent vertical transmission; non-primary infection is far lower
Amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction is deferred until after 21 weeks and at least 6 weeks from infection
Routine antenatal screening is not performed in Australia; hygiene advice is the preventive measure
explanation.pearls: Amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction is falsely negative if taken before 21 weeks, because fetal diuresis must be established for virus to appear in the amniotic fluid at detectable levels.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with absent uterus on imaging and normal female androgen levels
stem:
You are the registrar in an adolescent gynaecology clinic. A 16-year-old girl attends because she has never menstruated while all her friends began years ago. She has no cyclical pain and no abdominal swelling.

She is a competitive swimmer training 6 hours a week and eats well, with a stable weight. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and her sense of smell is normal.

On examination breast development is Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair are Tanner stage 5, and height is on the 70th centile. The external genitalia are normal in appearance with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple. Pelvic ultrasound reports no uterus identified, with two normal ovaries containing antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone is 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol is in the mid-follicular range, and total testosterone is 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female reference range). Renal tract ultrasound shows a solitary right kidney.

data_table.Examination: Breast Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair Tanner stage 5, height 70th centile, normal external genitalia with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: no uterus identified, two normal ovaries with antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol mid-follicular range, total testosterone 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female range). Renal tract ultrasound: solitary right kidney

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Complete androgen insensitivity with intra-abdominal testes and absent Mullerian derivatives
options.rationale: Androgen insensitivity produces testosterone in the male range and absent or very sparse pubic and axillary hair because hair growth depends on androgen receptor function, whereas this girl has full Tanner stage 5 sexual hair and female range testosterone. The near-pair distinction is that both conditions give an absent uterus and a blind vagina, but only androgen insensitivity gives male range androgens. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Congenital absence of the Mullerian duct derivatives with normally functioning ovaries
options.rationale: Female range testosterone with normal ovaries containing antral follicles and normal gonadotrophins establishes a 46,XX individual whose ovaries are working, so the absent uterus reflects failure of Mullerian duct development rather than androgen effect.
