The associated solitary kidney supports this, because the Mullerian and mesonephric systems develop in close association and renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Functional hypothalamic suppression from athletic training with reduced gonadotrophin secretion
options.rationale: Hypothalamic suppression gives low or low-normal gonadotrophins with low oestradiol and, critically, leaves the uterus present on imaging. It would explain secondary amenorrhoea in an athlete with a normal pelvic ultrasound and relative energy deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads and elevated gonadotrophin secretion from absent feedback
options.rationale: Streak gonads produce little oestradiol, so gonadotrophins rise markedly and spontaneous breast development does not occur without replacement. Here the ovaries contain antral follicles and gonadotrophins are normal, which excludes primary gonadal failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Transverse vaginal septum obstructing outflow above a normally developed uterine cavity
options.rationale: An obstructing septum leaves the uterus present and causes cyclical pain with accumulating blood, neither of which is present here. It would be the diagnosis in a girl with cyclical pain, a pelvic mass and a uterus visible on imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

explanation.summary: Mullerian agenesis is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhoea after gonadal dysgenesis, and it is diagnosed by the combination of normal secondary sexual characteristics, an absent uterus and female range androgens. The ovaries are derived from a different embryological origin and function normally, which means the girl ovulates, experiences no hormonal deficiency and needs no hormone replacement, points that are genuinely reassuring and often not explained clearly at diagnosis. Because the Mullerian ducts develop adjacent to the mesonephric system, renal anomalies such as a solitary or pelvic kidney occur in around a third of cases and skeletal anomalies in a smaller proportion, so imaging of the renal tract is part of the assessment. Management centres on creating vaginal length, usually with graduated dilator therapy as first-line and surgery reserved for failure, alongside psychological support. Fertility is possible through retrieval of the woman's own oocytes with gestational surrogacy, which is legally permitted on an altruistic basis in Australia.
key_points: Normal breast and sexual hair development with an absent uterus and female androgens defines Mullerian agenesis
Female range testosterone and normal sexual hair distinguish it from complete androgen insensitivity
Ovaries are of separate embryological origin, so ovulation and hormone production are normal
Renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases, warranting renal tract imaging
Graduated vaginal dilators are first-line management, with surgery reserved for dilator failure
explanation.pearls: Pubic and axillary hair is the bedside discriminator: it is fully developed in Mullerian agenesis and sparse or absent in complete androgen insensitivity, because sexual hair growth requires functioning androgen receptors.

subtopic_detail: Timing of antenatal deinfibulation planning for a woman with type 3 genital cutting
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 23-year-old woman who arrived in Australia 2 years ago attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy, accompanied by a professional interpreter she has agreed to.

She reports that passing urine takes several minutes and that periods before this pregnancy were prolonged and painful. She has no dysuria and no fever. She has not had intercourse difficulties raised as a concern by her or her partner.

On examination, with her consent, the vulva shows a horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip. The urethral meatus is not visible. There is no tenderness, no discharge and no infection. The uterus is consistent with dates and fetal heart tones are normal. She says she does not know what was done to her as a child and asks what this will mean for the birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip, urethral meatus not visible, no tenderness, discharge or infection, uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart tones normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Defer any procedure and plan deinfibulation during the second stage of labour with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Deinfibulation in the second stage is an acceptable fallback when a woman presents late or declines earlier intervention, but it is performed under time pressure with less opportunity for genuine consent. It would be the plan for a woman first seen in advanced labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Recommend planned caesarean section at 39 weeks to avoid vaginal birth, with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Previous genital cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean birth, and recommending one avoids rather than addresses the obstruction while committing her to abdominal surgery in every future pregnancy. Caesarean birth would be indicated for a standard obstetric reason arising independently. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Discuss and offer planned antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Elective deinfibulation before labour allows the procedure to be done with adequate analgesia, informed discussion and an interpreter, and it permits vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp access during labour. The second trimester is the preferred window because the pregnancy is established and there is time to heal well before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Arrange reinfibulation to be performed after the birth if she requests it, with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions and must not be performed or promised regardless of a woman's request, though the request itself deserves a respectful explanation. Repair after birth restores the anatomy to its deinfibulated state only. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Refer to the child protection team and defer any discussion of the birth plan until that assessment concludes
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting obligations concern girls at risk of cutting rather than adult women who were cut as children overseas, so notification here is not triggered by her own history. A report would be required if there were concern that a child in the family was at risk of undergoing the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

explanation.summary: Type 3 cutting, in which the introitus is narrowed by an occlusive seal, creates specific obstetric problems: vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp electrode placement may be impossible, and labouring against a rigid scar risks anterior tears involving the urethra and severe perineal trauma. Deinfibulation divides the scar tissue anteriorly to expose the urethral meatus and restore access, and it is best done electively in the second trimester when it can be planned with the woman rather than improvised. Doing it antenatally also allows the conversation to happen properly, with a professional interpreter rather than a family member, since women frequently do not know what was done to them and have never been offered an explanation. Chronic sequelae including obstructed urinary flow, dysmenorrhoea, recurrent infection and dyspareunia are common and often never raised, so the antenatal visit is a genuine opportunity. Reinfibulation is a criminal offence throughout Australia, and declining it requires a clear and non-judgemental explanation.
key_points: Type 3 cutting obstructs examination, catheterisation and fetal monitoring during labour
Elective second trimester deinfibulation is preferred to intrapartum division
Previous genital cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean birth
Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions
Use a professional interpreter rather than a family member for these discussions
explanation.pearls: Mandatory reporting in this context is triggered by risk to a girl in the family, not by an adult woman's own history, so ask specifically about daughters and planned overseas travel rather than notifying on the basis of the woman's examination.

sources.label: Department of Health: Female genital mutilation in Australia

subtopic_detail: Classifying and siting repair of a perineal injury where external sphincter fibres are partly torn
stem:
You are the registrar called to the birth suite to assess a perineal injury after a 26-year-old woman's first birth. The baby weighed 4020 g and was born by vacuum extraction with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage.

The midwife has applied pressure and bleeding is controlled. The woman has a working epidural and is comfortable.

With her consent you examine in lithotomy in the birth suite with good lighting. The episiotomy extends through the perineal body. Digital rectal examination shows intact rectal mucosa and intact anal epithelium. On pill-rolling the external anal sphincter between index finger and thumb, you find the torn fibres involve less than half the thickness of the external sphincter across its width, and the internal anal sphincter appears intact as a separate pale layer. She has had no previous perineal injury and no anal incontinence.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy extending through the perineal body; rectal mucosa and anal epithelium intact; external anal sphincter torn through less than half its thickness; internal anal sphincter intact; bleeding controlled; epidural working

lead_in: How should this injury be classified and repaired?

options.text: Second degree tear involving the perineal body, repaired in the birth suite by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: A second degree tear by definition spares the anal sphincter complex entirely, and here external sphincter fibres are divided. This classification would apply if pill-rolling had confirmed an intact external sphincter beneath a torn perineal body. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3b, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: The subclassification 3b denotes external sphincter disruption of more than half its thickness, whereas less than half is torn here. The near-pair distinction between 3a and 3b turns purely on the proportion of external sphincter thickness involved. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3c, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: The subclassification 3c requires the internal anal sphincter to be torn as well, and it is described here as an intact pale layer. Recognising internal sphincter involvement matters because it predicts worse continence outcomes than external disruption alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3a, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: Any disruption of the external anal sphincter makes this a third degree tear, and involvement of less than half its thickness defines the 3a subclassification. Sphincter repair requires theatre conditions with adequate lighting, assistance, anaesthesia and instruments, because repair quality in the birth suite is consistently poorer and long-term continence depends on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Fourth degree tear involving the anorectal complex, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: A fourth degree tear requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa, both of which are explicitly intact on rectal examination. That classification would apply if the examining finger were visible through the wound or mucosa were divided. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is substantially underdiagnosed, and the single biggest determinant of whether it is found is whether a systematic rectal examination and pill-rolling of the sphincter are performed after every vaginal birth, not only when a tear looks deep. The classification is not academic: it drives where the repair happens, who performs it, what antibiotics and laxatives are prescribed, and what the woman is told about future births. Grades 3a and 3b differ only in the proportion of external sphincter thickness torn, while 3c adds internal sphincter disruption, which carries the worst prognosis for continence because the internal sphincter maintains resting tone. Repair in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia allows adequate relaxation and exposure, and either end-to-end or overlap technique is acceptable for the external sphincter, while the internal sphincter is repaired end-to-end separately. Postoperative care includes a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy, and structured follow-up with symptom review before a subsequent pregnancy.
key_points: Any external anal sphincter disruption makes the tear third degree, regardless of perineal appearance
3a is less than half the external sphincter thickness, 3b more than half, 3c adds internal sphincter involvement
Fourth degree requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa
Repair belongs in theatre with anaesthesia, lighting, assistance and appropriate instruments
Digital rectal examination and pill-rolling after every vaginal birth is what makes the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Internal anal sphincter disruption, the 3c grade, is the finding that most strongly predicts long-term faecal urgency and incontinence, so identify it as a separate pale layer and repair it end-to-end rather than incorporating it into the external sphincter repair.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Switching antithyroid drug between trimesters when hepatic and teratogenic risks conflict
stem:
You are the registrar in a joint obstetric medicine clinic. A 27-year-old woman at 13 weeks in her second pregnancy has Graves disease diagnosed 3 years ago and has taken propylthiouracil since her positive pregnancy test, switched from carbimazole by her general practitioner at 5 weeks.

She reports feeling well with no tremor and no palpitations. Her first child, born before her diagnosis, is well. She has no personal or family history of liver disease and drinks no alcohol.

Thyroid function today shows free thyroxine at the upper end of the pregnancy reference range and thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed at 0.03 mIU/L. Thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody is 8.2 IU/L (<1.8). Liver function tests taken today show alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 152 U/L (<40), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (<20) and alkaline phosphatase within the pregnancy range. A repeat sample 4 days later confirms alanine aminotransferase 204 U/L. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and a liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: Free thyroxine at upper end of pregnancy reference range, thyroid stimulating hormone 0.03 mIU/L, thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody 8.2 IU/L (<1.8). Alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L then 204 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 152 U/L (<40), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (<20), alkaline phosphatase within pregnancy range. Viral hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal
data_table.Medications: Propylthiouracil since 5 weeks, switched from carbimazole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue propylthiouracil at the current dose and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity is idiosyncratic and can progress rapidly to hepatic failure requiring transplantation, so persisting with rising transaminases is not safe monitoring. Continuing would be defensible only in the first trimester if no alternative existed and liver enzymes were normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication now and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy causes miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction and thyroid storm, and her antibody titre is high, so stopping treatment exchanges one risk for a larger one. Withdrawal would be reasonable in late pregnancy for a woman whose disease has remitted with a low antibody titre on a minimal dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine ablation after the first trimester and monitor thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and ablates the fetal thyroid from about 10 to 12 weeks when it begins concentrating iodine. It is an option for definitive treatment once pregnancy and breastfeeding are complete, with conception deferred for 6 months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add oral prednisolone to the current propylthiouracil and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Corticosteroid does not treat idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury and adding it leaves the offending agent in place while introducing glycaemic and infective risks. Prednisolone has a place in thyroid storm and in Graves orbitopathy, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch back to carbimazole now and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester to avoid carbimazole embryopathy, but that window has passed at 13 weeks and the guidance is to switch back to carbimazole for the remainder of pregnancy. Rising transaminases with other causes excluded make continuing propylthiouracil unsafe, since its hepatotoxicity can progress to fulminant failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Managing Graves disease in pregnancy means trading two drug toxicities against each other across gestation. Carbimazole and its active metabolite methimazole are associated with an embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia and abdominal wall defects, concentrated in the 6 to 10 week organogenesis window, which is why propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester. Propylthiouracil, however, carries a small but genuine risk of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that can progress to fulminant failure, and this risk does not diminish with time on the drug. The resulting strategy is to use propylthiouracil through the first trimester and then switch back, which many clinicians forget to do. Treatment aims to keep free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy reference range on the lowest possible dose, deliberately accepting mild maternal hyperthyroidism, because both drugs cross the placenta and over-treatment causes fetal goitre and hypothyroidism.
key_points: Propylthiouracil in the first trimester avoids carbimazole embryopathy during organogenesis
Switch back to carbimazole after the first trimester because of propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity
Target free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy range on the lowest effective dose
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and ablates the fetal thyroid
A receptor antibody titre more than three times the upper limit predicts fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody at 18 to 22 weeks even in a woman rendered euthyroid or previously treated by surgery or ablation, because the antibody crosses the placenta and causes neonatal thyrotoxicosis independently of maternal thyroid status.

subtopic_detail: Responding to a falling lamotrigine concentration with breakthrough seizures in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in a joint obstetric medicine clinic. A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy has focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation, seizure free for 3 years on lamotrigine 300 mg daily before conception.

She has had two generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the past 5 weeks, the most recent while driving, and has surrendered her licence. She confirms she has not missed doses and a pill count supports this. She takes folic acid 5 mg daily and has no other medications and no vomiting.

Her pre-pregnancy trough lamotrigine concentration was 28 micromol/L. A trough sample taken today is 11 micromol/L. Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and magnesium are within normal limits, and she has no rash. Blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg with no proteinuria. Ultrasound today shows growth on the 40th centile with normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Trough lamotrigine 11 micromol/L today versus 28 micromol/L pre-pregnancy. Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and magnesium within normal limits. No proteinuria. Ultrasound: growth 40th centile, normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 300 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily; adherence confirmed by pill count

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by serial concentrations, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
options.rationale: Oestrogen-driven induction of glucuronidation increases lamotrigine clearance substantially through pregnancy, and the fall from 28 to 11 micromol/L with breakthrough seizures despite confirmed adherence is a pharmacokinetic problem requiring dose escalation to restore the pre-pregnancy concentration. Planning the postpartum reduction at the same time is essential because clearance returns toward baseline within 2 to 3 weeks of birth and toxicity otherwise follows. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Continue the current lamotrigine dose and repeat the trough concentration in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Clearance continues to rise through the second and third trimesters, so maintaining the dose means concentrations will fall further and seizures will continue. Holding the dose would be reasonable only if she remained seizure free with a stable concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Add sodium valproate to the current lamotrigine dose, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of any antiseizure medicine and is avoided in pregnancy whenever alternatives exist. Valproate also inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, which would raise lamotrigine concentrations unpredictably and increase rash risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Switch from lamotrigine to levetiracetam over 4 weeks, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
options.rationale: Changing agent during pregnancy exposes her to breakthrough seizures during cross-titration when her current drug was fully effective before conception at an adequate concentration. Switching would be considered before conception, not as a response to a clearance problem that dose adjustment solves. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Add a regular clobazam dose to the current lamotrigine, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
options.rationale: Adding a benzodiazepine treats the seizures without correcting the subtherapeutic concentration causing them, and it brings sedation plus neonatal withdrawal and floppy infant risk. Clobazam has a role as short-term seizure cluster cover, not as a substitute for optimising the primary agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is one of the preferred antiseizure medicines in pregnancy on teratogenicity grounds, but it has the most dramatic pregnancy-related pharmacokinetic change of the commonly used agents. Rising oestrogen induces uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase, so clearance can more than double and concentrations commonly fall by half or more by the third trimester even with perfect adherence. This is why pre-pregnancy baseline concentrations are worth obtaining: the target in pregnancy is the woman's own pre-pregnancy concentration at which she was seizure free, not a population reference range. Generalised tonic-clonic seizures carry real risk to both mother and foetus, including trauma, hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, so breakthrough seizures are not something to observe. The postpartum reduction is the step most often missed: clearance falls rapidly after birth and women maintained on their escalated pregnancy dose develop toxicity with ataxia, diplopia and sedation within a fortnight, usually while caring for a newborn.
key_points: Oestrogen induces glucuronidation, roughly doubling lamotrigine clearance during pregnancy
Target the woman's own pre-pregnancy concentration rather than a population reference range
Obtain a baseline concentration before conception in any woman planning pregnancy on lamotrigine
Breakthrough generalised seizures warrant dose escalation, not observation or a change of agent
Plan the postpartum taper in advance, since clearance normalises within 2 to 3 weeks of birth
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum lamotrigine taper into the birth plan at the time the pregnancy dose is increased, stepping back toward the pre-pregnancy dose over about 2 to 3 weeks after delivery, because toxicity typically appears around day 10 to 14.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological lactation suppression after stillbirth in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman on the ward. She gave birth two days ago at 34 weeks following an intrauterine fetal death, and is due for discharge tomorrow.

Her breasts have become firm, hot and painful overnight and milk is leaking through her clothing. She tells you she finds this 'unbearable to live with' and asks whether anything can be given to stop it. She has thought about donating milk and has decided against it.

Her blood pressure has been between 108/64 and 118/72 mmHg throughout the pregnancy and since birth, and her booking and postnatal blood pressure records contain no readings above 130/80 mmHg. She has no history of depression or psychosis, takes no regular medication and is not planning to feed a future infant in the coming weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1°C
data_table.Breast examination: Bilaterally firm, warm and tender with spontaneous leakage; no focal mass, no erythematous wedge, no fluctuance
data_table.History: Blood pressure never above 130/80 mmHg antenatally or postnatally; no psychiatric history; no regular medications

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Prescribe bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally twice daily for a fourteen day course
options.rationale: Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin effectively but has been associated with hypertension, seizures, stroke and myocardial infarction in postpartum women, and it requires two weeks of twice daily dosing. Cabergoline has replaced it because a single dose achieves the same effect with a better safety profile. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose with supportive breast measures
options.rationale: A single 1 mg oral dose of cabergoline is the Australian standard for lactation suppression after stillbirth or neonatal death, and it works best when given in the first days postpartum before full lactogenesis is established. Normal blood pressure throughout the pregnancy matters because hypertensive disorders and a psychotic illness history are the two main cautions against a dopamine agonist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe oestrogen therapy for one week with firm breast support and ice packs
options.rationale: High dose oestrogen was used historically to suppress lactation but was abandoned because it substantially raises the risk of venous thromboembolism in an already prothrombotic postpartum period. This woman has an additional thrombotic risk from recent birth and reduced mobility. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

options.text: Advise firm breast support and analgesia alone and avoid any drug treatment
options.rationale: Non-pharmacological measures are always offered and are the right answer for a woman who declines medication, but engorgement managed this way takes one to two weeks to settle. Withholding an effective and safe option from a bereaved woman who has explicitly asked for it is not neutral. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

options.text: Advise regular expression of milk to comfort and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Regular expression stimulates prolactin release and maintains supply, which is the opposite of the goal here, and it is advised only for women who choose to express and donate. Minimal expression for comfort only is the correct non-pharmacological approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

explanation.summary: Lactogenesis proceeds after any birth beyond about 16 weeks gestation, so women who experience stillbirth, late miscarriage or neonatal death face the physical reminder of milk production during acute grief. Suppression is offered rather than assumed, because some women choose to express and donate milk as part of their grieving and that choice should be supported. When suppression is chosen, cabergoline given as a single 1 mg oral dose is the Australian first-line agent, most effective within the first few days postpartum. Blood pressure should be checked first, as dopamine agonists are avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and there is a recognised though uncommon association with psychotic symptoms. Supportive measures continue alongside the drug: a firm supportive bra, cold packs, simple analgesia and minimal expression for comfort only.
key_points: Cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose is the Australian first-line suppressant
It works best in the first days postpartum before lactation is fully established
Check blood pressure first; avoid dopamine agonists in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Bromocriptine and oestrogen have both been abandoned on safety grounds
Offer suppression rather than assume it, as some women choose to express and donate
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline has a terminal half-life of around 60 hours, which is why one 1 mg dose suppresses prolactin for two to three weeks while bromocriptine needed twice daily dosing for a fortnight.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Lactation suppression

subtopic_detail: Duration of the magnesium sulfate infusion given for fetal neuroprotection before imminent preterm birth
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar called to the birth suite for a 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 28 weeks and 3 days. She arrived two hours ago saying she has had 'tightenings coming every three minutes' and a gush of fluid.

Speculum examination confirms ruptured membranes and vaginal examination finds the cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced with the vertex at the ischial spines. Contractions are palpably strong and regular and the midwife anticipates birth within a few hours.

She received the first dose of betamethasone six hours ago. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 150/min with normal variability and no decelerations. Her reflexes are normal, urine output is 60 mL per hour and renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Vaginal examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced, vertex at the ischial spines, membranes ruptured
data_table.Medications given: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly six hours ago
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 54 micromol/L (45-90), urine output 60 mL/hour, deep tendon reflexes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional treatment to give now?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after the birth
options.rationale: Continuing the infusion after birth is the pattern used for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia, where the maternal risk persists into the postpartum period. The neuroprotective effect operates on the fetal brain before and during birth, so there is no rationale for continuing once the baby is born. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously then 1 g per hour until birth or for 24 hours
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of imminent birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors, with a number needed to treat of about 63. The Australian regimen is a 4 g loading dose over 20 to 30 minutes followed by 1 g per hour, stopped at birth or after 24 hours, whichever comes first. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously as a single dose with no maintenance infusion
options.rationale: A loading dose alone does not maintain the fetal serum concentration through the period of birth, which is when the neuroprotective effect is exerted. The trials that demonstrated benefit all used a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 20 mg every six hours to prolong the pregnancy
options.rationale: Tocolysis is used to buy time for corticosteroids to act or for transfer to a tertiary centre, and it is not effective once the cervix is 4 cm dilated with ruptured membranes and strong regular contractions. Suppressing labour in the presence of ruptured membranes also raises the risk of chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

options.text: A second course of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly given 24 hours apart
options.rationale: The second dose of the current course is due at 24 hours, not a whole repeat course, and birth is expected long before that. Repeat courses are considered only when a woman remains undelivered and at risk more than 7 days after the first course. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Antenatal magnesium sulfate given shortly before very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, an effect established by the Australasian ACTOMgSO4 trial and confirmed by later meta-analysis. Australian guidance recommends it for women at risk of imminent birth before 30 weeks gestation, whether the birth is spontaneous or planned, with imminent meaning expected within 24 hours. The regimen is a 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 to 30 minutes followed by 1 g per hour, discontinued at birth or at 24 hours, and it is not repeated or continued postpartum. Monitoring is clinical, watching respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output for early magnesium toxicity, with serum magnesium levels reserved for renal impairment or suspected toxicity. Magnesium for neuroprotection is a separate indication from magnesium for eclampsia prophylaxis, and confusing the two regimens is a common source of error.
key_points: Give for imminent birth before 30 weeks, whether spontaneous or planned
Loading dose 4 g intravenously over 20 to 30 minutes, then 1 g per hour maintenance
Stop at birth or at 24 hours, whichever comes first, and do not continue postpartum
Monitor respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output rather than routine levels
Tocolysis has no role once the cervix is 4 cm with ruptured membranes and strong contractions
explanation.pearls: The first sign of magnesium toxicity is loss of the patellar reflex, which occurs at around 4 to 5 mmol/L, well before the respiratory depression that appears above roughly 5 mmol/L; calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously is the antidote.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy stratified by peak total bile acid concentration
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in a day assessment unit reviewing a 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 35 weeks and 2 days. She describes three weeks of itching that is worst on her palms and the soles of her feet and keeps her awake, and says she has scratched until she bleeds.

There is no rash apart from excoriations and no abdominal pain. Her urine and stools are of normal colour and she has had no nausea or vomiting.

Blood pressure and urinalysis are normal and fetal growth is on the 45th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Fasting total bile acids taken this morning are 118 micromol/L, having been 46 micromol/L two weeks ago. A viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies are negative and liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8°C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations with no primary rash; no right upper quadrant tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Total bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 19), previously 46 micromol/L two weeks ago; alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (less than 30); bilirubin within normal limits
data_table.Other results: Viral hepatitis serology and liver autoantibodies negative, liver ultrasound normal
data_table.Fetal assessment: Estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile, umbilical artery Dopplers normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour at 39 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Birth at 39 weeks is the plan for the mildest disease, where bile acids stay below 40 micromol/L and the stillbirth risk is close to background. Applying it to a peak above 100 micromol/L accepts a stillbirth risk several times the background rate across an extra month of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour at 38 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Birth between 38 and 39 weeks is appropriate for moderate disease with bile acids in the 40 to 99 micromol/L range, which is where this woman sat two weeks ago. Management follows the peak concentration reached, not the earlier value. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange weekly cardiotocography and plan induction of labour at 40 weeks
options.rationale: Cardiotocography and ultrasound do not predict the stillbirth of cholestasis, which is a sudden arrhythmic event caused by bile acid toxicity to the fetal myocardium rather than a gradual hypoxic decline. Surveillance offers false reassurance and cannot substitute for timing the birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour within the next week
options.rationale: A peak total bile acid concentration of 100 micromol/L or more marks the severe group, in which stillbirth risk rises steeply after 35 weeks, so birth is recommended at 35 to 36 weeks. Ursodeoxycholic acid is offered for maternal itch and biochemistry although it does not reduce the stillbirth risk, which is why the timing of birth carries the management. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange weekly bile acid testing and plan spontaneous labour at term
options.rationale: Serial monitoring is appropriate while bile acids remain below 40 micromol/L, and the result that would trigger action has already arrived. Awaiting spontaneous labour at term in severe disease exposes the pregnancy to the highest risk window. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus, classically of the palms and soles and worse at night, without a primary rash, and is confirmed by raised total serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases. The clinically important consequence is stillbirth, and the large 2019 individual patient data meta-analysis established that risk is concentrated almost entirely in women whose peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more. That finding reshaped practice into a three-band approach: below 40 micromol/L birth at around 40 weeks, 40 to 99 micromol/L birth at 38 to 39 weeks, and 100 micromol/L or above birth at 35 to 36 weeks. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and liver biochemistry modestly but the PITCHES trial showed it does not reduce perinatal death, so it is offered for symptoms rather than relied on for safety. Antenatal surveillance does not predict the event, and the condition resolves rapidly after birth with liver function checked at least 6 weeks postpartum to confirm normalisation.
key_points: Diagnosis rests on pruritus without a primary rash plus raised total bile acids
Peak bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more define the severe group with steeply raised stillbirth risk
Timing of birth follows the peak value: 40 weeks, 38 to 39 weeks, or 35 to 36 weeks by band
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but does not reduce stillbirth
Cardiotocography and ultrasound do not predict the stillbirth of cholestasis
explanation.pearls: Recheck liver function and bile acids at least 6 weeks postpartum: persistent abnormality points to an underlying chronic liver disease such as hepatitis C or primary biliary cholangitis, which is found in a small but real minority of women labelled with cholestasis of pregnancy.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Obstetric cholestasis
BMJ Best Practice: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Non-hormonal control of ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman actively trying to conceive
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman referred with two years of heavy periods. She says she floods through a super tampon and a pad together within an hour on her two worst days, passes clots the size of a fifty cent coin, and has twice had to leave work and go home.

Her cycles come every 28 days and last 7 days, and she has no bleeding between periods, no pain and no postcoital bleeding. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for four months and she tells you she does not want anything that would prevent pregnancy.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal sized uterus with an endometrial thickness of 7 mm, no fibroid and no polyp, and normal ovaries. Thyroid function, a coagulation screen and von Willebrand factor assays are within normal limits. Her haemoglobin is 103 g/L (115-155) with a ferritin of 7 microgram/L (15-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Menstrual pattern: Regular 28 day cycles, 7 day bleed, flooding through double protection hourly on the heaviest days, clots, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal sized uterus, endometrial thickness 7 mm, no fibroid or polyp, normal ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 103 g/L (115-155), ferritin 7 microgram/L (15-200), thyroid function, coagulation screen and von Willebrand factor assays within normal limits
data_table.Fertility plan: Trying to conceive for four months and declines anything that would prevent pregnancy

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and start oral iron replacement
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding and would be first line for a woman who did not want to conceive. It is contraceptive, which makes it unacceptable to a woman actively trying for a pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and start oral iron replacement
options.rationale: The combined pill reduces menstrual blood loss by around a third and is a reasonable second-line option, but it suppresses ovulation and is therefore incompatible with her stated goal. It would be the right choice if she also wanted contraception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start norethisterone from day 5 to day 26 of each cycle with oral iron
options.rationale: Long cycle oral progestogen does reduce blood loss but it suppresses ovulation across most of the cycle and so acts as contraception at this dose and duration. Short luteal phase progestogen courses, by contrast, are ineffective for heavy bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for endometrial ablation and start oral iron replacement beforehand
options.rationale: Ablation destroys the endometrium and is offered only to women who have completed their family, with reliable contraception afterwards because a pregnancy in an ablated uterus carries a high risk of abnormal placentation. It is definitively contraindicated in a woman seeking pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start tranexamic acid during menstruation and start oral iron replacement
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid taken only on the days of bleeding reduces menstrual blood loss by around 40 to 50 per cent, has no effect on ovulation or on conception, and can be continued while she is trying for a pregnancy. Iron replacement is given alongside because a ferritin of 7 microgram/L means her stores are exhausted and repletion before conception matters for both her and the pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its effect on the woman rather than by a measured volume, and the assessment separates structural causes, identified on examination and ultrasound, from non-structural ones including coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial disorders and iatrogenic causes. A coagulation screen with von Willebrand studies is warranted when heavy bleeding has been present since menarche or there is a personal or family bleeding history, as von Willebrand disease is found in a significant minority of these women. Treatment selection turns on whether contraception is wanted, because the most effective options are also contraceptive: the levonorgestrel intrauterine system first, then the combined pill or long cycle progestogen. For a woman trying to conceive, the non-hormonal options are tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, both taken only during menstruation, with tranexamic acid the more effective of the two. Iron deficiency is treated in every case, since it is the consequence that most often drives the symptoms of fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.
key_points: Whether contraception is wanted determines which treatments are available
Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by 40 to 50 per cent and does not affect fertility
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the other non-hormonal option and also help dysmenorrhoea
Endometrial ablation is only for women who have completed their family
Investigate for von Willebrand disease when bleeding has been heavy since menarche
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid is taken only on the days of heaviest bleeding, typically 1 g three times daily for up to 4 days, and it does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism in women without a thrombophilia, which is the commonest reason it is wrongly withheld.

subtopic_detail: Choice and duration of hormone replacement after biochemical confirmation of premature ovarian insufficiency
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. She says her periods 'just stopped' eight months ago and that she is waking three or four times a night drenched in sweat and feels dry and sore with intercourse.

She has never been pregnant and has an intact uterus. She takes no medications and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

A urine pregnancy test is negative. Follicle stimulating hormone measured four weeks apart is 58 IU/L and 62 IU/L with an oestradiol of 42 pmol/L on both occasions. Prolactin and thyroid function are within normal limits and a karyotype and fragile X premutation screen have been requested. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 58 IU/L then 62 IU/L four weeks apart (follicular 3-10); oestradiol 42 pmol/L on both occasions (follicular 110-400)
data_table.Other results: Urine pregnancy test negative; prolactin and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.History: Intact uterus, nulliparous, no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, body mass index 23 kg/m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oestrogen with a progestogen and continue it until about the age of 51
options.rationale: Two follicle stimulating hormone measurements above 40 IU/L a month apart with low oestradiol under the age of 40 confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, and systemic oestrogen replaces what the ovary would otherwise have produced until the average age of menopause. A progestogen is added because the uterus is intact, and physiological replacement at this age protects bone density and cardiovascular and cognitive outcomes rather than carrying the risk profile of postmenopausal therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her again in six months
options.rationale: The combined pill is an acceptable alternative for a woman who also wants contraception, but its ethinyloestradiol dose exceeds physiological replacement and the 7 day hormone free interval leaves a gap in bone protection. Standard hormone therapy is preferred when contraception is not the priority. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Start alendronate weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation for bone health
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates target bone alone and leave the vasomotor, urogenital, cardiovascular and cognitive consequences of oestrogen deficiency untreated. They are reserved for women who cannot take oestrogen, and their long half-life raises concerns in women who may later conceive. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor to control the vasomotor symptoms
options.rationale: Non-hormonal agents have a place when oestrogen is contraindicated, such as after hormone receptor positive breast cancer, and they do nothing for bone or cardiovascular risk. Withholding oestrogen from a 34-year-old with no contraindication accepts decades of avoidable deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: Arrange bone densitometry and defer any treatment until the result becomes available
options.rationale: Baseline densitometry is worth arranging, but the decision to replace oestrogen rests on the diagnosis rather than on the density result, and a normal scan would not change it. Deferring treatment allows further bone loss during the interval. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea for at least 4 months before the age of 40 with two follicle stimulating hormone measurements above 40 IU/L taken at least 4 weeks apart. About 90 per cent of cases have no identified cause, but the workup looks for Turner syndrome and other karyotypic abnormalities, the fragile X premutation, adrenal and thyroid autoimmunity, and iatrogenic causes including chemotherapy, radiotherapy and bilateral oophorectomy. Hormone therapy in this group is replacement rather than supplementation, and the risk-benefit balance is entirely different from that of women taking hormone therapy after a normal age at menopause, with benefits for bone, cardiovascular health, urogenital symptoms and quality of life. Treatment continues until at least the average age of menopause, around 51 years, at which point the decision is reconsidered on the usual grounds. Spontaneous ovarian activity returns intermittently in 5 to 10 per cent, so pregnancy remains possible and standard hormone therapy is not contraceptive.
key_points: Diagnosis needs amenorrhoea plus two follicle stimulating hormone levels above 40 IU/L a month apart
Replace with oestrogen plus a progestogen if the uterus is intact, continuing until about age 51
The risk-benefit balance differs entirely from hormone therapy started after a normal menopause
Investigate for karyotype abnormality, fragile X premutation and autoimmune disease
Standard hormone therapy is not contraceptive and spontaneous conception still occurs
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and carries no measurable excess venous thromboembolism risk, which makes it the preferred route in women who are obese, are migraineurs with aura, or have a thrombotic history.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Premature ovarian insufficiency

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment of endometrial hyperplasia without atypia in a woman wishing to keep her uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman in clinic with the result of an endometrial biopsy. She was referred with two years of heavy, prolonged and irregular periods that soak through a pad every hour on her worst days.

She has two children and has completed her family but tells you she 'really does not want an operation' and would like to keep her uterus if that is safe.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 16 mm with no focal lesion and normal ovaries. A pipelle biopsy reports endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. A full blood count shows haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155) with a ferritin of 9 microgram/L (15-200), and her thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 16 mm, no focal lesion, normal ovaries
data_table.Histology: Pipelle biopsy reports endometrial hyperplasia without atypia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 microgram/L (15-200), thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Arrange total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy on the next list
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is first line for hyperplasia with atypia, where up to 40 per cent harbour a concurrent carcinoma, and for hyperplasia without atypia only after medical treatment fails or the woman chooses surgery. Oophorectomy would also impose a surgical menopause on a premenopausal woman without indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

options.text: Start cyclical oral norethisterone for 10 days each month and resample at 6 months
options.rationale: Cyclical progestogen given for only part of the cycle produces lower regression rates than continuous progestogen exposure, because the endometrium is unopposed for the remainder of each month. Continuous oral progestogen is an acceptable second choice, but cyclical dosing is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and resample the endometrium at 6 months
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system achieves regression of hyperplasia without atypia in over 90 per cent of women, exceeding oral progestogens, and simultaneously treats the heavy bleeding that brought her in. Surveillance biopsies are taken at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative samples, with the device left in place for at least 5 years given her ongoing risk from obesity. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

options.text: Arrange endometrial ablation and repeat the endometrial sampling again at 6 months
options.rationale: Ablation is contraindicated when hyperplasia is present because incomplete destruction can leave islands of endometrium behind adhesions, where disease progresses and subsequent sampling becomes unreliable. It is a treatment for heavy bleeding with benign histology only. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

options.text: Advise weight loss alone and repeat the endometrial sampling again at 12 months
options.rationale: Weight reduction addresses the peripheral aromatisation of androgens in adipose tissue that drives the unopposed oestrogen and is an important adjunct, but it is too slow and unreliable to be relied on as sole treatment. Observation alone is reserved for women in whom an identifiable reversible cause has been removed. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is classified by the presence or absence of cytological atypia, and that single distinction drives management. Without atypia the risk of progression to carcinoma over 20 years is under 5 per cent, so medical treatment with surveillance is appropriate; with atypia the risk is an order of magnitude higher and a substantial proportion already harbour occult carcinoma, so hysterectomy is recommended. The underlying driver is unopposed oestrogen, whether from obesity, anovulation, polycystic ovary syndrome, tamoxifen or an oestrogen secreting tumour, and identifying and addressing that source is part of treatment. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system outperforms oral progestogens for regression and is first line, with endometrial sampling at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative biopsies are obtained. The device is then retained for at least 5 years in women whose risk factors persist, with annual surveillance considered for those who remain obese or anovulatory.
key_points: Atypia versus no atypia is the distinction that determines medical versus surgical management
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line and outperforms oral progestogens
Resample at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative biopsies
Endometrial ablation is contraindicated when hyperplasia is present
Identify and treat the source of unopposed oestrogen, most commonly obesity or anovulation
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen acts as an endometrial oestrogen agonist while antagonising the breast, so any abnormal bleeding in a woman taking it warrants sampling regardless of endometrial thickness, since the thickened heterogeneous appearance on ultrasound is unreliable in that setting.

subtopic_detail: Action on a borderline fetal scalp lactate result with a persisting pathological cardiotocograph
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in the birth suite with a 27-year-old woman in her first labour at 39 weeks and 4 days. The midwife called you because the trace 'has not looked right for the last half hour'.

She is 7 cm dilated with the vertex at the ischial spines and has an epidural in situ. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 155/min with reduced variability at 3 beats/min and repetitive late decelerations following more than half of the contractions, present now for 40 minutes.

You have already stopped the oxytocin infusion, turned her into the left lateral position and given a 500 mL crystalloid bolus, and the trace has not changed. There is no vaginal bleeding, the liquor is clear and the uterus is soft between contractions. A fetal blood sample taken five minutes ago gives a lactate of 4.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 155/min, variability 3 beats/min, repetitive late decelerations after more than half of contractions for 40 minutes
data_table.Vaginal examination: Cervix 7 cm dilated, vertex at the ischial spines, clear liquor
data_table.Fetal blood sample: Scalp lactate 4.4 mmol/L (normal less than 4.2, borderline 4.2 to 4.8, abnormal 4.8 or above)
data_table.Measures already taken: Oxytocin stopped, left lateral positioning, 500 mL crystalloid bolus, no change in the trace

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to immediate caesarean section under general anaesthetic in theatre
options.rationale: Immediate birth is indicated when the scalp lactate is 4.8 mmol/L or above, when sampling fails, or when there is an acute event such as prolonged bradycardia, abruption or cord prolapse. A borderline result in a stable woman with a working epidural does not justify a general anaesthetic. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Continue conservative measures and repeat the sample in two hours if unchanged
options.rationale: Two hours is the interval used after a normal result when the trace remains pathological, not after a borderline one. Waiting that long allows a foetus already at the edge of compensation to decompensate unobserved. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Apply a fetal scalp electrode and continue labour without further sampling
options.rationale: A scalp electrode improves the quality of the signal but adds no information about fetal acid-base status, which is the question the borderline lactate has raised. Continuing without resampling abandons the only test that can track the trend. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Continue conservative measures and repeat the fetal blood sample in 30 minutes
options.rationale: A lactate between 4.2 and 4.8 mmol/L is borderline, meaning neither reassuring nor an indication for immediate birth, and the recommended action is to resample within 30 minutes while conservative measures continue. The trend between two samples is far more informative than either value alone, and a rising lactate then mandates birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Start an oxytocin infusion to accelerate labour and reassess at full dilatation
options.rationale: Oxytocin increases contraction frequency and duration, which further reduces the placental perfusion window between contractions and worsens fetal acidosis. It was correctly stopped as part of the conservative measures and restarting it moves in the wrong direction. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

explanation.summary: Cardiotocography is sensitive for fetal compromise but poorly specific, and fetal blood sampling exists to reduce the operative birth rate driven by that false positive burden. Australian units predominantly use scalp lactate rather than pH because it needs a much smaller sample volume and fails less often, with thresholds of less than 4.2 mmol/L normal, 4.2 to 4.8 mmol/L borderline and 4.8 mmol/L or above abnormal. Interpretation is always paired with an action interval: a normal result is repeated within an hour if the trace stays pathological, a borderline result within 30 minutes, and an abnormal result mandates birth. Conservative measures, meaning stopping oxytocin, repositioning, correcting hypotension and considering tocolysis for hyperstimulation, continue throughout because they may correct the underlying cause. Sampling is contraindicated in suspected fetal bleeding disorders, maternal blood-borne viral infection, prematurity below 34 weeks, and any acute event requiring immediate birth.
key_points: Australian scalp lactate thresholds: normal below 4.2, borderline 4.2 to 4.8, abnormal 4.8 or above
A borderline result is repeated within 30 minutes, a normal result within 60 minutes
The trend between two samples matters more than any single value
Conservative measures continue while sampling is being repeated
Sampling is contraindicated by acute events, maternal blood-borne virus or prematurity below 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Fetal blood sampling is invalid during a prolonged bradycardia, because the lactate reflects the acid-base state up to the moment of sampling and will underestimate an injury that is happening right now; proceed straight to birth instead.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Fetal blood sampling
BMJ Best Practice: Fetal monitoring in labour

subtopic_detail: Switching antihypertensive therapy at the first antenatal visit for a woman on a renin-angiotensin blocker
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Dating by her last menstrual period puts her at 7 weeks and 1 day, and she says this pregnancy was not planned.

She has taken ramipril 5 mg daily for four years for essential hypertension diagnosed at age 29, and has taken it every day including this week. She takes no other medication and has never smoked.

Her blood pressure today is 142/92 mmHg, repeated after five minutes as 144/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows no protein. Renal function, electrolytes and a full blood count are within normal limits and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. She asks whether she needs to change anything about her tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 142/92 mmHg repeated at 144/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 5 mg orally daily for four years, taken daily including this week
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for protein; renal function, electrolytes and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Gestation: 7 weeks and 1 day by last menstrual period

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive treatment?

options.text: Continue ramipril until the end of the first trimester then change to labetalol
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are stopped as soon as pregnancy is recognised, not at an arbitrary later point, because exposure at any gestation carries risk and the second and third trimester foetopathy is the most severe. Continuing deliberately for another 6 weeks has no justification. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop ramipril today and withhold all antihypertensive treatment until 20 weeks
options.rationale: Blood pressure does fall physiologically in the first half of pregnancy, but a reading of 142/92 mmHg already meets the threshold for treatment and leaving it untreated risks progression to severe hypertension. Treatment of chronic hypertension continues throughout pregnancy with the agent changed, not paused. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop ramipril today and start oral labetalol, titrating to a target below 140/90
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are discontinued at the first knowledge of pregnancy because of oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, skull hypoplasia and limb contractures, and labetalol is the Australian first-line replacement with the largest safety dataset. Tight control to below 140/90 mmHg reduces progression to severe hypertension without increasing small for gestational age babies, as shown in the CHIPS trial. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop ramipril today and start oral atenolol, titrating to a target below 140/90
options.rationale: Atenolol is the one beta blocker specifically avoided in pregnancy because first trimester exposure is associated with fetal growth restriction, an effect not seen with labetalol. Labetalol differs by virtue of its combined alpha and beta blockade and preserved uteroplacental flow. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Halve the ramipril dose today and start low dose aspirin at 100 mg each night
options.rationale: Aspirin is correctly indicated for her, since chronic hypertension is a high risk factor for pre-eclampsia, but it is started from 12 weeks and does not substitute for withdrawing a teratogenic agent. Dose reduction rather than cessation leaves the foetus exposed to the same mechanism at lower intensity. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Chronic hypertension complicates a growing proportion of Australian pregnancies and carries a threefold to fivefold increase in superimposed pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction and preterm birth. Pre-pregnancy or early pregnancy review has two tasks: switching to an agent with an acceptable safety profile, and starting the preventive measures that reduce the superimposed pre-eclampsia risk. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are stopped at the first knowledge of pregnancy, as is any direct renin inhibitor, while labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted alternatives with labetalol usually first. The CHIPS trial settled the target debate by showing that tight control reduces severe hypertension without harming fetal growth, so a diastolic target of 85 mmHg is now standard. Low dose aspirin from 12 weeks, calcium supplementation where dietary intake is low, serial growth scans and early morphology assessment complete the package.
key_points: Stop angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers at the first knowledge of pregnancy
Labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted alternatives; atenolol is avoided
Treat to below 140/90 mmHg; tight control does not increase small for gestational age babies
Start low dose aspirin from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in chronic hypertension
Arrange serial growth scans because of the raised risk of fetal growth restriction
explanation.pearls: The renin-angiotensin foetopathy is a second and third trimester effect on fetal renal perfusion producing oligohydramnios and skull hypoplasia, so first trimester exposure alone, as here, warrants a detailed morphology scan rather than any discussion of termination.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of scar dehiscence during labour after caesarean when an epidural masks the pain
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar called urgently to a 34-year-old woman in her second labour at 40 weeks and 1 day. She had a caesarean section at full dilatation in her first pregnancy and has chosen to labour this time. She has a working epidural and an oxytocin infusion running for slow progress.

Fifteen minutes ago she began saying she can feel 'a burning ache across my tummy that will not go away', which is breaking through an epidural that had been effective. The midwife notes her pulse has risen from 88 to 126/min over the same period.

The cardiotocograph shows a prolonged deceleration to 70/min now lasting four minutes. On vaginal examination the vertex, which was at the ischial spines twenty minutes ago, is now 2 cm above them, and there is fresh blood at the introitus. Her uterus feels tense and tender between contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126/min, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C, fetal heart rate 70/min
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Prolonged deceleration to 70/min lasting four minutes
data_table.Vaginal examination: Vertex 2 cm above the ischial spines, having been at the spines twenty minutes earlier; fresh blood at the introitus
data_table.Abdomen: Tense and tender between contractions; constant pain breaking through a previously effective epidural
data_table.Infusions: Oxytocin infusion running for slow progress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give a tocolytic, reposition her and continue labour with close monitoring
options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is a holding measure for a prolonged deceleration caused by uterine hyperstimulation, where the uterus is contracting excessively but intact. It does nothing for a defect in the uterine wall and delays the only definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Call for immediate laparotomy and transfer her to theatre without any delay
options.rationale: Loss of station with an abnormal fetal heart rate, new constant abdominal pain breaking through a working epidural, maternal tachycardia with hypotension and fresh bleeding is uterine rupture until proven otherwise, and fetal and maternal outcomes depend directly on the interval to laparotomy. The oxytocin is stopped, blood is cross-matched and the massive transfusion protocol is put on standby while she is moved. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Perform fetal blood sampling to clarify the significance of the abnormal trace
options.rationale: Sampling is contraindicated during a prolonged bradycardia because the result reflects the state before the acute event and will falsely reassure. It also consumes minutes that determine whether this baby survives intact. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

options.text: Increase the epidural top-up and reassess her abdominal pain in ten minutes
options.rationale: Pain that breaks through a previously adequate epidural is one of the most specific warning signs of scar dehiscence, and deepening the block removes the signal rather than the cause. This is the classic mechanism by which rupture is recognised late in women labouring with regional analgesia. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Start an oxytocin infusion and plan an assisted birth at full dilatation
options.rationale: Oxytocin is already running and must be stopped, since augmentation raises intrauterine pressure across a scar that has failed. Planning an assisted vaginal birth also presumes descent, whereas the presenting part has risen. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates roughly 0.5 per cent of labours after a single lower segment caesarean section and is the complication that dominates counselling about vaginal birth after caesarean. The textbook description of sudden tearing pain with cessation of contractions is uncommon in practice, because most women labouring after caesarean have regional analgesia that blunts the pain and because oxytocin maintains the contraction pattern. The most reliable early sign is an abnormal cardiotocograph, present in the large majority of cases, and it is usually the first abnormality; loss of station of the presenting part, new constant pain breaking through a working block, maternal tachycardia, haematuria and vaginal bleeding follow. Induction and augmentation both raise the risk, and prostaglandin induction raises it most, which is why mechanical methods are preferred in this group. Management is immediate laparotomy with delivery of the foetus and repair or, if the defect cannot be repaired, hysterectomy.
key_points: An abnormal cardiotocograph is the earliest and commonest sign of scar rupture
Loss of station of the presenting part is highly suggestive and easy to miss
Pain breaking through a previously effective epidural is a warning sign, not a block failure
Oxytocin and prostaglandin both increase the risk of rupture in a scarred uterus
Treatment is immediate laparotomy; nothing medical relieves a defect in the uterine wall
explanation.pearls: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended for the whole of labour after a previous caesarean precisely because the cardiotocograph abnormality typically precedes the maternal signs by 10 to 30 minutes, which is the interval in which intact fetal survival is won or lost.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Stopping rule when a trial of vacuum extraction in theatre fails with repeated cup detachment
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar conducting a trial of instrumental birth in theatre for a 28-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 41 weeks. She has an epidural that has been topped up to a surgical block, the bladder has been emptied and the anaesthetist and paediatric team are present.

She has been fully dilated for three hours with two hours of active pushing. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 170/min with absent variability and recurrent variable decelerations.

On examination the head is at station plus 1 with the occiput in the left transverse position. There is caput of 2 cm and the parietal bones override and cannot be reduced. You have applied a posterior vacuum cup twice with correct placement over the flexion point; on each pull the cup detached with no descent of the presenting part.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2°C, fetal heart rate 170/min
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 170/min, absent variability, recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Vaginal examination: Station plus 1, occiput left transverse, caput 2 cm, overriding parietal bones that do not reduce
data_table.Instrumental attempts: Vacuum cup applied twice over the flexion point; detachment on each pull with no descent
